title: ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents for Efficient Robot Control
authors: Zexin He,Rui Li,Yushi Lan,Chengkai Jin,Zhi Hou,Xingang Pan
abstract: Coding agents can construct and revise robot behavior during execution, but using one agent for the whole robot can delay otherwise independent work. We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes one robot as a team of persistent agents. Each member reasons and acts for a configurable control group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution. However, different robot components often have physical dependencies that require coordination. To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that assigns tasks, coordinates dependencies, and dynamically allocates control between the lead and member agents. This allows independent work to progress concurrently while supporting tightly coupled manipulation when necessary. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across all eight Collaborative settings, ACAP also achieves lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where only member agents can control their assigned groups. An additional 90-rollout study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We further demonstrate mobile manipulation using the same member interface for chassis and torso control. We present the framework and a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, actions, and feedback to support research on how coding agents reason and act in the physical world.
introduction:
Recent coding-agent policies can inspect a scene, construct numerical models, and write and revise robot-control programs during execution (Jia et al., 2026, Fu et al., 2026). They extend the executable-policy interface of Code as Policies (Liang et al., 2023) into sustained interaction with physical feedback. While learning from demonstrations produces increasingly capable visuomotor policies (Chi et al., 2023, Kim et al., 2024a, Black et al., 2024), coding agents can construct task-specific procedures. This flexibility raises a practical question: how can we organize coding agents to achieve efficient robotic manipulation?

Reasoning takes time. In a typical coding-agent policy, a single agent is responsible for the entire robot. Although it can issue concurrent motion commands, decisions about different robot components still pass through the same reasoning process. For example, diagnosing a failed grasp with one arm may delay an independent action with the other. This suggests that distributing reasoning across different robot components could improve task efficiency.

We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes a single robot as a team of persistent coding agents. Each agent is assigned to a control group, such as an arm with its gripper or a body group comprising the torso and chassis. Each member observes, reasons, and acts within its scope while other members continue their work, enabling parallel reasoning and execution. Member agents can use lightweight reasoning configurations for local tasks, while a more capable coordinating agent reasons about the overall task.

However, independent reasoning does not imply independent physical actions. The agents share one physical robot, where one group’s actions can affect another’s reach, support, or clearance. A straightforward approach assigns each control group permanently to a member agent. While this can work well for independent tasks, tightly coupled manipulation, such as folding cloth or opening a bottle, requires close coordination between agents. Repeated communication and synchronization can introduce substantial overhead, while one agent’s recovery actions may change the object state and invalidate another’s plan. The challenge is therefore to coordinate agents efficiently as physical dependencies change.

To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that orchestrates the member agents. Unlike a fixed delegation scheme, the hyper-agent decides not only what tasks to delegate, but also when the lead should take direct control of multiple robot components. It uses task progress and execution feedback to coordinate dependencies and dynamically allocate control between the lead and member agents. For example, in four-flower insertion (Figure 1), the hyper-agent coordinates access to the shared vase while member agents prepare flowers independently. For a shared towel-folding action, the lead can instead directly control both arms while members continue their analysis. The division of control can therefore adapt to the physical dependencies of the task.

We evaluate ACAP on real-world manipulation tasks, including Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces the task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across all three task categories. To evaluate agentic coordination, we compare ACAP with Fixed Delegation, where only members control their assigned groups. ACAP achieves lower mean time cost across all eight evaluated Collaborative settings, supporting the benefits of flexible coordination for collaborative manipulation. An additional 90-rollout repeated-trial study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We also demonstrate ACAP in mobile manipulation. Furthermore, we collect a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, agent interactions, actions, and physical feedback to support future research on embodied coding agents.

Our contributions are threefold:

Asynchronous agentic policy framework. We introduce ACAP, which organizes a single robot as a team of persistent coding agents assigned to configurable control groups, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution across different robot components.

Agentic coordination. We introduce a hyper-agent that coordinates task dependencies and dynamically manages control allocation between the lead and member agents, supporting both independent and tightly coupled manipulation.

Real-world evaluation and rollout dataset. We evaluate the efficiency and coordination capabilities of ACAP across diverse real-world manipulation tasks. We also present a rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, agent interactions, and physical execution feedback.

title: Embo-Harness: Towards Understanding Frontier-Model-as-Policy Harness
authors: Xiao-Ming Wu,Kang Liao,Yuexiao Ma,Taolin Zhang,Mingqian Zhou,Nuo Chen,Ziming Li,Yihang Luo,Rui Li,Zhonghua Wu,Tianyu Xie,Xiawu Zheng,Zhongang Cai,Zhi Hou,Chen Change Loy
abstract: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model’s native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.
introduction:
Recent advances in frontier models, such as GPT-6-Astra [49], are reshaping robotic manipulation [74, 62]. Their remarkable generalization capabilities enable them to handle complex instructions, diverse environments, long-horizon manipulation, and failure recovery, substantially outperforming existing robot foundation models (RFMs), such as Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [78, 6, 38, 36, 67] and World Action Models (WAMs) [71, 42, 73], on recent benchmarks [46, 77, 68, 14], offering a different possibility for future robotic policies.

A robotic harness is the software loop that connects observations and instructions to planning, tool use, action generation, execution, and feedback. As illustrated in Figure 2, existing robotic harnesses can be broadly divided according to how actions are produced. Tool- or code-as-policy [31, 44, 33, 32, 20, 24, 16, 65, 29] harnesses use multimodal models [3, 27] for high-level planning but execute actions through predefined tools or generated code. Model-as-policy [58, 75, 56] harnesses instead delegate action generation to specialized learned policies. Recent frontier-model-as-policy harnesses take a further step by using the frontier model itself to plan and generate robot actions within a closed loop. Recent studies have established the feasibility of this paradigm [15, 61, 74, 43, 63, 62]. For example, SenseNova-RoboRSI [62] improves a frontier-model policy through recursive self-improvement based on prior training datasets and test-time execution rollouts, while GPT-as-Policy [61] and related studies [49, 17] profile the native robotic capabilities of frontier models. However, these works primarily demonstrate or improve the performance of particular systems. They do not systematically study which harness components are responsible for the gains, or why general-purpose frontier models can outperform policies specialized for robotic control.

We address these questions through Embo-Harness, a controlled study for frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. Starting from a common baseline, we vary individual design factors and progressively integrate the effective choices, rather than optimizing the complete system as a single configuration. Our study covers four dimensions of the robotic agentic loop: prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use. The resulting six findings can be summarized into three principles. First, suitable action representations and execution strategies are essential: frontier models more effectively generate end-effector actions than joint-space actions and favor short, fixed-length action chunks over adaptive chunking. Second, their performance benefits substantially from stronger reasoning and richer visual observations, including higher resolutions and complementary viewpoints. Third, tools and learned policies should complement the model’s native capabilities rather than replace them: manually designed plans and failure-derived reminders provide limited benefits, whereas short multi-action sequences and VLA refinement improve effectiveness and efficiency. Guided by this recipe, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3% success rate on RoboLab-120, compared with 57.1% for SenseNova-RoboRSI, the strongest existing baseline. It also completes 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks.

Beyond performance, we further investigate why frontier models succeed as robotic policies. Although they can generate joint-level and trajectory-level actions commonly learned by VLAs and WAMs, explicitly requiring such generation degrades performance. In contrast, directly predicting the final EEF destination outperforms short-range action generation, suggesting a stronger reliance on spatial perception than low-level action generation. We further validate this hypothesis through spatial position estimation experiments, observing broadly aligned trends with manipulation performance across reasoning efforts and visual resolutions, as well as comparable errors between direct position estimates and gripper positions in failed grasps, both measured against ground-truth target positions. These findings further highlight the central role of spatial perception in frontier models’ robotic capabilities.

title: VITA-WAM: Manifold-Aligned World-Action Modeling for Real-Time Robot Control
authors: Boqi Zhao,Dechen Gao,Hanchu Zhou,Hang Wang,Junshan Zhang
comment: Project page.this http URL. Equal Contributors: Boqi Zhao, Dechen Gao. Corresponding Author: Junshan Zhang
abstract:
World action model (WAM) is a promising paradigm for visuomotor control by jointly modeling world dynamics and actions. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large generative models and iterative sampling which incur substantial latency for action generation, limiting real-time deployment. In particular, there are two root causes of inefficiency in conventional flow matching or diffusion based action models in WAMs: 1) transporting uninformative Gaussian noise into precise actions necessitating multiple ODE steps, and 2) repeatedly injecting task context through expensive cross-attention modules. Our key insight is that jointly learning and aligning the source and action manifolds streamlines the transport between them, substantially accelerating action generation.
Building on this insight, we introduce VITA-WAM, a WAM architecture with manifold-aligned flow-matching (VITA flow matching) that directly transports latent observation representations containing visual, language, and proprioceptive information into latent actions. More specifically, a flow latent alignment (FLA) mechanism is employed to facilitate manifold alignment between latent observation and action representations, enabling accurate generation with few ODE steps. The resulting architecture also eliminates costly attention for observation conditioning during repeated denoising steps. Notably, with a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and by 1.65 pp on LIBERO, achieving these gains through the FLA objective without distillation, while inferring at 55.67 ms latency, a 2.10×2.10\times speedup compared to FastWAM.
introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot learning by jointly modeling physical dynamics and robot actions (Zhu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026). Learning to predict future dynamics encourages representations that capture how the environment evolves, supporting physical understanding and policy generalization. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large diffusion or flow matching based video and action models that require iterative sampling. The resulting latency during inference limits robots’ ability to incorporate new observations and respond promptly to environmental changes for real-time control. A central challenge is therefore to reduce the computational cost of action generation while retaining the benefits of world modeling.

Recent work has made attempts to address this challenge. Fast-WAM eliminates explicit future video generation at inference while retaining video co-training to learn representations that enhance action prediction (Yuan et al., 2026). Nevertheless, its action model uses conventional flow matching, with multiple ODE integration steps, repeating cross-attention conditioning on task observations at each step. Action generation still remains a computational bottleneck. Complementary approaches reduce the number of sampling steps through distillation or specialized few-step training objectives (Geng et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Akbari et al., 2026), which may incur costly training procedures or even degrade performance.

A primary objective of this work is to overcome the inefficiency of action generation for WAMs, while maintaining the performance (e.g., success rate). Our earlier work, VITA flow matching (Gao et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026), identified the sampling from uninformative Gaussian noise as a potential bottleneck to low-latency action generation. More specifically, conventional flow matching begins with a Gaussian prior as the source of the flow and progressively transforms it into actions, which is inherently inefficient for two reasons: 1) Complex Gaussian-to-action transport. Gaussian noise is uninformative and distant from the target action manifolds, necessitating multiple ODE steps for denoising into precise actions; 2) Heavy computational cost associated with cross-attention based conditioning. When starting from uninformative Gaussian sources, conventional flow-matching models must incorporate task contexts through heavy cross-attention based conditioning at each ODE step.

VITA addresses these inefficiencies by jointly learning the source and target latent manifolds and directly modeling the flow from observation latents to action latents. To the best of our knowledge, VITA (Gao et al., 2025) is the first work to apply a non-Gaussian source to flow matching policies, and to develop learnable source and target latents for flow matching. VITA proposed two flow latent objectives, flow latent decoding (FLD) and flow latent consistency (FLC), to enable source–target co-adaptation while preventing latent collapse arising from the training–inference discrepancy, in the sense that during training the target latent is provided by an action encoder, whereas at inference the action latent is generated by solving the ODE using the learned velocity field. The resulting joint optimization promotes alignment between the source and target manifolds, simplifying their transport and facilitating accurate action generation with fewer ODE steps. Moreover, since the source is grounded by observations, VITA eliminates the need for repeated conditioning modules.

Nevertheless, VITA studied FLD and FLC mainly through empirical studies, and is task-specific, constrained by a smaller-scale network of around 30M parameters without language conditioning. In this work, we develop VITA-WAM, scaling up VITA to a 6B WAM architecture, formalize flow latent objectives under a unified Flow Latent Alignment (FLA) mechanism, and establish a theoretic foundation for manifold alignment. A key challenge is to learn an informative flow source from visual, language, and proprioceptive representation while matching the dimensionality of latent actions, as required by flow matching.
To address this, we develop a Q-Former-based source encoder to effectively extract and fuse multimodal observations into a compact, learnable source representation. The FLA mechanism, designed to minimize the reconstruction loss using ODE-generated latent actions, effectively boils down to the co-optimization of flow matching, and the source and target manifolds in VITA-WAM, thereby driving the source observations and target actions towards aligned manifolds. Our theoretic study shows that aligning the source and target latent representations reduces the coupling cost, facilitating simpler, less curved flow trajectories, and allowing the corresponding ODE to be solved accurately with fewer steps, thereby reducing inference latency, as illustrated in Figure 1. From an optimization perspective, this joint learning shifts part of the action generation burden from the flow matching model to the source encoder, which learns an action-relevant initialization that simplifies the subsequent transport to latent actions.
In essence, through FLA-enabled manifold alignment, VITA-WAM streamlines the flow between source latent and action latent, and speeds up the action generation process.

We conducted comprehensive empirical evaluations across four real-world tasks using a Franka Research 3 robot arm, as well as on the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus simulation benchmarks. With a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and 1.65 pp on LIBERO. On LIBERO-Plus, this improvement stems from FLA learning action-relevant representations that are invariant to visual perturbations, thereby improving robustness. With a single ODE step and repeated language and proprioception cross-attention removed, VITA-WAM achieves an inference latency of 55.67 ms, compared to 116.65 ms for 10-step FastWAM and 62.32 ms for 1-step FastWAM. We emphasize that these results are achieved without distillation.

Our contributions are:

1) VITA-WAM: A highly efficient WAM architecture. We introduce VITA-WAM, a novel world-action model for visuomotor control that substantially reduces action-generation latency. By jointly optimizing the source and target manifold representations with flow matching, VITA-WAM begins generation from an informative, learnable source and avoids repeated attention to multi-modal observations during denoising.
In particular, VITA-WAM learns manifold-aligned source and target latent representations for flow matching, simplifying transport and enabling low-latency action generation for real-time robot control.

2) Flow Latent Alignment (FLA). We formalize FLA that enables VITA flow learning, and provide theoretic studies to demonstrate that FLA enforces the source and target manifold alignment of flow matching, thus simplifying the transport from the source to the target and reducing the ODE steps needed. The VITA flow using FLA is a general flow matching method that can be applied to the WAM or VLA architecture.

3) State-of-the-art success rates and efficiency. We conduct empirical studies on both real-world and simulation tasks. With a single ODE step, VITA-WAM achieves higher success rates than 10-step FastWAM while providing an 2.1×2.1\times inference speedup.

title: EmboEagle: An Efficient Agentic Embodied Framework for Long-horizon Robotic Manipulation
authors: Fan Xu,Zhongtao Wang,Hao Wu,Yitong Zhu,Wenzhuo Ma,Long Li,Zhuohao Li,Zhisheng Chen,Rui Su,Kun Wang,Xian Wu,Wanli Ouyang
abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation demands reliable execution across interdependent stages, yet standalone World-Action Models (WAMs) suffer from compounding physical errors, while stateless Vision-Language Model (VLM) supervision incurs prohibitive chunkwise latency and lacks 3D spatial persistence. We present EmboEagle, a closed-loop agentic framework that unifies subtask-conditioned WAM control, latent-space adaptive supervision, and memory-guided geometric recovery. First, we adapt sequential WAMs via decoupled two-stage flow matching that preserves cross-stage visual history while calibrating truncated action supervision at subtask boundaries. Second, without an auxiliary vision encoder, we distill teacher intervention decisions into a lightweight routing gate driven solely by the WAM Action Expert’s pre- and post-chunk latent transitions and subtask embeddings. Third, upon invocation, the VLM decouples diagnostic status from discrete routing actions and executes parameterized recovery primitives grounded in structured memory (initial references, active grasp bindings, and tool traces), followed by mandatory post-repair verification. Across RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, EmboEagle achieves 91.3% and 90.6% average success, surpassing the strongest baselines by 8.0 and 9.8 percentage points, while boosting real-world success over VoLoAgent under identical executor weights. Moreover, adaptive gating cuts VLM calls by 74.2% versus chunkwise monitoring (91.3% vs. 93.7% success).
introduction:
Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires a robot to preserve task intent across changing object configurations and grasp states, deciding when a subtask completes, retaining spatial cues needed by subsequent stages, and correcting physical errors before they compound.
World-Action Models (WAMs) establish a strong foundation for this execution layer by coupling visual dynamics prediction with continuous action generation. Recent advances extend this paradigm through history-conditioned control in Long-WAM (Huang et al., 2026) and episodic visual guidance in MaP-WAM (Zhao et al., 2026a).
Nevertheless, turning a capable visuomotor executor into a reliable long-horizon agent raises a complementary control question: how should a system allocate high-level supervision and translate its decisions into physical corrections during an ongoing task?

VLM-based orchestration bridges learned policies with explicit planning, monitoring, and manipulation tools (Chen et al., 2026a; Gu et al., 2026b), yet the timing of this supervision imposes a sharp efficiency–responsiveness trade-off.
As contrasted in Figure 1(a–b), open-loop execution lacks error recovery, whereas querying a VLM after every action chunk repeatedly returns routine continuation commands and incurs unnecessary overhead; conversely, lengthening a fixed checking interval delays the detection of subtask completions, auxiliary tool opportunities, and failed grasps.
While progress-based and event-driven triggers mitigate parts of this cost (Gu et al., 2026b), existing triggers often rely on heuristic rules or auxiliary visual processing.
We instead investigate whether a lightweight predictor can use the executor’s internal representations to anticipate a teacher’s intervention decisions, including stage advancement, proactive assistance, and failure recovery.

Beyond knowing when to intervene, effective recovery requires a persistent physical reference for what to restore.
Returning a displaced object to an earlier location requires retaining that location after the object has moved, and placing a held object requires accounting for the spatial offset between its geometric anchor and the gripper.
Because the live observation, the initial scene reference, and the active grasp record each supply distinct geometric evidence, structured memory is essential both for semantic interpretation and for synthesizing corrective trajectories.
Moreover, once a corrective motion finishes, fresh observations must be reassessed before low-level policy control safely resumes.

To address these challenges, we propose EmboEagle, an agentic framework that integrates subtask-conditioned WAM execution with adaptive VLM invocation and memory-guided geometric recovery (Figure 1(c)).
Crucially, its design separates the decision to request supervision from the supervisory decision itself, uniting three tightly coupled components:
✿ Boundary-aware subtask WAM adaptation. Starting from pretrained Long-WAM checkpoints, we perform decoupled two-stage flow-matching adaptation (Video DiT LoRA followed by full Action DiT fine-tuning) on subtask-conditioned demonstrations, preserving cross-stage visual history while truncating action supervision at subtask boundaries via a calibrated fixed-horizon loss.
✿ Latent-delta adaptive VLM invocation. Rather than duplicating visual encoding with an external perception network, we train a lightweight routing gate distilled from teacher decisions using the WAM Action Expert’s pre- and post-chunk token transitions and subtask embeddings, keeping post-intervention verification outside optional gating.
✿ Decoupled orchestration and memory-guided recovery.
When invoked, the VLM separates diagnostic status from discrete routing actions.
Assist operations can establish gripper–object bindings for subsequent recovery or directly support execution.
Recovery draws on these bindings, initial references, and recent tool feedback to select tool primitives, with immediate verification after each intervention.
Our main contributions are threefold:

Closed-loop agentic architecture. We present EmboEagle, which unifies subtask-conditioned WAM execution, decoupled VLM task orchestration, and persistent geometric memory with mandatory post-repair verification.

Closed-loop agentic architecture. We present EmboEagle, which unifies subtask-conditioned WAM execution, decoupled VLM task orchestration, and persistent geometric memory with mandatory post-repair verification.

Latent-space adaptive VLM invocation. We formulate selective monitoring as teacher-decision distillation over WAM action-token transitions and subtask semantics, enabling lightweight runtime gating without an auxiliary vision backbone.

Boundary-aware WAM adaptation and empirical validation. We develop a two-stage subtask adaptation scheme to adapt to the long-horizon settings. We validate our method alongside closed-loop evaluations on RMBench and LIBERO-Mem.

title: WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Zien Wang,Yuhao Pan,Yunfeng Fan,Nan Cheng,Xin Xia,Wenchao Xu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit.
To address this challenge, we introduce WeaveVLA, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations.
WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references.
Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context.
A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation.
We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and π0.5\pi_{0.5}, achieving over 98% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9% to 82.0% and from 85.7% to 87.8%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D→\rightarrowD.
On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6% to 70.0% under standard conditions and from 33.3% to 53.3% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline in both settings.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained vision-language representations with robot demonstrations to learn instruction-conditioned manipulation policies.
Representative approaches such as OpenVLA and OpenVLA-OFT have advanced general-purpose manipulation, while recent systems have expanded these capabilities across robotic embodiments Kim et al. (2024); Kim et al. (2025); NVIDIA (2026).
Flow-based policies, including π0\pi_{0}, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and π0.7\pi_{0.7}, further advance continuous action generation, generalization, and steerable control Black et al. (2025b); Black et al. (2025a); Physical Intelligence et al. (2026).
Despite these advances, understanding and maintaining the spatial relationships that govern manipulation remains an important challenge.

Robot actions depend on different relative 3D relations at different stages of manipulation. For example, placing a cup into a bowl requires reasoning about gripper–cup relations during grasping and cup–bowl relations during placement, while other object pairs may be less relevant.
These relations change with robot and object motion, while geometric estimation errors, viewpoint changes, and occasional occlusion can make their current configurations difficult to determine reliably Peng et al. (2026).
SpatialVLA and 3DS-VLA improve spatial awareness through geometric representations and sequential spatial constraints Qu et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025). GraphCoT-VLA and TriRelVLA further explore structured 3D relations for manipulation Huang et al. (2026); Zhou et al. (2026).
This raises a central question: How can VLA models explicitly model task-relevant 3D relations and continuously update their representations as manipulation unfolds to support action generation?

To address this challenge, we introduce WeaveVLA, a framework that explicitly models task-relevant relative 3D relations and their evolution during manipulation to enhance VLA action generation, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
Its object-centric representation combines visual features with estimated 3D geometry, using the robot’s tool center point (TCP) to anchor gripper–object relations.
A task-conditioned graph connects instruction-relevant objects, the gripper, and nearby spatial references, while edge-aware graph attention encodes their relative 3D geometry.
To maintain evolving spatial context, WeaveVLA assigns a recurrent state to each selected entity pair and updates it with valid geometric evidence across observations.
The resulting relation features are conditioned on the vision-language context and summarized into compact relational tokens. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages the learned relational features to preserve spatial structure.
Together with the original vision-language representations, these tokens condition a continuous action expert for robot manipulation.

We instantiate WeaveVLA on two VLA backbones, StarVLA-GR00T and π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and evaluate its effectiveness on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN Mees et al. (2022).
On the four standard LIBERO suites, WeaveVLA achieves average success rates of 98.3% and 98.2%, respectively, improving both backbones.
On LIBERO-Plus, it improves StarVLA-GR00T from 74.9% to 82.0% and π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 85.7% to 87.8%, demonstrating consistent gains across the two architectures.
On CALVIN D→\rightarrowD, WeaveVLA increases the average completed sequence length from 3.645 to 3.910 for StarVLA-GR00T, surpassing the original π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline, and from 3.885 to 3.997 for π0.5\pi_{0.5}.
Across three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based WeaveVLA achieves average success rates of 70.0% under standard conditions and 53.3% under perturbations, outperforming both baselines.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce WeaveVLA, a 3D relational grounding framework that explicitly models task-relevant spatial relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references to enhance VLA action generation.

We develop pair-specific recurrent relational updating to maintain evolving 3D relations across observations, integrating valid geometric evidence while preserving historical relational context.

We demonstrate consistent improvements across two VLA backbones on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN D→\rightarrowD, and validate WeaveVLA on three real-world manipulation tasks, outperforming both baselines under standard and OOD conditions.

title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
authors: Yanzhe Chen,Zhijun Cao,Zechen Bai,Wenzheng Zeng,Kevin Yuchen Ma,Yiqi Lin,Guoqiang Liang,Xiaokang Liu,Ke Sun,Kevin Qinghong Lin,Mike Zheng Shou
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Multimedia (cs.MM)
abstract:
Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging.
We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions.
To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation.
We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control.
In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent’s success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions.
Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.
introduction:
Foundation models are moving from understanding the physical world to acting in it [74, 2, 39].
While vision-language-action models learn to predict robot actions [7, 43, 6], recent agentic systems enable general-purpose models to control robots through tool calls and executable programs [52, 76, 15, 27, 45, 16].
This introduces a critical design choice beyond the model itself: how should an agent interact with a robot?
We define the robot-use interface (RUI) as the actions an agent can command and how they are organized for execution.
From low-level motion commands [3, 4] and image-grounded points [25, 57] to semantic skills [1, 37] and executable programs [52, 71], the RUI determines what the agent must decide, what can be delegated to execution, and when control returns to the agent.

This distinction becomes critical in complex physical tasks.
These tasks require agents to gather missing information, react to dynamic events, and correct errors through physical feedback.
An interface that demands a new model decision for every small movement can make execution costly and error-prone, while one that provides insufficient feedback may fail when the world deviates from the plan.
Thus, reliable execution depends not only on what an agent knows, but also on how decisions and feedback are distributed between the agent and the robot.

However, existing embodied benchmarks compare models under fixed interfaces [47, 82, 18, 84, 23], while interface studies typically examine selected design choices [27, 64, 68].
Consequently, the impact of interface design remains poorly understood.
In our experiments, changing only the RUI shifts Claude Code’s success rate from 45% to 81%, far exceeding the average performance gap between two frontier agents (Fig. 1a).
This raises our central question: What makes a good robot-use interface?

To answer this question, we introduce RUIBench, a benchmark combining 30 agentic manipulation tasks with a controlled evaluation protocol.
These tasks go beyond simple pick-and-place, requiring agents to reason, acquire information through interaction, and adapt to changing physical conditions.
They span five suites: world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation.
The protocol limits agents to RGB-D observations and robot states, keeps the environment evolving during model reasoning, and evaluates task success independently of the agents’ claims.
We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that disentangles two design choices: action abstraction, which determines what an agent can command, and interaction form, which determines how actions are organized and executed.
RUIKit crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms to instantiate 12 interfaces, plus a free-choice interface, all within a shared harness where only the RUI varies (Fig. 1).

Across frontier and small models in simulation and 650 real-robot episodes with frontier agents, we find that effective RUIs reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback (Fig. 1b), which also makes them easier for small models to learn (Fig. 1d).
Fine-grained interaction can fragment a clear plan into excessive model decisions, a failure we call execution fragmentation.
Composing actions into programs reduces this burden when agents effectively exploit multi-step execution and intermediate feedback.
However, real-world execution changes which interfaces are effective, as physical uncertainty demands more opportunities for local correction (Fig. 1c).
We further uncover a verification gap: agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, while checking individual actions does not guarantee task completion.
Together, these findings highlight the importance of allocating decisions, feedback, and verification at appropriate levels.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Agentic benchmark. We introduce RUIBench with 30 manipulation tasks across five suites and a controlled evaluation protocol for systematically studying RUIs.

Unified framework. We develop RUIKit, spanning 13 interfaces across six action abstractions and two interaction forms under shared perception and control.

Empirical insights. We reveal how decision burden, physical feedback, and task-level verification shape embodied performance across agents and environments.

1. Agentic benchmark. We introduce RUIBench with 30 manipulation tasks across five suites and a controlled evaluation protocol for systematically studying RUIs.

2. Unified framework. We develop RUIKit, spanning 13 interfaces across six action abstractions and two interaction forms under shared perception and control.

3. Empirical insights. We reveal how decision burden, physical feedback, and task-level verification shape embodied performance across agents and environments.

title: NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
authors: Lemeng Qi
abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token’s exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3–1.7×\times larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token’s input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error–reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the π0.5\pi_{0.5} prefix by up to 1.61×\times, stays 2.7–2.9×\times closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models act from camera images and language [1, 2]. In π0.5\pi_{0.5}, a PaliGemma backbone [3] encodes two camera views and the instruction into an 18-layer key-value cache, and a smaller action expert reads this cache to generate the action chunk. The backbone runs on every control call. In our measurements the three feed-forward products of its gated MLP, of size 2048×163842048\times 16384, 2048×163842048\times 16384 and 16384×204816384\times 2048, take about 73% of the prefix’s GPU time, and in our earlier profiling of the compiled policy each of them ran at the device’s arithmetic throughput. Saving reads does not help a compute-bound product; only skipping arithmetic does.

A low-rank approximation skips most of the arithmetic, and its error is uneven across tokens. With an output-optimal rank-256 draft [4], the low-rank prefix applied to every token deviates from the original policy by 8.9 seed units and fails every closed-loop episode we ran (0/10). Yet when the right 20–40% of tokens per layer are computed exactly, the deviation falls below that of every static compression we tested at equal arithmetic. The question is which tokens are the right ones.

The intuitive answer is to verify the product: estimate each token’s output error and compute exactly where it is largest. Verification by random projection makes this cheap, since for a fixed draft W~\tilde{W} the error x⁡(W−W~)​Sx(W-\tilde{W})S can be computed before either product exists. We implemented this rule and an oracle that knows the exact error of every token’s MLP output. Both lose to a simpler signal, the relative residual of the token’s input outside the calibrated subspace, the gate of Gated Subspace Inference [5]. Even the oracle deviates 1.31–1.74×\times more, across three exact fractions and two disjoint held-out sets. The local error is concentrated in tokens the action expert does not rely on: the oracle spends 28% of its exact budget on the third-person camera, the input test 17%, and approximating the wrist camera alone harms the action twice as much as approximating the third-person camera alone.

The second finding concerns where to decide. Deciding separately for each product moves 16384-wide rows between the paths, and on our GPU that movement costs as much as the saved arithmetic: in eager execution, per-product dispatch reaches at most 1.12×\times and falls below 1 at larger exact fractions. Deciding once per token and layer, at the 2048-wide MLP input, reaches 1.50×\times at the same exact fraction and the same deviation. A fixed quota per layer also keeps every tensor shape static, so the dispatched prefix can be captured as a single CUDA graph, where it reaches 1.61×\times. We call the resulting training-free method NoveltyGate: it computes exactly the tokens that are new to the calibrated subspace and sends the rest through a low-rank MLP.

title: Real2Worlds2Real: Scaling Self-Improving Agentic Real2Sim2Real for Robot Manipulation
authors: Jinzhong Gu,Jiakai Chen,Xinyi Cao,Yan Shen,Hangke Sui,Shutian Zheng,Xiang Xiao,Haoran Lu,Fan Xu,Lu Shi,Daochen Shi,Ruihua Zhang,Wei Zhan,Masayoshi Tomizuka,Ruihai Wu
abstract: Scaling robot manipulation learning remains challenging due to the high cost of collecting real-world interaction data. Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) offers a promising route by enabling policy learning in simulation grounded in real-world observations, yet scaling this paradigm across diverse tasks and physical interactions remains difficult. We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic framework that integrates scalable simulation-world construction with policy development. Given limited visual observations and task descriptions, its tool-orchestration harness constructs faithful digital twins and expands them into diverse, physically executable digital cousins. The agent adaptively selects tools and revisits construction decisions, using visual and execution feedback to refine geometry and physical behavior. Building on these worlds, the agent orchestrates policy development by coordinating data generation, policy learning, and refinement based on task requirements and simulation rollout feedback. Across both stages, the agent distills validated procedures into reusable skills that guide subsequent tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved world fidelity and successful real-world policy transfer, with performance gains from increasing world diversity and interaction-data volume. Skill reuse further improves world-building efficiency and long-horizon task success. Project website: real2worlds2real.github.io.
introduction:
Recent advances in robotic foundation models, including vision-language-action (VLA) policies [28, 3, 2] and world-action models (WAM) [4, 27, 57], have demonstrated the importance of large and diverse data for generalizable robot manipulation. Yet collecting such data on physical robots remains costly, requiring substantial human effort for teleoperation, supervision, and repeated scene setup and resets.
These costs make it difficult to cover the breadth of manipulation tasks needed for generalization.
Real2Sim2Real offers a promising way to overcome this bottleneck. By grounding simulation in limited real-world observations, this paradigm offers the potential to scale both the diversity of training environments and the volume of robot interaction data, supporting policies that transfer to the real world.

Recent work has enabled the construction of visually realistic, interactive simulation environments from real observations [16, 48, 22, 20, 21], while automated scene generation and digital-cousin synthesis have expanded their diversity [11, 44, 5, 35]. However, scaling Real2Sim2Real requires more than generating additional scenes.
Simulation worlds must faithfully reproduce task-relevant appearance and physical interactions while supporting diverse, physically meaningful variations that remain executable. Beyond world construction, effective robot learning also requires adapting data generation and policy refinement to different tasks, using failures observed in simulated rollouts to guide subsequent policy improvements. Together, these challenges motivate adaptive, feedback-driven approaches to both world building and policy development.

We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic Real2Sim2Real framework that transforms limited real-world observations into faithful digital twins and diverse, physically executable digital cousins for scalable robot policy development (Fig. 1).
For simulation-world construction, a tool-orchestration harness enables a general-purpose agent to adaptively coordinate world building across diverse scenes and physical interactions. Guided by visual and execution feedback, the agent iteratively identifies and corrects errors in scene geometry and physical behavior. Successful correction procedures can be distilled into reusable skills, allowing experience from previous scenes to guide subsequent world building.
Starting from RGB images or videos, the agent reconstructs a scene-level digital twin that faithfully captures the real-world appearance and spatial structure.
It then creates a diverse family of digital cousins by introducing variations at both the object and scene levels, while ensuring that the resulting environments remain plausible and suitable for the intended manipulation tasks.
Beyond rigid objects, our framework supports the generation and physics-based simulation of articulated and deformable objects, enabling realistic robot interactions across a broader range of manipulation scenarios.
To further improve physical fidelity, when interaction recordings are available, the harness compares simulated rollouts with observed real-world motion, using their discrepancies to calibrate physical parameters.
These capabilities enable high-fidelity simulation world building to scale across diverse scenes and physical interactions without scene-specific human intervention.

Building on the simulation worlds, Real2Worlds2Real employs agentic tool orchestration for robot policy development. Rather than following a fixed training pipeline, the agent adaptively selects tools and learning strategies based on task requirements and available demonstrations.
It can synthesize executable control programs through tool-assisted grasp and motion planning, train reinforcement learning policies with agent-designed rewards, or employ model predictive control for online planning.
These methods can directly execute tasks or generate demonstrations across diverse simulation environments for training visuomotor policies through imitation learning.
Through simulated rollouts, the agent evaluates policy performance and uses failure feedback to guide further data generation and policy refinement, iteratively improving the resulting policies.
Across iterations, validated development procedures are distilled into reusable skills, allowing accumulated experience to guide policy development on subsequent tasks.

We evaluate Real2Worlds2Real across diverse manipulation scenes and physical interactions, assessing both the quality of simulation worlds and their effectiveness for robot policy learning.
Real-robot experiments demonstrate that policies trained in simulation successfully transfer to physical robots.
World-quality evaluations show that constructed worlds faithfully reproduce real-world appearance and physical interactions.
We further identify two complementary scaling trends: increasing interaction data improves policy performance, while increasing world diversity enhances policy generalization under a fixed interaction-data budget.
Finally, we demonstrate self-improvement in both world building and policy development, showing that reusing skills from previous tasks reduces world-building token consumption and improves long-horizon task success.

To summarize, our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a scalable Real-to-Sim-to-Real framework that constructs faithful digital twins and diverse digital cousins from limited real-world observations for agent-orchestrated policy development.

We develop agentic tool-orchestration workflows for both world building and policy development, enabling iterative refinement through feedback and cross-task self-improvement through skill reuse.

We demonstrate the transfer of simulation-developed policies to real robots, validate the visual and physical fidelity of constructed worlds, and reveal scaling trends in world diversity and interaction-data volume.

1. We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a scalable Real-to-Sim-to-Real framework that constructs faithful digital twins and diverse digital cousins from limited real-world observations for agent-orchestrated policy development.

2. We develop agentic tool-orchestration workflows for both world building and policy development, enabling iterative refinement through feedback and cross-task self-improvement through skill reuse.

3. We demonstrate the transfer of simulation-developed policies to real robots, validate the visual and physical fidelity of constructed worlds, and reveal scaling trends in world diversity and interaction-data volume.

title: Wrist-Camera Video Diffusion as Generalizable Robot Policies
authors: Jingyuan Liu,Yongwei Chen,Yishan Yang,Zexin He,Xingang Pan,Zhi Hou
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: A generalist manipulation policy should perform new tasks, operate in unfamiliar scenes, and transfer skills across robot embodiments. We present Wrist Video Policy (WVP), a closed-loop manipulation framework that learns how manipulation unfolds through video prediction and recovers executable motion through geometric estimation. Our key idea is to represent robot motion through wrist-camera trajectories, which determine the corresponding end-effector poses through a fixed hand-eye transformation. We pair a video generator that predicts future wrist views with a pose estimator adapted from a pretrained 3D model to recover the corresponding camera trajectories. Model stitching maps the generator’s predicted latents directly into the estimator’s intermediate feature space, bypassing RGB decoding. This decomposition allows task knowledge to expand through broad human and robot video data while reusing geometric motion estimation across tasks and embodiments. The resulting pose estimator transfers across Franka Panda, PiPER-X, and Galaxea R1 Pro without further fine-tuning. Across tabletop and laundry-room settings, WVP generalizes to tasks ranging from precise grasping and inserting to handling deformable objects, achieving a success rate of over 50% in zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluations. Our project page is at https://wrist-video-policy.github.io.
introduction:
Generalization in robotic manipulation requires policies to perform new tasks and transfer familiar skills across scenes and robot embodiments [12]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge with robot demonstrations, enabling manipulation across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments [8, 5, 22]. Scaling these capabilities through action-labeled demonstrations, however, creates an expensive coverage problem, as the training data must capture a broad range of tasks, environments, and robot motions. Video-based approaches, including world-action models (WAMs), offer a way to learn much of this task and interaction knowledge from a broader supply of human and robot videos, without requiring corresponding action labels for video pretraining [52, 63]. Recent advances demonstrate the potential of this approach through transfer from human videos and zero-shot execution of new tasks [41, 20]. Yet learning to faithfully translate visual predictions into executable motion still typically requires action-labeled robot trajectories [55, 20].
Even with this reliance on action labels, separating task knowledge from motion execution opens a promising path to scalable robot learning.

Building on this separation, we aim to achieve zero-shot transfer across tasks, scenes, and embodiments without additional action-labeled demonstrations for deployment. A natural foundation for this goal is the 3D geometry of manipulation. Different robots may need different joint commands to approach and manipulate an object, but their motion can be described in the same way across embodiments by how far the gripper moves and how it is oriented relative to the object. Recent policies incorporate 3D scene features into action prediction [23, 40], but still rely on robot demonstrations to learn the mapping from geometry to actions, limiting zero-shot generalization across tasks, scenes, and embodiments. Pretrained 3D models, on the other hand, suggest a more direct role for geometry. They can already estimate camera poses from images across diverse scenes and viewpoints [49, 32, 50]. Treating motion execution as a well-defined geometric estimation problem could extend these pretrained capabilities to robot control and, together with video prediction, provide a scalable path towards learning manipulation in 3D visual space.

A wrist-mounted camera makes this idea concrete by connecting video prediction with geometric estimation. Because it is rigidly attached to the end effector, their poses are related by a fixed hand-eye transformation. We can therefore plan the robot’s motion by predicting future wrist-camera views, estimating the camera trajectory, and converting it into end-effector poses for execution. The prediction target remains the motion of the observing camera regardless of which robot carries it, allowing the same estimator to transfer across embodiments through each robot’s hand-eye calibration. This lets task knowledge expand through video prediction while reusing the geometric mechanism that translates those predictions into actions.

To this end, we introduce Wrist Video Policy (WVP), a policy that connects pretrained video and 3D models through wrist-camera motion. Given a language instruction and current observations, the generator predicts how wrist views will evolve, drawing on pretrained video models that generalize across manipulation tasks and scenes [29, 20]. The pose estimator builds on a pretrained 3D model [49], whose geometric priors we adapt to robot control through fine-tuning on public wrist-camera videos and trajectories. Once adapted, it is reused across tasks and embodiments without further fine-tuning. We then connect the two components through model stitching [19], mapping the predicted video latents directly into the estimator’s intermediate feature space. This bypasses RGB decoding and yields action trajectories that more closely follow the visual plan.

We evaluate WVP on real robots across tasks, scenes, and embodiments. Trained solely on public robot datasets, the pose estimator transfers across all three settings without further fine-tuning. Paired with a video generator, it enables zero-shot manipulation with a success rate of over 50% in our out-of-distribution tests. Across tabletop and laundry-room settings, the system performs tasks ranging from pick-and-place and stacking to wiping, inserting, retrieving clothes, and opening articulated fixtures. Its capabilities span fine-grained manipulation of small rigid objects, handling of deformable garments and towels, and precise stacking of transparent tableware (Fig. 3). In summary, our contributions are threefold.

We represent robot actions using wrist-camera motion, formulating action prediction as estimating the camera poses of future wrist-camera views.

We present a pose estimator built on a pretrained 3D model, and use model stitching to estimate wrist-camera motion directly from a video generator’s latents.

We demonstrate that WVP generalizes across tasks, scenes, and embodiments in the real world, achieving a success rate of over 50% in zero-shot evaluations.

1. We represent robot actions using wrist-camera motion, formulating action prediction as estimating the camera poses of future wrist-camera views.

2. We present a pose estimator built on a pretrained 3D model, and use model stitching to estimate wrist-camera motion directly from a video generator’s latents.

3. We demonstrate that WVP generalizes across tasks, scenes, and embodiments in the real world, achieving a success rate of over 50% in zero-shot evaluations.

title: Completing analytical conversion scheme among DH, Hayati, CPC and POE models for manipulator calibration
authors: Oleg Yu. Sumenkov,Danil D. Kulminskiy,Sergei V. Gusev
abstract: Kinematic model selection is an important aspect of robotics, particularly in trajectory planning, motion control, and, most notably, robot calibration. Building on Mooring’s decomposition of the calibration procedure into four stages — modeling, measurement, identification, and correction — this paper investigates the role of analytical kinematic model conversion algorithms within the overall calibration framework and their potential to improve calibration performance.
introduction:
Kinematic model selection is a fundamental step in robotics, as it affects the accuracy and reliability of a wide range of tasks, including trajectory planning, motion control, and, in particular, kinematic calibration and parameter identification. One of the earliest and most influential kinematic models is the Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) convention, introduced in (Denavit and Hartenberg, 1955). Despite the development of numerous alternative formulations, the DH convention remains a widely used standard in both the robotics community (Joubair and Bonev, 2014; Kamali et al., 2016; Kolyubin et al., 2019; Žlajpah and Petrič, 2023) and industry. Its continued use is largely due to its compact parameterization, which can simplify kinematic computations, and its systematic rules for assigning coordinate frames.

Since its first application to kinematic calibration in (Wu, 1983), the DH convention has been widely used to calibrate industrial manipulators (Zhen, 1985; Payannet et al., 1985; Ibarra and Perreira, 1986). However, a significant limitation was later identified in (Hayati, 1983; Mooring, 1983): small geometrical variations in consecutive nominally parallel joint axes can cause abrupt changes in the corresponding DH parameters. This effect, known as a parameter singularity, can complicate parameter identification and reduce the reliability of calibration results.

To evaluate the suitability of kinematic models, two important criteria were established in (Everett et al., 1987): completeness and parametric continuity, the latter originally termed proportionality. A kinematic model is complete if it can describe the relationship between the tool pose and the joint variables of an arbitrary manipulator while including the required number of independent kinematic parameters (Everett and Hsu, 1988). Parametric continuity requires that small changes in the physical geometry of a manipulator produce correspondingly small changes in its kinematic parameters. These properties are particularly important in calibration, where the model must represent geometric deviations accurately and allow the corresponding parameters to be identified reliably.

The classical DH convention has limitations with respect to both completeness and parametric continuity. These limitations have motivated the development of alternative kinematic models. For example, the S-model proposed in (Stone et al., 1986) extends the DH parameterization with two additional variables to achieve completeness and allow more flexible frame assignment. Other alternatives include the model introduced in (Veitschegger and Wu, 1986) and the “Zero-Reference” model proposed by (Mooring and Tang, 1984), which uses Rodrigues’ formula to ensure parametric continuity. These are among the many formulations developed to address the limitations of the classical DH convention.

Among these alternatives, the convention proposed by Hayati (1983) is particularly notable because it can be viewed as a natural extension of the DH convention. Specifically, an additional rotation about the yy-axis is introduced for consecutive revolute joints that are nominally parallel. As demonstrated in (Hayati, 1983), small variations in the Hayati (HAY) parameters can represent small changes in the relative positions and orientations of consecutive links, thereby addressing the parameter singularity associated with parallel joint axes. The HAY convention remains in use (Chen et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024) because it is intuitive, uses a compact parameterization, and requires only limited modifications to the classical DH convention while providing parametric continuity.

However, as in the DH convention, the HAY convention imposes specific rules for assigning the {Base}\{\mathrm{Base}\} and {Tool}\{\mathrm{Tool}\} frames. Consequently, neither convention allows these frames to be assigned arbitrarily, which limits their completeness according to the criteria in (Everett et al., 1987).

These limitations motivate the need for a kinematic convention that retains the simplicity of the DH approach while satisfying both parametric continuity and completeness. This need was addressed by the Complete and Parametrically Continuous (CPC) model proposed in (Zhuang et al., 1990; Zhuang et al., 1992; Zhuang, 1989). The CPC model is based on a theoretically minimal four-parameter representation of a line (Roberts, 1988), which provides parametric continuity. To achieve completeness, the model introduces two additional parameters for defining the {Base}\{\mathrm{Base}\} and {Tool}\{\mathrm{Tool}\} frames. Thus, the CPC model combines a continuous representation of the manipulator geometry with flexible frame assignment, addressing the two principal limitations of the classical DH convention.

At the same time, minimality, which requires a kinematic model to use the minimum number of parameters necessary to describe the manipulator, was identified as a third criterion for a good kinematic model in (Everett and Hsu, 1988; Everett and Suryohadiprojo, 1988; Schröer et al., 1997). These studies examined the effect of model minimality on robot calibration and parameter identification. In particular, (Everett and Suryohadiprojo, 1988) rigorously established an upper bound on the number of independently identifiable parameters, regardless of the kinematic model used.

Using tools from differential geometry, (Schröer et al., 1997) subsequently showed that non-redundant kinematic models are subject to parameter singularities arising from fundamental topological constraints (Gottlieb, 1986; Baker, 1990). In particular, a Euclidean parameter space cannot, in general, be mapped continuously and bijectively onto a sphere. For example, the parametric continuity of the CPC model is achieved using a redundant seven-parameter representation and restricting joint-axis vectors to the upper half-space (Zhuang et al., 1992). However, the analysis in (Schröer et al., 1997) did not address the use of smooth mappings between Lie algebras and Lie groups, as employed in the Product of Exponentials (POE) formulation proposed in (Brockett, 1984).

Owing to the smoothness of the exponential map and its foundation in screw theory, the POE formulation provides a natural framework for achieving parametric continuity and completeness. However, until the analysis presented in (Yang et al., 2014), the minimality and identifiability of POE-based kinematic models had not been systematically addressed. This raised questions about the number of independently identifiable parameters and the reliability of parameter identification when using POE-based models.

Early assessments of the POE formulation suggested that its mathematical description and computational implementation were more complex than those of the DH convention. However, this view was challenged by (Park, 1994), which demonstrated that POE-based calculations can be computationally less demanding. Furthermore, the examples presented in (Murray et al., 1994; Lynch and Park, 2017) illustrate that constructing a POE model can be both natural and intuitive. An important advantage of this formulation is that it does not require the strict frame-assignment rules imposed by other kinematic conventions.

At present, the POE and DH conventions remain among the most widely used kinematic representations in robotics (Lynch and Park, 2017; Wu et al., 2017; Kim and Kwon, 2026). Nevertheless, alternative models, particularly the HAY and CPC conventions discussed above, continue to be used in robot calibration and parameter identification (Meng and Zhuang, 2007; Zeng et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). To examine the relative prevalence of these approaches, we searched Google Scholar 11

https://scholar.google.com/; search performed on 24 September 2026. and analyzed the number of citations associated with the corresponding publications. The results are summarized in Table 1.

It should be noted that the choice of kinematic model is indeed a crucial step in solving the calibration problem. In the case of parametric singularity — such as in the DH model — it is evident that numerical issues will encounter at identification, at least with optimization methods calculating the objective functional gradient, point noted in numerous studies (Hayati and Mirmirani, 1985; Okamura and Park, 1996; Kuti and Galambos, 2024; Karhan and Bingül, 2025).

If a model possesses the parametric continuity property, then the objective function us a smooth function on the parameter manifold. In that case, a numerical solver will converge to a certain point, depending on the initial conditions, manifold dimension, boundary conditions for the parameters — in other words, it is highly likely that the final calibration result will differ for various kinematic models describing the same nominal object — a point emphasized from a theoretical perspectives Schröer et al. (1997) and also observed in experiments Xuan and Xu (2014); Zhang et al. (2021); Kuti and Galambos (2024); Boschetti and Sinico (2024); Malyshev and Kulminskij (2026); Károly et al. (2026) and many others.

Thus, parameter conversion algorithms which allows to express one kinematic model in terms of another — preferably in analytic form to preserve the accuracy — are of particular of interest and seems beneficial in calibration field. For the models discussed herein (Table 1), most such conversions have already been established, and we present them systematically in Fig. 1 (left).

In the accompanying figure, colored arrows denote established parameter conversion pathways. The orange arrow signifies the conversion initially formulated for transitioning from the DH convention to the POE model in (Murray et al., 1994; Okamura and Park, 1996; Lynch and Park, 2017). Due to generality of POE model, proposed methodology can be naturally extended to other transitions: CPC–POE and HAY–POE, as indicated by the dashed arrows in different colors. The green arrows correspond to conversions derived from (Zhuang et al., 1992), where a general procedure for extracting CPC model parameters from specifically structured homogeneous transformation matrices was established. The relative simplicity of these transitions provides a compelling justification for the CPC model usage. Later, an analytical method for converting between the DH and HAY conventions was proposed in (Kuti and Galambos, 2024). The magenta arrow highlights a contribution in (Wu et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019), where an analytical solution for the important POE–DH conversion was suggested. Then, the POE and CPC model relations were revealed in (Sumenkov, 2026) together with conversion algorithm.

The paper extends existing conversion schemes (Fig. 1 (left)) suggesting an analytical framework for transitions in solid red (Fig. 1 (right)), namely, POE–HAY, HAY–POE, CPC–HAY and HAY--CPC22

This transition is marked with dotted lines, emphasizing that this transition was previously known in the literature (Zhuang et al., 1992, Section V), but has advantages and disadvantages that will be discussed further in the section 4.4 (see Tables 12, 13, and 14).. It could be argued that the transitions between HAY and POE may be performed using at least two–step (up to three) conversion procedure, for example, consequent POE–DH  (Wu et al., 2017) and DH–HAY Kuti and Galambos (2024) transitions. However, compared with the two-step method, the proposed approaches are expected to achieve higher accuracy and lower computational cost, since it requires only a single step, performed to machine precision, and thus avoids the additional error and computation associated with the second step.

Moreover, is known that sequential conversions that include DH model, i.e., POE–DH or POE–DH–CPC, retain DH model singularities — significant parameter growth while small geometry changes, see, e.g., (Wu et al., 2019, Table II) and (Sumenkov, 2026, Tables III and IV), where the algorithms were tested on 6R33
