Puma 560 model (Okamura and Park, 1996) with two near parallel consequent joints. To ensure the comparability of the presented results, we use this model as a benchmark for the POE–DH–HAY algorithm (Wu et al., 2019; Kuti and Galambos, 2024), in which the significantly modified parameters are marked in red. The same holds here: the artifacts in the translation parameters of the DH model, which do not reflect the actual link geometry (see −567.6554-567.6554 and 552.7518552.7518 (Wu et al., 2019, Table II)), were neglected when the DH–HAY algorithm was applied in (Kuti and Galambos, 2024).

Detailed information on the Puma 560 nominal and actual model (Okamura and Park, 1996), as well as the results on proposed POE–HAY and their comparison with POE–DH–HAY (Wu et al., 2017; Kuti and Galambos, 2024) is provided further in Section 4.

In this way, the proposed analytical conversions — POE–HAY, HAY–POE, CPC–HAY and HAY–CPC — complete the existing DH, HAY, CPC, and POE conversion scheme in Fig. 1 (left) made by Hayati (1983); Zhuang et al. (1990); Murray et al. (1994); Okamura and Park (1996); Lynch and Park (2017); Wu et al. (2017); Wu et al. (2019); Kuti and Galambos (2024).

First, this allows to compare the calibration methods, algorithms, techniques and tools applied (and developed) on different kinematic conventions, e.g., (Zhuang et al., 1992; Okamura and Park, 1996; Yang et al., 2014; Toan and Khoi, 2018; Yang et al., 2024), enhancing their comparability.

Second, this enables the user to select the most appropriate kinematic convention for a given problem, regardless of the model in which the system is originally described, and subsequently to return to the required model through the proposed conversion procedures. In particular, for a manipulator with a modified geometry not specified in its datasheet, even describing it in DH parameters is a far from trivial task compared to the approaches mentioned above. It is much more simpler, to describe it in HAY, CPC or POE and then convert to DH.

Second, the user can choose the most suitable kinematic convention for a given problem, regardless of the model in which the system is originally described, and then return to the required model via the proposed conversion procedures. In particular, for a manipulator with a modified geometry not covered by its datasheet, a direct description in DH parameters is far from trivial; it is much simpler to describe it in HAY, CPC or POE and then convert to DH.

Moreover, the main result of this paper addresses the manipulator calibration problem within a general framework, as shown below.

The methodological idea of the paper is to demonstrate that parameter conversion schemes in Fig. 1, including the paper contribution: POE–HAY, HAY–POE, CPC–HAY and CPC–HAY transitions, can be fruitfully incorporated in manipulator calibration framework. According to Mooring et al. (1991), kinematic calibration is typically divided into the following stages, which are modeling, measurements, identification and correction.

Modeling refers to the choice of a mapping from joint configuration space to the end-effector’s pose in task space, which takes into account the manipulator geometry — namely, DH, HAY, CPC, and POE models considered in this paper. At the next stage, the end-effector poses (or its components) are measured for a given manipulator configuration set, as well as these configurations. At the identification step we estimate the kinematic model parameters based on a formulated optimization problem to fit better the end-effector pose obtained with forward kinematics and measured. Finally, the parameter estimation is implemented in a real robot — at the correction step.

The proposed calibration framework is schematically shown below in Fig. 2.

On the modeling step (depicted as red rectangle), we suggest to describe the given manipulator with nominal (manual) parameters using any of the four models of our choice — the POE model is selected in the example. Then, using the conversion scheme in Fig. 1, we convert the chosen model to others, i.e., employing results in (Wu et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019) for POE–DH, results in (Sumenkov, 2026) for POE–CPC and POE–HAY.

Next, on identification step (marked as yellow rectangle), using measured data (TCP pose and configurations, for instance) we formulate and solve four distinct (DH, HAY, CPC, and POE) optimization problems. Then, testing estimated parameters on some validation set, we choose the model showing best performance — accuracy — in our example the CPC model.

Finally, on the correction step (in green rectangle) we convert the most accurate model to a model, that given manipulator uses. In Fig. 2 it is DH model, so result in (Zhuang et al., 1992) are applied for CPC–DH transition.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a comprehensive overview of the core principles underlying the DH, HAY, CPC, and POE kinematic models, thereby establishing the necessary theoretical background. Section 3 constitutes the primary contribution of this work — completing the conversion scheme in Fig. 1 — presenting a detailed exposition of the proposed parameter conversion framework. In Section 4, the efficacy of this framework is evaluated through simulation results obtained from its application to a RRRP SCARA robot (Lynch and Park, 2017) with all joint axis being near parallel and well-known calibration benchmark PUMA 560 manipulator (Okamura and Park, 1996). Following this, Section 5 provides a practical example of the proposed method applied to the ABB IRB 1600 open-loop calibration, illustrating the conversion scheme (Fig. 1) utility in general, and the paper contribution in particular.

title: ReWeave: Emergent Physical Task Topologies for Embodied Harness Optimization and Cross-Task Meta-Distillation
authors: Yicheng Xu(1),Wencan Jiang(1),Zihao Zhu(2 and 4),Keru Zhou(3),Chang Zhou(4),Li Liu(4),Maoqing Yao(4),Yong Liu(1),Jiangning Zhang(1) ((1) Zhejiang University, (2) Stanford University, (3) Tsinghua University, (4) AGIBOT Innovation)

introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation depends on establishing physical conditions needed by downstream actions [20, 15]. Plausible high-level plans often fail because key physical requirements, such as contact stability, clearance margins, and assembly tolerances, emerge only during execution. These dynamics cannot be anticipated a priori, making physical trial-and-error necessary yet costly. Maximizing what each trial teaches is thus vital for adaptation and reuse.

Recent work repairs programs and evolves skills from execution feedback [28, 5, 22], distills playbooks [17], or organizes repairs with workflow graphs [29]. These advances leave a distinct question: when new evidence changes our understanding of a physical prerequisite, how should already collected trials be reassessed? Keeping their interpretation fixed can hide partial progress behind failure labels. Likewise, storing a successful routine does not identify which local mechanism another task needs. Revisable dependencies connect retrospective credit, harness revision, and condition-based transfer (Fig. 1).

Research question. How can we continually revise physical task understanding through interaction to reinterpret experience, improve agent harnesses, and transfer mechanisms across tasks?

[Challenge 1] Nominal task plans mask latent physical bottlenecks [Sec. 3.2.1]. 
Execution can expose missing physical requirements. Revised understanding calls for re-reading past trials to assess retained progress.

[Challenge 2] Diagnosing a bottleneck does not reveal a remedy [Sec. 3.2.2]. 
Context, action routines, and feedback loops are coupled. Several edits can address one failure, but each needs physical validation.

[Challenge 3] Task-specific success does not guarantee transfer [Sec. 3.2.3]. 
Specialists depend on their scenes and objects. New tasks may need one local mechanism or parts from several specialists, each with prerequisites.

We introduce ReWeave, which uses an emergent physical task topology to make changes in task understanding explicit (Fig. 2). It links physical dependencies and alternative routes to evidence and harness mechanisms. Beyond using old traces to propose repairs, topology revision changes how the same archived trials are credited and compared (Challenge 1). Reprojected progress and bottlenecks then guide harness search (Challenge 2). Across tasks, matching verified transition effects to unmet conditions identifies which specialist mechanisms to combine in a shared harness for transfer and continual learning (Challenge 3).

On LIBERO-PRO and RoboDojo, ReWeave achieves strong performance: 98.75%98.75\% and 58.25%58.25\% SR, gains of 9.759.75 and 32.7532.75 points over H0H_{0}, respectively. Re-reading 159 failed RoboDojo development trials on their final topologies finds retained progress in 89%89\% (median 0.330.33; Fig. 3). On unseen tasks, direct distillation reaches 41.3%41.3\% SR and the shared harness reaches 51.3%51.3\%.

Our contributions are threefold:

Emergent Physical Task Topology. We introduce an emergent representation of task understanding that connects physical dependencies, alternative routes, execution evidence, and reusable harness mechanisms.

Topology-Guided Harness Optimization. We develop joint harness optimization guided by emergent task understanding and the physical cost of further search.

Topology-Guided Meta-Distillation. We develop meta-distillation matching specialist mechanisms to unmet conditions for cross-task consolidation and transfer.

2. Topology-Guided Harness Optimization. We develop joint harness optimization guided by emergent task understanding and the physical cost of further search.

title: SurgeCount: A Protocol-Guided Composition Harness for Bimanual Surgical Sponge Counting
authors: Sung Eun Kim,Xiaoman Zhang,Xucheng Wang,Pranav Rajpurkar
comment: . Accepted to the Findings Track of Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026
abstract: We present SurgeCount, a system for auditable robotic surgical sponge counting that composes learned skills under a written procedural protocol. Retained sponges cause preventable harm, and surgical teams count every sponge before closure to reduce that risk. The robot repeatedly isolates one deformable sponge from a tangled pile and places it in the next numbered counting-tray slot, requiring handling of occluded grasp threads while preserving step order. We train one subtask-conditioned policy on eleven short skills and learn when each skill ends. At each learned boundary, a stateful vision-language model selects the next skill from an operator-authored specification of step order, visual verification, and recovery. This creates temporal commitment to each subtask and enables failures to be recovered by recomposing existing skills rather than using a dedicated recovery policy. We evaluate five methods across 100 real-robot trials using 20 matched layouts. SurgeCount fills 47 of 60 ordered slots and completes 12 of 20 procedures, compared with 27 of 60 and 3 of 20 for the strongest of four end-to-end policies trained on the same data. Replacing the detailed protocol prompt with a minimal prompt reduces performance to 29 of 60 slots and 5 of 20 completed procedures. These results show that long-horizon performance depends not only on visuomotor capacity, but also on how learned skills are committed, verified, and composed. This tabletop proof of concept motivates further evaluation of protocol-guided robotic sponge counting in clinically representative settings.
introduction:
Retained surgical sponges can cause serious adverse events, and prevention depends on accounting for every sponge before wound closure (Gawande et al., 2003). Automating such a workflow poses a broader challenge for learned healthcare robotics: procedural competence requires not only accurate visuomotor actions, but also maintaining step order, committing to a subtask until completion, verifying its outcome, and recovering when an imperfect skill fails.

End-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically absorb these functions into a continuous sequence of predictions. For long-horizon procedures, however, hierarchical prediction alone may be insufficient if the policy repeatedly reconsiders its active subtask before completion. In our evaluation, the hierarchy-aware π0.5\pi_{0.5} model re-issues its subtask prediction before each action chunk and frequently changes that prediction between consecutive chunks, despite operating on the same underlying visuomotor backbone as π0\pi_{0}. This motivates a different formulation: rather than asking a single policy to infer procedural structure implicitly, learned policies can execute bounded skills while explicit procedural knowledge determines when transitions are allowed, how outcomes are verified, and how failures are recovered.

We study this question through robotic surgical sponge counting. Three red-ink-stained surgical sponges overlap in a source tray, and each carries a blue radiopaque thread that serves as the preferred grasp landmark for isolating a single sponge. The robot must transfer one sponge at a time into counting-tray slots I, II, and III in order. When the thread is visible, the right arm can grasp it directly; when it is occluded by overlapping sponges, the left arm must first manipulate the pile to expose the thread before the right arm can grasp and transfer the isolated sponge. The task therefore couples deformable-object manipulation, visual ambiguity, bimanual coordination, ordered placement, and repeated verification.

We introduce SurgeCount, a protocol-guided composition harness over an off-the-shelf π0\pi_{0} policy that externalizes procedural hierarchy through three coupled mechanisms (Figure 1). First, a single subtask-conditioned π0\pi_{0} checkpoint executes eleven learned skills, and a learned stop head establishes temporal commitment: once a skill is selected, it runs until a learned completion boundary rather than being re-decided at every action chunk. Second, only at these boundaries does a stateful vision-language model select the next skill under an operator-authored protocol specifying legal orderings, two nominal strategies (visible-thread grasp and occluded-thread reveal-then-grasp), and per-skill visual verification gates. Third, when a gate fails, recovery is achieved by recomposing release-and-return subtasks already present in the learned skill library, without a dedicated recovery policy (Dai et al., 2025). Representative rollouts, including the bimanual reveal and composed recovery, are shown in the supplementary videos at https://github.com/rajpurkarlab/SurgeCount.

This design deliberately preserves procedural knowledge as an explicit supervisory layer rather than requiring it to be rediscovered entirely from robot demonstrations. Beyond the shared teleoperation data, SurgeCount uses operator-entered subtask tags, stop labels derived from those segmentations, and an operator-authored protocol specification; it uses no transition-level reasoning annotations, no learned recovery policy, and no engineered affordance API. Every orchestrator transition, verification decision, and recovery step is logged, making failures localizable at explicit subtask boundaries and the resulting execution trace directly auditable.

Protocol-guided skill composition: a single subtask-conditioned VLA, learned completion boundaries, and a stateful VLM constrained by operator-authored ordering and verification rules.

Protocol-guided skill composition: a single subtask-conditioned VLA, learned completion boundaries, and a stateful VLM constrained by operator-authored ordering and verification rules.

Temporal commitment and compositional recovery: learned boundaries prevent per-chunk subtask re-decoding and provide explicit points for verification and recovery using already-trained skills.

Real-robot evaluation: 100 matched-layout trials against four end-to-end policies, with mechanistic diagnostics and a protocol-specificity ablation.

1. Protocol-guided skill composition: a single subtask-conditioned VLA, learned completion boundaries, and a stateful VLM constrained by operator-authored ordering and verification rules.

2. Temporal commitment and compositional recovery: learned boundaries prevent per-chunk subtask re-decoding and provide explicit points for verification and recovery using already-trained skills.

3. Real-robot evaluation: 100 matched-layout trials against four end-to-end policies, with mechanistic diagnostics and a protocol-specificity ablation.

title: RoboUniverse-10K: Toward the Scaling Era of Agentic Robotics via Real-to-Sim Environments
authors: Jinkun Liu,Yingze Wang,Situ Wang,Deyao Hong,Mingju Gao,Wenyi Li,Yizhe Chi,Youjie Zheng,Kaisen Yang,Xiangyang Wang,Bingxiang He,Yuxin Zuo,Boyuan Chen,Yue Chen,Cheng Qian,Tianxing Chen,Huichi Zhou,Huaxiu Yao,Hao Tang,Hao Zhou,Ya-Qin Zhang,Calvin Xiao,Tiga Altman,Huan-ang Gao
abstract:
Agentic Robotics, in which foundation models act as coding agents to control robots through executable programs, has emerged as a compelling paradigm for embodied intelligence. Yet unlike software engineering, where massive executable environments power post-training, robotics remains constrained by small, manual benchmarks and in-distribution evaluation.
To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboUniverse-10K, 10,807 interactive, resettable, and verifiable physics environments built from real-world videos via an automated Real2Sim and quality assurance pipeline. Each runs in an isolated, Harbor-compatible harness that hides privileged states and grading logic to mirror real-world sensing.
From the same pipeline, we hold out 500 unseen tasks to establish RoboUniverse-Verified, an expert-verified zero-shot benchmark.
Evaluating 11 closed- and open-source models reveals a huge gap: frontier models reach 85.8% success, while open-source baselines lag at 2.6% to 10.0%, bottlenecked by low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control.
Finally, we collect about 17K multi-turn trajectories totaling 0.79B tokens with GPT-6 Astra and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, yielding RoboUniverse-35B-A3B.
Our model achieves substantial zero-shot gains on RoboUniverse-Verified, lifting the success rate from 0.8% to 21.2%, while achieving zero-shot task completions across LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real Franka arm.
We open-source the RL-ready environments and model to lay the foundation for large-scale reinforcement learning in Agentic Robotics.
introduction:
Recently, Agentic Robotics—a paradigm in which frontier foundation models act as Coding Agents to control robots—has emerged rapidly. Rather than relying solely on end-to-end visuomotor mappings, these agents write and execute code that invokes perception tools, planning routines, and low-level control interfaces in a closed-loop manner [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], already surpassing end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies on several mainstream leaderboards [7, 8, 9]. Looking to the trajectory of software engineering (SWE), the rapid capability leap of coding agents has been fundamentally driven by large-scale, executable, and automatically verifiable post-training environments [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. By mining real-world pull requests to construct hundreds of thousands of interactive repositories, the SWE community unlocked large-scale trajectory distillation and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) [17, 18, 19], yielding substantial gains for open-source models on benchmarks such as SWE-bench [20]. We posit that the cornerstone of general-purpose Embodied Intelligence is generalization, and the root of generalization lies in the scale and diversity of training environments.

Yet Agentic Robotics has not truly entered its scaling era, primarily due to two fundamental bottlenecks. First, the bottleneck of environment scale and construction cost. Existing robotic simulation benchmarks—such as LIBERO, RoboCasa, RoboTwin, and RoboDojo [21, 22, 23, 24, 25]—rely heavily on manual scene authoring and handcrafted success criteria, keeping their task counts limited to tens or a few hundred. Even recent efforts that leverage LLMs or real-world videos to synthesize simulation tasks (e.g., Real2Gym and Gym-Anything for Robotics) [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33] remain modest in scale. Unlike software engineering tasks that can be mined directly from existing code repositories, each robotic task requires constructing a physically plausible interactive scene and authoring rigorous verification logic, incurring a far higher construction cost. Second, the lack of generalization caused by “train on test.” Constrained by limited environment scale, prior works [34, 35, 36, 37] typically train and evaluate agents within the same task settings and environment distributions. Training and testing in homogeneous environments not only risks overfitting, but also fails to faithfully demonstrate an agent’s true generalization to unseen physical scenes and novel manipulation tasks.

To address these challenges, we introduce RoboUniverse-10K, a suite of 10,807 interactive, resettable, and automatically verifiable Isaac Sim [38] environments across 4,132 single-arm Franka and 6,675 dual-arm AgileX tasks for Agentic Robotics post-training and evaluation. Inspired by mining SWE tasks from real-world pull requests, we convert diverse real-world robot manipulation videos into distinct concrete tasks via hierarchical deduplication and normalization. Specifically, an end-to-end Real2Sim construction and quality assurance (QA) pipeline equips a coding agent with SAM 3.1 [39], DA3 [40], a curated asset library, and physics-modeling skills to reconstruct scenes, author reference solutions, and write verifiers, which an independent QA agent audits for physical fidelity, reset consistency, and verifier robustness against reward hacking. Meanwhile, a Harbor-compatible isolated harness separates the code-execution sandbox from the simulator and verifier, restricting interaction to public observations and control APIs while hiding ground-truth states and grading logic to mirror real-world constraints and support parallel rollouts.

From the same pipeline, we hold out 500 unseen, expert-verified tasks (200 single-arm and 300 dual-arm) across all eight task families to establish the zero-shot benchmark RoboUniverse-Verified, on which we systematically evaluate 11 leading closed- and open-source models.
Our evaluation reveals two core findings. First, a sharp capability gap persists: frontier closed-source models such as GPT-6.2 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 reach 85.8% and 76.8% overall success, whereas open-source baselines lag at 2.6% to 10.0% and struggle sharply on dual-arm coordination. Second, failures stem predominantly from physical execution rather than task comprehension. Weaker models are bottlenecked by low-level grasping, dropping to 0% to 4% success on grasp-required tasks. Even frontier models struggle with deformable-object manipulation, where cloth tasks barely benefit from capability gains, and roughly 80% of their failures occur after contact, pointing to fine-grained post-contact physical control as the primary remaining bottleneck.

To validate the utility of RoboUniverse-10K as a scalable post-training infrastructure, we conduct supervised post-training and generalization experiments. Using GPT-6 Astra [41], we collect about 17K multi-turn interaction trajectories across the training environments, totaling 0.79B tokens, and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the open-source Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model, yielding RoboUniverse-35B-A3B.
SFT yields substantial zero-shot gains on RoboUniverse-Verified, lifting the overall success rate from 0.8% to 21.2% (single-arm from 2.0% to 40.5% and dual-arm from 0.0% to 8.3%).
Furthermore, zero-shot probes on LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin 2.0 in the Embodied First Exam [8] format, alongside a sim-to-real test on a real Franka arm, achieve zero-shot task completions beyond our environments.

In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

RoboUniverse-10K: We present an automated Real2Sim construction and agent-based quality assurance pipeline, and open-source 10,807 Harbor-compatible, isolated, RL-ready simulation environments, overcoming the scale bottleneck limitation of prior benchmarks.

RoboUniverse-Verified Benchmark: We curate an expert-verified zero-shot test suite of 500 tasks, benchmark 11 closed- and open-source models, and pinpoint low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control as the primary bottlenecks of current embodied coding agents.

RoboUniverse-35B-A3B Model: We train and open-source an SFT model on RoboUniverse-10K, lifting zero-shot success on RoboUniverse-Verified from 0.8% to 21.2% while achieving zero-shot task completions across external benchmarks and a real Franka arm.



1. RoboUniverse-10K: We present an automated Real2Sim construction and agent-based quality assurance pipeline, and open-source 10,807 Harbor-compatible, isolated, RL-ready simulation environments, overcoming the scale bottleneck limitation of prior benchmarks.

2. RoboUniverse-Verified Benchmark: We curate an expert-verified zero-shot test suite of 500 tasks, benchmark 11 closed- and open-source models, and pinpoint low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control as the primary bottlenecks of current embodied coding agents.

3. RoboUniverse-35B-A3B Model: We train and open-source an SFT model on RoboUniverse-10K, lifting zero-shot success on RoboUniverse-Verified from 0.8% to 21.2% while achieving zero-shot task completions across external benchmarks and a real Franka arm.

title: Generalizing Agentic Robotics via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
authors: Xinxin Liu,Anh Dao,Wenrui Bao,Rafid Ahmed,Bingxin Xu,Ming Li,Chen Chen,Yuzhang Shang
abstract: Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. In large language model (LLM) post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) has been used to consolidate domain specialists into a single generalist. Yet whether MOPD can build a generalist planner for agentic robotics, how well it performs, and how it compares with other consolidation methods remain unexplored. In this paper, we systematically study these questions: we introduce Robo-MOPD, which trains a single student on closed-loop rollouts in simulation under token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists, and compare it with weight merging, off-policy specialist supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-domain online RL. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9% and 44.8% success (58.9% average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on LIBERO-10.
introduction:
Building general-purpose robots has long been a central goal, and agentic robotics has recently emerged as a promising path toward it [34, 14, 76]. In this paradigm, a multimodal planner interprets the instruction, decomposes the task, and acts by calling tools: callable functions that either perceive the scene (e.g., segmenting an object or locating it in 3D) or invoke a frozen low-level executor, such as a motion primitive or a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. After each call, the tool returns feedback from the environment, such as the execution status and updated camera views. This loop closely resembles how recent coding agents work. Because low-level executors handle embodiment-specific control, the planner only reasons and calls tools rather than directly outputting motor commands. As with coding agents, achieving general capability then comes down to obtaining a capable planner.

However, most existing planners are proprietary models prompted through APIs [14, 7, 76], whose per-call cost and latency accumulate over long closed-loop episodes and rule out on-device deployment. To remove this dependence, recent post-training methods [37, 36, 12] train open-weight models with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL). Each resulting planner is trained for a single domain, i.e., one robot environment together with its executors and tools. Because tools differ across domains in names, arguments, and feedback formats, every domain requires its own planner, and serving NN domains means deploying NN planners (Figure 1a). This raises a natural question: Can we train a single open-weight planner to operate across multiple domains, as a step toward general-purpose robots?

A natural approach is to consolidate specialist planners across domains into a single generalist planner. Large language model (LLM) post-training offers four common consolidation methods: weight merging [59, 25, 43], off-policy specialist SFT [43, 17, 65], multi-domain online RL [68, 43, 17], and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) [60, 68, 43, 17]. Agentic robotics, however, differs fundamentally from the language and software domains where these methods were developed, so conclusions drawn there do not transfer directly. First, domains differ in robot embodiment, camera views, and low-level tools. Second, the planner acts over dozens of turns from multi-view camera images, repeatedly recovering when stochastic physical execution slips or fails. Third, a physical task often fails because a single step selects the wrong tool or a slightly inaccurate spatial parameter, yet the episode outcome reveals only success or failure, not where the error occurred. Under these conditions, it remains unclear how these consolidation methods should be adapted to agentic robotics and which of them actually work.

To answer this question, we compare the four methods on the same Qwen3.5-9B backbone [49], with the three training-based methods starting from a shared cross-domain SFT initialization under a matched consolidation rollout budget. To include MOPD in this comparison, we adapt it to agentic robotics as Robo-MOPD (Figure 2). In Robo-MOPD, the generalist student runs closed-loop rollouts in simulation, and the matching frozen specialist scores each token of the student’s reasoning and tool call via token-level reverse KL, correcting errors such as a wrong tool or an inaccurate coordinate at the step where they occur. This same scoring scheme works across all robots because, even when embodiments and tools differ, every turn shares the same format: camera images and tool feedback go in, and reasoning plus a tool call come out. Across all training-based methods, we drop prior-turn reasoning from the context [77], subsample a random subset of turns per episode [37], and balance the loss across episode lengths [19, 43, 65] and domains [17] to keep training efficient and balanced over long, multi-view episodes (Section 3). All low-level executors [48, 26] remain frozen throughout. At test time, a single generalist planner operates robots across all domains without any specialist.

We evaluate on tabletop LIBERO-PRO [35, 81] and mobile-kitchen RoboCasa365 [45, 46] and obtain three findings. First, a single generalist planner can outperform the specialists. Robo-MOPD reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-PRO and 44.8% on RoboCasa365, the only method to surpass both 9B specialists, achieving a 58.9% average while all baseline methods fall below the specialists’ 56.9% (Figure 1b,c and Table 1). Second, the gap concentrates on long-horizon tasks. On the long-horizon LIBERO-10 suite, neither off-policy SFT nor online RL improves over the shared SFT initialization, while Robo-MOPD leads online RL by 13.0 percentage points (Figure 4). Third, Robo-MOPD changes how the planner fails. On LIBERO-PRO, budget-exhaustion failures drop from 31.6% under online RL to 20.3%, while voluntary finish() calls on unsolved episodes rise from 2.6% to 6.8%: on hard tasks, Robo-MOPD stops voluntarily after failed attempts rather than repeating actions until the 100-turn limit like the baselines (Section 4.3 and Figure S3).

Our contributions are as follows:

Systematic comparison. We present the first systematic comparison of four consolidation methods for agentic robot planners: weight merging, off-policy specialist SFT, multi-domain online RL, and MOPD.

Robo-MOPD. To our knowledge, we are the first to bring MOPD to agentic robotics, adapting it to closed-loop multimodal planning so that a single generalist planner spans incompatible robot domains toward general-purpose robots.

Findings and performance. Consolidation works best when it combines on-policy rollouts with token-level supervision, and its advantage is largest on long-horizon tasks. A single 9B generalist planner surpasses both 9B domain specialists.

1. Systematic comparison. We present the first systematic comparison of four consolidation methods for agentic robot planners: weight merging, off-policy specialist SFT, multi-domain online RL, and MOPD.

2. Robo-MOPD. To our knowledge, we are the first to bring MOPD to agentic robotics, adapting it to closed-loop multimodal planning so that a single generalist planner spans incompatible robot domains toward general-purpose robots.

3. Findings and performance. Consolidation works best when it combines on-policy rollouts with token-level supervision, and its advantage is largest on long-horizon tasks. A single 9B generalist planner surpasses both 9B domain specialists.

title: WorldLeague: Benchmarking Physical Agency
authors: Xinyang Zhou,Qi Li,Xinchao Wang
abstract:
AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms.
What range of physical goals can today’s AI systems achieve autonomously?
Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action.
We introduce WorldLeague, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of 60 simulated robot tasks by measuring progress toward each task’s physical goal from the robot’s trajectory.
Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in WorldSeek, rearrange objects in WorldShape, and adapt to changes in WorldShift.
Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared.
In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls.
For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate).
Together, these measures form the system’s Physical Agency Profile.
Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100).
Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks.
Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8% of those episodes.
WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion.
introduction:
Foundation models have recently become a promising direction for building general-purpose robots [51].
In digital environments, agents built on frontier models can follow instructions in open-world video games [4] and turn visual references into editable 3D scenes in Blender [12].
The range of tasks that physical robots can perform has also grown [14, 31].
Robots have performed long-horizon household tasks, such as cleaning a kitchen or bedroom, in homes they had never seen during training [19].

To clean an unfamiliar kitchen, a robot must use what it sees to decide what to do next. Embodied AI systems connect perception to action in different ways [16]. A vision-language model (VLM) can identify an object from a spatial description [7] and estimate its distance from other objects [5]. With a robot interface, it can use such judgments to choose where to move or grasp [9]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models produce robot actions directly from instructions and visual observations [20]. For example, Gemini Robotics 1.5 interleaves reasoning and action during multi-step manipulation [50]. World-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions [23, 44, 57, 26]. This approach has enabled closed-loop manipulation on new tasks and in new environments [63].

Across these approaches, the ambition is the same. A person specifies a physical goal and leaves the system to decide how to achieve it [30, 9, 27, 25, 39, 42]. We call the system making those decisions the agent and its capacity to choose and execute actions through a body its physical agency. The decisions an agent must make depend on the goal. To find a hidden object, it must decide where to look and what to move out of the way [11, 10, 17]. To put that object through a narrow opening, it must also choose an orientation that fits.
An agent may therefore find the right object and still fail to put it away.
This leads us to the central question of our study.
What range of physical goals can today’s AI systems achieve autonomously?

Organizing robot benchmarks around household activities [21, 37] obscures what success on each activity establishes about an agent. Consider a robot asked to deliver a cup. If the user names the cup and it is in plain sight, the robot can select it from its current view. If the user asks for the cup that has moved since the robot last visited the room, the robot must use an earlier observation to decide what to pick up. Both tasks count as cup delivery. Yet success on the first leaves the decisive requirement of the second entirely untested. To establish the range of an agent’s physical abilities, we must vary what the agent has to work out for itself and verify that its actions bring about the requested outcome.

We introduce WorldLeague, a benchmark of 60 simulated robot tasks organized by the physical demands that determine success.
We evaluate VLMs, VLAs, and WAMs against shared goals and constraints.
For each task, the robot’s trajectory shows which goal requirements it satisfies and whether it completes the task.
The tasks span three tracks, each defined by what the robot must do to achieve its goal.
WorldSeek tests navigation and goal grounding as systems explore and gather evidence. WorldShape tests geometric reconfiguration and physical reasoning as systems change the scene. WorldShift tests temporal memory and constraint management as systems track a changing world and recover from disturbances. The three tracks span six capability dimensions (Sec. 3.1). We group each task by its primary challenge, and a single task can draw on capabilities from several dimensions.

To compare systems across these tasks, we instantiate each goal in a scene with specified objects, initial conditions, and constraints. Physical predicates check conditions such as stable placement or recovery after a disturbance. We inspect all 60 task–scene pairs, verify that reference runs meet the goals and constraints, and check the scoring conditions against the task specifications.
Each system pursues its goal through physical interaction. For VLMs, our decision-preserving action abstraction draws on how sensorimotor mechanisms coordinate fine-grained human movement [53, 59, 13]. The interface executes motions, and the agent chooses the targets, action parameters, sequences, and responses to feedback that shape the outcome. We adapt a motion interface [9] to implement this abstraction on R1 [21]. VLA and WAM policies use their native interfaces under shared task goals, constraints, and physical scoring rules.

We score the resulting trajectory for progress toward individual requirements and for physical success, which requires satisfying the full goal and all task constraints. A Physical Agency Profile reports Interactive Score for progress and physical success rate for complete goal achievement in each capability dimension. For VLMs, terminal question answering (QA) provides an auxiliary measure of scene understanding, outcome recognition, and memory within the same episodes.

Among the 13 evaluated embodied AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 earns the highest overall Interactive Score, 28.58 out of 100, and achieves physical success on 13 of its 60 tasks. Fable leads in navigation, goal grounding, geometric reconfiguration, and temporal memory, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra lead in constraint management. The trajectory analysis also identifies goal requirements that remain unmet after systems make physical progress. Of 347 VLM episodes with full terminal QA credit, 249 (71.8%) receive an Interactive Score of zero. These results show that goal-relevant understanding and successful intermediate actions can coexist with unmet physical goals.

Turning demonstrated capabilities into desired physical outcomes is central to Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI, which share the ambition of building systems that can pursue human goals through their own actions in the world. WorldLeague turns this ambition into a common experiment. A person specifies the desired outcome, an agent determines how to pursue it through a body, and the evaluation verifies what it achieves in the physical environment. Evaluating systems against common goals and physical success criteria allows advances in perception, reasoning, and control to be assessed in terms of what they enable these systems to accomplish [56]. Our broader aim is to make autonomous goal achievement a shared measure of progress for AI systems that act in the world.

We make three contributions to the evaluation of physical agency in embodied AI systems.

We test physical agency by goal achievement on tasks with different capability combinations.

We build and validate WorldLeague, a suite of 60 tasks that measures progress and physical success across six capability dimensions using shared goals and scoring rules.

We compare the capability profiles of 13 systems and identify goal requirements that remain unmet in episodes with correct answers or partial physical progress.

1. We test physical agency by goal achievement on tasks with different capability combinations.

2. We build and validate WorldLeague, a suite of 60 tasks that measures progress and physical success across six capability dimensions using shared goals and scoring rules.

3. We compare the capability profiles of 13 systems and identify goal requirements that remain unmet in episodes with correct answers or partial physical progress.

title: Foresight Forcing: Learning Spatial Foresight for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Mishuo Han,Zhixuan Liang,Zhaoyuan Wan,Wendi Chen,Jiarui Chen,Xinkai Wang,Yue Ma,Yu Zhou,Junting Chen,Yao Mu,Jun Lv,Chuan Wen,Cewu Lu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit.
To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing (ℱ2\mathcal{F}^{2}), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space.
During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, ℱ2\mathcal{F}^{2} achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation has progressed from task-specific systems designed for controlled environments towards generalist policies that operate across diverse objects, instructions, and settings. A general-purpose robot must interpret task instructions, perceive objects in its surroundings, and execute precise actions under varying conditions. Recent advances in large-scale robot learning and pretrained vision-language models have enabled Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions Zitkovich et al. (2023); Kim et al. (2025b); Black et al. (2025b); Black et al. (2025a); Kim et al. (2025a).
However, action labels do not directly supervise the visual outcomes of those actions. To incorporate this information into policy learning, World Action Models (WAMs) build on visual generative models and couple action learning with world modeling objectives Zhang et al. (2026b); Cen et al. (2025); Bi et al. (2026); Yuan et al. (2026). The resulting visual prediction task provides an additional training signal alongside action supervision and enables robot policies to benefit from pretrained generative representations.

Most WAMs learn how a scene evolves by predicting future RGB observations or visual latents. These objectives encode task-relevant spatial relationships alongside object appearance, background, and viewpoint, leaving the geometric transitions that matter for control implicit.
Geometry Forcing shows that pretrained 3D features can improve the geometric consistency of video generation Wu et al. (2026), and geometry-aware WAMs have explored geometric supervision for manipulation Ma et al. (2026a); Zhang et al. (2026a); Li et al. (2026c).
For robot control, the 3D changes needed to advance the task provide a natural target for this supervision.
Placing an object requires changing its pose relative to a target, while opening a drawer requires changing the configuration of an articulated object.
Modeling such transitions gives the policy a way to anticipate how the scene needs to change when generating actions.

Therefore, we introduce Foresight Forcing (ℱ2\mathcal{F}^{2}), a WAM that fuses correspondence-aligned transitions in 3D geometry feature space of foundation models into spatial transition queries for action generation, rather than directly predicting explicit 3D motions (Figure 1). During training, a frozen VGGT teacher Wang et al. (2025a) extracts patch features from an aligned observation pair, and their temporal differences serve as dense targets for the queries. A shared updater progressively refines the queries after each double block of the visual backbone using information from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state. We supervise the queries to match the direction and scale of the teacher targets and feed the refined queries directly to the action expert. At inference, the policy predicts the queries from its current inputs without access to future observations or the teacher. We evaluate ℱ2\mathcal{F}^{2} on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks to assess manipulation performance, robustness, and inference efficiency. ℱ2\mathcal{F}^{2} achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real robot.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Transition-centric geometric supervision. We introduce correspondence-aligned 3D teacher feature differences as supervision for spatial transition learning for action generation in a World Action Model.

Teacher-guided spatial transition learning for action generation. We introduce dedicated latent queries that a shared updater progressively refines across the visual backbone. During training, we align the refined queries with the frozen 3D teacher targets in direction and scale. The queries directly condition the action expert.

Manipulation performance and robustness. Evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, with state-of-the-art average success rates on RoboTwin 2.0 Full and Clean-to-Random. On six real-world tasks, ℱ2\mathcal{F}^{2} achieves a mean task score of 85.8%, exceeding ImageWAM and π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 15.6 and 2.3 percentage points, respectively.

1. Transition-centric geometric supervision. We introduce correspondence-aligned 3D teacher feature differences as supervision for spatial transition learning for action generation in a World Action Model.

2. Teacher-guided spatial transition learning for action generation. We introduce dedicated latent queries that a shared updater progressively refines across the visual backbone. During training, we align the refined queries with the frozen 3D teacher targets in direction and scale. The queries directly condition the action expert.

3. Manipulation performance and robustness. Evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, with state-of-the-art average success rates on RoboTwin 2.0 Full and Clean-to-Random. On six real-world tasks, ℱ2\mathcal{F}^{2} achieves a mean task score of 85.8%, exceeding ImageWAM and π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 15.6 and 2.3 percentage points, respectively.

title: SayDo: Benchmarking the Safety of Frontier Models from Chat to Closed-Loop Robot Control
authors: Benjamin Alt
abstract: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.
introduction:
Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) have been used to decompose open-ended instructions into robot skills (Ahn et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2023), and general-purpose models have been shown to control robot arms without task-specific training (Zhang et al., 2026). These capabilities make VLMs candidates for high-level robot control in laboratories, homes and factories. In such deployments, whether an action is safe depends on context, and a specification of safe behavior cannot enumerate every context. Pouring a clear liquid into a waste beaker is routine laboratory practice, unless the liquid is bleach and the beaker holds acid washes (Mazeika et al., 2024). Moving a knife off a cutting board is helpful, unless the only free surface is a child’s toy box (Grover, 2026, adapted from). In both cases the instruction is benign and the hazard lies in the scene, so a safe robot must decline a request that is unobjectionable in itself (Briggs & Scheutz, 2017).

Whether frontier models decline such requests when they control a robot has not been measured systematically, as most published safety evaluations of these models present both the request and the hazard as text. Several early results indicate that text evaluations may be poor predictors of model behavior in embodied conditions. Digital agents that refuse harmful requests in conversation have been found to execute them through tool calls (Cartagena & Teixeira, 2026), and models that refuse a request in chat have been reported to comply with it when it arrives through a robot control loop (Grover, 2026; Sun et al., 2026). These small-scale studies compare propensities to follow harmful instructions across text and embodied conditions. They do not identify which aspect of embodiment produces the effect (egocentric vs. allocentric perspectives, image vs. text inputs, action vs. prose outputs, or closed-loop vs. open-loop control), nor whether their findings extend to benign instructions in hazardous scenes.

We introduce SayDo, a benchmark designed to address both questions. We propose eleven tasks, each pairing a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Each task is implemented in six settings that form an embodiment gradient, from a single chat question to closed-loop control in a robot simulator (Figure 1). The information that reveals the hazard is present in the model’s input in every setting, so that the settings only differ in interface, not in available information. Two further conditions, a benign control without the hazard and a variant that admits a safe way to carry out the instruction, distinguish unsafe compliance from overcaution and from failure to find the safe option. Scripted operator pushback, which does not add information about the hazard, measures whether refusals persist.

Our contributions are:

SayDo, a benchmark of eleven latent-hazard tasks in laboratory and household settings. Each task is implemented in six settings that change how the model is embodied while keeping the information about the hazard the same. Matched benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback separate unsafe compliance from overcaution.

Evidence that safety in chat does not predict safety in robot control. Across six frontier VLMs, the unsafe-action rate rises from 14% in chat to 47% in closed-loop simulation (Figure 3), in all eleven tasks. The increase is confined to the three open-weight models.

Evidence that the failures are not failures to perceive the hazard. In 73% of unsafe episodes the model identifies the hazard before acting. In the closed loop, models give way to pushback more often and take an available safe alternative less often than in chat.

1. SayDo, a benchmark of eleven latent-hazard tasks in laboratory and household settings. Each task is implemented in six settings that change how the model is embodied while keeping the information about the hazard the same. Matched benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback separate unsafe compliance from overcaution.

2. Evidence that safety in chat does not predict safety in robot control. Across six frontier VLMs, the unsafe-action rate rises from 14% in chat to 47% in closed-loop simulation (Figure 3), in all eleven tasks. The increase is confined to the three open-weight models.

3. Evidence that the failures are not failures to perceive the hazard. In 73% of unsafe episodes the model identifies the hazard before acting. In the closed loop, models give way to pushback more often and take an available safe alternative less often than in chat.

2. 是否属于 World Model：否。虽然论文涉及到模型在不同环境下的表现和安全性评估，但并没有明确强调模型学习环境演化或进行未来状态预测的过程。其重点在于模型如何处理潜在危险，而不是对世界模型的学习和规划。

title: Personalization of a Commercial Powered Knee Prosthesis Under Clinically Realistic Conditions via Reinforcement Learning: A Feasibility Study
authors: Xinyi Liu,Atli Örn Sverrisson,David Langlois,Ming Liu,Varun Nalam,He Huang
abstract: Personalization of powered prosthesis control to individual user needs remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE), a reinforcement learning (RL) tuning approach, has been developed and validated. This feasibility study investigated whether the developed approach can personalize a commercial powered knee prosthesis under clinically realistic conditions. To reduce the time for personalization, tuning was initialized with a policy learned offline from one non-disabled participant walking on a treadmill and was then applied to three other non-disabled participants walking with the knee through a bypass adapter on a 5-meter walkway. All participants reached the goal within 8–18 tuning steps (1.7–4.2 minutes of walking), reducing the knee-kinematic feature error by 64–90% on average. These results support the feasibility of implementing the RL-based tuning approach in clinically realistic conditions with space and equipment constraints.
introduction:
For individuals with transfemoral amputation, powered knee prostheses can generate positive mechanical power during gait, which passive knees cannot [1]. Research prototypes have demonstrated clinical benefits in laboratory settings [2],
and clinical evaluations of commercial devices have reported improved biomechanical outcomes and favorable user feedback [3], yet these benefits are not fully realized across users [4, 5, 6]. This inconsistency has limited the adoption of powered prostheses in clinical practice and everyday use [3].
A major bottleneck is personalizing the controller to each user [7, 8]. Across robotic lower-limb prostheses, user outcomes depend on how the controller is configured [3, 9, 10]. Commonly used prosthesis control approaches, from finite-state impedance control [11, 2], continuous impedance control [12], hybrid kinematic–impedance control [13], and model-based control [14] to recent learning-based controllers trained in simulation [15], all require per-user customization to achieve clinical benefits [9].

Personalization must account for many user-specific factors and is predominantly performed manually without a standardized procedure. Parameters must be adjusted to each user’s body size and gait style [16, 5].
Some factors also change over time:
users re-weight movement goals such as efficiency and stability as environmental risk changes [17, 18], and users adapt their motor control to the device [19], so a configuration tuned once may need to be revisited. In current practice, prosthetists tune the parameters by observing the user across walking trials [11], which is time-consuming and relies on expert knowledge of many interacting parameters: even with a structured starting configuration, 24 of the 140 parameters of a powered knee–ankle prosthesis had to be adjusted for each user, taking up to 5 hours in one such approach [11]. Moreover, clinical evaluations often do not report the tuning procedure or criteria used [3, 5], which makes outcomes difficult to compare across studies.

Automating tuning toward a prescribed goal could shorten clinic visits, standardize fitting procedures, reduce dependency on subjective expert tuning, which could be biased, and let users benefit more fully from powered prostheses. Such automation is commonly framed as human-in-the-loop optimization (HILO) [8]. Black-box optimizers that search for a single best parameter set, such as covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy and Bayesian optimization, have reduced the metabolic cost of walking with exoskeletons [20, 21], but have not outperformed generic control for prosthesis users [22], likely because users’ motor control and objectives change as they adapt to the device [22, 19]. Another common HILO framework is reinforcement learning (RL) with human-subject testing in the loop, which instead drives the prosthesis motion toward a target profile [23, 15]. Rather than searching for a single optimum, it learns a tuning policy that maps the observed knee-motion error to incremental parameter adjustments [7], which can be reapplied whenever the user’s condition changes. Policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE) [24] tuned 12 impedance parameters within 45 tuning steps, and the resulting policies remained effective across users and task modifications. RL tuning has since been extended to continuous impedance control [12] and to shaping the user’s thigh motion [25]. RL tuning frameworks such as PICE could therefore serve as a general tuning mechanism, but there are still challenges to be addressed to ensure practical implementation in clinics [7, 24, 12].

Our previously validated PICE algorithm [24] has so far been used to tune prosthesis impedance only during treadmill walking, where continuous walking at a fixed speed keeps gait variability low [26]. In clinical practice, however, prostheses are typically tuned during self-paced overground walking [13], which produces more variable gait and is interrupted by frequent stops and turns imposed by limited walkway space. Whether PICE can tune a prosthesis effectively under these clinically realistic conditions remains an open question.
In this study, we tested PICE on a commercial powered knee prosthesis under such conditions. We further asked whether tuning for a new user can be accelerated by reusing prior experience from another user. Building on [24], which showed that offline data can improve tuning efficiency, we initialized tuning with a policy learned offline from one non-disabled participant walking on a treadmill, rather than starting from scratch. We then used this policy to tune the knee for three other non-disabled participants walking overground with a bypass adapter, and, for one participant, toward a second set of target knee kinematics. We show that all participants reached the goal within 8–18 tuning steps, corresponding to 1.7–4.2 minutes of walking, reducing the knee-kinematic feature errors by 64–90%. These results are a preliminary step toward clinically relevant automated prosthesis tuning.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II describes the system setup and formulates the problem,
Section III describes the tuning method and evaluation protocol, Section IV reports results, and
Section V discusses limitations
and concludes.

title: CoSel: Cooperation as Selection for End-to-End Driving
authors: Yiping Li,Haohua Que,Zhipeng Bao,Wenjie Zhao,Qianwen Li
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Cooperative driving can extend a vehicle’s awareness beyond its own sensors, but existing cooperative end-to-end methods inject shared information into the planner and rely on cooperative driving demonstrations to learn how to use it. The moments in which shared information should change a driving decision are rare in such data, providing limited supervision for learning this behavior. We argue that cooperation need not be learned by the planner. Instead, reacting to shared information requires predicting how surrounding agents will move and selecting a response from the candidate trajectories of an ego planner. We introduce CoSel, a cooperation-as-selection framework that leaves the planner and its ego-only input unchanged. A separately trained cooperative predictor uses observations from the ego vehicle, roadside units, and connected automated vehicles to predict surrounding agents and their future motion. CoSel evaluates the planner’s candidate trajectories against these predictions, preserves the planner’s choice when it remains safe, and selects the closest safe alternative when shared information reveals additional risk. Each safety intervention is traceable to the shared evidence that triggers it. In closed-loop evaluation, CoSel achieves a driving score of 70.7 on V2Xverse, outperforming the best compared cooperative method by 7.5 points, and the highest average driving score of 85.8 on MDrive. Under missing ego detections, the collision count of CoSel increases only from 17 to 19 in 72 scenarios, compared with 19 to 32 for an existing cooperative end-to-end model.
introduction:
Cooperative driving extends a vehicle’s awareness with the perception [71, 70, 24, 76, 77]
and intent [45, 19] shared by roadside units (RSUs) and other connected automated vehicles
(CAVs).
A single vehicle, however good its end-to-end planner [59, 51], cannot obtain this information from
its own sensors: what lies behind an occluder, such as a pedestrian behind a kiosk (Fig. 1), and what other
vehicles intend, as at an unsignalized intersection.

Existing cooperative end-to-end methods fuse the shared information into the planner, as raw data [75] or as
features or queries [46, 78, 57], and train the planner on cooperative driving data.
Language-based methods instead pass shared messages to a large language
model [20, 19, 48, 45, 15]. In the fusion-based methods the perception that
feeds the planner can be supervised with labels, but how the planner uses it is learned from the expert’s trajectory.
The planner has to infer from imitation alone when shared information should change its decision.

This is hard to learn, because the frames that could teach it are rare. Imitation supervises a planner with
one ego trajectory per frame, a sparse signal [7, 37], and the frames in which the expert
changes its action because of an event in the scene, such as a light turning green or a pedestrian stepping out, are
a very small fraction [12, 64]. As a result, a learned planner can reach a low
imitation error by continuing its own speed and past
motion [12, 64, 39], and an additional input is not guaranteed to be
used correctly [17]. Of these frames, only a subset can teach the planner anything about shared
information: those in which the event is reported by an RSU or a CAV and is not visible to the ego’s own sensors. We
call these frames decision-changing moments: only in them should shared information change the decision. In
every other frame it adds little to what the ego already sees, and the demonstration gives no signal for using it.
In V2Xverse training data, 97.7% of the 7,158 brake causes of the expert are visible to the ego, and none is an agent ahead
that only the RSU sees (Sec. 7).
A recent closed-loop benchmark also reports that sharing perception does not
always improve planning [13].

We argue that shared information need not enter the planner at all. Two observations support this. First, predicting the future motion of the
surrounding agents from shared detections is densely supervised: the future track of every observed agent in every frame is a
training target [6], and an agent that only another source sees is obtained by dropping its ego detection, without a new
expert action. Shared observations have been shown to
improve forecasting [54, 62, 81]. Second, an
ego planner that scores candidate trajectories [31, 38, 41, 36, 43, 68]
typically has the kind of response that a decision-making moment demands. Candidates who follow the same path at different speeds cover slowing and
yielding. Recent vocabularies also vary the path: they are factorized into paths and speed
profiles [59], and candidates ranked below the executed one can include lateral alternatives such as
lane changes [43], so taking a neighboring path is also a candidate. The planner lacks only
the information to prefer one of them. Given predicted futures, we can test in every frame whether each candidate is safe,
and when to react follows from this test. We cast cooperation as selection: the planner proposes, and shared
information decides which candidate from its vocabulary is executed. Selecting among a learned planner’s own candidates with an explicit
safety check has been used for the safety of ego-only planners [53, 31]. We make it the only place where
cooperation enters.

We propose CoSel, a cooperative driving system built on this formulation (Fig. 2). Its planner uses
ego-only input, in training and at test time. A cooperative predictor estimates an existence probability and several possible futures for every surrounding agent
from the detections of the ego, RSUs and CAVs. Some inputs enter the same scene with a given future: the plan that a
CAV shares and the static obstacles that a roadside LiDAR sees. Among
the candidates that satisfy a chance constraint on predicted collision risk with a fixed risk budget, a selector
executes the one closest to the planner’s choice. Only the predictor is trained on cooperative data,
and its targets are the future tracks of all agents.

Cooperation as selection gives CoSel three properties by design, where an intervention is a step at which
the executed candidate differs from the planner’s choice. Planner first: the planner’s choice is executed
unchanged unless the predicted risk rules it out or progress requires a move (Sec. 3.4). One safety rule for every
source: an agent or obstacle enters the chance constraint as one factor of the same form whether the ego, an RSU or
a CAV reported it, and a source that reports nothing contributes no factor and leaves the rule unchanged
(Secs. 3.3 and 4.3). Traceable interventions: every safety intervention is attributed to the
agent or obstacle that contributes most to the predicted risk of the planner’s choice, together with the source
that reported it (Sec. 4.2).

On the 85 closed-loop routes of V2Xverse [46], the planner alone reaches a driving score of 57.6,
the selection on the ego’s own detections 62.9, and with the detections of the RSU 70.7, the highest among the compared
methods. CoSel surpasses the cooperative method CoDriving (59.1) and has 67% fewer collisions per kilometer. CoSel is robust to unreliable ego perception. In a stress test of 72 scenarios that removes the pedestrians from the ego’s sensors,
it collides in 19 scenarios, against 17 without the removal. CoDriving collides in 32, against 19, and the planner alone in 50.
On MDrive [13], which tests interaction among multiple CAVs, CoSel attains the highest
average driving score among the compared methods (85.8, Tab. 2). Our contributions are:

Formulation. Cooperation as selection: the planner is trained on ego-only demonstrations, and shared
information decides which of its candidates is executed.

Method. CoSel: a lightweight, densely supervised cooperative predictor and an interpretable selector
that applies one safety rule to every source and leaves the planner untouched.

Evidence. Closed-loop results on V2Xverse and MDrive, a stress test that isolates the shared
information, and an analysis of each source and of the interventions (Secs. 4.3 and 4.2).

1. Formulation. Cooperation as selection: the planner is trained on ego-only demonstrations, and shared
information decides which of its candidates is executed.

2. Method. CoSel: a lightweight, densely supervised cooperative predictor and an interpretable selector
that applies one safety rule to every source and leaves the planner untouched.

3. Evidence. Closed-loop results on V2Xverse and MDrive, a stress test that isolates the shared
information, and an analysis of each source and of the interventions (Secs. 4.3 and 4.2).

title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation
authors: Vinay Udit Mohan,Xuchuan Huang,Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM’s reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available on our project page.
introduction:
Developing world models that generalise across diverse robot embodiments remains a central challenge in robotic manipulation. Embodiments differ substantially in their morphologies, kinematics, and action spaces, making it difficult to learn predictive dynamics that transfer across platforms. This motivates learning a unified action representation that enables a world model to capture reusable interaction dynamics across different embodiments, including those unseen during training.

A promising direction is to learn action representations directly from observed manipulation, without relying on embodiment-specific action labels [31]. Human manipulation videos provide a rich source of such observations, but representations learned from human motion alone may not generalise across robot morphologies. Retargeting these demonstrations to different robot embodiments produces corresponding manipulation trajectories that preserve the underlying interaction despite differences in morphology [33]. These correspondences provide a natural basis for learning a shared latent action space that captures motion rather than embodiment-specific variation.

Manipulation involves physical interactions that evolve over space and time. Explicit 3D geometry provides a natural way to represent this evolution, capturing the spatial relationships and contact geometry between interacting entities [14, 1]. Representing scene evolution through particle displacements provides direct supervision of physical motion, allowing predictive dynamics to focus on how the scene evolves rather than its visual appearance. We therefore seek to ground both latent action inference and predictive dynamics in a common geometric representation, enabling actions to be learned and their consequences to be predicted in the same physical space.

In this work, we introduce DexLatentWorld, a unified 3D latent-action world model for prediction and control, learning continuous action representations directly from action-unlabelled manipulation observations (Fig. ). We represent these observations as temporally corresponding 3D scene particles derived from tracked hand–object trajectories, with human manipulation trajectories retargeted to different robot embodiments. A cross-embodiment contrastive objective aligns corresponding human and robot transitions within a shared latent action space, while a forward dynamics model uses these representations to predict scene evolution in 3D particle space. At deployment, we perform closed-loop model-predictive control (MPC) directly in the learned latent action space, evaluating candidate latent-action sequences through their predicted geometric consequences. We then recover executable robot commands from predicted motion using known robot geometry and kinematics, without additional action-labelled demonstrations for training an embodiment-specific latent-to-action decoder.

The learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, enabling consistent geometric predictions across unseen robot embodiments. To evaluate the effectiveness of these capabilities in robotic manipulation, we employ MPC in both simulation and real-world deployment. We further demonstrate zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries without embodiment-specific adaptation. Extending to dexterous manipulation, our framework achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing following task-agnostic domain adaptation, compared with DexWM [9]’s 72%, 58%, and 28%. In real-world deployment, the original pretrained model achieves 86% success on five manipulation tasks with an unseen dexterous hand, without any fine-tuning. Our contributions include:

A unified 3D latent-action world model.
We introduce a self-supervised framework that combines
particle-based scene dynamics with a shared continuous
latent action representation, enabling cross-embodiment
world modelling and direct latent-space planning and control.

A geometry-based prediction-to-control framework. We plan directly in the learned latent action space and recover executable robot targets from predicted 3D motion, avoiding the need for a learned embodiment-specific latent-to-action decoder.

Cross-embodiment generalisation and dexterous manipulation. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to held-out end effectors, including real-world dexterous manipulation without world-model adaptation, and task generalisation following task-agnostic domain adaptation.

We introduce a self-supervised framework that combines
particle-based scene dynamics with a shared continuous
latent action representation, enabling cross-embodiment
world modelling and direct latent-space planning and control.

2. A geometry-based prediction-to-control framework. We plan directly in the learned latent action space and recover executable robot targets from predicted 3D motion, avoiding the need for a learned embodiment-specific latent-to-action decoder.

3. Cross-embodiment generalisation and dexterous manipulation. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to held-out end effectors, including real-world dexterous manipulation without world-model adaptation, and task generalisation following task-agnostic domain adaptation.
