title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Surprisingly Effective In-Context Robot Learners
authors: Zhen Xu,Hao-Run Cai,Heng-Zhuang Li,Si-Yang Liu,Jun-Peng Jiang,Han-Jia Ye
abstract:
Can foundation models pretrained for generic
numerical prediction serve as in-context robot
learners? We investigate this question through
tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are
pretrained to infer input–output relationships from
labeled examples in context. We introduce TabAct, which
casts visual imitation as numerical prediction: frozen visual features and
robot proprioception form the inputs, future action
chunks form the targets, and each demonstration time step
provides one labeled example that conditions a frozen
TFM for closed-loop control.
The predictor receives no robot-specific training
or target-task fine-tuning.
With one target-task demonstration available to each
method, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest
average success among all evaluated methods on both
LIBERO and Meta-World, exceeding the strongest baseline
by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points, respectively.
Additional demonstrations improve control without
updating model weights: with five demonstrations,
success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object. These results demonstrate that generic
numerical pretraining can provide an effective
foundation for in-context robot learning.
introduction:
Providing a few demonstrations is a natural way to teach
a robot a new behavior. In-context learning (ICL) makes
this possible without task-specific parameter updates,
using demonstrations as context for action prediction at
deployment. Robot-trained in-context policies acquire this
ability through training on robot demonstrations and
trajectories [11, 22, 7, 13, 33, 10, 49, 46].
Language and multimodal foundation models offer another
route, drawing on in-context capabilities acquired through
general-purpose pretraining [3, 9, 50, 27].
In this work, we investigate whether pretraining for generic
numerical prediction can provide this capability.

The connection starts with the structure of a demonstration.
Each time step pairs an observation with an action, so even
a single trajectory provides a small labeled dataset.
Acting from a new observation then requires predicting an
action from these examples. Once observations and actions
are represented numerically, this structure matches the
prediction interface of tabular foundation models (TFMs),
which are pretrained to infer input–output relationships
from labeled examples in context [18, 41].
A demonstration can therefore supply the context for a TFM,
while the robot’s current observation supplies the query.
Can a frozen predictor whose pretraining uses no robot
data use these numerical examples to support visual,
closed-loop robot control?

We show that this is possible with TabAct, a numerical
formulation of visual imitation for frozen TFMs.
TabAct converts demonstrations into compact input–output
examples: frozen visual features and robot proprioception
form the inputs, while short action chunks form the targets.
Projections fitted on the supplied demonstrations compress
visual features and future motion, reducing the dimensions
of the inputs and prediction targets. At deployment, the
TFM predicts an action chunk for the current observation,
conditioned on these demonstration examples. The robot
executes the predicted actions, obtains a new observation,
and repeats, placing the predictor directly in the control
loop. The visual encoder and TFM remain frozen throughout,
with no robot-specific policy training or target-task
fine-tuning.

We evaluate TabAct in simulation on held-out manipulation
tasks from LIBERO [26] and
Meta-World [51]. With one target-task
demonstration available to each method, TabAct with frozen
TabICLv2 [41] achieves 62.7% average success
across three held-out LIBERO subsets and 49.3% on
Meta-World. On both benchmark averages, it outperforms all
evaluated baselines, including robot-trained in-context
policies, retrieval-based imitation, and pretrained robot
policies fine-tuned on the target demonstration
(Table 1).

Beyond overall success, we examine how the frozen model
uses its demonstration context. Providing five demonstrations
instead of one raises average LIBERO success from 62.7%
to 81.3%, while all pretrained weights remain fixed
(Sec. 4.4). Figure 2
illustrates the gains on LIBERO-Object.
In a controlled goal-switching
evaluation, we hold the initial observation fixed and change
the supplied demonstration to specify different goals.
TabAct completes the demonstrated goal in 75.6% of
rollouts, showing that the same frozen model can produce

Table 6). These results show that

We further examine whether effective control depends on a

and execution held fixed, replacing TabICLv2 with

(Table 2). At the same time,

and 5), rather than being confined
to a single model pairing. Together, these findings support
generic numerical pretraining as a viable foundation for
in-context robot learning.

Our main contributions are:

Frozen TFMs as in-context robot learners.
We show that TFMs pretrained on generic numerical tasks
without robot data can support visual, closed-loop robot
imitation through demonstration context.

TabAct, a numerical formulation of visual imitation.
We represent demonstrations as input–output examples for a
frozen TFM, using frozen visual features and proprioception
as inputs and compact action chunks as targets.

An empirical characterization of this capability.
We evaluate one-shot control, demonstration-conditioned goal
switching, and improvement with additional demonstrations,
and examine predictor choice and generality across TFMs
and visual encoders.

title: Bridging Continuous-Time MAPF and Industrial AGV Fleet Coordination with Lazy Priority-Based Search
authors: Federico Signorile,Raffaele Carli,Alessandro Bertogli,Roberto Olmi,Sven Koenig,Mariagrazia Dotoli
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
abstract: Continuous-time multi-agent path finding on roadmaps (MAPFR) offers a principled way to coordinate robot fleets with geometric collision avoidance, yet its deployment on industrial automated guided vehicle (AGV) infrastructures remains challenging, as highly connected and redundant roadmaps amplify both safe-interval reasoning and multi-agent interaction handling. To bridge this gap, we formalize AGV-MAPFR-CTC, a configuration-space variant of MAPFR with precomputed continuous-time conflicts that enables the reuse of MAPFR solvers for AGV fleet coordination with minimal changes. We then revisit continuous-time priority-based search (CPBS), identifying the boundary conditions required by its safe interval path planning (SIPP) low-level planner under priority-induced constraints and enabling earlier solution detection. As a central contribution, we analyze the structure of the priority search space, clarifying which agents are affected by each priority refinement and when replanning can be avoided. Building on this analysis, we introduce a novel algorithm, Lazy-CPBS, which materializes high-level nodes lazily: a child’s plans are computed only when it is expanded, so siblings that are never expanded cost no low-level search. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks and on industrial AGV roadmaps imported from a proprietary digital-twin simulator show that CPBS-based solvers remain effective well beyond the agent counts reachable by optimal MAPFR solvers, while Lazy-CPBS substantially reduces CPBS overhead and offers the most consistent robustness/runtime trade-off across industrial layouts.
introduction:
Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) has emerged as a central problem in both AI and robotics, providing algorithmic foundations for coordinating large fleets of robots under collision-avoidance constraints. Its techniques have been successfully applied in domains such as warehouse logistics [1], office service robots [2], airport towing [3], and video games [4], and have also inspired solutions to related problems including 3D pipe routing [5], autonomous driving in urban environments [6], and other complex routing and scheduling tasks.
In the classical MAPF formulation, the environment is discretized into a grid and agents move synchronously in discrete time steps, seeking non-colliding paths that minimize global objectives such as the sum of arrival times [7, 8]. Over the last decade, this setting has led to a rich algorithmic landscape, ranging from optimal [9] and bounded-suboptimal search [10] to suboptimal methods that scale to hundreds or even thousands of agents in seconds [11, 12]. However, discrete-time, grid-based MAPF remains an abstraction: it disregards the continuous nature of time, the geometry of real roadmaps, and the kinematic constraints of industrial vehicles, limiting its direct applicability in real-world domains such as warehouses with automated forklifts and other car-like automated guided vehicles (AGVs).

To address these limitations, the continuous-time variant MAPFR has been proposed, in which agents move along a generic roadmap, collisions are detected geometrically rather than via grid-cell conflicts, and actions have arbitrary real-valued durations [13]. A key component in this context is safe interval path planning (SIPP) [14], an A∗-based algorithm that performs continuous-time planning by encoding dynamic obstacles as time-varying safe intervals on vertices and edges. SIPP serves as the single-agent planner underlying most MAPFR algorithms, such as continuous-time conflict-based search (CCBS) [15]. CCBS and its recent refinements based on wait discretization [16] or improved branching rules [17] currently represent the main optimal and solution-complete baselines for MAPFR.

Unlike autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), which navigate primarily through onboard intelligence [18], industrial AGVs are designed to operate on fixed, predefined roadmaps [19].
Recent advances in MAPFR therefore appear as a natural algorithmic candidate for AGV fleet coordination, seemingly lowering the barrier to a direct integration of multi-agent planning into industrial systems.
In practice, however, most deployments still follow a decoupled architecture: each vehicle plans as if it were alone, while a separate traffic-management layer resolves interactions online [20].
Such controllers typically ensure safety and liveness through priority rules, local negotiation over shared resources [21], hierarchical control schemes [22], or segment-reservation policies [23], rather than through a globally coordinated multi-agent planner.
Although well established, these approaches can degrade in dense, customized warehouse layouts, where congestion, deadlocks, and suboptimal traffic patterns become increasingly frequent as fleet sizes grow [24].

A key reason why MAPFR techniques remain challenging to deploy at scale lies in the structure of industrial AGV roadmaps.
Such roadmaps are typically highly connected and redundant, providing strong connectivity, broad coverage of the free space, and multiple alternative routes between most locations [21, 25].
While this redundancy is desirable for robustness and for handling local disturbances, it amplifies the combinatorial complexity of both layers in MAPFR solvers.
At the single-agent level, many methods rely on SIPP, which represents temporal constraints by maintaining, for each vertex and edge, the time windows in which it can be safely occupied.
Large and edge-dense industrial roadmaps inflate the number of vertex/edge safe intervals, raising memory and bookkeeping overhead.
Moreover, redundancy offers many alternative outgoing edges that traverse similar regions of the roadmap, increasing the branching factor that the low-level planner must consider.
At the multi-agent level, the same structural property induces dense clusters of temporally overlapping interactions, which in CCBS-like approaches translates into an explosion in the number of conflicts to detect and resolve through branching and repeated replanning.
As a consequence, the scalability observed on standard MAPFR benchmarks often fails to transfer to real industrial layouts, and practitioners still overwhelmingly rely on faster coordination schemes.

Within this landscape, priority-based planning offers a natural compromise between the speed of decoupled coordination and the adaptability of conflict-driven MAPF solvers.
In classical prioritized planning, a total order over the agents is fixed in advance, and each agent plans its path while treating all higher-priority agents as moving obstacles [26].
This yields a simple and fast framework, but it is well known to be incomplete: a fixed priority ordering may fail to admit any solution even when an alternative ordering would succeed [27].
To mitigate this limitation, restart-based variants repeatedly modify the priority order, either by random resampling [28] or by deterministic promotion rules for agents that fail to find a path [29].
A more principled alternative is priority-based search (PBS), which systematically explores the space of priority orderings and searches for a priority structure that is consistent with a conflict-free solution [30].

Continuous-time priority-based search (CPBS) extends this idea to MAPFR by combining a PBS-style high-level search over partial priority relations with a SIPP-based low-level planner operating in continuous time [31].
In roadmap-based settings, CPBS can exploit precomputed continuous-time conflict annotations (CTC).
These annotations specify, offline, which pairs of roadmap actions or resources may lead to a collision for given relative execution times.
At runtime, they allow the trajectory of a higher-priority agent to be converted into time-varying reservations for lower-priority agents without performing geometric collision checks online. Related offline conflict-detection and annotation strategies are widely used in industrial AGV systems [23] and have also been explored in roadmap-based MAPF planning [32, 33].

The resulting framework is attractive for industrial AGV coordination, but its performance is strongly affected by the cost of repeated replanning.
Each new priority refinement may require recomputing the path of the lower-priority agent and, through transitivity, the paths of all agents whose set of higher-priority predecessors has changed.
We refer to this computation of the multi-agent plan of a high-level node as its materialization.
On large or highly connected industrial roadmaps, this operation can be expensive because each replanning step requires rebuilding priority-induced safe intervals and running SIPP over a roadmap with many alternative outgoing motions.
At the same time, the benefit of this effort depends on the interaction density of the instance.
In dense or highly constrained layouts, where bottlenecks generate many conflicts, revising priorities is essential because fixed-order prioritized planning is brittle.
In sparse layouts, instead, a simple priority ordering may already be sufficient, and eager materialization of high-level nodes can introduce overhead with limited conflict-resolution benefit.

These observations motivate a lazy variant of CPBS that avoids materializing nodes that are never expanded. Rather than replanning immediately for every generated child node, the proposed Lazy-CPBS delays materialization until node expansion, so that siblings that are never expanded cost no low-level search. The goal is to preserve the robustness of systematic priority revision in congested regimes while approaching the efficiency of prioritized planning when interactions are sparse.

This paper makes the following contributions. First, we analyze the priority-search space induced by partial priority orderings in priority-based continuous-time MAPFR solvers. The analysis clarifies how priority decisions propagate through the search, which agents are affected by a priority refinement, and why different priority branches can be reasoned about independently. This structural view also provides implementation-level consequences for CPBS-style solvers, including the identification of the SIPP boundary conditions required by priority-induced reservations and the possibility of detecting solutions earlier during node materialization.
Second, building on this structural analysis, we introduce Lazy-CPBS, which delays node materialization until expansion, avoiding the low-level search for children that are never expanded. This reduces redundant SIPP calls and safe-interval updates while preserving the priority-search-space semantics of the eager formulation.
To ground these algorithmic contributions in industrial AGV coordination, we formalize AGV-MAPFR-CTC as a configuration-space variant of MAPFR with precomputed continuous-time conflicts. We then evaluate
CPBS and Lazy-CPBS both on standard MAPF benchmarks converted to continuous-time roadmaps and on industrial AGV roadmaps imported from a proprietary digital-twin simulator.
Taken together, these results strengthen the connection between continuous-time MAPF and industrial AGV coordination, while identifying priority-search-space structure as a concrete lever for reducing replanning overhead and enabling further acceleration.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 formalizes the continuous-time multi-agent problem, introducing the MAPFR-CTC model and its AGV-specific instantiation.
Section 3 revisits the CPBS framework, describes a SIPP-based low-level planner that ensures sound behavior under priority constraints, and formalizes structural properties of the CPBS high-level search that support efficient implementations.
Section 4 presents the novel Lazy-CPBS algorithm and discusses its relation to standard CPBS.
Section 5 reports the experimental setup and results on standard MAPFR benchmark instances. Section 6 then presents the industrial evaluation on warehouse roadmaps imported from a proprietary digital-twin simulator and derived from real AGV installations. Section 7 presents an ablation study that isolates the contributions of lazy materialization and child ordering to the speed-up of Lazy-CPBS over CPBS.
Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.

title: HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation
authors: Qiwei Liang,Zhengtu Liang,Minghao Lai,Yikeng Chen,Yiming Wang,Boyang Cai,Yuetong Fang,Taowen Wang,Baiqiao Yin,Tianxing Chen,Yue Chen,Jiaming Liang,Guangyu Chen,Shaolong Zhu,Daolin Ma,Renjing Xu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment Codebase & Benchmark Zoo.
introduction:
Robot manipulation policies increasingly reuse pretrained visual encoders instead of learning vision from scratch, which transfers poorly across objects, robots, and viewpoints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The candidates come from very different signals, including self-supervision, language alignment, 3D reconstruction, robot data, and vision–language models [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Choosing among them still means training and rolling out a policy. A benchmark with a shared policy can reveal which representations transfer, and whether inexpensive measurements explain their successes and failures across different training conditions.

Earlier evaluations often read a pooled third-person feature and relate scene reconstruction to control [2, 11, 12, 13, 14, 3, 15]. Bimanual policies do not use that interface. They attend to dense patch tokens, which keep the local detail that separates nearby grasps [16, 17, 18, 19], and they see through head and wrist cameras that move with the robot and are often occluded [20, 21, 22, 23]. We therefore ask how encoders compare when one policy reads their patch tokens from onboard cameras, and which properties of those tokens track the resulting success.

We introduce HIVE-Bench (Figure 1), to our knowledge the first comprehensive benchmark of patch-level representations for egocentric bimanual manipulation that jointly studies control and diagnostic correlations across training regimes. A flow-matching action head [24, 25] reads 20 encoders from seven families on two egocentric bimanual suites [26, 22]. We train it frozen and fine-tuned, on one task and on a shared suite, and we sweep data, model size, and the extracted layer, because a ranking from a single regime is easy to over-read. The same tokens are then scored in several ways: token statistics, state and object readouts, published vision benchmarks, and an inverse-dynamics readout (IDM) that recovers the commanded motion.

Those runs support three simple conclusions. Keeping the patch tokens, rather than averaging each view into one, accounts for most of the success of the encoders we compare this way. Fine-tuning improves every encoder we adapt, and one policy shared across tasks keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The measurements are the second half of the study. Several of them correlate with success somewhere, but none is stable enough to prove which encoder a robot should use. IDM is among the strongest readouts, especially on RoboTwin, yet even its ranking misses the best encoder and fails to predict gains from adaptation. Our goal is to map these relationships and their limits; finding measurements that improve on IDM remains an open research problem. Our contributions are:

An egocentric patch-level benchmark: one shared policy reads the dense patch tokens, not a pooled vector, of 20 encoders from onboard cameras on two bimanual suites under one shared update budget, through documented token interfaces (Section 3).

Evaluation from many angles: single-task and multi-task training, frozen and fine-tuned encoders, demonstration and model-size scaling, extraction layers, pooling, and optional robot state, with the action head and optimizer held fixed (Section 4).

A study of what tracks success, and where it stops: token statistics, action and state readouts, and published vision scores, compared across suites, task sharing, and adaptation, with the cases where a frozen ranking fails to predict improvement kept separate from the cases where it holds, and with IDM among the strongest metrics (Sections 5 and 6).

1. An egocentric patch-level benchmark: one shared policy reads the dense patch tokens, not a pooled vector, of 20 encoders from onboard cameras on two bimanual suites under one shared update budget, through documented token interfaces (Section 3).

2. Evaluation from many angles: single-task and multi-task training, frozen and fine-tuned encoders, demonstration and model-size scaling, extraction layers, pooling, and optional robot state, with the action head and optimizer held fixed (Section 4).

3. A study of what tracks success, and where it stops: token statistics, action and state readouts, and published vision scores, compared across suites, task sharing, and adaptation, with the cases where a frozen ranking fails to predict improvement kept separate from the cases where it holds, and with IDM among the strongest metrics (Sections 5 and 6).

title: Beyond Domain Randomization: Real-World Policy Adaptation in Learned Dynamics for Legged Robots
authors: Rui Dai,Shunpeng Yang,Zhen Fu,Maolin Lei,Jiaqi Song,Hua Chen,Nikos Tsagarakis
abstract:
Reinforcement learning policies are often trained with static domain
randomization for real-world deployment. However, real-world environments often exhibit unmodeled dynamic variations, such as payload changes or friction shifts,
that lie outside the randomization distribution, leading to performance
degradation upon deployment.
We propose a framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by adapting
a learned dynamics model to the deployed target conditions, with a
concurrent teacher-student paradigm applied to both the policy and dynamics
model.
This framework integrates the dynamics model into an on-policy reinforcement learning
pipeline, letting the performance of the policy align with the empirical
target dynamics. Experimental validations on bipedal locomotion tasks demonstrate
competitive adaptability under extreme physical variations,
including a payload reaching 80% of self-weight and an oil-lubricated
low-friction surface.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning has recently achieved remarkable success in robotic
control. This success is largely driven by high-fidelity simulators that
enable massive trajectory rollouts and systematic policy
evaluation [1, 2]. Within this paradigm,
domain randomization (DR) has established itself as a cornerstone technique to
bridge the reality gap, effectively handling modeling errors by exposing the
agent to a spectrum of physical parameters during
training [3, 4].
However, relying on a static
randomization range during training imposes inherent limitations when facing
significant dynamic variations. Fixed randomization ranges cannot fully capture extreme conditions encountered during deployment, such as substantial payload shifts or severe hardware degradation. Consequently, learned policies can either become overly conservative, sacrificing task performance to maintain stability, or fail catastrophically when faced with large dynamics mismatches [5, 6].

Alternative approaches focus on reducing the
reality gap through system identification (SysID) [7]
or learned actuator networks [2]. While SysID
effectively leverages analytical physics priors to calibrate simulation
parameters, its performance is fundamentally bounded by the structural
assumptions of rigid-body dynamics. Variations that fall outside this
parametric family introduce structural bias,
and
additional interaction data cannot expand the expressive capacity of
SysID [8]. Learned actuator networks
introduce
neural flexibility to capture nonlinearities, but typically require dense
supervision from high-accuracy torque sensors [2].
Moreover, as component-level models, they often fail to generalize to
system-level perturbations. Consequently, effective adaptation should benefit from flexible system-level dynamics models that capture effects beyond predefined physical parameterizations and can be learned directly from interaction data without requiring sophisticated sensing setups.

In this work, we incorporate learned system-level dynamics models into policy optimization within a model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) paradigm tailored to real-world domain adaptation.
Existing MBRL approaches include methods that augment off-policy training with model-generated transitions [9, 10], as well as methods that combine model and policy learning with continued environment interaction [11, 12]. We instead consider a practical setting in which only a limited batch of real-world interaction data is available from the target domain.
In the proposed framework, as illustrated in Fig. 1, offline real-world trajectories are collected with diverse behavior policies from simulation pre-training. These trajectories serve solely to align
the dynamics model with the target domain, after which the pre-trained
policy is fine-tuned via on-policy proximal policy optimization (PPO) entirely
inside this surrogate without any further environment interaction in the real
world. This decoupling of offline data collection from on-policy optimization
combines two properties usually held in tension by prior MBRL methods. The dynamics
model is policy-agnostic and ingests data from arbitrary, diverse behavioral
policies, while policy improvement remains on-policy and benefits from the
stability and data-scaling of PPO that have proven crucial for
locomotion [1].
We demonstrate the approach on a real robot locomotion task under extreme domain shifts.
Our main contributions are as follows.

We propose a target-specific domain adaptation framework that uses
real-world data to drive on-policy optimization through a learned dynamics
model,
enabling the policy to adapt to real-world physical variations beyond the
training randomization range.

We design a unified architecture for concurrent pre-training
of the policy and dynamics model in a single stage. This architecture enables
both components to operate on proprioceptive
inputs, facilitating subsequent post-training using the limited observations
available in the real world.

The framework is empirically validated on a real bipedal robot
platform, demonstrating competitive adaptability under extreme physical
variations compared with conventional baselines.

1. We propose a target-specific domain adaptation framework that uses
real-world data to drive on-policy optimization through a learned dynamics
model,
enabling the policy to adapt to real-world physical variations beyond the
training randomization range.

2. We design a unified architecture for concurrent pre-training
of the policy and dynamics model in a single stage. This architecture enables
both components to operate on proprioceptive
inputs, facilitating subsequent post-training using the limited observations
available in the real world.

3. The framework is empirically validated on a real bipedal robot
platform, demonstrating competitive adaptability under extreme physical
variations compared with conventional baselines.

title: Object Count Generalization Is an Interface Problem: Warping a Frozen Skill Instead of Retraining It
authors: Paul Mattes,Ayman Abdeldayem,Denis Shcherba,Wojciech Samek,Marc Toussaint
comment: . Submitted to International Conference on Learning Representations 2027. Code, videos and full results are available atthis https URL
abstract:
Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects NN in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on NN. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all NN objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget. Code,
videos and full results are available at https://hhi-robot-learning.github.io/wave-website/.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) learns a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward of
an agent interacting with an environment (Sutton & Barto, 2018). Policies trained this way for
robot manipulation solve the scene they were trained in and often degrade when that scene
changes (Kirk et al., 2023). This work addresses a covariate shift (Shimodaira, 2000), a change of the state
distribution under unchanged dynamics. In our case the number of objects in the scene
changes, so a policy trained with a few objects is deployed with many. Such a
shift also changes the dimension of the state, and appears for example when a
robot that has learned to manipulate a few plates is asked to fill a dishwasher. This work asks what can be learned around a frozen pretrained skill to enable zero-shot generalization to object counts unseen during training.

Two families of prior work address this shift. Set and relational architectures let a policy act
at any object count (Zaheer et al., 2017; Zambaldi et al., 2019). Robot policies built this way learn the
manipulation behavior itself (Li et al., 2020; Haramati et al., 2024; Lanier et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022). That is, a learned policy
issues the robot command at every control step, and no primitive, planner or model supplies
the motion. Such policies report whole-task success of at most 0.750.75 at six objects (Li et al., 2020) and at most 0.360.36 at eight (Park et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025) on their respective benchmarks.
Further, the theory of size
extrapolation shows that networks which pool over every entity can fail to generalize to sets
larger than those seen in training (Xu et al., 2021; Veličković et al., 2025; Haramati et al., 2024). Works that keep a trained skill frozen and learn
a correction around it (Silver et al., 2018; Johannink et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2025; Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Hirschowitz & Ramos, 2026; Zhang et al., 2023; Alqithami, 2026; Park & Lee, 2026) absorb dynamics shifts, sensor changes and
task mismatch, but none edits both the input and the output interface of a frozen skill to
generalize across the object count.

We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which learns a warping policy around
a frozen skill. Because the skill can already place one object, training only has to learn the
corrections needed for many.
Figure 1 gives an overview, and our contributions are as follows.

We propose WAVE, which composes a frozen single-object skill with a learned warping
policy. The policy applies an affine edit to every input and output channel of the skill and
is trained with PPO. It uses the skill as a black box, so it applies to any goal-conditioned skill trained on the same robot and to any task that gives every object a goal pose. We show which shifts such a warp can absorb (Section 3).

We propose WAVE, which composes a frozen single-object skill with a learned warping
policy. The policy applies an affine edit to every input and output channel of the skill and
is trained with PPO. It uses the skill as a black box, so it applies to any goal-conditioned skill trained on the same robot and to any task that gives every object a goal pose. We show which shifts such a warp can absorb (Section 3).

We train WAVE on six cube arrangement tasks, on a gantry robot and on a Franka Panda
arm with a gripper and with a pusher, with at most nine objects and evaluate it zero-shot
on up to thirty. On the gantry, this is two to five times the largest count to which published
methods that learn the manipulation itself generalize.

We compare WAVE with ten baselines spanning skill fine-tuning, distillation, subgoal control, scratch-trained entity transformers (Haramati et al., 2024), and a fixed-per-episode input edit (Zhang et al., 2023). They either fail beyond six cubes, even with a non-learned scripted selection of fulfillable goals, or learn their training counts but extrapolate worse. We also ablate the parts of WAVE’s architecture.

title: Place-Revisit Consistency Evaluation of Reference Poses
authors: Jianzhu Huai,Yujia Zhang,Grzegorz Jozkow
abstract: Reference trajectories are widely used to evaluate odometry and simultaneous localization and mapping systems. However, local inconsistencies in benchmark reference poses can bias such evaluations. This paper presents a place-revisit consistency evaluation method for reference poses in mobile sensing datasets. When a platform revisits a previously observed place after a sufficient temporal gap, the relative pose implied by the reference trajectory should agree with relative poses estimated directly from onboard sensors. We instantiate this idea with lidar scan registration and stereo-image pose estimation, and apply it to the KITTI Odometry and SNAIL Radar. The KITTI analysis identifies several revisit regions where the public reference poses disagree with sensor-derived relative poses, with median translation discrepancies up to 6.60 m. Representative point-cloud overlays further localize these discrepancies and support the use of place revisits as a benchmark-validation tool.
introduction:
Reference trajectories are central to odometry and SLAM benchmark evaluation,
where trajectory-level error metrics are commonly used to compare systems Sturm et al. (2012).
They are widely treated as ground truth for evaluating visual odometry, lidar odometry, and SLAM systems.
However, reference trajectories are not strictly error-free.
They are produced through sensor processing pipelines and calibration procedures that inevitably introduce systematic errors.
In many benchmarks, the accuracy characteristics of the reference poses are not fully documented, which limits the ability to assess their reliability.
A high-quality benchmark should ideally provide reference trajectories that are demonstrably more accurate than the methods being evaluated;
otherwise, evaluation results may be biased and the benchmark itself becomes less trustworthy.

This paper studies reference-pose consistency with a key observation.
When a vehicle revisits a previously observed place after a sufficient temporal gap,
the relative pose derived from the reference trajectory should agree with the relative pose estimated directly from sensor measurements.
If independent modalities such as lidar scan matching and stereo geometry produce consistent relative poses that disagree with the reference trajectory,
this indicates a potential local inconsistency in the reference poses rather than a failure of a specific sensing method.

The proposed analysis is related to prior work on odometry benchmarking, scan registration, and visual relative-pose estimation.
Unlike conventional odometry evaluation, which assumes that the benchmark trajectory is correct,
we use independent sensor-derived relative poses to evaluate the reference trajectory itself.
The method is particularly suited to repeated-route or looped mobile-sensing datasets where place revisits occur naturally.
The principal contributions are summarized in three aspects.
First, we formulate a place-revisit consistency check for reference poses in mobile sensing benchmarks.
Second, we instantiate the check using lidar Generalized ICP and stereo PnP as independent relative-pose estimates.
Third, we apply the method to KITTI Odometry sequences 00–10 and identify revisit regions with multi-meter reference-pose discrepancies.
We also evaluate lidar scans and stereo images from the SNAIL Radar dataset, with motion compensation applied to the lidar scans.

title: LLM-Guided Compositional Continual Learning for Robot Manipulation with Gated Low-Rank Experts
authors: Nilay Kushawaha,Abdalla Swikir,Fares Abu-Dakka
abstract:
General-purpose manipulation robots must acquire new skills over time without
forgetting prior ones or retraining from scratch. We present a continual
learning framework that represents each skill as a dedicated expert sub-network in a
Progressive Neural Network (PNN). New tasks reuse prior knowledge through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on lateral connections controlled by learnable per-parent gates, enabling explicit attenuation of individual transfer paths while reducing the parameter cost of dense PNN laterals. For long-horizon deployment, a frozen
local large language model decomposes natural-language instructions into
sub-tasks, routes them to suitable experts, and requests a new expert only when
the library is insufficient. Using a shared task-space action interface, we evaluate the framework on twelve MetaWorld tasks and in a Sawyer-to-Panda-to-UR5e cross-embodiment transfer experiment, showing improved task success relative to learning from scratch when demonstrations are limited. Real-robot manipulation experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework supports compositional execution and expert orchestration.
introduction:
Robots operating in unstructured environments must acquire new manipulation
skills throughout their lifetime without losing previously learned ones. This
requirement is difficult to satisfy with the dominant paradigm of training a
single monolithic policy across all tasks. When new tasks are added, previously
acquired knowledge can be partially or completely overwritten, leading to
catastrophic forgetting [1]. Continual learning (CL) addresses this problem by
enabling incremental skill acquisition while preserving earlier capabilities.
However, forgetting is not the only limitation of monolithic policies [2]. Because
different skills are entangled within the same set of parameters, it is difficult
to identify which part of the network is responsible for a particular behavior or
to quantify how much a new skill reuses prior knowledge. In safety-critical
robotics [3], this lack of transparency limits inspection,
verification, and selective deployment of individual competencies.

We address these issues by learning each skill as a dedicated expert that is
preserved after training and composed only when needed, as shown in Fig. 1. Our architecture is based
on a Progressive Neural Network (PNN) [4], where every task is assigned a
new column, or sub-network, that is frozen once learned. This prevents parameter overwriting in previously learned columns. To enable forward knowledge transfer with a lower per-connection parameter cost than dense lateral connections, prior knowledge is reused through LoRA-style low-rank lateral adapters  [5]. Each adapter is modulated by a learnable
per-parent gate, allowing the new column to draw selectively from relevant prior
experts while suppressing unhelpful ones. This design reduces the quadratic
parameter growth of vanilla PNNs, mitigates negative knowledge transfer, and exposes
transfer as a measurable quantity. Depending on the experiment, experts are trained either with soft actor-critic (SAC) augmented by behavior cloning or from demonstrations using conditional flow matching  [6].

A library of reusable experts becomes most useful when paired with a planner that
can decide which skill to invoke. We therefore integrate a frozen, locally served
large language model (LLM) as a high-level supervisor. Given a natural-language
instruction, the LLM decomposes it into an ordered sequence of sub-tasks, selects
the appropriate expert for each step, and requests that a new expert be trained
only when the current library is insufficient. The LLM operates purely at the
symbolic planning level and is never fine-tuned, keeping task reasoning separate
from low-level control and making the high-level task decomposition and routing explicit.

Using shared task-space action conventions, we also evaluate the gated transfer mechanism across robot embodiments. We study transfer from a Sawyer arm in MetaWorld [7]
to Panda and UR5e arms in Robosuite [8], and finally to a real Franka Research 3 (FR3) arm performing a long-horizon manipulation task. In the simulated cross-embodiment experiments, the framework achieves higher mean task success than learning from scratch at every tested demonstration budget. The main contributions of this article are summarized as follows:

We introduce a continual reinforcement learning (CRL) framework that combines frozen PNN
columns with LoRA lateral adapters and learnable per-parent gates, enabling selective and parameter-efficient forward transfer.

We introduce a continual reinforcement learning (CRL) framework that combines frozen PNN
columns with LoRA lateral adapters and learnable per-parent gates, enabling selective and parameter-efficient forward transfer.

We develop a frozen local LLM planner that decomposes long-horizon instructions,
routes sub-tasks to learned expert policies, and requests a new expert when the
library cannot solve the task, while remaining separate from low-level control.

We evaluate the framework against representative CL methods in the MetaWorld simulator, and demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer to the Robosuite simulator and then to an FR3 robot.

We demonstrate a six-stage real-world manipulation sequence on the FR3, where the LLM planner coordinates dedicated expert policies across all the sub-tasks.

1. We introduce a continual reinforcement learning (CRL) framework that combines frozen PNN
columns with LoRA lateral adapters and learnable per-parent gates, enabling selective and parameter-efficient forward transfer.

2. We develop a frozen local LLM planner that decomposes long-horizon instructions,
routes sub-tasks to learned expert policies, and requests a new expert when the
library cannot solve the task, while remaining separate from low-level control.

3. We evaluate the framework against representative CL methods in the MetaWorld simulator, and demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer to the Robosuite simulator and then to an FR3 robot.

4. We demonstrate a six-stage real-world manipulation sequence on the FR3, where the LLM planner coordinates dedicated expert policies across all the sub-tasks.

title: Active Observation for Robust Visual Servoing in Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zhilun Hu,Yuqi Cheng,Yuxiang Tan,Wenpan Li,Weiming Shen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Published in 2026 IEEE 22nd International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (CASE), pp. 3026-3031
abstract:
Robust visual servoing during robotic grasping remains challenging, as approach-phase occlusion frequently disrupts closed-loop control. To address this, we present an active observation framework in which one arm of an existing dual-arm platform carries an RGB-D camera as an active observer while the other executes grasping. The observer repositions to maintain or recover a shared target–gripper view within the feasible shared-view workspace.
Occlusion during the final approach is particularly acute: fixed eye-to-hand lacks an active recovery mechanism once the target is hidden, while eye-in-hand can suffer from self-occlusion and sensitivity to hand–eye calibration.
The observer first uses an active two-phase viewpoint strategy to align high-precision RGB-D axes with task-relevant error components. If visibility later degrades, an occlusion-triggered exploration module pauses the worker arm and scores candidate viewpoints by observation quality to recover a shared target–gripper view. Because both objects are detected in a single RGB-D image, the resulting Relative Servo Error avoids differencing two independently transformed target and gripper estimates.
We evaluate the system on a dual 6-DoF Piper platform using an open-vocabulary detector with text prompts, without task-specific fine-tuning or demonstrations.
Across 50 randomized trials per object, the system achieves 94% grasp success versus 76% for a reactive viewpoint baseline and 64% for a fixed camera. On triggered severe-occlusion trials, recovery takes 1.8±\pm0.6 s on average.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation increasingly relies on visual feedback for accurate and flexible interaction in unstructured environments. Visual servoing closes the perception–action loop for such tasks: the robot continuously observes the scene, estimates the discrepancy between the current and desired configuration, and updates its motion online, compensating for perception errors, kinematic uncertainty, and environmental disturbances. It has thus become a fundamental tool for visually guided robotic manipulation [1, 2, 3].

Despite its effectiveness, visual servoing critically depends on the availability of reliable visual observations. In real-world manipulation, however, this requirement frequently fails to hold. During grasping, alignment, or object approach, the manipulator itself may partially or completely occlude the target. Meanwhile, fixed sensor placement can easily create unfavorable viewing angles or depth-dominant observations. Once the target or the end-effector leaves the camera view, the visual feedback loop is broken, and the manipulation process may fail. Ensuring stable observability of task-relevant features is therefore a central challenge for robust visual servoing [4, 5].

Most existing visual servoing methods implicitly assume that observation conditions remain sufficiently reliable throughout execution. In typical setups, cameras are mounted either in a fixed eye-to-hand configuration or in an eye-in-hand configuration rigidly attached to the manipulator. While these arrangements simplify system integration, they also constrain the available viewpoints and make the perception process vulnerable to self-occlusion and visibility loss, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Classical position-based visual servoing (PBVS) and image-based visual servoing (IBVS) pipelines [1, 2] are effective when task-relevant features remain observable, but visibility recovery is usually outside the controller design. Learned or keypoint-based variants [6, 7] strengthen feature extraction or pose estimation, yet they still largely rely on the assumption that the necessary observations remain available.

Several research directions attempt to mitigate this limitation, but each addresses only part of the problem. Occlusion-aware visual-servo constraints [5] improve robustness by enforcing visibility conditions, but the sensing geometry is still externally specified rather than actively maintained online. Active vision and next-best-view methods [8, 9, 10] explicitly move the camera to improve visibility, yet they typically operate at planning frequencies and optimize scene coverage or information gain, instead of sustaining servo-rate visual feedback during manipulation. Dual-arm manipulation systems [11, 12] improve coordination and dexterity, but the visual feedback still comes from a static viewpoint that does not adapt to the evolving manipulation geometry.

Another limitation lies in how the servo signal itself is formed and whether the perception stack requires task-specific supervision. In standard position-based pipelines, the target and the end-effector are often estimated through separate kinematic and camera transformation chains before the control input is computed [2]. This design makes the servo error sensitive to calibration inaccuracies, especially when the two estimates are produced independently. Meanwhile, recent learning-based active manipulation systems, including recent bimanual active-vision systems [13], reduce hand-crafted engineering but often require task-specific teleoperation data, policy training, or task-level adaptation.

These gaps motivate a different formulation: rather than treating perception as a passive upstream module, we make observation an explicit and adaptive part of the servoing process. To this end, we propose an active observation framework for robust visual servoing in robotic manipulation. In this framework, one arm of an existing dual-arm platform carries an RGB-D camera as an active observer and regulates the camera viewpoint to maintain or recover a shared target–gripper view when feasible. Specifically, the framework combines three key mechanisms: viewpoint adaptation to reposition the observer arm toward more informative views, occlusion-triggered exploration to restore a shared view when detection quality drops, and a Relative Servo Error computed from the target–gripper displacement in a single camera image, avoiding differencing two independently transformed target and gripper estimates. By coupling active visibility maintenance with Relative Servo Error feedback from a single camera image, the proposed system uses recovered observations to update the servoing signal after occlusion begins.
Overall, the main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We propose an active observation framework for robotic manipulation that repurposes one arm of an existing dual-arm platform as an active observer carrying an RGB-D camera. The observer maintains or recovers target–gripper visibility within a feasible shared-view workspace via anisotropy-aware two-phase positioning and occlusion-triggered exploration.

title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?
authors: Hiroaki Honda,Koya Sakamoto,Shu Morikuni,Yusuke Iwasawa,Taiki Miyanishi
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds.
We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10–0.40 m/s).
Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt.
Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds.
We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames.
For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one.
Past frames raise the success rate by 10–40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three.
Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain.
These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames.
Project page: damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench
introduction:
Robot policies trained from demonstrations are largely evaluated on benchmarks in which objects remain stationary until robot contact [25, 28].
Manipulating a moving object requires the robot to adjust the timing and location of contact to the object’s speed.
Recent studies report that vision-language-action (VLA) models struggle with moving objects [46] and examine temporal motion cues [14], inference latency [44], and physical prediction [49].
However, it remains unclear whether these policies adapt their actions to object speed when that speed can be inferred from past frames.

Answering this question requires evaluating success rates across speeds to reveal speed-dependent failures and across diverse manipulation skills so that the findings are not tied to a few tasks.
Each task must also be solvable at the tested speeds so that failures reflect policy limitations rather than task infeasibility.
Existing moving-object benchmarks rarely provide all three.
Those with larger task sets report success rates at no more than three speeds or provide no per-speed results; those reporting more speeds do so for at most four tasks.
Few also check during task construction that an expert solves every task at several speeds.

We introduce SWEEP-Bench (Speed-Wise Evaluation of Embodied Policies), a simulation benchmark for moving-object manipulation on a conveyor belt.
We use a conveyor because we can set its speed while keeping the rest of the scene fixed, it supports many manipulation skills, and its motion is visible in the camera images.
The benchmark contains 80 conveyor-belt tasks in 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 speeds from 0.10 to 0.40 m/s, with constant speeds in the main protocol and within-episode speed changes in an acceleration setting.
To isolate the effect of speed, each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds, and the training demonstrations span the full speed range.
To ensure that failures reflect the policy, a scripted expert solves every task at four speeds spanning the range, and each task has a static counterpart that checks whether it can be learned with a stationary object.

We fine-tune six VLA models and two video-based world-action models [20, 48].
For each model, we compare the current frame alone with the current frame plus two past frames and evaluate both policies on every task at every speed.
For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds with or without past frames, as the policies tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed.
Measuring success at 13 speeds makes this pattern visible, whereas averaging over speeds hides it.

A small network on the optical flow between two frames 0.1 s apart estimates the belt speed with a mean absolute error of 0.010 m/s.
Past frames, however, raise the mean success rate by 10–40 percentage points for three models and by at most one point for the other five.
Linear probes on the fine-tuned policies show that the belt speed is most linearly decodable from these three (R2=0.86R^{2}=0.86–0.990.99 at the action module), whereas the other five reach at most R2=0.58R^{2}=0.58 and gain little from past frames.
The speed is useful once a policy has it: on a 20-task subset, adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and an image-based speed adapter recovers most of this gain.
In 720 real-conveyor trials, past frames raise Fast-WAM’s score slightly more than π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s, as in simulation, and adding belt speed input raises π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s score from 31 to 80, and to 66 when the adapter estimates the speed.

Our contributions are:

We introduce SWEEP-Bench, with 80 tasks across 16 skill categories and 13 speeds, paired evaluation scenes, an expert check of every task at four speeds, and a static counterpart for every task.
We will release the code, demonstrations, and evaluation protocol.

We evaluate eight VLA and world-action models with and without past frames on every task at every speed, showing that six of them peak at intermediate speeds and tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed.

Using linear probes and speed-conditioned policies, we find that past frames help only the three models from which the belt speed is most linearly decodable, and that a speed estimated from the images keeps most of the gain from ground-truth speed input.

1. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, with 80 tasks across 16 skill categories and 13 speeds, paired evaluation scenes, an expert check of every task at four speeds, and a static counterpart for every task.
We will release the code, demonstrations, and evaluation protocol.

2. We evaluate eight VLA and world-action models with and without past frames on every task at every speed, showing that six of them peak at intermediate speeds and tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed.

3. Using linear probes and speed-conditioned policies, we find that past frames help only the three models from which the belt speed is most linearly decodable, and that a speed estimated from the images keeps most of the gain from ground-truth speed input.

title: ABI: Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations for Zero-Shot Test-Time Guidance
authors: Yifei Yao,Yude Zou,Guanbo Jiao,Jianming Ma,Xing Gao,Chunhua Shen
abstract: Behavior-cloning policies show strong ability in sequential control by generating coherent multi-step action chunks, yet their purely imitative objective limits zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks. While offline reinforcement learning offers principled policy improvement, existing methods either require task-specific reward supervision or remain tied to a specific actor during critic training or policy deployment, inflating training cost and restricting cross-policy generalization. We observe that evaluating actions under the data-collecting behavior largely preserves their relative value ordering across target policies, offering a way around actor coupling. Combining this property with reward-free successor prediction, we propose Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations (ABI) to learn multi-horizon action-chunk representations from unlabeled trajectories without reward supervision or actor training. At test time, pairing the frozen representation with lightweight task readouts forms a chunk critic that guides target policies without parameter updates and transfers directly across distinct unseen policies. Our analysis establishes when the value ordering is preserved across policies and when selecting among proposed chunks improves closed-loop return. Across 65 locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks, ABI’s chunk critic guides weak imitation policies to match or surpass zero-shot RL baselines with high sample efficiency, outperforms existing zero-shot critics on identical proposals, and improves externally trained RL actors without retraining. From raw pixels, ABI delivers substantial guidance gains and surpasses prior zero-shot RL baselines on visual manipulation, highlighting its potential for visuomotor control.
introduction:
Modern generative policies in manipulation and other control domains widely rely on behavior cloning from demonstrations to predict multi-step action chunks [59]. Representative approaches include diffusion [14] and flow-matching policies [35], as well as large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models [9, 28, 42] and world-action models (WAMs) [57, 29, 58, 52]. Imitating demonstrations at the chunk level captures multimodal action patterns while maintaining temporal consistency across long horizons. However, collected demonstrations often cover only specific tasks or local state regions. Purely imitative policies can reproduce demonstrated behaviors, but still lack evaluative signals to recombine them for unseen objectives.

Several paradigms leverage offline trajectory datasets to improve policies beyond pure imitation. Reward-supervised offline reinforcement learning, such as IQL [30] and its extensions to generative or chunked policies [23, 36, 39, 32], learns value critics without online interaction, but still depends on task-specific reward labels and per-task retraining. Zero-shot reinforcement learning reduces this requirement by pretraining task-agnostic representations on unlabeled trajectories to solve unseen tasks at test time [37], as in Forward–Backward (FB) [49, 50] and TD-JEPA [6]. These representations underlie frontier control policies such as Meta Motivo [47] and BFM-Zero [34]. However, existing zero-shot methods mostly rely on jointly training a task-conditioned actor for bootstrapping, which induces out-of-distribution overestimation [26] and unstable convergence [61]. Coupling critic learning to an actor also escalates training cost with policy complexity and weakens generalization across policies. To avoid this coupling, one-step FB [61] removes the actor from critic training by evaluating single actions under the data-collecting behavior [11], yet still trains a task-conditioned actor for execution. Whether zero-shot RL can remove actor dependence in both training and execution to guide independently trained policies has not been fully explored.

Our observation, that evaluating actions under the data-collecting behavior largely preserves their relative value ordering across target policies, suggests a way around this coupling. Combining this property with task-agnostic successor representations [15, 8] allows value representations to be trained without a target policy or rewards. Since test-time guidance only compares actions proposed by a policy, a critic formed from these representations can guide that policy without updating it. Building on this principle, we introduce Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations (ABI) for chunked control, as shown in Fig. 1. ABI pretrains a multi-horizon encoder–predictor backbone over multi-step action chunks from unlabeled state or pixel trajectories without rewards, task inputs, or simulators. Paired with lightweight task readouts on cached states, ABI forms a test-time chunk critic without gradient updates [50, 6, 2]. This critic guides both chunked and single-step policies via candidate selection or Q-guided flow (QGF) [62]. We further establish when it preserves cross-policy ranking, improves closed-loop return under selection, and yields local gains under gradient guidance.

We evaluate ABI on 65 locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks across 13 state and pixel datasets [6], as summarized in Fig. 1. Pretrained once per dataset without an actor, ABI guides a weak Flow BC policy from 58.4 to 655.2 return on DMC and from 3.0% to 38.6% success on OGBench, matching or surpassing multiple zero-shot RL baselines while using 24×24\times fewer DMC pretraining samples than TD-JEPA reproduced from its official code and reported settings. To verify that these gains stem from the critic itself, we compare zero-shot critics on identical action proposals: ABI leads on both suites, more than doubles OGBench success over TD-JEPA and one-step FB critics, and avoids the sharp drop of single-step critics when executing full action chunks. Moreover, the same frozen critic transfers across policies without retraining, improving external TD-JEPA and one-step FB actors trained with their own critics and achieving higher task success with stronger base proposers. Finally, ABI scales directly to raw pixels, substantially lifting visual Flow BC and surpassing prior pixel zero-shot RL baselines across all four visual manipulation datasets. We summarize our contributions as follows:

We propose ABI, an efficient actor-free framework that pretrains reward-free multi-horizon chunk representations from states or pixels and forms zero-update critics for test-time policy guidance.

We establish theoretical conditions for ABI guidance, covering cross-policy value-ordering preservation, closed-loop gains under whole-chunk and rolling selection, and data-supported gradient steps.

We empirically demonstrate that ABI guides weak imitation policies to match or surpass zero-shot RL baselines, outperforms prior critics on shared proposals, and improves external actors without retraining.

title: GeoMerge-OPD: Balanced Skill Integration in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Le Yang,Haoyang Lyu,Honglei Jin,Wenshuo Chen,Jiawei Liang,Wenqiang Wang,Yutao Yue,Xiaochun Cao
comment: . The first four authors contributed equally. Wenshuo Chen is the project leader. Yutao Yue and Xiaochun Cao are co-corresponding authors
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models excel at individual robotic skills, yet integrating heterogeneous skills into a single policy remains a key challenge for general-purpose robotic control, especially in whole-body tasks with differing manipulation and locomotion requirements. Common multi-skill integration strategies, such as joint fine-tuning and parameter merging, can induce unintended actions during closed-loop execution, severely degrading individual skills. Task-conditioned analysis of expert updates reveals response energy concentrated in a few dominant directions and opposing expert responses along high-energy directions within a shared, task-relevant response subspace. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, combining response-space regularization, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation. During independent expert fine-tuning, G-isometry constrains update-response gains within task-activation subspaces; the expert parameters are then statically merged into a student with preliminary multitask capabilities. Fine-tuned task experts serve as teachers, providing velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate action-flow states visited by the student to calibrate residual behavioral deviations. Experiments with two VLA backbones show strong, balanced humanoid skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, outperforming joint fine-tuning and multitask reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining robustness under perturbations.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language models to robotic control using demonstration data, combining semantic understanding and referential grounding with strong performance on individual manipulation tasks (Driess et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025; Hancock et al., 2026). Generalist robots, however, must integrate multiple skills within one policy; humanoids must additionally coordinate upper-body manipulation and lower-body locomotion (Jiang et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026a). This makes reliable integration of heterogeneous skills a central challenge for VLA models.

A common approach is joint fine-tuning on demonstrations pooled across skills. Although effective for homogeneous tasks, it can improve some skills at the expense of others when task demands differ (Kim et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). These trade-offs also arise with a shared control interface: with a π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone, joint training on a stream of real-robot tasks improved one normalized task score from 52 to 92 while reducing another from 100 to 33.3 (Zhu et al., 2026). On whole-body tasks, jointly fine-tuned Ψ0\Psi_{0} underperformed its single-task counterparts across all evaluated tasks, with some skills nearly lost (Wei et al., 2026a).

An alternative is to fine-tune experts separately and merge their parameters, an approach effective in language and vision models (Yadav et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2026; Marczak et al., 2025). MergeVLA extends this approach to VLAs through task masks, dedicated action heads, and test-time routing (Fu et al., 2026). However, we find that directly merging whole-body VLA experts can severely degrade individual skills, even when the task-specific experts retain those skills. In our Ψ0\Psi_{0} experiments, the merged policy issued unintended locomotion commands during BendPick, a task requiring bending and grasping in place, resulting in task failure. These failures motivate our central question: how can heterogeneous task behaviors be retained in shared parameters to form a balanced, robust policy without maintaining separate models for individual tasks?

Prior work documents concentrated update spectra and interference arising from disagreements in parameter signs or singular directions (Yadav et al., 2023; Gargiulo et al., 2025; Marczak et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). It also shows that the functional effects of updates depend on inputs and may concentrate in low-dimensional activation or output-shift subspaces (Cheng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). Building on these findings, we analyze task-conditioned responses of Ψ0\Psi_{0} experts, using task activation statistics to characterize the functional effects of their parameter updates. We observe opposing components within a shared task-relevant response subspace, concentrated along high-energy response directions. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging, suggesting that energy concentration can amplify the impact of opposing responses. These observations motivate regularizing update responses before merging and calibrating the resulting policy afterward.

We propose GeoMerge-OPD, which combines regularized expert fine-tuning, static parameter merging, and on-policy distillation (OPD). Starting from a common pretrained backbone, each expert is fine-tuned with G-isometry to constrain update-response gains in task-activation subspaces. This regularizer acts on responses induced by task inputs, reducing excessive dominance by a few directions. Static merging then establishes a balanced initialization with preliminary multitask competence. Inspired by multi-teacher OPD for integrating heterogeneous expert capabilities in language and text-to-image models (Ma et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026), we use OPD to consolidate skills from task-specific VLA experts into a unified student policy. The student interacts with the environment in closed loop and generates its own action-flow trajectories. The corresponding task expert provides dense velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate flow states actually visited by the student. This supervision calibrates residual behavioral deviations under the student’s own state and action-generation distributions, further coordinating multitask skills within the shared model.

We evaluate GeoMerge-OPD on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025), and SIMPLE (Wei et al., 2026b), using π0.5\pi_{0.5} and Ψ0\Psi_{0} as the two VLA backbones, covering tabletop manipulation, whole-body loco-manipulation, and generalization to perturbed evaluation conditions. Our main contributions are:

Empirical diagnosis of multitask VLA integration. We characterize failures in merging task-specific VLA experts and identify concentrated update responses and opposing components in shared task-relevant subspaces, connecting these observations to unintended behavioral shifts in closed-loop execution.

Empirical diagnosis of multitask VLA integration. We characterize failures in merging task-specific VLA experts and identify concentrated update responses and opposing components in shared task-relevant subspaces, connecting these observations to unintended behavioral shifts in closed-loop execution.

A framework for balanced skill consolidation. GeoMerge-OPD combines G-isometry regularization and static merging to establish a balanced initialization, followed by task-routed OPD to calibrate residual behavior on student-visited states and action-flow trajectories, consolidating heterogeneous skills in shared parameters.

Skill consolidation and robustness across two backbones. GeoMerge-OPD achieves 26/30 whole-body successes on SIMPLE versus 22/30 for Joint FT from the same G-regularized merge, reaches 97.1% on LIBERO versus 96.2% for Joint FT from the pretrained base, and attains the highest average LIBERO-PRO success (67.3%) across five perturbation axes among the evaluated policies.
