title: VeriTouch: Verified Visuo-Tactile World Models that Improve Robot Policy Learning
authors: Shuxun Wang,Xiaonan Jiang,Zhaoyu Wang,Ziyuan Chu,Xihang Yue,Pengfei Liu,Haodong Zhu,Shiqi Liu,Mingzhi Zheng,Liang Su,Linchao Zhu
abstract:
Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions.
To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos.
Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.
introduction:
Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to reason about physical contact, which is often difficult to infer from visual observations alone. By providing direct feedback on contact states, tactile sensing enables visuo-tactile policies to better handle contact-rich tasks [37, 50, 6]. However, collecting visuo-tactile data in the real world requires expensive tactile sensors [11] and labor-intensive teleoperation [9, 44]. Simulation reduces the need for real-world data collection but requires realistic environments and accurate modeling of objects’ physical properties [1, 51, 42]. To reduce these costs, recent work synthesizes manipulation videos and
extracts the corresponding actions for policy training [19, 15].

However, extending video-based synthesis to visuo-tactile demonstrations requires generating plausible tactile responses that are synchronized with visible contact. Existing approaches
augment training with synthetic rollouts [17] or
corrective segments for policy failures [25], with repeated
rounds of data generation and policy retraining. Other approaches rely on simulation to generate or validate physically feasible trajectories [20, 14]. Meanwhile, existing verification methods assess kinematic and tactile plausibility [25] or score predicted tactile signals against task instructions [46]. While these methods improve different aspects of data generation and quality control, several challenges remain. Iterative augmentation requires repeated data generation and policy retraining, while simulation-based approaches depend on additional environments, increasing the cost and complexity of generating training data. Existing verification methods can identify specific errors, but lack a joint assessment of tactile plausibility and temporal alignment with visual contact throughout complete demonstrations. These quality requirements, together with the costs of iterative augmentation and simulation, motivate a more efficient and comprehensive pipeline for generating reliable visuo-tactile training data.

As shown in Fig. 1, we introduce VeriTouch, a framework that jointly generates visual and tactile observations, verifies the resulting sequences without iterative retraining and simulation replay, and extracts actions from the sequences that pass verification. Our world model, VeriGen, extends a pretrained video backbone [30] with a dedicated tactile expert. It uses cross-view attention to combine scene context with close-up contact details and jointly models visual and tactile dynamics. Alongside checks for physical plausibility and instruction following, our multimodal verifier, VeriEval, assesses tactile reconstruction error and task-dependent contact forces, and checks the temporal alignment of visual and tactile contact intervals. By filtering out unreliable sequences before action extraction, VeriTouch produces higher-quality synthetic visuo-tactile training data.
Finally, VeriIDM uses local gripper cues and temporal context to extract actions from the retained videos.

We evaluate VeriTouch on five real-world contact-rich tasks using two vision-based and two visuo-tactile policies. Augmenting real demonstrations with our synthetic data improves all four policies, increasing the overall average success rate from 19.4% with real data alone to 33.8%. Moreover, policy performance continues to improve as the synthetic dataset scales without collecting additional real-world demonstrations, more than doubling the average success rate from 33.0% to 67.0% when the amount of synthetic data reaches four times that of real data. Ablations show that generated tactile signals improve policy performance and that training on data selected by our multimodal verifier yields higher success rates than training on synthetic data with visual-only filtering or no filtering. These results demonstrate that verified synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories improve policy performance on contact-rich manipulation tasks.
Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce VeriTouch, a framework for synthesizing high-quality visuo-tactile training trajectories. Its world model jointly captures visual and tactile contact dynamics, while an IDM preserves fine motion details to recover precise actions.

We develop a multimodal verifier that checks tactile plausibility and visual–tactile contact consistency alongside visual quality, filtering unreliable observations before extracting actions without physical or simulated replay.

We improve all four policies and show that scaling synthetic data more than doubles average success rate over the real-data baseline without collecting additional real-world demonstrations.

1. We introduce VeriTouch, a framework for synthesizing high-quality visuo-tactile training trajectories. Its world model jointly captures visual and tactile contact dynamics, while an IDM preserves fine motion details to recover precise actions.

2. We develop a multimodal verifier that checks tactile plausibility and visual–tactile contact consistency alongside visual quality, filtering unreliable observations before extracting actions without physical or simulated replay.

3. We improve all four policies and show that scaling synthetic data more than doubles average success rate over the real-data baseline without collecting additional real-world demonstrations.

title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation
authors: Jiawei Guo,Yu Huang,Dijiang Dong,Yue Liu,Peiran Ren,Wei Shen
abstract:
Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution.
Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes.
Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions.
We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction.
For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed.
Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution.
The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact.
We evaluate leading manipulation policies (π0.5\pi_{0.5} and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash).
All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.
introduction:
Embodied manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO [34], RoboTwin [39, 6], and RoboCasa [40] have helped establish a common evaluation ecosystem for language-conditioned robot manipulation. They provide diverse tasks and environments for measuring capabilities such as task execution, generalization, and object interaction, and have become important testbeds for evaluating vision–language–action (VLA) models [62, 29] and emerging world-action models [51, 54]. Recent benchmark audits also caution that high aggregate scores can reflect shortcuts rather than the intended capabilities [24]. Yet a successful task outcome does not necessarily mean that a policy has followed the instruction faithfully. A policy may reach the required final configuration while performing operations in the wrong order, taking an unintended route, contacting a region other than the one requested, or stopping at an imprecise target angle. Such executions may satisfy a coarse task-success criterion while violating the behavior explicitly requested by the instruction. This raises a complementary question for embodied evaluation: beyond whether a robot completes a task, can we measure whether it completes the task in the way it was instructed to?

Recent work has increasingly explored how to make robot manipulation policies more controllable through fine-grained language instructions, allowing users to specify not only what the robot should achieve, but also how it should execute the task [7, 16, 8]. However, evaluating this capability remains challenging, as existing benchmarks often entangle instruction following with other capabilities, including object generalization, visual recognition, and multi-step planning. For example, InstructVLA [53] evaluates instruction tuning on SimplerEnv-Instruct, where performance is also affected by unfamiliar objects and visual distractors, while VLABench [58] includes tasks requiring implicit goal inference and multi-step planning. Consequently, improvements in task success may arise from better perception or planning, rather than a stronger ability to execute instructions faithfully. This makes it difficult to isolate whether a policy actually responds to the specific behavioral constraints expressed in language. We therefore need a dedicated benchmark that isolates instruction fidelity by testing whether, under otherwise identical conditions, a robot adjusts its actions as a revised instruction requires.

To make such an evaluation possible, we argue that a benchmark for instruction fidelity should meet two requirements. First, it should compare different instructions from the same initial scene and robot state. If the scene or initial conditions change together with the instruction, differences in execution may reflect changes in perception, object configuration, or task difficulty rather than the policy’s response to language. We therefore require each initial state to admit multiple feasible instruction branches that vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation details. Second, evaluation should check the parts of execution that the instruction actually constrains, rather than relying only on final-state success. This is essential when different procedures lead to the same final configuration, or when a task is considered complete despite imprecise execution. Figure  illustrates both cases: different switch orders yield the same final state, while a laptop can reach the requested angle even if the robot contacts the wrong part of the lid. Together, these requirements let us assess whether a policy’s behavior changes appropriately with the instruction and whether the resulting execution satisfies its constraints.

Following these principles, we introduce RoboInF, a benchmark for evaluating instruction fidelity in language-conditioned manipulation, built on RoboTwin [39, 6]. RoboInF contains eight base tasks, each with six to twelve instruction branches from shared initial states. To generate demonstrations that satisfy these branch-specific requirements, we extend RoboTwin’s vision–language model (VLM)-based expert policy generator to synthesize a multi-branch expert policy for each task. Each policy program takes a branch specification as input and executes the corresponding goal, procedure, and fine-grained requirements from the same initial state. We refine these programs iteratively using execution videos and structured simulator logs, together with task-specific compliance checks. During data collection, a structured intermediate representation (IR) collector extracts task and interaction annotations directly from simulator states and execution records, avoiding video-based estimation and manual label verification. The resulting RoboInF-4K dataset contains post-training demonstrations with detailed IR annotations, supporting evaluation of task-only policies and policies trained with IR-derived commands using the same branches and checks.

With the benchmark and dataset in place, we study instruction fidelity across different policy settings. We evaluate VLA policies in terms of both task completion and compliance with instruction-specific requirements, and examine post-training and an IR-supported hierarchical control configuration. We also evaluate inference-only agents separately, accounting for their different action interfaces. By distinguishing final task outcomes from the goals, procedures, and manipulation details specified by an instruction, RoboInF provides a common testbed for studying how reliably embodied policies can be controlled through language.

title: Body and Soul: Decoupling Robotic Brain and Policy with RoboHarness-Zero
authors: Yihao Shen,Yuxuan Chen,Xuantong Liu,Jun Gao,Weijian Luo,Tianyang Hu
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our RoboHarness-Zero is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA.
The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, RoboHarness-Zero with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from 57.5% to 70.5% and preserves 90.4% of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy.
introduction:
A vision-language-action (VLA) policy can have the motor skills a task requires and still fail to finish it (Hu et al., 2026). In some RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026) episodes, a robot acted on the wrong object, turning the wrong burner knob or taking the wrong item from a drawer (Figure 2a,b). Even when it chose the right item, it could move on too soon. Asked to put two pieces of broccoli in a pot and stir them, it added one and began stirring while the other was still on the counter. Across failed RoboCasa365 episodes with Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (Xiaomi Robotics Team, 2026b), we estimate that 43% of failures arise from choosing the wrong target or losing track of which steps remained (§3.1, Table A.2).

A natural response to these decision errors is to put a vision-language model (VLM) in charge of tracking the task while the VLA executes it. Existing harnesses improve performance by learning how to guide the robot in a particular setting.
In its few-shot RoboCasa365 evaluation, Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b) finds a successful sequence of subtask instructions on one reference scene per task and reuses it in new scenes. EmbodiedRSI (Song et al., 2026) runs robot trials to decide which changes to its code and skills to keep, while AdaHVLA (Tang et al., 2026) revises its prompting and recovery code separately for each robot and policy. How much of the resulting gain survives when the task set or the policy changes? Although Harness VLA gains 29.2 percentage points on RLDX-1, transferring its released task memories to Xiaomi-Robotics-1 on our 50-scene benchmark solves 29 scenes, compared with 30 for Xiaomi alone (−2.0-2.0 percentage points).

We argue that an ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) avoid breaking what the policy already solves. We introduce RoboHarness-Zero, a VLM harness that gives a frozen VLA the full task and monitors progress within each substage during execution, without interfering while the policy advances.
When progress stalls or the robot acts on the wrong target, RoboHarness-Zero first revises the instruction and, if needed, briefly takes over the arm via VLM-generated code over generic motion primitives before handing control back.
Our core insight is that the instruction and the scene alone determine which object the robot should act on, what must happen next, and whether the current step is complete, so a VLM can judge them zero-shot and identically across policies.
This allows RoboHarness-Zero to supervise different tasks and frozen VLA backbones during execution with a single fixed set of rules; onboarding a new policy requires no task-specific demonstrations or scripts—only a thin interface adapter and a one-time automatic calibration (§3).

Our method builds on the premise that a VLM can interpret an instruction, plan its steps, and detect execution drift zero-shot, while the frozen VLA provides reactive, contact-rich motor control without needing task-specific scripts or skills.
When asked to place a suitable tool for peeling a cucumber on a cutting board (Figure 2b), RoboHarness-Zero gives the frozen VLA the full instruction while the VLM forms its own step-by-step plan from the robot’s camera views. Judging progress against the active step, the VLM sees that reaching the drawer completes the approach, but the grasp stalls while the peeler remains inside. It first intervenes through language—“Place the green-handled peeler on the cutting board”—and only when the VLA grasps and delivers the knife instead does the harness invoke generic motion primitives via generated code on the fly to position the gripper at the peeler, before returning control to the VLA to finish (§3.5–3.6).

Task-level completion criteria can be shared across policies, whereas execution reliability and timing vary.
For example, if a task requires two pieces of broccoli in a pot, placing only one leaves the goal incomplete regardless of the policy (Figure 2c). Automatic profiling estimates each policy’s skill success rates and completion times, allowing the same supervision rules to accommodate different execution speeds.

Across 200 RoboCasa365 evaluation scenes spanning 50 tasks, RoboHarness-Zero with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from 57.5% to 70.5% (Figure 1). It preserves 104 of the 115 episodes the policy solves on its own (90.4%) and rescues 37 of its 85 failures, for a net gain of +26 episodes; multi-step tasks account for +23 of this net gain, including +13 on previously unseen task compositions. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, from π0.5\pi_{0.5} (16% to 24%) to RLDX-1 (40% to 50%). Recovery remains a bottleneck: in a separate trajectory audit, 22 of 35 failed skill attempts still do not reach their goal after the harness intervenes (§4.7).

In summary, our core contributions are:

RoboHarness-Zero, a VLM harness that supervises a frozen VLA during execution; its rules need no task-specific demonstrations or scripts and are calibrated to a new policy automatically (§3).

A paired evaluation protocol, with a no-VLM control, that separates the successes a harness preserves from the failures it rescues (§4.1).

Evidence that the same rules improve five frozen policies (Xiaomi-Robotics-1, RLDX-1, WorldDreamer, GR00T N1.5, and π0.5\pi_{0.5}) on the same scenes, while retaining 90.4% of Xiaomi-Robotics-1’s standalone successes (§4.2–4.3).

1. RoboHarness-Zero, a VLM harness that supervises a frozen VLA during execution; its rules need no task-specific demonstrations or scripts and are calibrated to a new policy automatically (§3).

2. A paired evaluation protocol, with a no-VLM control, that separates the successes a harness preserves from the failures it rescues (§4.1).

3. Evidence that the same rules improve five frozen policies (Xiaomi-Robotics-1, RLDX-1, WorldDreamer, GR00T N1.5, and π0.5\pi_{0.5}) on the same scenes, while retaining 90.4% of Xiaomi-Robotics-1’s standalone successes (§4.2–4.3).

title: DelayOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation from a Synchronous Teacher for Real-time Asynchronous Policies
authors: Hyeonjae Kim,Jeongsol Kim,Sunwoo Park,Chanyu Moon,Yoojin Oh,Youngjun Jun,Kyumin Choi,Jong Chul Ye
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising.
Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases.
We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times.
We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy’s own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes.
Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy’s own rollouts.
Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed.
The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process.
Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%.
Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment.
On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
introduction:
Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies such as π0\pi_{0} [3], π0.5\pi_{0.5} [28] and SmolVLA [31] generate action chunks, short sequences of future actions [43], by solving a flow ODE initialized with Gaussian noise.
Generating each action chunk requires a forward pass of a large vision-language backbone and multiple denoising steps, taking tens to hundreds of milliseconds on a desktop GPU and even longer on edge or networked hardware [2, 40].
Under synchronous execution the robot stops while each chunk is generated, increasing task completion time and preventing the robot from reacting during generation [4, 35].
Asynchronous execution [4] removes these pauses by generating the next chunk while the current chunk is being executed, making it essential for VLA deployment [4, 31].
However, asynchronous execution introduces a mismatch between the observation used for action generation and the state at which the generated actions are executed. While a new chunk is generated, the robot continues executing the committed actions of the current chunk for KK control steps (the delay). Consequently, the new chunk generated from observation 𝒐t{\bm{o}}_{t} is executed from step t+Kt+K, when the environment has already evolved to 𝒐t+K{\bm{o}}_{t+K}, which was unseen by the policy during generation (Fig. 2a).
Since flow-based policies trained with behavior cloning do not account for this mismatch, executing them asynchronously leads to a drop in task success rate, which becomes more pronounced as the delay increases (Fig. 3).

Existing remedies keep the new chunk consistent with the committed actions at inference time [4, 21], predict the missing observation with an added module [12], or fine-tune the policy on demonstrations [5, 22, 19, 36, 45, 46]. While these approaches mitigate the effects of execution delay, our goal is to directly improve the delayed policy under its own execution dynamics. In particular, the observation-action mismatch can lead the delayed policy to visit states different from those in demonstrations, where the policy may require different actions to recover. In our measurements, the delay barely changes the policy’s actions on demonstration states but changes them substantially on its own delayed rollouts, especially in failed episodes (Sec. 5.2). This motivates on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), which trains the student on its own rollouts rather than relying solely on demonstration states.

Here, we introduce DelayOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework for asynchronous VLA execution. Our key insight is to construct an asymmetric teacher-student pair from the same policy through different conditioning.
Specifically, the synchronous teacher obtains the execution-time observation 𝒐t+K{\bm{o}}_{t+K}, while the asynchronous student conditions on 𝒐t{\bm{o}}_{t} and the committed actions. By querying the teacher along the student’s delayed rollouts, we obtain improved supervision even at states where the student fails, without an external teacher model or ground-truth action annotations. We then distill the teacher into the student by matching their velocity fields along the student’s own denoising trajectory, providing dense supervision beyond matching the final actions.

In practice, repeatedly collecting student rollouts online during training is expensive, since it requires interaction with the environment. We therefore collect delayed rollouts once before training and perform distillation offline, as in offline on-policy distillation [39, 42]. In our experiments, the evaluated online collection variants give no significant gain over this one-time collection. DelayOPSD requires no external expert or additional inference-time module, preserving the original policy architecture and sampler at deployment. Our contributions can be summarized as:

Asynchronous execution as on-policy self-distillation from the synchronous policy. We train the policy on its own delayed rollouts, and its teacher is the same policy run synchronously on the execution-time observation. SmolVLA then reaches 78.7% at K=10K{=}10, against 70.2% when trained on demonstrations.

Asynchronous execution as on-policy self-distillation from the synchronous policy. We train the policy on its own delayed rollouts, and its teacher is the same policy run synchronously on the execution-time observation. SmolVLA then reaches 78.7% at K=10K{=}10, against 70.2% when trained on demonstrations.

title: JEPA-ICL: Progress-Aligned Latent Plans for In-Context Robotic Manipulation
authors: Tingjun Dai,Jianxiang He,Mingfei Han,Qihao Yu,Longtao Jiang,Changlin Li,Minghao Jin,Zhihui Li,Xiaojun Chang
abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot’s current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot’s own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.
introduction:
Demonstrations provide more than examples of successful actions: they reveal how a task progresses toward completion. To use this experience, a robot must relate the demonstrated process to what remains to be accomplished in its own execution, even when embodiment, appearance, and execution speed differ. This calls for a representation that supports both anticipating task progress and identifying relevant guidance. Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) offer a natural basis for learning such representations through future feature prediction without requiring image reconstruction.

Recent work has advanced both predictive control and demonstration learning. JEPA-WAM [30] uses latent transition supervision for action generation, while HOST [8] connects demonstration localization with future observation prediction. JEDI [28] learns predictive representations for demonstration compression, and MUTEX [45] demonstrates the benefits of learning from complementary task specifications. These advances motivate a more specific question: how can the plan that guides a robot’s own actions also organize its use of demonstration experience? Future prediction alone does not establish correspondence across executions, while access to relevant context does not by itself ensure better planning. We study it through the state changes that remain before subtask completion.

We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that connects predictive planning and demonstration learning through progress-aligned latent plans. Our central idea is to describe an execution stage by the ordered state changes that remain before the current subtask is complete (Fig. 1). We learn this representation through a plan-conditioned Markov predictor, a latent world model that forecasts future states in JEPA feature space. The resulting plans support action generation and provide progress keys for locating relevant stages in demonstrations. Prediction and demonstration alignment jointly supervise these plans, connecting the ability to anticipate an execution with the ability to learn from another.

Specifically, plan queries from the VLA backbone condition this world model, which starts from the current JEPA state and predicts four ordered checkpoints in the remaining subtask, one shared Markov transition at a time; supervising the intermediate checkpoints as well as completion makes the plan retain the remaining process, not only the endpoint. For demonstration use, the same backbone produces plans for robot observations and demonstration frames, and a learned indexer associates their stages under stage and temporal-consistency supervision. The policy then reads JEPA-supervised content features from a short window around the aligned stage through memory tokens, and the retrieved context is updated during execution so that guidance stays tied to the robot’s observed progress.

We evaluate these capabilities separately and in combination. On LIBERO [32] and LIBERO-Plus [15], JEPA-ICL achieves 97.6% and 73.2% success without contextual demonstrations, respectively; demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at test time further raise LIBERO-Plus success to 75.2%. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM [63] (68.0%) by 12.0 percentage points. Under C45 pretraining, it reaches 85.5% unseen-task success after fine-tuning on 10 robot demonstrations per task. Real-robot gear assembly further demonstrates the use of recorded experience: JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% success with a deployment-setup demonstration, compared with 40.0% for the kai0 (π0.5\pi_{0.5}) baseline. Controlled comparisons separate the contributions of latent planning, of progress-aligned retrieval, and of context at test time.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Markov-supervised latent planning.
We learn progress-aware plans through recurrent prediction of ordered future JEPA states within the remaining subtask, supervised at intermediate checkpoints and at subtask completion.

Progress-aligned demonstration context.
We use latent plans to locate relevant demonstration stages and read separate JEPA-supervised content features through memory tokens, which separates progress correspondence from content retrieval and updates guidance as execution progresses.

Joint planning and demonstration learning.
We combine future prediction, demonstration alignment, and action supervision to train one shared policy that runs both with and without contextual demonstrations.

2. Progress-aligned demonstration context.
We use latent plans to locate relevant demonstration stages and read separate JEPA-supervised content features through memory tokens, which separates progress correspondence from content retrieval and updates guidance as execution progresses.

3. Joint planning and demonstration learning.
We combine future prediction, demonstration alignment, and action supervision to train one shared policy that runs both with and without contextual demonstrations.

authors: Joonhee Lim,Seonmyeong Lee,Sihwan Hwang,Hanbin Jang,Hiwon Shin,Dogun Kim,Hyelin Jo,Hyeonjun Jeong,Yongjae Lee,Junseong Kwak,Junhyeok Park,Satyam Mishra,Juyeb Shin,Uisung Kim,Hyeonseo Kim,Saparkhan Kassymbekov,Hailemichael Molla Gashaw,Abi Rahman Syamil,Mingyu Kim,Hyeongjun Kim,Yeina Lee,Moogeun Park,Dongsuk Kum

abstract: This report presents a comprehensive pipeline for developing an end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving model for the Physical AI AV Track. The framework consists of data curation, HD map auto-labelling, data-driven imitation learning, and simulator-based reinforcement learning. To ensure safety in the closed-loop setting, we introduce a selection-based E2E planning approach that leverages object detection and BEV segmentation to filter out trajectory candidates likely to cause collisions or off-road driving. Trained on NVIDIA NuRec and the NVIDIA PAI-AV dataset, our method scores a fixed vocabulary of trajectory candidates for collision, drivable-area compliance, and progress learned from simulated rollouts, and selects the best candidate that passes the filter. This design highlights the effectiveness of combining E2E planning with perception-based trajectory filtering for safe and reliable closed-loop autonomous driving.
introduction:
Our proposed method for the Physical AI AV Track comprises an end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving pipeline designed to achieve robust performance in closed-loop execution. As illustrated in Figure 1, the framework follows a sequential development and training pipeline comprising five core stages, from data curation and imitation learning to reinforcement learning-based policy refinement.

Data Curation: We curate 1,400 additional PAI-AV clips using scenario-based, semantic, and spatiotemporal feature-based selection to address coverage gaps and model failures. The selected clips are subsequently auto-labeled and used for end-to-end policy training.

Data Curation: We curate 1,400 additional PAI-AV clips using scenario-based, semantic, and spatiotemporal feature-based selection to address coverage gaps and model failures. The selected clips are subsequently auto-labeled and used for end-to-end policy training.

HD Map Auto-labeling:
HD map annotations for the PAI-AV dataset are automatically generated using a 3DGS-based method.
We extend PseudoMapTrainer [1] with LiDAR supervision and DINOv3 [2] distillation to ensure annotation quality.

End-to-End Autonomous Driving Model: We develop an E2E architecture that encodes multi-view temporal observations into a BEV representation and selects a safe trajectory from 8,192 candidates via perception-based feasibility checks and coarse-to-fine scoring.

Data-driven Imitation Learning: We train the E2E model on NVIDIA NuRec data and auto-labeled PAI-AV data using perception, imitation, and scoring losses.

Simulator-based Reinforcement Learning: Finally, to address compounding errors and enhance robustness in out-of-distribution states, we fine-tune the policy using reinforcement learning within a realistic closed-loop simulator, NVIDIA AlpaSim.

title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations
authors: Haoran Zhang,Haokai Ding,Han Zhou,Zuxing Lu,Heng Zhang,Xingxing Zuo
abstract:
Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation.
We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration.
DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other’s states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases.
Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11–41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation.
Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human’s contacts better in 117 cases.
Code and videos are available on our project page.
introduction:
People routinely manipulate objects with both hands, such as holding a bottle while opening its lid. Learning such dexterous skills from human demonstrations offers a natural approach to robotic manipulation [37, 36, 46, 5].
However, differences between human and robot hands prevent demonstrations from being directly replayed on robots.
Recent methods bridge this gap by retargeting human motions to robot hands and training policies in simulation to track demonstrated object trajectories [30, 21, 63].
Nevertheless, a fundamental limitation of these methods is their reliance on object trajectory tracking as the primary learning objective.
Even when a robot accurately tracks the demonstrated trajectory, its hands may contact the wrong object parts or slide on the object, resulting in unstable manipulation.
Faithful bimanual manipulation requires not only reproducing where the object moves, but also preserving how the hands interact with it.

However, achieving contact-preserving bimanual manipulation presents three key challenges.
First, bimanual manipulation requires coordinated yet role-specific control.
Existing methods either control both hands through a unified policy [30, 63] or train separate policies independently [62], limiting explicit coordination or shared learning between hands.
Second, preserving human hand-object contacts across different embodiments remains difficult.
Although existing methods incorporate contact-related rewards [30, 63, 22], robot hands can still contact the object differently from human hands, particularly in which hand holds an object part and whether the contact is maintained.
Third, learning complex demonstrations is hindered by difficult manipulation phases.
To make training tractable, prior methods assist the object early in training, with a virtual object controller (VOC), a proportional-derivative (PD) controller that pulls the object toward its demonstrated trajectory [30, 63], or with relaxed physics [21], and gradually withdraw this assistance.
However, the assistance is typically reduced uniformly across the demonstration, allowing a difficult phase, such as a handover, to stall the entire training process.

To address these challenges, we introduce DexDuet, a framework for learning contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration ().
To coordinate the two hands, DexDuet factorizes the bimanual policy into two per-hand policies that share network parameters while observing each other’s states.
This allows each hand to perform its own role, adapt to its partner, and benefit from shared learning.
To preserve human hand-object interactions, DexDuet introduces two complementary interaction rewards.
The first encourages each robot hand to match the orientation and finger configuration of its human counterpart relative to the object.
The second encourages each hand region, such as the palm or a finger, to contact the object where the corresponding human region does.
Together, these rewards guide the robot to reproduce the demonstrated contacts rather than merely track object motion.
Furthermore, to facilitate learning through difficult manipulation phases, we propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts VOC assistance separately for each demonstration segment based on its learning progress.
It also initializes episodes from previously reached states and prioritizes failing segments, enabling the policy to learn complex demonstrations without assistance.
In summary, our contributions are:

We present DexDuet, a framework for learning contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from human demonstrations through factorized, weight-sharing per-hand policies that enable role-specific control and partner-aware coordination.

We introduce two complementary interaction rewards that preserve human hand-object interactions by aligning object-relative hand configurations and region-level contacts across different robot embodiments.

We propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that combines segment-specific VOC assistance, initialization from previously reached states, and failure-aware sampling to improve learning through difficult manipulation phases.

We evaluate DexDuet on four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, demonstrating consistent improvements in object tracking and contact preservation, with additional demonstrations on two real robot systems.

1. We present DexDuet, a framework for learning contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from human demonstrations through factorized, weight-sharing per-hand policies that enable role-specific control and partner-aware coordination.

2. We introduce two complementary interaction rewards that preserve human hand-object interactions by aligning object-relative hand configurations and region-level contacts across different robot embodiments.

3. We propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that combines segment-specific VOC assistance, initialization from previously reached states, and failure-aware sampling to improve learning through difficult manipulation phases.

4. We evaluate DexDuet on four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, demonstrating consistent improvements in object tracking and contact preservation, with additional demonstrations on two real robot systems.

title: EgoStudy: How Does Scaling Egocentric Data Affect VLA and WAM Pretraining?
authors: Puzhen Yuan,Yanjiang Guo,Yichen Liu,Xiang Zhu,Qingzhou Lu,Chenxin Liu,Tun Ban,Haodong Yan,Zhide Zhong,Jianyu Chen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots.
We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)?
Our experiments yield three main findings.
First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer.
Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements.
Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases.
Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.
introduction:
Learning general-purpose dexterous manipulation requires experience spanning diverse objects, environments, and interaction patterns.
Robot demonstrations provide direct supervision for control, but collecting them at scale requires substantial hardware resources and effort for operation and maintenance.
Egocentric human videos offer an attractive source of manipulation experience: people perform a broad range of everyday activities, exposing models to interactions that are expensive to reproduce through robot data collection.
Recent efforts have made this experience increasingly accessible through hand-motion annotations [42, 34, 12], creating opportunities to pretrain Vision–Language–Action Models (VLAs) [18, 33, 51] and World–Action Models (WAMs) [41, 10] with growing amounts of human experience.
However, limited attention [22, 10, 50] has been given to the fundamental questions about scaling egocentric data for robot foundation model pretraining:

Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data?

Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data?

How do egocentric scaling effects differ between VLAs and WAMs?

Answering these questions requires examining more than data volume alone.
Existing studies have shown that egocentric human videos can improve robot policy learning, but their conclusions are difficult to compare. Different studies typically use different robot datasets, action representations, model architectures, optimization budgets, and evaluation protocols. Consequently, it remains unclear whether an observed improvement comes from additional human experience, a particular data-processing choice, or a model-specific training recipe.
Moreover, most evaluations report an aggregate action loss, leaving open which components of dexterous control actually benefit from egocentric pretraining and whether these offline gains translate to closed-loop control.

Studying VLAs and WAMs together is particularly informative because they learn from different pretrained priors and objectives.
Representative VLAs adapt vision-language representations for action prediction [18, 2, 17, 50, 27, 3], while video-based WAMs combine action learning with future visual prediction [43, 13, 10, 8].
These differences suggest that the same egocentric experience may benefit the two model families in different ways.

To investigate these questions, we conduct a systematic empirical study named EgoStudy, a unified pretraining and evaluation protocol for VLAs and WAMs.
EgoStudy combines egocentric human demonstrations and bimanual robot data through a shared dexterous action interface describing wrist motion and fingertip poses, providing common action targets across embodiments and supporting comparisons between model families.
We vary only the scale and construction of the egocentric human data, including episode curation, source diversity, caption detail, and temporal sampling, while holding robot training data and exposure fixed.
We assess human-to-robot transfer using a common evaluation protocol with held-out samples, component-wise action metrics, and validation loss on robot data.
Finally, standardized robot posttraining and evaluation on target robot domain ensure that pretraining improvements translate into better deployment outcomes.

The results reveal that the benefits of egocentric pretraining are selective rather than uniform.
Controlled comparisons in EgoStudy show that VLAs show larger gains from scaling egocentric data, and WAMs generally attain lower robot-domain validation loss.
Semantically complete episodes, detailed language captions, diverse egocentric data, fixed-step sampling for VLA and event-level sampling for WAM pretraining all contribute to lower robot validation loss and stronger human-to-robot transfer.
Scaling egocentric data improves wrist-motion prediction more than finger-motion prediction.
Furthermore, we compare how the visual representations of VLAs and WAMs evolve as egocentric data increases and how their gains vary with backbone capacity, providing a basis for explaining why the two model families scale differently.
Together, these findings provide practical guidance and empirical insights for training VLAs and WAMs with human videos, while revealing the capability gains and limitations of scaling egocentric data.

Our contributions are as follows:

title: OVOGO: Offline Value-Guided On-Policy Generative Optimization for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Rongzheng Yang,Jiaming Guo,Yuxuan Guo,Zihao Zhang,Yunkai Gao,Siming Lan,Shaohui Peng,Rui Zhang,Tianyun Ma,Xing Hu,Yunji Chen
abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action models can benefit from robot experience collected during deployment, but repeatedly acquiring new physical interactions for policy improvement is costly. Offline reinforcement learning provides a natural way to reuse collected experience, while flow-based policies offer an additional opportunity because fresh generation trajectories can be cheaply resampled from the current policy at replay observations. This motivates separating offline value learning from on-policy optimization of the generative process. We propose OVOGO, an offline reinforcement learning framework that realizes this separation for flow-based VLAs. A central challenge in this formulation is to learn a critic that remains grounded in logged robot experience while providing useful value signals for newly generated actions. OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that combines in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, improving discrimination among generated actions without assigning them artificial return targets. The frozen critic then provides group-relative value signals for selected-transition optimization of fresh action candidates sampled from the current flow policy. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and LIBERO, as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task, show that OVOGO improves the initial VLA across all four settings and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated offline adaptation and value-guided baselines. These results suggest that offline robot experience can be repeatedly reused for value learning while inexpensive generative sampling supports policy optimization, providing an effective approach to experience-based post-training of flow-based VLAs.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities and generalization by combining large-scale, cross-task robot data with pretrained vision-language representations Kim et al. (2024); Black et al. (2024); Intelligence et al. (2025b).
However, further improving these models still relies heavily on collecting high-quality demonstrations, whose acquisition is expensive and difficult to scale.
In contrast, deployment and autonomous execution naturally produce large amounts of experience spanning successful, failed, and suboptimal behaviors, together with task-outcome signals that behavior cloning cannot fully exploit.
Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a natural mechanism for learning from such experience, and offline RL is particularly attractive for robotics because it can repeatedly reuse previously collected interactions and their reward feedback without requiring new physical interaction for every policy update Kostrikov et al. (2021); Intelligence et al. (2025a); Wang et al. (2026b).
As VLA training moves beyond imitation pretraining toward experience-based post-training, offline RL is emerging as a promising approach for improving large generative VLAs from accumulated robot experience.

Applying offline RL to flow-based VLAs, however, is not straightforward. Because actions are produced through a multi-step flow process, a central question is how value information should be translated into updates of the generative policy. Existing approaches adopt different value-to-policy interfaces. RECAP converts estimated advantages into conditioning variables and extracts an improved policy through supervised training on collected experience Intelligence et al. (2025a). This design is simple and scalable, but its improvement supervision is attached to replayed actions rather than actions freshly sampled from the current policy. Other approaches, such as LWD and Q-VGM, use the critic’s action gradient to construct improvement targets for the flow dynamics Wang et al. (2026b); Wang et al. (2026c). These methods enable more direct value-based policy improvement, but make the update depend on reliable action-gradient information from the critic around policy-generated actions. Flow policies offer a complementary opportunity because physical interactions are expensive and should be reused extensively, whereas generation trajectories are inexpensive computational samples that can be repeatedly resampled from the current policy at the same replay observation. This asymmetry suggests that physical experience and generation trajectories need not be consumed at the same rate during policy improvement.

Motivated by this observation, we decouple flow-based VLA reinforcement learning by separating offline value learning from on-policy generative policy optimization. The former learns long-horizon values from a fixed robot dataset, while the latter repeatedly samples fresh actions from the current flow policy at replay observations.
The critic serves as the key interface between these two processes. Directly incorporating policy-generated actions into Bellman updates would make temporal targets depend on value estimates for actions without observed environment outcomes. Errors in these estimates, especially overestimation, can then propagate through bootstrapping and be further exploited during policy improvement.
Keeping Bellman value propagation in-sample provides a more stable foundation for learning long-horizon returns because temporal targets remain grounded in replayed experience. However, restricting all critic supervision to replayed actions would leave the critic unable to reliably distinguish fresh candidates sampled from the evolving policy.
The key challenge is therefore to preserve in-sample temporal value propagation while extending the critic’s discriminative ability beyond replayed actions, without compromising the return-grounded value estimates on which offline learning relies.

In this paper, we propose OVOGO (Offline Value-Guided On-Policy Generative Optimization), an offline RL framework for flow-based VLAs that combines stable offline value learning with fresh on-policy optimization of the generative process. For offline value learning, OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic (RARC) that separates long-horizon return propagation from local action discrimination. RARC uses in-sample distributional value learning to propagate long-horizon values through real replay transitions without bootstrapping through policy-generated actions, and augments this return-grounded objective with local ranking supervision around replayed actions. Synthetic actions receive only relative preference supervision rather
than artificial Bellman targets, while a guarded ranking objective
combines temperature-dependent gradient decay with a gap cutoff to
control ranking pressure, helping preserve the return scale established
by real experience. With RARC frozen, OVOGO repeatedly samples groups of fresh action candidates from the current flow policy at replay observations and constructs group-relative improvement signals directly from their scalar critic values, without differentiating through the critic. We further adopt a selected-transition flow update inspired by Flash-GRPO He et al. (2026), making on-policy generative optimization tractable for large flow-based VLAs.

In our experiments, we evaluate OVOGO on RoboTwin 2.0 Chen et al. (2025b), DexJoCo Wang et al. (2026a), and LIBERO Liu et al. (2023), as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task. The results demonstrate that OVOGO more effectively improves flow-based VLAs from collected robot experience than existing offline adaptation and value-guided methods, while additional comparisons and ablations analyze the contributions of its critic design and generative policy optimization.

title: CHAMP: Coordinated Humanoid Loco-Manipulation with Whole-Body Motion Priors
authors: Lijun Han,Muyuan Ma,Zichen Wang,Siyuan Liu,Yuxi Liu,Yutong Wang,Bohao Zhang,Heng Zhou,Wei Sui
abstract:
Coordinating locomotion and dexterous manipulation is fundamental to humanoid robots operating in human environments.
A key challenge is learning motion priors from diverse data and using them effectively for coordinated robot control.
We present CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive feature extraction.
CHAMP pretrains a vision-language model to predict future body and hand motion from approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot data.
A shared motion representation enables unified whole-body motion learning across embodiments from datasets with body annotations, hand annotations, or both.
To ground these motion priors in robot control, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) and train it on replay data generated using the target controller.
Through sparse routing, CAE adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from multiple layers of the pretrained model to jointly generate body and hand actions.
In experiments, CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks with a Unitree G1, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings.
In particular, CHAMP achieves 70.0% success on the long-horizon popcorn-serving task, compared with 40.0% for the best-performing baseline.
introduction:
Humanoid robots hold the promise of assisting people across a wide range of everyday activities [8, 10, 26].
Fulfilling this promise requires a broad repertoire of motor skills.
A key capability is loco-manipulation, which integrates locomotion and object manipulation through whole-body coordination [6, 14].
Locomotion and manipulation are tightly coupled.
Body motion enables the hands to reach and interact with objects, while the demands of manipulation shape how the robot moves and maintains balance [12].
These dependencies evolve throughout execution, requiring a policy to coordinate body and hand motion over time.
We therefore aim to enable coordinated humanoid loco-manipulation by learning whole-body motion priors that capture these relationships and integrating them into robot policies.

Learning such priors requires diverse examples of body and hand motion, yet collecting demonstrations on physical humanoids is costly and difficult to scale [35, 22].
Existing human and robot motion datasets offer a broader source of supervision beyond demonstrations collected for a target robot [15, 25, 5].
Ψ0\Psi_{0} pretrains a vision-language model (VLM) to predict wrist poses and fingertip positions [28], while WholeBodyWAM learns body-motion priors by predicting the future rotations of 21 body joints [31].
Despite these advances, these methods do not jointly model body motion and fine-grained hand motion during pretraining.
This motivates us to learn unified whole-body motion priors that explicitly capture body–hand coordination through joint motion prediction, using heterogeneous datasets with annotations for body motion, hand motion, or both.

Translating these whole-body motion priors into coordinated robot behavior requires adapting representations learned for motion prediction to robot action generation.
Ψ0\Psi_{0} conditions its action expert on final-layer VLM features [28].
GR00T N1.6 [19] and N1.7 [21] instead use intermediate VLM features.
DiT4DiT [18] and MotionWAM [34] use features from a fixed video-model layer for action generation, with DiT4DiT reporting better performance using intermediate rather than final-layer features.
These methods use features from a source layer selected in advance.
However, as the task or observation changes, the features most suitable for robot control may come from different layers.
We therefore investigate whether jointly learning which layers to read and how to adapt their features, under robot-action supervision, can better support coordinated whole-body control.

To achieve coordinated whole-body control for humanoid loco-manipulation, we present CHAMP, a unified framework that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive motion feature extraction (Fig. 1).
First, we pretrain a VLM to predict future body and hand motion from heterogeneous human and robot data, supervising only the motion targets available in each sample.
Second, we use SONIC-replayed robot trajectories [17] to ground the learned representations in robot control.
In this stage, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) that adaptively selects and fuses features from the pretrained VLM.
Through joint layer–expert routing, CAE uses the fused features to condition flow-matching generation of SONIC motion latents and hand actions.
Finally, we fine-tune the policy with task-specific demonstrations collected through whole-body teleoperation.
Our contributions are threefold:

We propose CHAMP, a unified framework for coordinated humanoid loco-manipulation.
It learns whole-body motion priors from heterogeneous human and robot motion data and transfers the learned priors to robot control.

We introduce CAE to adaptively extract motion features from the VLM pretrained for whole-body motion prediction.
It jointly selects source layers and projection experts for each input token, transforming and fusing these features for coordinated whole-body control.

Experiments demonstrate CHAMP’s effectiveness for coordinated humanoid loco-manipulation, including long-horizon execution.
CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings.

1. We propose CHAMP, a unified framework for coordinated humanoid loco-manipulation.
It learns whole-body motion priors from heterogeneous human and robot motion data and transfers the learned priors to robot control.

2. We introduce CAE to adaptively extract motion features from the VLM pretrained for whole-body motion prediction.
It jointly selects source layers and projection experts for each input token, transforming and fusing these features for coordinated whole-body control.

3. Experiments demonstrate CHAMP’s effectiveness for coordinated humanoid loco-manipulation, including long-horizon execution.
CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings.

title: ROSE-Drive: Runtime Orchestration and System Evolution for Autonomous Driving
authors: Qihang Huang,Zhidong Wang,Zirui Li,YuJie Yan,Jingsong Liang,Shiyu Fang,Collister Chua,Zhan Chen,Chen Lv
abstract: End-to-end driving models have made substantial progress, yet reliable closed-loop driving in complex traffic remains challenging. Beyond improving individual models, system-level orchestration offers a complementary approach by coordinating driving capabilities and computation. We introduce ROSE-Drive (Runtime Orchestration and System Evolution), a model-agnostic framework that jointly orchestrates driving execution and computation. It coordinates frozen driving models with driving skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers. A distilled vision–language model (VLM) proposes driving tasks and scene relations. Shared physical state and persistent tasks support capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling. The orchestrator combines model and skill outputs across control channels, maintains task responsibility through handover, and uses execution feedback to select controllers, reuse valid motion references, and schedule model inference. Offline revisions use execution records to refine skills and their coordination through a stable task interface. Successive system stages inherit these revisions while model, perception, and VLM weights remain fixed. Evaluations with four driving models on Bench2Drive v0.0.3, Bench2Drive v0.0.4, and Fail2Drive show accumulated capability and transfer before target-benchmark revision. On held-out Longest6, driving score (DS) rises from 25 to 52 for AutoMoT and from 22 to 47 for SimLingo across system stages, while both systems skip new model inference on over 71% of control steps.
introduction:
End-to-end driving policies have made substantial progress across diverse traffic scenarios [14, 22, 31, 17, 6]. Beyond improving individual policies, a complementary direction is to coordinate their use with driving skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers at the system level. A runtime harness exposes these capabilities through common interfaces. System-level orchestration determines how their contributions are combined and when new computation is needed.

The central difficulty is coordinating these choices throughout an ongoing maneuver. A skill can regulate speed while retaining a compatible model path. When the model supplies both motion channels, persistent tracking error can trigger a controller change. A navigation change can prompt a new model call. The maneuver may also need to continue after the latest scene assessment no longer requests it. These decisions require task state that persists across changing observations and capability outputs.

We introduce ROSE-Drive, a model-agnostic framework that jointly orchestrates driving execution and computation (Fig. 1). A distilled vision–language model (VLM) proposes driving tasks and scene relations. The orchestrator binds these proposals to observed objects and road regions to form task requests. Shared physical state and persistent tasks guide capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling. These mechanisms determine which outputs to combine, how to maintain responsibility through a maneuver, and when computation is needed.

A shared task interface also supports cumulative improvement. Skills address physical requirements that recur across benchmarks, including traffic-interaction timing and obstacle clearance. Current geometry and motion determine each task’s constraints, allowing the same implementation to handle different objects and layouts. The VLM’s relation vocabulary and skill families stay fixed as execution records guide offline improvements to skill implementations and orchestration rules. Successive system versions, called stages, inherit these improvements.

We study four frozen models across Bench2Drive v0.0.3, v0.0.4, and Fail2Drive, including transfer before target-specific revision. Longest6 is reserved for evaluating frozen systems throughout this process. AutoMoT’s driving score (DS) progresses from 25 alone to 36, 44, and 52 across system stages, while SimLingo progresses from 22 to 36, 39, and 47. Both systems skip model inference on over 71% of Longest6 control steps. Our contributions are:

Model-Agnostic Runtime Framework. We introduce a unified architecture that connects frozen driving models, skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers through shared physical state and a common task interface. Model adapters preserve each model’s inputs and outputs while making it available to the same runtime.

Coordinated Execution and Scheduling. The orchestrator combines model and skill outputs across control channels while persistent tasks maintain responsibility through handover. The same task state and execution feedback guide controller selection, motion-reference reuse, and model inference, coupling capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling.

System Evolution and Transfer. A stable task interface supports offline refinement of shared skills and orchestration rules with model, perception, and VLM weights fixed. Successive versions inherit these changes and transfer across benchmarks and driving models.

We introduce a unified architecture that connects frozen driving models, skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers through shared physical state and a common task interface. Model adapters preserve each model’s inputs and outputs while making it available to the same runtime.

2. Coordinated Execution and Scheduling. The orchestrator combines model and skill outputs across control channels while persistent tasks maintain responsibility through handover. The same task state and execution feedback guide controller selection, motion-reference reuse, and model inference, coupling capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling.

3. System Evolution and Transfer. A stable task interface supports offline refinement of shared skills and orchestration rules with model, perception, and VLM weights fixed. Successive versions inherit these changes and transfer across benchmarks and driving models.

title: AgentMoT: An Agentic Mixture-of-Transformers for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
authors: Qihang Huang,Collister Chua,YuJie Yan,Shiyu Fang,Zhan Chen,Haoran Xu,Zirui Li,Chen Lv
abstract: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. The relative-capability principle guides these choices by relating the benefit of additional computation or intervention to its cost. After open-loop initialization, dual-loop evolution trains the Router, agent, and self-scheduler from closed-loop experience while failure-driven updates refine skills and execution feedback. AgentMoT achieves state-of-the-art results on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4, with 94.48/92.33 driving score and 85.45/82.73% success rate, respectively. With skills disabled, learned routing improves over the strongest fixed pathway by 1.79 driving-score points and 4.09 percentage points of success rate on v0.0.3. Ablation studies further show gains from closed-loop agent learning, two-view queries, and event-triggered wake-up.
introduction:
End-to-end driving connects sensor observations to motion through learned perception and planning [12, 20]. Vision-language reasoning enriches scene interpretation [27, 14], while world prediction anticipates traffic evolution [13, 6]. Driving agents further provide access to specialized tools [29, 36, 24]. Together, these capabilities expand what a driving model can do. Their value in a particular scene depends on which capabilities the model chooses to use and when it revisits that choice.

Using these capabilities requires choosing a native pathway, deciding whether to delegate to a skill, and determining when to reconsider (Fig. 1). Each choice depends on context. Reasoning and prediction cost computation. A skill suited to a blocked lane may be inappropriate for an ordinary stopped vehicle. Repeated confirmation wastes agent calls, while new interactions demand attention.

We present AgentMoT, which embeds agent capabilities into a driving Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT, Fig. 2). A Router selects among direct-action (A), vision-language-action (VLA), and world-action model (WAM) pathways formed by agent, world, and action experts. The agent expert supplies reasoning within VLA and WAM. System scheduling combines task selection by GG with call timing from the agent self-scheduler. GG selects native driving or a skill and target. The execution layer builds the skill–target menu and sends wake-up requests with updated driving context. The agent self-scheduler screens ordinary requests, choosing reconsider or keep. Mandatory requests call GG directly and can add a rear view to identify an approaching vehicle before deciding whether to yield.

Under the relative capability principle, an option is useful when its expected benefit over the default justifies its cost. The appropriate choice depends on both the scene and the capabilities available to the model. This motivates updating scheduling as those capabilities evolve.

Dual-loop evolution keeps these learned choices aligned with the available capabilities. After joint native training and open-loop initialization of the Router and GG, the inner loop trains the Router, GG, and the agent self-scheduler on closed-loop training-route experience. The outer loop attributes failures and refines skills and execution feedback. Rollouts with the updated model and skills supply experience for the next round.

Our contributions are threefold. (1) We introduce AgentMoT, which unifies three native driving paradigms with a shared agent expert for reasoning and tool use. The model learns to select native computation, delegate tasks, and reconsider decisions in response to execution feedback. (2) We develop dual-loop evolution that connects scheduling learned from closed-loop experience with failure-driven refinement of skills and execution feedback. (3) We achieve state-of-the-art performance on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4. Ablation studies demonstrate the benefits of learned routing, agent learning, and execution feedback.

title: SOAR: temporal Structure-guided One-step Action generation for Robotic manipulation
authors: Di Xin,Mingfei Han,Genming Cui,Yuanxiang Chen,Xiaolong Wu,Siyu Ning,Xiaojun Chang,Zhihui Li
