introduction:
Learning visuomotor policies from expert demonstrations enables robots to acquire complex manipulation skills without manually designing task-specific controllers.
However, given the same observation and task goal, multiple action trajectories may succeed while differing in approach direction, motion timing, or contact strategy.
Unlike deterministic behavior cloning, which can average across distinct action modes,
diffusion- and flow-based policies address this ambiguity by modeling the action distribution itself and have shown strong performance in robotic manipulation [8, 60].

Despite their effectiveness, generative policies often rely on iterative inference. Diffusion policies progressively denoise action trajectories, while flow-based policies typically integrate learned velocity fields over multiple steps.
Such interactive strategy repeats network evaluations, introducing substantial inference latency
that reduces responsiveness to dynamics and can leave predicted actions stale as the scene evolves [4].
Some recent efforts seek to reduce inference steps through accelerated sampling, distillation, consistency learning, or shortened flow trajectories [43, 39, 36, 19, 46], even pushing them to a single network evaluation [13, 41, 11].
However, such efficiency comes at the cost of iterative refinement.
Multi-step generation repeatedly revisits the action trajectory, progressively correcting its temporal organization; a one-step policy must instead determine the entire trajectory structure at once, with no subsequent opportunity for correction.

To provide explicit temporal structure guidance
without relying on iterative refinement, we propose
SOAR, a temporal Structure-guided
One-step Action generation framework
for Robot manipulation, as shown in
Fig. 1.
Unlike velocity-parameterized one-step flow policies
that recover clean actions indirectly, SOAR directly
generates clean action trajectories in action space,
aligning the model output with the executable control
target and enabling direct structural calibration.
Given the current observation, SOAR predicts a
multi-band discrete cosine transform (DCT)
representation of future actions to provide temporal
structure guidance [1, 65].
The predicted structure is incorporated into the
observation condition to guide base action generation
and is subsequently used to calibrate the generated
trajectory according to their spectral discrepancy,
without additional evaluation of the generative
backbone. During training, the calibrated action is mapped to
the corresponding MeanFlow velocity for consistency
and endpoint supervision.
SOAR thus improves action quality while retaining
NFE=1\mathrm{NFE}=1 inference and millisecond-scale latency.

Our contributions are:

We propose SOAR, a direct one-step action generation policy that generates clean action trajectories in action space with NFE=1\mathrm{NFE}=1 and millisecond-scale inference.

We introduce temporal structure-guided generation and calibration, which explicitly models key temporal structural characteristics of action trajectories and corrects structural discrepancies in generated actions without additional backbone evaluations.

SOAR consistently outperforms compared one-step policies on Adroit and Meta-World while retaining NFE=1\mathrm{NFE}=1, and further demonstrates competitive performance in the VLA setting on LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0.

2. We introduce temporal structure-guided generation and calibration, which explicitly models key temporal structural characteristics of action trajectories and corrects structural discrepancies in generated actions without additional backbone evaluations.

title: One Policy, Many Bodies: Cooperative Human-Object Interaction with Heterogeneous Teams
authors: Zhihao Cao,Tianxu An,Chenhao Li,Chenyangguang Zhang,Stelian Coros,Marco Hutter
abstract: Physics-based human-object interaction (HOI) has enabled multiple characters to cooperatively transport objects, but existing cooperative controllers largely assume homogeneous embodiments and predefined interaction tasks. We ask whether a single physics-based policy can enable cooperation across diverse embodiments, team compositions, and interaction skills. We present MorphHOI, a decentralised framework built on a key insight: effective heterogeneous cooperation requires a unified representation across embodiments while accounting for differences in their physical capabilities. To realise this insight, we introduce a canonical body interface that unifies observation and action spaces, together with an embodiment-conditioned transformer that adapts cooperative decisions to the physical capabilities of each agent and its teammates. To extend cooperation to new interaction skills, we reuse the learned cooperative policy through task-specific tokens and lightweight adaptation, preserving its original capabilities. Our framework achieves success rates of up to 96.7% on seen embodiments, 95.6% on unseen embodiments, and 91.4% on novel payloads. Furthermore, the learned cooperation extends to diverse interaction skills with high success rates, including box carrying, transport on stairs, and waypoint following, while preserving previously acquired cooperative capabilities.
introduction:
Cooperative human-object interaction (HOI) requires multiple agents to coordinate their actions towards shared goals while adapting to one another’s physical capabilities. In practice, participants often differ in body proportions, joint configurations, and strengths, making such coordination particularly challenging. For instance, carrying a large object together requires partners to agree on where to grasp, when to lift, and how to move while sharing the load.
Physics-based HOI [43, 45] has progressed from individual manipulation skills [19, 59, 62, 40] to cooperative transport [16, 34]. However, existing cooperative controllers largely assume homogeneous teams, limiting their ability to coordinate agents with diverse embodiments. Moreover, extending learned cooperative behaviours to new interaction skills often requires updating the shared policy, potentially compromising previously acquired capabilities [29]. These limitations raise a central question: can a single policy enable physically plausible cooperation across heterogeneous embodiments and team compositions while remaining extensible to new interaction skills?

Answering this question poses two closely related challenges. First, cooperative control must generalise across embodiments and team compositions. Characters with different skeletons have incompatible observation and action spaces [31, 17], making it difficult to share a policy. More importantly, effective cooperation requires understanding both one’s own capabilities and those of one’s partners: characters of different heights and strengths must coordinate where to grasp, how high to lift, and how to move. This becomes harder as teams grow and diversify [5]. Second, cooperative skills should be unified and extensible across interaction tasks. Following routes, handling objects of different shapes, and traversing uneven terrain share fundamental cooperative behaviours but require different task-specific interactions. Training separate controllers limits the reuse of learned cooperation [62, 40]. A unified policy should therefore retain these shared capabilities while flexibly adapting to new interaction requirements.

We introduce MorphHOI, a framework for physics-based cooperative HOI across heterogeneous embodiments and extensible interaction skills. A canonical body interface unifies observations through the links of a shared skeleton and maps canonical joint targets to each character’s own hinges, enabling one policy to control bodies with different skeletons and degrees of freedom (DoFs). Within this shared representation, an embodiment-conditioned transformer (ECT) accounts for differences in physical capabilities: each agent’s own description conditions its network layers and action head, while teammate descriptions guide cooperative reasoning through corresponding tokens. Trained on mixed teams with body-adapted rewards and masked AMP [45, 34] for motion imitation, the policy learns to coordinate agents with diverse capabilities. To extend this learned cooperation to new interaction skills, we condition the shared policy on task-specific tokens and introduce lightweight adaptation, enabling new behaviours while preserving the original cooperative policy.

With a single policy across diverse embodiments, MorphHOI achieves success rates of 96.7%, 94.5%, and 87.8% with two, four, and eight agents, respectively. Across the same team sizes, it further generalises to unseen embodiments with success rates of 95.6%, 93.9%, and 80.0%, and unseen objects with 90.0%, 91.4%, and 84.9%, while extending to new skills with harmonic-mean success rates of 88.5% to 92.2% without compromising the original task. In summary, our contributions are:

Unified control across heterogeneous embodiments.
We introduce a canonical body interface that unifies the observation and action spaces of characters with diverse body proportions and joint configurations, enabling a single decentralised policy to control heterogeneous teams.

Embodiment-conditioned cooperative reasoning.
We develop an embodiment-conditioned transformer that separately models inter-agent coordination and task interactions through structured attention, while conditioning cooperative decisions on the physical capabilities of each agent and its teammates.

Extensible cooperative interaction.
We develop a progressive training framework that learns reusable cooperation across heterogeneous teams and extends it to new interaction skills by conditioning the shared policy on task-specific tokens with lightweight adaptation, while preserving previously learned cooperative behaviours.

1. Unified control across heterogeneous embodiments.
We introduce a canonical body interface that unifies the observation and action spaces of characters with diverse body proportions and joint configurations, enabling a single decentralised policy to control heterogeneous teams.

2. Embodiment-conditioned cooperative reasoning.
We develop an embodiment-conditioned transformer that separately models inter-agent coordination and task interactions through structured attention, while conditioning cooperative decisions on the physical capabilities of each agent and its teammates.

3. Extensible cooperative interaction.
We develop a progressive training framework that learns reusable cooperation across heterogeneous teams and extends it to new interaction skills by conditioning the shared policy on task-specific tokens with lightweight adaptation, while preserving previously learned cooperative behaviours.

title: Seeing Together, Acting Apart: Shared Environmental Understanding for Multi-Robot Navigation
authors: Haihong Hao,Lei Chen,Mingfei Han,Chenglong Yan,Dong An,Yuqiang Yang,Changlin Li,Minghao Guo,Salman Khan,Xiaojun Chang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment?
We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context.
To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens.
Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.
introduction:
Multi-robot embodied systems are commonly expected to collaborate by coordinating their behaviors: agents may communicate, share experience, divide tasks, avoid conflicts, or jointly decide what to do next.
This question naturally extends classic embodied navigation and vision-and-language navigation settings, where an agent must ground observations and instructions into actions in realistic environments [1, 2].
It has also motivated a large body of work on multi-robot coordination, communication, task allocation, and multi-agent decision making [3, 4, 5, 6], as well as recent embodied multi-agent systems that share semantic maps, messages, frontier assignments, action plans, or generated rollouts for cooperative navigation and planning [7, 8, 9].
However, most existing approaches frame collaboration at the level of agent-centric traces, such as sharing actions, trajectories, maps, or intermediate decisions. While effective, these methods tightly couple collaboration with policy design and communication protocols. This raises a fundamental question: can collaboration emerge from shared perception before shared decision-making? In other words, instead of exchanging what agents do, can they first share what they understand about the environment?

In realistic settings, different robots naturally observe complementary parts of the same environment from diverse viewpoints and at different times. Aggregating these partial observations can yield a richer representation of the environment than any single agent can obtain alone. Crucially, such a representation can serve as a policy-agnostic interface: it can be shared across agents while allowing each agent to make decisions independently using its own policy. We therefore propose to shift collaboration from policy space to representation space. We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates multi-robot observations into a shared latent description of the environment. This shared representation provides a common environmental context, while allowing each agent to act independently with its own policy.

In this paper, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that learns shared latent world representations from multi-robot, multi-view observations. SEER organizes distributed observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are exposed as continuous tokens and injected into downstream navigation agents, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context.
We evaluate SEER from both representation and task perspectives. Our results show that the learned representations capture action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improve downstream navigation across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents.

title: ConsisX: Cross-View Consistency Thinking in 3D for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Yunhe Zhang,Long Gao,Yuedong Fu,Gang He,Li Xu,Chang Wu,Pengyu Li
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.
introduction:
In modern embodied intelligence systems, robots take natural language instructions and multi-view visual observations as input to predict actions for task execution. Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation by extending the visual and language understanding of pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) [1, 2] to robot control through an action prediction module optimized via demonstration learning [31, 39]. RT-2 and OpenVLA adapt VLMs into robotic policies to predict actions as discrete tokens [44, 16]. Subsequently, π0\pi_{0} introduces an action expert to predict continuous action sequences [3]. Building upon the π0\pi_{0}, π0.5\pi_{0.5} combines diverse robot and vision-language data during training for enhanced generalization to unseen environments [12].

A common setup for robotic policies incorporates multi-view visual inputs from environment and wrist cameras to provide complementary observations of the current scene for reliable action prediction. To integrate these observations, VLA models enable interactions between visual features from different views through jointly processing within the VLM. However, the joint processing can introduce cross-view ambiguity. As shown in Fig. 1(a), both cups appear in the environment view but only one is visible in the wrist view, and feature interactions may link the front one to the rear one. In Fig. 1(b), the two cameras capture different faces of the same triangular prism, and 2D feature similarity alone may fail to link the local observations.

The above cases highlight a challenge: cross-view interactions in VLMs rely on learned similarities between 2D features and can therefore lead to physically inconsistent action execution. Specifically, the challenge involves two forms of cross-view ambiguity. (Q1) Visually similar observations may be incorrectly associated despite corresponding to distinct physical entities. (Q2) Cross-view information remains fragmented despite coming from the same physical entity.

Do visually similar observations across views actually refer to the same physical entity? How should fragmented information from different views of the same physical entity be organized? We regard these ambiguities as a 3D cross-view consistency problem and argue that cross-view thinking should jointly consider cross-view association and entity coherence in 3D. Specifically, visual similarity alone is insufficient to establish physical identity, and cross-view association is therefore needed to provide 3D spatial constraints. The fragmented information from the same entity also requires entity coherence to guide its organization into physically consistent evidence. The above considerations lead to the central question: How to think about cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency in 3D?

To answer this question, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that combines cross-view association and entity coherence for cross-view consistency thinking in 3D. Specifically, the consistency thinking follows a progressive process. Firstly, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to organize 3D features from each view in a shared 3D coordinate system and infer cross-view association with spatial proximity constraints and feature similarity. (A1) CAM provides cross-view correspondences under 3D spatial constraint, thereby reducing cross-view incorrect association. Secondly, Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) groups fragmented local 3D feature within each view into entity candidates through spatial affinity and feature compatibility before organizing cross-view entity pairs according to the cross-view association from CAM. (A2) ECO organizes cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thus addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Finally, Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) retrieves candidate entity pairs from ECO according to task relevance, providing the corresponding 3D entity features for cross-view consistent action prediction. ConsisX thus jointly considers cross-view association and entity coherence, enabling cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for reliable robotic manipulation. The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows.

To address the challenge of cross-view physical inconsistency, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D.

We design CAM to reduce cross-view incorrect associations through 3D spatial constraint, ECO to organize fragmented local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, and CAC to provide task relevant 3D entity features for cross-view consistent action prediction.

We evaluate ConsisX on 4 simulation benchmarks and conduct real-world experiments on 3 manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness and competitive performance of the proposed framework.

2. We design CAM to reduce cross-view incorrect associations through 3D spatial constraint, ECO to organize fragmented local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, and CAC to provide task relevant 3D entity features for cross-view consistent action prediction.

3. We evaluate ConsisX on 4 simulation benchmarks and conduct real-world experiments on 3 manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness and competitive performance of the proposed framework.

title: Robust Lateral String Stability and Error Attenuation for Heterogeneous Vehicle Platoons
authors: Sixu Li,Swaroop Darbha,Yang Zhou
abstract:
Keeping an entire vehicle platoon close to its planned path is essential for navigating road boundaries and obstacles safely. Followers may rely on predecessor information for lateral guidance, which couples their lateral dynamics and allows errors to propagate downstream. This paper develops a robust lateral string stability framework to study this propagation and achieve downstream error attenuation in heterogeneous platoons under varying longitudinal motion and local perturbations. Arc-length-based feedback linearization gives each vehicle the same nominal lateral error dynamics, with parameter uncertainty and external disturbances represented as local perturbations. We define robust ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} lateral string stability in terms of platoon-length-uniform error bounds and derive a sufficient condition for achieving it. Furthermore, we show that the same condition guarantees platoon-length-uniform ℒ∞\mathcal{L}_{\infty} error bounds. For the considered control formulations, predecessor
tracking (PT) can accumulate lateral errors, whereas
desired-path tracking (DT) prevents this accumulation.
We propose a learn-from-predecessor (LFP) strategy
with explicit gains for downstream error attenuation
and characterize how intervehicle perturbation
differences limit this attenuation. Simulations validate the theoretical findings under vehicle heterogeneity, varying longitudinal motion, and local perturbations.
introduction:
Connected and automated vehicle platoons offer
opportunities to improve traffic throughput and energy efficiency
[1]. Realizing these benefits requires
attention to how errors arising at individual vehicles propagate
through the platoon, as their amplification can compromise
platoon performance. This concern motivates string stability,
which has been studied extensively for longitudinal spacing
errors [2, 3], with controller
design and information exchange playing important roles
[4, 5, 6].

Lateral coordination is also important when platoons follow curved roads or perform obstacle-avoidance maneuvers. In a platoon, a vehicle can obstruct the field of view of onboard cameras and LiDARs on the vehicle behind it [7, 8]. Consider the obstacle-avoidance scenario in Fig. 1. The lead vehicle detects the obstacle and plans a safe avoidance path, as shown in Fig. 1(a), but blocks the second vehicle’s view of the obstacle. By the time the second vehicle detects it, the remaining distance may be insufficient to independently plan and execute a safe maneuver, as shown in Fig. 1(b). This delayed perception effect can further accumulate downstream as the platoon size increases. This motivates using the leader’s planned path as the desired path for the platoon, allowing followers to benefit from the leader’s earlier perception and planning [9, 10, 11]. Guidance for following this path may be obtained through onboard sensing of a predecessor’s traveled path or through vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication of the desired path. When predecessor information
is used for lateral control, the vehicles’ lateral
dynamics become interconnected, allowing lateral
errors to propagate downstream. This motivates
examining whether these errors amplify along the
platoon through the study of lateral string stability
[11].

The spatial nature of lateral motion also matters when
assessing error propagation. Road curvature and physical
boundaries vary along the path, while vehicles occupy
different locations at the same time instant. Comparing
their lateral errors at that instant therefore mixes the
effects of different road geometries with error propagation
along the platoon. Comparing errors as vehicles pass the
same desired-path location avoids this ambiguity. This
motivates the arc-length-based framework for lateral string
stability developed in [11] for homogeneous
platoons at constant longitudinal speed.

Practical platoons, however, may contain vehicles
with different physical parameters and operate under
varying longitudinal motion. Moreover, parameter
uncertainty and external disturbances introduce local
perturbations that affect lateral error propagation.
This paper develops a robust lateral string stability
framework for this setting and proposes a
learn-from-predecessor (LFP) strategy for downstream
error attenuation. The analysis establishes conditions
for bounded lateral errors throughout the platoon
and characterizes how differences between vehicles’
local perturbations affect the guaranteed attenuation.

Longitudinal string stability was formally established in the work of Swaroop and Hedrick [2, 3] to characterize how spacing errors propagate along automated vehicle platoons and has since been studied under various spacing policies and information topologies [4, 5, 6]. Subsequent work has addressed communication imperfections, including packet loss, noise, and delay [12, 13, 14], and extended the analysis to mixed traffic and human-driven vehicles [15, 16, 17]. Theoretical developments include ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p}-based input–output formulations [18] and disturbance string stability accounting for disturbances at individual vehicles [19]. Among the norm-based criteria, ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} string stability is widely used because error amplification in stable LTI interconnections can be assessed in the frequency domain [5, 18]. Under additional assumptions, it also yields bounds on peak errors [12].

Lateral string stability has received comparatively less
attention, with existing studies adopting different error
measures and stability criteria. For example, [9] employed
ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} norms of transfer functions to characterize
lateral string stability, while [10] considered
ℒ∞\mathcal{L}_{\infty} attenuation of tracking error vectors and
identified limitations of relying solely on predecessor
information. Bounded tracking errors and the benefits of
leader information were examined in
[20]. However, much of this early work
focused on straight-line paths. Moreover, the quantities
analyzed for lateral string stability in these studies,
such as yaw rate or predecessor-relative errors, do not
directly characterize lateral deviations from the desired
path, which determine whether vehicles maintain the clearance
from obstacles and road boundaries intended by the path
planner. These limitations motivated the arc-length-based
framework in [11], which explicitly considers
desired-path errors and compares them at common locations
along curved paths. That framework introduced an
ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} lateral string stability definition,
established a necessary and sufficient condition for the
considered stable LTI interconnections, and examined the
effects of information modes, control strategies, and error
measures. Its analysis, however, was restricted to homogeneous
platoons at constant longitudinal speed.

Practical platoons may consist of vehicles with different physical parameters and operate under varying longitudinal speeds and accelerations, motivating an extension beyond the homogeneous, constant-speed setting. Moreover, parameter uncertainty and external disturbances can affect lateral control performance and error propagation. These considerations motivate developing a robust notion of lateral string stability and studying downstream error attenuation for heterogeneous platoons under varying longitudinal motion.

This paper develops a framework for robust lateral string stability and downstream error attenuation in heterogeneous vehicle platoons under varying longitudinal motion and local perturbations. The main contributions are as follows:

A feedback linearization formulation is developed directly in the arc-length domain to account for vehicle heterogeneity and varying longitudinal motion. It yields the same nominal lateral error dynamics for each vehicle, with parameter uncertainty and external disturbances represented as local perturbations, enabling a unified analysis of lateral error propagation.

A robust ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} lateral string stability notion is introduced to characterize platoon-length-uniform lateral error bounds in terms of initial conditions and local perturbations. A sufficient condition is established for the considered one-predecessor LTI interconnections. Furthermore, the same condition guarantees platoon-length-uniform ℒ∞\mathcal{L}_{\infty} lateral error bounds.

Predecessor tracking (PT) and learn-from-predecessor (LFP) control are formulated for the heterogeneous, perturbed setting. The analysis establishes that the considered PT configuration fails to guarantee robust lateral string stability and derives sufficient learning-gain conditions under which LFP satisfies it.

An explicit LFP gain design makes the predecessor-to-follower propagation map contractive in both the ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} and ℒ∞\mathcal{L}_{\infty} norms. Under zero initial conditions, exact downstream error attenuation is established for common perturbations, while error envelopes characterize how intervehicle perturbation differences limit the guaranteed attenuation.

Numerical studies of the reduced arc-length error dynamics
first validate the theoretical bounds and examine how
perturbation repeatability affects downstream error attenuation.
Simulations with heterogeneous vehicle dynamics then evaluate
performance under varying longitudinal motion, parameter
uncertainty, and road-bank disturbances. Both studies compare
PT, desired-path tracking (DT) without learning, and LFP to
distinguish the benefits of desired-path information from the
additional error attenuation achieved through LFP.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the arc-length-based feedback linearization for heterogeneous vehicles and the local perturbation model. Section III formulates platoon control under the two information modes. Section IV introduces robust lateral string stability and establishes sufficient conditions. Section V analyzes robust lateral string stability under the two information modes and establishes downstream error attenuation results for LFP. Section VI presents the numerical evaluation, and Section VII concludes the paper.

title: Beyond Which: Where, How, and When in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Yunhe Zhang,Long Gao,Yuedong Fu,Gang He,Li Xu,Chang Wu,Songyuheng Gao
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically rely on vision-language model (VLM) features as the primary perceptual source for action prediction, showing strong generalization across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. Although VLM features can identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, precise manipulation also requires understanding where task-relevant entities are located within the spatial layout, how their geometric structure constrains physical interaction, and when spatial or geometric information should make a greater contribution to action prediction. To this end, we introduce 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA to organize VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. Specifically, 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA retains VLM-based semantic entity perception (which) and further introduces spatial distance perception (where) and geometric structure perception (how) with adaptive spatial-geometric guidance (when) to enrich the perceptual information available for action prediction. Experiments across real-world settings and simulation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA.
introduction:
Robot policies optimized for specific tasks often suffer from limited generalization [14]. Meanwhile, recent advances in large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-modal learning and reasoning [1, 2]. The advances provide a strong basis for visual perception and language understanding, enabling robot policies to leverage broad vision-language knowledge for interpreting visual observations and language instructions across the physical world. Building upon these, vision-language-action (VLA) models combine a pre-trained VLM for perceptual and semantic understanding with an action prediction module that maps observations and instructions to robot actions, enabling robot policies to generalize across diverse tasks [45, 14, 3, 11, 40, 20].

Despite the strong generalization, most VLA models still rely on the VLM-based 2D visual perception, resulting in a primary focus on the semantic information about the entities relevant to the action prediction. Recent efforts have begun to enrich perception with spatial depth information [25] and 3D scene representations [39]. Although these advances show the benefits of richer perception, they also motivate a broader question: what perceptual information is required to support precise action prediction in a VLA model?

Consider the task of placing a blue cube surrounded by other cubes onto a cube tower. Given 2D visual observations and a language instruction, the VLM provides semantic information for identifying which cube to manipulate. Semantic information therefore remains essential throughout the manipulation process to ensure that action prediction remains grounded in relevant entities. Beyond this, precise action prediction also depends on knowing where the cube, the tower, and the end effector are located relative to one another. Furthermore, the model must also account for how the shapes and local geometric details of the entities constrain grasping, alignment, and placement. During manipulation, it is also required to decide when action prediction should emphasize spatial relationships for localization or prioritize geometric constraints for grasping, alignment, and placement.

Accordingly, we argue that precise action prediction requires not only VLM-based semantic entity perception but also spatial distance perception, geometric structure perception, and adaptive spatial-geometric guidance, which together advance VLA perception beyond Which with the consideration of Where, How, and When.

As shown in Fig. 1, we introduce 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA, a novel framework that organizes VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. For which, 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA follows the standard VLA paradigm, using a VLM to derive semantic entity perception from 2D visual observations and language instructions, thereby preserving the full semantic information as the primary task-relevant context throughout action prediction. In terms of where, 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA introduces spatial distance perception by incorporating task-relevant distance relationships and spatial layout features derived from a pre-trained depth estimation model [35]. About how, 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA enables geometric structure perception by capturing task-relevant geometric structure features from a pre-trained visual geometry model [31]. For when, 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA integrates adaptive spatial-geometric guidance into action prediction by coordinating the contributions of spatial distance perception and geometric structure perception, conditioned on the current task semantic context and evolving action state. By unifying which, where, how, and when, 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA complements semantic entity perception with spatial distance perception, geometric structure perception, and adaptive spatial-geometric guidance to support precise action prediction in the complex physical world.

To validate the effectiveness of 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA, we conduct extensive experiments on 4 benchmarks, LIBERO [17], LIBERO-Plus [6], CALVIN [21], LIBERO-PRO [44], and 4 real-world manipulation tasks. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows.

We formulate VLA perception and action prediction in terms of which, where, how, and when, extending VLM-based semantic entity perception with spatial distance perception, geometric structure perception, and adaptive spatial-geometric guidance.

Building on the formulation and the corresponding perceptual design, we propose 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA, a novel VLA framework that incorporates a broader range of perceptual information into action prediction.

We evaluate 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA on 4 benchmarks and 4 real-world manipulation tasks, showing its effectiveness and superior performance in simulated and physical settings.

1. We formulate VLA perception and action prediction in terms of which, where, how, and when, extending VLM-based semantic entity perception with spatial distance perception, geometric structure perception, and adaptive spatial-geometric guidance.

2. Building on the formulation and the corresponding perceptual design, we propose 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA, a novel VLA framework that incorporates a broader range of perceptual information into action prediction.

3. We evaluate 𝒲3​ℋ\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}-VLA on 4 benchmarks and 4 real-world manipulation tasks, showing its effectiveness and superior performance in simulated and physical settings.

title: Skill-Adaptive Noise Scheduling for Diffusion Policies
authors: Woo Kyung Kim,Gwangpyo Yoo,Eunyoung Park,Honguk Woo
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
abstract:
Recent advances in diffusion policies have demonstrated strong effectiveness when integrated into hierarchical skill-based learning frameworks, leveraging offline data to capture multimodal and temporally abstracted behaviors. However, prior approaches have rarely considered the diffusion process as a learnable component, adopting fixed noise schedules applied uniformly across skills, regardless of their distinct behavioral contexts. Such a design fundamentally limits the achievable performance, particularly for contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks where different skills exhibit distinct couplings between action dimensions.
In this paper, we present a skill-adaptive noise diffusion framework (SaND) which introduces a learnable, skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates the diffusion process per action dimension, adapting the noising dynamics to each skill.
To prevent the learned noise schedule from collapsing into trivial solutions, we employ an auxiliary inverse objective that reconstructs the skill embedding from the Legendre coefficients of the derivative of the noise schedule, encouraging the schedules to remain skill-discriminative.
This formulation naturally enables adaptive control over the denoising steps for each skill, where noise schedules are clustered in the Legendre coefficient space, and the appropriate number of denoising steps is determined at the point where reconstruction error abruptly increases.
At inference, we identify each skill embedding’s cluster from its noise schedule and apply the corresponding number of denoising steps, dedicating more compute to skills requiring fine-grained control and less to simpler ones.
Through experiments in simulation and on real robot hardware, we demonstrate that SaND outperforms existing skill learning and planning baselines on contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, achieving higher success rates while requiring fewer denoising steps.
introduction:
Hierarchical skill-based learning has emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation by abstracting temporal behaviors into latent skill representations [33, 12]. Meanwhile, diffusion policies have demonstrated strong capability in modeling sequential decision-making tasks, owing to their ability to capture multimodal action distributions [31, 1, 47] and generate coherent trajectory-level plans [15, 25, 5]. Building on these successes, recent works have augmented skill-based frameworks with diffusion models to further enhance the expressiveness of skill decoders [6, 19, 49, 22, 52].

Despite their effectiveness, prior methods share key limitations due to their reliance on a fixed noise schedule across all skills and action dimensions. Such uniform denoising prevents the model from leveraging mutual information among actions, i.e., using easily inferred dimensions to guide the harder ones. This is particularly important in contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, where kinematic contact constraints and dynamic equilibrium tightly couple action dimensions. Moreover, these coupling patterns vary across skills, as different behaviors yield distinct contact and force structures.
Theoretically, a fixed noise schedule yields a loose bound on the diffusion ELBO [37]. Under the deterministic denoising process of diffusion policies [1, 35, 10], the resulting inaccuracy propagates irreversibly and cannot be mitigated by additional denoising steps (see Appendix C.2).

To address this, inspired by adaptive noise schedules in image diffusion models [20, 37], we propose to learn a skill-conditioned noise schedule that adapts the denoising rate per action dimension for each skill.
Such adaptive scheduling enables prioritized denoising across action dimensions, first resolving dimensions that are easier to predict and subsequently refining more contact-sensitive ones, yielding a tighter ELBO on the action distributions.
This is analogous to the Knothe–Rosenblatt map, which guarantees exact likelihood evaluation by decomposing a joint distribution into a chain of conditionals [2]. In Figure 1, we visualize the per-step denoising residuals along each action dimension for two different skills learned with a skill-conditioned noise schedule.
When approaching the target object, rotational dimensions (yaw, roll) resolve first to align the end-effector orientation, while positional dimensions (xx, yy) converge later. In contrast, during grasping, the gripper actuation dimension commits early to secure a firm grasp on the object, while positional dimensions are refined later.
This skill-aware prioritization
yields average success rate gains of 11.711.7 percentage points (pp) on contact-rich tasks and 13.013.0 pp on dexterous manipulation tasks over the most competitive baseline, SkillDiffuser [22], as shown on the rightmost side of the figure.
Beyond improving generation quality, the geometry of the learned schedule naturally reveals the denoising budget required for each skill, thereby enabling adaptive allocation of denoising steps at inference time.

To this end, we propose the Skill-Adaptive Noise Diffusion (SaND) framework, designed to learn robust skills for contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks that demand fine-grained coordination across tightly coupled action dimensions.
Building on skill diffusion, a hierarchical skill-learning paradigm with a skill encoder and a diffusion-based decoder, we introduce a skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates the noise injection across action dimensions based on the skill embedding. To prevent the schedule from collapsing into a skill-agnostic (fixed) one, we employ an auxiliary inverse schedule that reconstructs the skill embedding from the Legendre coefficients of the noise schedule’s derivative. Furthermore, the learned noise schedule naturally encodes the denoising demand of each skill, which allows us to adaptively determine the number of denoising steps without additional training. We introduce a schedule-driven adaptive denoising mechanism, which allocates denoising steps per skill based on the geometry of the learned schedule.
Specifically, we cluster skills by the Legendre coefficients of their corresponding noise schedules and identify, for each cluster, the minimal denoising budget that maintains reconstruction quality. At inference, we select the total number of denoising steps based on the inferred skill, yielding improved inference efficiency with negligible impact on task performance.
The contributions of our work are summarized as follows:

We propose the SaND framework, skill diffusion augmented with a skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates noise injection across action dimensions based on the skill embedding, paired with an auxiliary inverse schedule to prevent the schedule from collapsing.

We introduce a schedule-driven adaptive denoising mechanism that assigns a distinct number of denoising steps for each skill based on the geometry of the learned noise schedule, enabling efficient inference without sacrificing task performance.

Through extensive experiments on contact-rich and bimanual dexterous tasks, we show that SaND consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based skill learning and planning baselines while accelerating inference.

1. We propose the SaND framework, skill diffusion augmented with a skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates noise injection across action dimensions based on the skill embedding, paired with an auxiliary inverse schedule to prevent the schedule from collapsing.

2. We introduce a schedule-driven adaptive denoising mechanism that assigns a distinct number of denoising steps for each skill based on the geometry of the learned noise schedule, enabling efficient inference without sacrificing task performance.

3. Through extensive experiments on contact-rich and bimanual dexterous tasks, we show that SaND consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based skill learning and planning baselines while accelerating inference.

introduction:
The physical world is open-ended, partially observable, and dynamically evolving, where actions have
uncertain consequences and failures may incur irreversible costs.
While foundation models have substantially advanced embodied intelligence, standalone foundation
models still struggle to sustain reliable behavior over long horizons, particularly when execution
requires self-correction and adaptation.
Extending their capability boundaries therefore requires coupling native model capabilities with
persistent agentic reasoning [yao2023react, schick2023toolformer],
memory [nvidia2026gr00t2, lu2026aspire], and
interaction [zitkovich2023rt2, kim2024openvla, gemini2025robotics].
However, simply integrating models and agents may not fully realize their combined potential.
Inconsistencies between planning and control may lead to unreliable physical execution and limited
adaptation from accumulated experience.
This motivates a shift from a standalone embodied model toward a
native embodied world system.

To this end, we characterize native through three core capabilities:
Plan lays the foundation for the system to accomplish long-horizon tasks by coordinating model execution across subtasks;
Recover further bolsters the system, enabling it to handle uncertainties and recover from unexpected failures during real-world execution; and
Evolve extends the system to continuously adapt to new environments and scenarios through accumulated experience.
To jointly realize these capabilities, we introduce Innata-0, a model-agent co-designed
system that advances native embodied intelligence.
As illustrated in \figreffig:native_codesign, our co-design establishes complementary roles for
the embodied model and agent, allowing the model to fully leverage its native capabilities while the
agent extends its effective operating scope.

On the model side, Innata-0-WAM serves as the physical execution foundation of the system.
We adopt a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture [liang2024mixture0of0transformers0],
which provides understanding, prediction, and action generation capabilities.
The model is conditioned on the complete instruction, active subtask, and verified task history. By
incorporating current- and history-plan annotations during training, Innata-0-WAM aligns its learned
conditioning interface with the agent’s evolving representation of task progress.

On the agent side, Innata-0-Agent serves as the system coordinator, supporting long-horizon
planning, failure recovery, and continual evolution.
It orchestrates model execution across subtasks while maintaining hierarchical memory.
Grounded in observations and execution feedback, the agent verifies against intended physical outcomes and
invokes tool-based recovery upon deviations.
Verified interactions and experiences are consolidated into reusable skills that refine subsequent
decisions and recovery strategies.
Innata-0-Agent aligns its execution logic with the model’s capabilities, enabling coordinated
execution, outcome verification, and experience-driven adaptation.

Realizing Plan, Recover, and Evolve requires the model and agent to work
together and play complementary roles.
We therefore establish a co-design protocol that enables them to operate in concert, leveraging
their respective strengths while guiding their subsequent design.
Crucially, this protocol operates in both directions: the model’s execution capabilities shape how the
agent organizes and delegates tasks, while the agent’s requirements for planning, recovery, and
adaptation guide model design and training.
Our protocol aligns the model’s training data with the agent’s task instructions, subtask plans, and
recovery commands, allowing complex tasks to be carried out through coordinated execution.
The agent, in turn, validates execution outcomes and consolidates experiences to refine its task
commands and reusable recovery strategies. It also feeds successful rollout segments, including
corrective actions and post-recovery continuations, into the shared data pipeline for subsequent
policy training.
These principles guide our data construction, model training, and agent design, laying the
foundation of native embodied intelligence.

We evaluate the physical capabilities underlying Innata-0 and their use in closed-loop task
execution. Among the compared models, the understanding tower ranks first on nine benchmarks and within the top two on fourteen. On WorldArena 2.0 Track 1 [li2026worldarena2], Innata-0 achieves an
EWM score of 67.63, the highest among the open-source models. Policy evaluations on
RoboCasa365 [robocasa365] and RoboDojo-Sim [chen2026robodojo] examine manipulation and
task completion.
On RoboCasa365, Innata-0 achieves 60.2% overall success and ranks first on Atomic-Seen tasks with
an 88.4% success rate.
These evaluations characterize the model’s grounding, prediction, and control capabilities, as well as its
use within an agent-guided execution loop.

To conclude, we propose Innata-0, a native embodied world system that extends physical
intelligence beyond individual task execution. Our approach jointly designs the embodied model and agent to
leverage their complementary strengths. A shared interaction protocol aligns model capabilities with
agent requirements and guides data construction, model training, and agent design. Together, these
designs enable long-horizon planning, failure recovery, and continual evolution. Our system
co-design establishes a basis for studying how aligned task context, physical-outcome verification,
and validated experience contribute to reliable open-world interaction.

title: RoboAda: Adapting Frozen Robot Policies at Test Time to Physics They Cannot See
authors: Yunbei Zhang,Zijian Jin,Shuaicheng Niu,Baian Chen,Weirui Ye,Jihun Hamm,Yilun Du
comment: Project page and code:this https URL
abstract: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from that of the training data, the plan is often still right, but it is executed as if nothing had changed, and the robot falls short. Existing methods either train on such variations in advance or adapt once deployed. The former cannot handle changes unseen in training. The latter change what the robot plans, which leaves the miscalibrated commands in place, or update a model of the robot by gradient steps. Such updates do not know how reliable they are, so they can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. Our key observation is that the robot’s own motion reveals the change. After each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model trained on the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands the original robot would have needed, which yields free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under the weighted hypotheses. For example, if the robot moves only half as far as commanded, RoboAda infers a weaker robot and scales up its next commands. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and it largely preserves the policies’ success when nothing has changed. On the bimanual RoboTwin 2.0, commanded in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.
introduction:
World action models (WAMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have made
pretrained robot policies broadly capable. A WAM predicts how the scene will
evolve and decodes the actions that produce this future, either from predicted
frames [10, 25, 53, 19] or by denoising video
and actions jointly [30, 77, 22, 60].
A VLA maps observations to actions
directly [6, 23, 5, 43]. We call the chunk of actions that either kind of policy outputs its plan. Both kinds learn to plan under the physics of their training data, and their plans are executed as if that physics still held. Yet some of the physics that decides whether a plan succeeds is not visible. A full mug looks like an empty one, a block that looks wooden may be made of iron, and a worn joint or a lagging controller looks the same as a healthy one. In each case, the physics at deployment differs from that of the training data, and the camera cannot reveal the difference.

Such hidden physical shifts are common once robots leave the lab, where
actuators wear, controllers are tuned differently from robot to robot, and the
objects to be handled vary in weight. They are also costly. In
Fig. 1, a hidden 35 N payload acts on the robot while it carries
a cream cheese box. The policy plans the same motion as on the training robot
and sends the same commands, and the box falls short of the basket. On
RoboTwin-Phys, randomizing physical conditions, together with table geometry and
camera pose, lowers the success of Fast-WAM from 91.8% to 44.2% and of
π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 76.8% to 31.6%, whereas visual and layout randomization alone
costs at most 6 points [66].

Existing remedies fall into two groups (Tab. 1). The first prepares
the policy in advance, either by training on randomized
dynamics [42, 16] or by inferring a latent physical
context from recent
interaction [61, 75, 27, 26, 65].
Both handle only variations seen during training. The second adapts at deployment. Some of these methods change what the robot plans or predicts, by adapting the world model to the observed
outcome [62, 54, 41, 70]
or by sampling several plans and keeping the one a verifier
prefers [44, 68, 64], and the plan is still executed
with the same miscalibrated commands. Others update a dynamics
model [36, 51] or a residual on the
commands [49, 50] by gradient steps. These updates carry no
estimate of how reliable they are, so they also move when nothing has changed
and can make an unchanged robot worse.

We argue that under such shifts the plan is usually still right, and only the
commands that carry it out are wrong. If the robot executes only half of every
command, it reaches only half of the motion that Cosmos Policy imagines for it
(Fig. 5). We therefore treat test-time adaptation as inferring how the robot turns commands into motion and correcting the commands accordingly. We refer to the actuators, the controller and any load the robot carries, which together turn commands into motion, as the robot’s body. This is hard because the shift cannot be seen, no reward or label
is available at test time, and a correction that chases execution noise can
make an unchanged robot worse.

We introduce RoboAda to address this (Fig. 1). After each action
chunk, an inverse-dynamics model trained on the nominal robot, the one
the policy was trained on, returns the command the nominal robot would have
needed for the motion that actually happened, as in hindsight
relabeling [1, 15]. If the robot executes only
half of every command, this label is half the command sent, so every step yields
a free label of how the robot responds. Per action axis, RoboAda fits three
competing hypotheses to these labels, namely that the robot is unchanged, that
it scales and offsets every command, or that its response depends on its state,
as when a payload appears at the grasp. Each hypothesis is weighted by how well
it predicted each new label, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that
best realize the plan under these weights. A systematic shift moves the weight
away from the unchanged hypothesis within a few chunks, while pure noise leaves
the weights spread, so the commands do not chase it. Only the priors and
features of the hypotheses are learned in advance, from the nominal robot alone.
The fitting and weighting follow multiple-model adaptive
control [35, 37], which we apply around a
frozen foundation policy with its own plan as the target and no robot model or
reward. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on
LIBERO [32], two WAMs and three VLAs from 2B to 7B parameters,
and with Fast-WAM on the bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 [7]. With
the same settings for every policy, it more than doubles their average success
under eleven physical shifts, from 27.8% to 62.9% (Tab. 2). Our
contributions are threefold:

Test-time adaptation as inferring the body. We reframe adapting a
frozen robot policy to unseen physics as inferring a posterior over explicit
hypotheses of the robot’s body, in the policy’s own action space, from
hindsight labels of the robot’s own motion. It needs no reward, no retraining
and no data from the changed robot.

Test-time adaptation as inferring the body. We reframe adapting a
frozen robot policy to unseen physics as inferring a posterior over explicit
hypotheses of the robot’s body, in the policy’s own action space, from
hindsight labels of the robot’s own motion. It needs no reward, no retraining
and no data from the changed robot.

RoboAda. We weigh body hypotheses by their predictive evidence and command under the posterior, with priors meta-learned on synthetic changes of the nominal robot. Unlike latent-context inference, which recognizes variations seen in training, RoboAda fits the body at hand from the robot’s own motion and needs no data from the changed robot. Unlike world-model adaptation and verifier-based
steering, it changes how a plan is executed rather than which plan is chosen.

Evidence on five policies and two simulators. RoboAda more than doubles the average success under eleven physical shifts, recovers much of the
success lost to objects 100 times heavier than they look, keeps its gains
under perception, language and world changes, outperforms seven test-time
adaptation methods, and transfers to a bimanual robot commanded in joint
space. Its posterior recovers the true command gain within four to six chunks.

title: Counterfactual Velocity Steering for World Action Models
authors: Xufeng Zhan,Yuanzhi Liang,Ye Lu,Haibin Huang,Chi Zhang,Xuelong Li
abstract:
Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional
velocity field. This makes test-time bias correction appear deceptively simple:
query the action expert under a task-agnostic or nominally stationary condition,
then subtract the resulting velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We
show that this interpretation is often wrong. On Fast-WAM evaluated over 50
RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, predictions obtained from a mean instruction are highly
aligned with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.940.94–0.950.95).
Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: the
norm of their mean is 98.3%98.3\% of the mean individual norm. Thus, reference
branches contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and
aggressive subtraction damages the generative trajectory. We develop a
same-state diagnostic framework and a shrinkage analysis showing that the
optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates
geometry-calibrated action debiasing (GCAD), which removes only the
component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small, task-dependent
scale from within-task and cross-task instruction geometry. Controlled
RoboTwin experiments reveal three findings: corrupting the instruction still
permits 25.1%25.1\% success on a complete 50-task, 20-episode study, whereas
dynamic corruption of visual observations nearly eliminates success; a fixed centered
orthogonal correction reaches 92.7%92.7\% versus a 92.1%92.1\% baseline in one
randomized 1,000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within observed
run-to-run variation; and an angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated
upper bound of 94.5%94.5\%, while its best learned online realization reaches
92.5%92.5\%. Our results identify shared flow and train–serve mismatch as central
obstacles, and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction
rather than claiming that reference subtraction is universally beneficial.
introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising framework for embodied intelligence by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. Unlike conventional vision-language-action policies that directly map observations and instructions to actions, WAMs also learn how the observed world changes during interaction. This additional objective can encourage representations of object motion, contact dynamics, spatial relations, and task progression. It may also broaden the sources of supervision available for robot learning. Videos collected from humans, other robots, or passive observations can reveal how objects move and how manipulation unfolds, even when action labels for the target robot are unavailable. Recent WAMs have demonstrated promising transfer across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments, while large-scale video representation models have shown that visual pretraining can support physical reasoning and downstream robot planning [33, 2]. In parallel, the broader AI Flow perspective emphasizes that capable generative models must be coordinated across heterogeneous models, devices, and interaction contexts rather than treated as isolated predictors [1, 30]. These results suggest that video modeling can provide useful knowledge beyond what is available from narrowly collected robot demonstrations, making it an increasingly important component of general-purpose robot learning.

However, learning to predict visual futures and learning to select an appropriate action are not equivalent objectives. A video model must account for many changes in the visual input, including object appearance, texture, lighting, camera motion, and background structure. A control policy, in contrast, should preserve the information that determines the correct action under the current task and environment while ignoring changes that are irrelevant to control. Consequently, visually accurate prediction does not necessarily imply reliable action selection, causal physical understanding, or robust adaptation to changes in the robot and its surroundings. Recent evaluations show that video generation models can produce plausible visual futures while failing to extrapolate physical rules beyond familiar cases [12, 26]. Fast-WAM further demonstrates that much of the benefit of video modeling may come from shaping the learned representation during training, since competitive action performance can be retained after explicit future-video generation is removed at inference [34]. These findings leave open a broader question about conditional control: after video and action learning are combined, does the policy adapt its action to the full conditioning state—including task intent, visual observations, robot proprioception, and interaction context—or does it primarily reproduce a behavior associated with the current observation? This question is closely related to a broader concern in generative-model post-training: optimizing a convenient surrogate, whether a likelihood term or a learned reward, can improve the measured objective while failing to preserve intended semantics, controllability, or robustness [19, 21].

A potential failure mode is that WAM predictions become dominated by the current visual observation. When similar visual scenes repeatedly co-occur with particular actions in the training data, the policy may learn to reproduce the visually associated behavior while paying insufficient attention to the task instruction and robot state. Recent VLA studies report related modality imbalance, in which strong visual-action priors weaken the influence of language and proprioception [7, 32]. This is also analogous to the non-visual statistical shortcuts exposed in visual-relationship recognition, where models can exploit predictable relationships without using the image evidence intended to support the decision [18]. We observe a similar asymmetry in Fast-WAM: replacing the instruction with one sampled from another task still yields 25.1%25.1\% success on randomized RoboTwin episodes, whereas dynamically replacing the visual observation reduces success to 1.5%1.5\% on the same condition. These results are consistent with the possibility that Fast-WAM relies strongly on visual observations and may not always respond adequately to non-visual conditioning.

In this paper, we propose a counterfactual velocity-steering framework for
diagnosing and mitigating conditioning imbalance in WAMs. Our starting point
is to query the action expert under alternative instruction contexts while
holding the visual observation, proprioception, noisy action, and flow time
fixed. A mean context constructed from training instructions serves as a
task-agnostic reference, allowing us to examine which components of the action
prediction persist when task-specific language is attenuated. This reference
is a probe, not a ground-truth estimate of bias: neither averaging embeddings
nor removing task intent guarantees that the resulting prediction should
correspond to a stationary robot.

The main challenge is to distinguish an unwanted action tendency from the
transport required by the generative process itself. Even a stationary action
endpoint generally requires a nonzero velocity at an intermediate noisy state.
Consistent with this distinction, our diagnostics reveal strong alignment
between task-conditioned velocities and both mean-instruction and
completed-state reference velocities. Directly subtracting a reference can
therefore remove useful transport together with any unwanted component. We
address this ambiguity by constructing centered residuals and retaining their
components orthogonal to the task velocity. This preserves the instantaneous
projection along the original prediction, while allowing a controlled change
in direction; it does not assume that the original prediction is always
correct or that the residual is purely harmful.

We instantiate this framework as geometry-calibrated action debiasing
(GCAD). A noisy-reference analysis motivates shrinking the correction
according to its signal-to-noise ratio rather than applying a uniform, large
scale. We use within-task and cross-task instruction geometry as observable
proxies for this calibration, separating the correction amplitude from a gate
that estimates whether an intervention is beneficial. The same residual also provides a training-time signal: we use it to define
two detached sample-weighting rules based on angular displacement and relative
correction norm. These objectives test whether reference information can be
incorporated during learning without requiring an auxiliary branch at
deployment.

Our RoboTwin study combines input interventions, same-state velocity
diagnostics, and controlled correction sweeps. The results show that reference
geometry is informative but does not make debiasing automatic: small
corrections help some tasks, while stronger corrections can hurt, and offline
scale-selection gains need not transfer to online rollouts. We therefore
distinguish evidence of conditional dependence, the quality of a candidate
bias estimate, and the downstream utility of applying it. Our contributions
are:

A controlled diagnostic framework that probes conditioning
dependence in Fast-WAM and distinguishes action-space stationarity from
shared transport in velocity space.

A geometry-aware correction formulation combining centered
residuals, orthogonal projection, and calibrated scales, together with
training-time extensions based on corrected supervision and detached
loss weighting.

An empirical analysis of reference selection and correction
strength on RoboTwin, identifying task-dependent benefits, failure modes
of naive subtraction, and the gap between offline calibration and
deployed control.

1. A controlled diagnostic framework that probes conditioning
dependence in Fast-WAM and distinguishes action-space stationarity from
shared transport in velocity space.

2. A geometry-aware correction formulation combining centered
residuals, orthogonal projection, and calibrated scales, together with
training-time extensions based on corrected supervision and detached
loss weighting.

3. An empirical analysis of reference selection and correction
strength on RoboTwin, identifying task-dependent benefits, failure modes
of naive subtraction, and the gap between offline calibration and
deployed control.

title: Calibrating World Action Models: From Adaptive System 2 Takeover to Self-Evolution
authors: Wenhao Li,Yu Han,Xiu Su,Dehao Wu,Keke Huang,Shan You,Fei Wang,Chang Xu
abstract:
World action models (WAMs) deliver fast visuomotor control, yet degrade sharply in challenging scenes and act blindly when about to fail; conversely, foundation-model-based agents generalize and recover reliably, but incur prohibitive latency and cost when queried at every step.
To achieve both WAM (System 1)-level speed and agent (System 2)-level reliability— we propose Judgment-in-the-Loop (JiL), a framework that calibrates WAMs’ confidence— adaptively triggering System 2 only when necessary, and distilling System 2’s knowledge to form an evolving System 1.
First, JiL equips a frozen WAM with calibrated self-assessment: a single lightweight judgment token reading internal video–action features is trained via our proposed cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning using only binary rollout success/failure signals. It can predict a calibrated success probability at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions.
Second, this calibrated success probability schedules control chunk by chunk—invoking System 2 to resolve bottlenecks when confidence drops, and handing control back to the WAM once confidence recovers, preserving WAM-like speed while approaching System 2 reliability.
Third, as System 2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, its takeover trajectories directly capture the WAM’s capability gaps. JiL distills these takeovers into the WAM to repair those gaps so System 1 can operate standalone without System 2 at test time, while our mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating prevent degrading existing capabilities.
Across Fast-WAM, LingBot-VA, and Kairos on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation, JiL System 1 & 2 outperforms all baselines—e.g., cutting Fast-WAM failures on RoboTwin 2.0 by 57.6%57.6\% at a 30%30\% agent budget (vs. 16.3%16.3\% for random calls)—while our consolidated standalone WAM improves success rates by +13.1%+13.1\% to +24.7%+24.7\% with zero agent calls.
introduction:
Generalist robotic manipulation has recently advanced rapidly along two complementary paradigms. On the reactive side, World action models (WAMs) [7, 25, 21, 23, 43, 39, 19] couple action generation with world modeling for fast visuomotor control [5, 28], yet degrade sharply in challenging OOD scenes and lack self-assessment—blindly executing erroneous actions even in scenarios beyond their capability [47, 8]. On the deliberative side, manipulation agents built on frontier foundation models such as GPT-6-Astra [18, 45, 13, 29, 9] offer high task capability, broad generalization, and reliable error recovery, but incur high latency and token cost when queried at every step. Bridging a fast WAM (System 1) with a foundation-model-based agent (System 2) (Fig. 1) promises the best of both worlds, yet faces two fundamental bottlenecks: (1) the Scheduling Gap and (2) the Consolidation Gap.

The Scheduling Gap lies in knowing when to invoke System 2: calling a slow agent only on impending failures requires a fast, calibrated estimate of System 1’s success probability before executing each chunk. Some existing methods achieve this estimation by querying external VLMs [10, 24], but incur heavy latency and miss System 1’s internal action intent. Others compute multi-sample consistency [1, 50, 31] or simulate world-model rollouts  [44, 48, 22, 32], which require repeated forward passes or future generation, sacrificing reactive speed. Single-pass feature and conformal detectors [33, 2, 11, 15, 35] instead output uncalibrated anomaly alarms [33, 2, 11, 35] or action-agnostic observation scores [15], rather than calibrated task-success probabilities. Meanwhile, the Consolidation Gap lies in turning System 2’s help into permanent System 1 capability: existing dual-system frameworks [46, 24, 37, 9] treat System 2 as a permanent runtime dependency, repeatedly paying its high latency and cost without internalizing its experience into System 1.

To bridge both gaps, we propose Judgment-in-the-Loop (JiL), a self-evolving System 1 & 2 framework that equips the WAM with calibrated self-assessment—enabling adaptive System 2 takeover at runtime and continual skill consolidation into System 1.
To resolve the Scheduling Gap, JiL appends a lightweight judgment token to the frozen WAM’s final denoising step via a causal mask and token-gated adapters [14], reading internal video–action features without affecting action predictions. Trained solely on binary rollout success/failure signals via our cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning, which propagates multi-step value estimates without self-bootstrapping bias, this token outputs a calibrated success probability in only 1.61.6 ms per chunk.
Guided by this probability, JiL runs the WAM by default, invokes System 2 below a confidence threshold, and returns control to the WAM once confidence recovers.

To resolve the Consolidation Gap, JiL progressively distills knowledge from System 2’s takeovers into System 1, turning runtime rescues into permanent skills and eliminating the need to call System 2 at test time. Because System 2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, these takeover trajectories automatically pinpoint System 1’s capability gaps without manual labeling. However, we prove via a competence shrinkage law (Sec. 3.5) that directly fine-tuning the base WAM on off-distribution recovery data pulls it away from its original behavior, fixing those gaps at the cost of hurting mastered skills. Guided by this law, JiL keeps the base WAM frozen, trains a separate repaired action expert on System 2 takeovers mixed with mastered-skill anchor data (own successes and pre-training replay), and reuses the base WAM’s calibrated confidence to switch to the repaired expert only on low-confidence states—preserving mastered skills while achieving multi-round self-evolution.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose Judgment-in-the-Loop (JiL), a two-system framework uniting WAM speed with agent reliability—slashing agent calls via on-demand takeover and evolving System 1 to run standalone.

We design a non-invasive judgment token trained via cross-fitted TD learning on binary outcomes alone, predicting unbiased, calibrated success probabilities in 1.61.6 ms per chunk without altering actions.

We prove a competence shrinkage law revealing the repair–erosion trade-off, guiding mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating for erosion-free gap repair and self-evolution.

Across Fast-WAM, LingBot-VA, and Kairos on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world tasks, JiL beats all 30%30\%-call baselines and boosts standalone WAM success by +13.1%+13.1\% to +24.7%+24.7\% with zero agent calls.
