title: OmniSLAM: Evidence-Authorized Revision of Persistent Object Maps
authors: Haoxiang Jie,Yaoyuan Yan,Zhiyou Heng,Liang Li,Zhaosong Li,Lifeng Liu
abstract: Persistent object maps must incorporate new surfaces while retaining valid identities and correcting earlier associations. We present a map-revision module that separates historical identity changes from new-surface admission. Proposed merges are tested against shared and separate mask explanations across views; a merge is allowed only if its evidence margin remains positive after removing any one observed frame. New measured points are assigned through local identity competition, with a mask witness and a seed-frame stability check. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the fixed method increases mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 under a local evaluation protocol. Controlled output interventions attribute the gains to fragment consolidation, protection against harmful overwrites, and local assignment of new points. Four additional spatial holdouts increase mean AP from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision is slightly higher at 23.251. The extra seed-frame check yields no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment in either set. A 330-frame garage recording demonstrates offline integration with LiDAR–inertial–visual odometry. These results identify where observation-supported revision improves object maps and where conservative decisions still limit recovery.
introduction:
Object maps associate physical surfaces with persistent identities. When a robot revisits a scene, new observations can extend an object’s geometry or reveal that earlier observations were assigned incorrectly. These updates require different decisions: evidence that a surface belongs in the map does not necessarily justify merging every old identity that overlaps it.

Outdoors, partial views can fragment a building, while a broad surface component can absorb a neighboring vehicle or an unrelated structure. Keeping every old assignment preserves such fragments; replacing all assignments inside an accepted component can erase valid identities. We address this tradeoff by separating surface proposals from the evidence required to change persistent labels.

Our revision module takes an existing object map, posed images, masks, and measured 3D points. It compares shared and separate mask explanations before allowing an old identity to merge into a proposed receiver. The evidence must survive removal of one observation, and all identities in the merged group must be pairwise compatible. New points are assigned through local competition among witnessed identities. The module preserves the original measurement coordinates and records the observations supporting each decision.

The contributions are (1) a historical-revision rule based on competing multi-view explanations and group compatibility; (2) a measured-point admission rule combining mask support with local identity competition; and (3) controlled interventions that separate the effects of historical edits, identity preservation, and new-point assignment. A seed-frame deletion certificate provides a fixed-graph stability property; its additional accuracy benefit is tested separately.

The method is evaluated within omni_slam, where LIVO supplies robot poses and geometry and public benchmarks supply reference poses. Two preselected KITTI-360 windows improve by 1.503 mean AP points over the frozen backbone. Four further spatial holdouts improve by 2.908 points, with one regression and a slightly stronger unconditional control. We retain an earlier fixed-identity filtering study as V1 and report it separately from the current method. The experiments evaluate object-map revision with a fixed pose source.

title: Trustworthy agentic lunar robotics: safety-constrained contingent planning with a foundation-model planner
authors: Bingqi Huang,Bingchuan Wei,Yingkai Cai,Zhaokui Wang
abstract: Sustained lunar-base operations require robots that restore equipment and deliver cargo under conditions unforeseen before deployment. Flown space autonomy executes pre-validated procedures and enters a safe hold outside their scope, whereas foundation models synthesize plans on site that cannot be verified before execution. We formulate these operations as safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued physical evidence, and costly, deadline-constrained sensing. We propose asymmetric knowledge-level replanning (AKR), which treats the planner as an untrusted black box: reversible actions run on the planner’s assumptions, and irreversible actions run only after a minimum-cost sensing cover verifies every precondition. Under sound measurements, no irreversible action executes on a false precondition for any planner or record, the sensing cost before an irreversible action is bounded below for every sound knowledge-based policy, and execution with a complete planner ends in a verified goal or a certified hold. AKR executed no hazardous action in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials with sound observations or in 58 full-stack runs; the FF-Replan acting rule executed one in 7% of those trials. The median AKR run took 1.10 times the fastest run on the same mission, against 1.50 under the K-replanner acting rule. AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model; the original PLEXIL and EUROPA→\rightarrowPLEXIL procedures completed none. The project page: https://bingqi-huang.github.io/thoth-website/
introduction:
The Moon is the primary proving ground for sustained infrastructure operation beyond Earth. Contemporary lunar exploration architectures envision surface assets operating continuously across extended uncrewed intervals [12, 18], building on recent operational milestones including autonomous lunar sample collection by Chang’e-6 [46] and pinpoint landing within 100 m by SLIM [40].

Uncrewed surface facilities must be assembled and maintained largely by robotic systems. Engineering analyses of lunar outposts establish both the environmental constraints and the structural requirements of surface habitats [5, 10]. Sherwood’s operational assessment concludes that robotic systems must perform the majority of outpost maintenance between crewed missions, down to the removal and replacement of failed orbital replacement units (ORUs) [37], while multi-robot construction planning continues to mature [11]. Agency capability assessments identify inspection, maintenance, repair, logistics and fault management as primary gaps for sustained uncrewed operations [8]. Although routine in category, surface maintenance is unpredictable in detail: power distribution units, battery storage, scientific payloads and in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) plants experience breaker trips, thermal faults, filter blockages and module failures, while cargo must be routed continuously between surface supports.

Planetary surface robots deployed to date have operated primarily under ground-commanded or short-horizon workflows [43, 30]. Yutu-2 has traversed the lunar far side under waypoint teleoperation since 2019 [13], while International Space Station dexterous servicing relies on ground control [35] and low-latency orbital telerobotics has been investigated for lunar science [9].

Direct ground teleoperation does not scale to continuous outpost maintenance. Signal propagation and ground review introduce multi-minute latencies, and at polar sites direct-to-Earth links close periodically as Earth sets below the local horizon. Anomaly diagnosis and procedure generation already consume a substantial fraction of planetary mission operations effort [19].

Flown on-board autonomy addresses communication constraints by executing task models validated prior to launch: Remote Agent demonstrated model-based spacecraft execution [29], PLEXIL provides deterministic plan execution [17], EUROPA performs constraint-based temporal planning [4], and CADRE extends autonomous coordination to multi-rover lunar teams [33]. At the skill level, planetary rover autonomy and visual-servoed space manipulation are well established [41, 15, 16, 24]. Across all such architectures, causal task knowledge is authored and verified before flight; when execution encounters an unmodelled fault, the executive enters a safe hold and awaits ground intervention. Planetary operations enforce this conservatism because irreversible execution errors can permanently degrade mission capability. In 2009, the Mars rover Spirit broke through a sulphate crust at Troy and became embedded; months of recovery commands failed to free the vehicle [2], ending its mobile mission. Flight operations therefore retain ground-in-the-loop oversight and qualify autonomous capabilities incrementally, as demonstrated by Enhanced Autonomous Navigation on Perseverance [41].

Foundation models alter what a surface robot can synthesize on site. Given equipment telemetry and visual observations, a foundation model can infer unmodelled fault causes and compose registered robot skills into repair sequences not authored prior to deployment [42, 23]. Yet runtime plan synthesis precludes pre-flight verification: a model may act on unsubstantiated assumptions or declare mission completion prematurely. Space-autonomy and safety-critical engineering address this assurance gap through trusted-AI frameworks [39] and runtime assurance architectures that isolate unverified high-level planners behind formal safety filters [21]. Existing uncertainty-aware foundation-model planners resolve ambiguity by querying a human operator [36], which presupposes immediate and continuous communication that is unavailable at a lunar pole. Sustained lunar-base autonomy requires combining the execution guarantees of authored flight executives with the open-world diagnostic flexibility of foundation models.

Three operational characteristics of lunar-base maintenance complicate this synthesis. First, certain operations are irreversible relative to the robot’s capabilities: removing a module from an energized unit permanently damages its connector, and handing over cargo at its destination cannot be undone autonomously. Second, facility state is only partially observable: inventory records drift from physical reality, and actuation effects can fail silently unless verified by measurement. Third, observation incurs mission time costs and visibility deadlines, most notably when requesting ground authorization before Earth sets. Consequently, when a rover receives plans from an untrusted foundation model, an execution policy must guarantee that no irreversible action executes on a false precondition, bound the sensing overhead required for safety, and preserve mission completion.

Contingent planning addresses partial observability with sensing actions [32, 22], and its online variants differ in how they act on unverified assumptions. Online contingent planners such as the K-replanner [6] and SDR [7], along with compilation-based methods [28], plan optimistically under assumed state values but act conservatively: every action requires verified preconditions prior to execution. Their completeness guarantees rely on accurate initial beliefs, deterministic effects and dead-end-free state spaces [6, 7]; recent extensions relax dead-end or unsafe-fact assumptions individually [38, 34]. Conversely, determinized replanners such as FF-Replan [45] and closed-loop foundation-model agents such as ReAct [44] act on unverified assumptions, which keeps execution overhead low and provides no safeguard before irreversible actions. Frameworks that pair foundation models with external formal critics [25] validate plan syntax and domain transitions offline without addressing online sensing costs, irreversibility or physical evidence. To our knowledge, no existing formulation jointly addresses erroneous records, stochastic action effects, irreversible operations and deadline-constrained sensing under an untrusted planner.

The central premise of this work is that optimistic and conservative acting rules suit distinct action classes: acting on assumption is appropriate when a false assumption incurs only a bounded time penalty, whereas acting on verified knowledge is mandatory when an effect cannot be undone (Fig. 1). The contributions of this paper are:

A formal model (Section 2) casting lunar-base maintenance and logistics as safety-constrained contingent planning across four departures from classical formulations: potentially erroneous records, failing effects evaluated by three-valued physical evidence, irreversible actions, and sensing with time costs and deadlines.

Asymmetric knowledge-level replanning (AKR, Section 3), an online execution algorithm wrapping an untrusted planner with three proved guarantees: no irreversible action on a false precondition under sound evidence for any planner or record (Theorem 1), per-decision sensing cost lower bounds for every sound knowledge-based policy (Theorem 2), and bounded episode termination in verified goal achievement or a certified hold for complete planners (Theorem 3).

Evidence that the guarantees hold in operation (Sections 4 and 5): AKR executed no hazardous action in any trial with sound observations of the main Monte Carlo grid or in any full-stack run, and it completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model, where the original PLEXIL and EUROPA→\rightarrowPLEXIL procedures completed none. The evaluation covers 254,000 mission-level Monte Carlo trials and 165 full-stack runs on sixteen maintenance and delivery missions, against the K-replanner and FF-Replan acting rules, PLEXIL and EUROPA→\rightarrowPLEXIL.

Section 2 formulates the planning model. Section 3 presents AKR and proves its theoretical guarantees. Section 4 details the rover instantiation and experimental protocol, Section 5 analyses the results, and Section 6 discusses on-board operation and scope.

title: Quantizing in the Loop: Drift-Aware Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Yanlong Chen,Thongthornpatch Chamadol,Yichen Guo,Yunfei Gao,Mohan Liu,Addison Lin Wang,Yawei Li
comment: The paper is currently under review. Code and models:this https URL
abstract:
Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths (≤\leq 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy’s own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, π0.5\pi_{0.5} still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit π0.5\pi_{0.5} runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1×\times smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at 

 github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [5, 17, 4, 27, 3] have become the standard recipe for generalist robot policies: a pretrained vision-language backbone, a flow-matching or diffusion transformer action head [20, 9], and several billion parameters evaluated many times per second on onboard hardware. While language models of this scale are routinely compressed to 2 bits per weight with modest loss [30, 10, 31], VLAs resist such extreme compression. Existing VLA quantizers stop at 4 bits or keep the action head in higher precision [36, 37, 1]; applying the strongest 2-bit quantizers across an entire VLA drops perturbed success by 4 to 62 points. Figure 1a illustrates this failure: from the same initial state and noise, the full-precision policy opens the drawer, whereas its 2-bit counterpart reaches for the upper drawer and stalls.

Why does a recipe that works for language models break a policy? Because a policy acts in closed loop: its outputs determine its next inputs. This single fact invalidates two core assumptions behind standard post-training quantizers, explaining both why they fail and how to fix them.

Quantization drift. Layer-wise quantizers minimize output error on static calibration data (human demonstration frames), pushing the unavoidable ultra-low-bit error into input directions that those frames never excite. While a language model rarely encounters this hidden error because its test and calibration distributions align, a closed-loop robot inevitably does: a 2-bit policy acts slightly differently from full precision, enters an unseen state, triggers the error hidden there, and deviates further. We term this self-reinforcing divergence quantization drift. Figure 1b traces it in a real episode, where the 2-bit end-effector leaves the reference path and never recovers. Across every VLA module, policy-induced states dominate the input distribution shift at deployment, accounting for 45% in the language model and up to 83% in the action head.

Readout corruption. Because the action head interacts with the backbone solely through attention readouts over backbone tokens, action generation depends not on raw weights, but on what the head reads. Ultra-low-bit quantization systematically displaces this interface, shifting the readout by a nearly constant offset at every step of an episode (Fig. 1c). The head is not reading a noisier copy of the same content; it is reading something else.

LoopQ translates both diagnoses into two steps atop a trellis-coded format [25, 31]. Closed-loop calibration quantizes every layer on the states the quantized policy itself visits, so the quantizer can no longer hide error where the policy will go; it requires a few hundred rollouts and no training. Readout-aligned fine-tuning then updates only a 512-entry lookup table and a scale vector per layer around the frozen codes, aligning the action head’s readouts with the full-precision model. Neither step alters the storage format, bit budget, or decoder.
The result is a VLA quantized end to end, across both backbone and action head, that behaves like the original (Fig. 1d). Without any training, closed-loop calibration alone outperforms the strongest post-training quantizer on LIBERO-Plus, reaching 73.4% vs. 72.6% on π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 57.5% vs. 55.9% on GR00T N1.7. Adding readout alignment brings the 2-bit policies to 74.9% and 60.4%, within 1.6 and 1.4 points of full precision, recovering three quarters of the degradation incurred by the best existing 2-bit quantizer on GR00T. Nor does our approach stop at 2 bits: at 1 bit per weight, π0.5\pi_{0.5} still completes 80.0% of LIBERO, far surpassing the 48.0% reported for 2-bit backbone-only quantization [1]. Finally, the compressed policy is directly deployable: with 8-bit activations, the 2-bit π0.5\pi_{0.5} executes on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor with 4.1×4.1\times smaller weights and 44% less memory (Fig. 1e). On a real AgileX Piper arm, the 2-bit policy succeeds in 58 of 75 trials, against 59 for full precision. Our contributions are:

A closed-loop diagnosis. We show that ultra-low-bit VLAs fail due to two phenomena rooted in closed-loop execution: quantization drift, caused by calibration statistics that miss policy-induced states, and readout corruption, a systematic displacement of the representations consumed by the action head under layer-wise objectives.

LoopQ. We propose closed-loop calibration to align calibration statistics with the policy’s own state distribution, outperforming the strongest post-training quantizers on two VLAs without any training, followed by readout-aligned fine-tuning, which optimizes only per-layer lookup tables and scales while keeping all stored codes and the decoder untouched.

End-to-end VLAs at 2 bits and below. We present the first VLAs with both backbone and action head quantized entirely to 2 bits that stay within two points of full precision under perturbation, while remaining functional policies even at 1 bit. Furthermore, we deploy the 2-bit policy on a physical AgileX Piper arm, demonstrating reliable closed-loop execution across three real-world manipulation tasks: precision stacking, two-stage lidded-bin lemon placement, and multi-object grasping in clutter, each within one success of full precision.

1. A closed-loop diagnosis. We show that ultra-low-bit VLAs fail due to two phenomena rooted in closed-loop execution: quantization drift, caused by calibration statistics that miss policy-induced states, and readout corruption, a systematic displacement of the representations consumed by the action head under layer-wise objectives.

2. LoopQ. We propose closed-loop calibration to align calibration statistics with the policy’s own state distribution, outperforming the strongest post-training quantizers on two VLAs without any training, followed by readout-aligned fine-tuning, which optimizes only per-layer lookup tables and scales while keeping all stored codes and the decoder untouched.

title: Confidently Lost: Silent Failure and Edge Deployment of Dense Visual SLAM under Photon Starvation
authors: Shrikrishna Bhagirath Rajule,Srinath Neelamagam,Aniket Bera
abstract: Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM’s network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1 605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism’s signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.
introduction:
A robot inspecting a tunnel at night needs a SLAM system that runs on the computer it carries, in the light it has. Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is the strongest candidate: MASt3R-SLAM [1] regresses dense pointmaps and descriptors from a foundation model and reconstructs without calibration in real time. But every quantitative result for this class of system is measured in good light, on the edge as throughput alone [2], or on the pairwise network alone under synthetic darkening [3]; whether it can be deployed in the dark on an edge computer was untested. This paper asks what happens when it is: the specific form its failure takes under photon starvation, the mechanism, the health signal that exposes the failure at no cost, what the available remedy buys and costs, and which of these carry to a Jetson AGX Orin on a legged robot.

The obvious remedy exists: Dark3R [4] adapts the same MASt3R backbone to photon-starved raw imagery by LoRA distillation [5], offline, where every image is available and geometry is globally optimized. SLAM is causal and must commit to a keyframe, a match and a pose now; whether a distilled low-light prior survives that transition was untested.

We find that it survives as behavior but not as geometry, and that the more interesting result is what happens to the system it was meant to fix. Loading Dark3R’s weights into MASt3R-SLAM, changing nothing else, takes usable trajectories on the ETH3D-SLAM dark sequences [6] from 1 of 6 to 5 of 6, usable being a workload criterion (≥50\geq 50 keyframes, a converging alignment), not an accuracy one: every dark trajectory has meter-scale error, and over 95% of the correspondences either model accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry (Sec. IV-B). Retuning two of the stock system’s gate thresholds also reaches 5 of 6 (Sec. IV-A), with the same wrong correspondences; no gate retuning leaves the degenerate regime at the shipped acceptance radius, and adaptation does. On sofa_dark_1 stock MASt3R-SLAM consumes 1 605 frames, emits 7 keyframes and reports 14.6 FPS, and every signal a deployment could monitor reads nominal: 0 skipped frames, 0 Cholesky failures, 0 relocalization attempts, no factor-graph edge rejected, a trajectory file the standard evaluation scores. It leaves a seven-keyframe map of a 1 605-frame walk (Fig. 1), silent to the system, to the evaluation protocol (an ATE over the keyframe file cannot tell a seven-keyframe map from a complete one) and to any downstream consumer.

The mechanism is a property of the network’s output at the matcher’s acceptance radius, not of any gate threshold. MASt3R-SLAM validates a correspondence by geometric self-consistency: a pixel carried through the network’s cross-view pointmap must land within 10 cm of the other view’s own pointmap. In near-darkness the two predictions become spuriously consistent, the network emits geometry that agrees with itself about a scene it cannot see, and validity reaches 0.93. The keyframe rule fires when its confident-match operand falls below 0.333; on the silent runs that operand’s median is 0.85–0.89, so the rule fires six times in 1 605 frames. Relocalization accepts a candidate when the same quantity rises above 0.3: on plant_dark it accepts 497 of 543 attempts, rejecting 21.5% of the edges they propose. One cause, two opposite symptoms, which we call the silent exit (starved keyframing at nominal FPS) and the loud exit (thrashing: unbounded relocalization onto wrong anchors).

The diagnosis yields a detector that costs no computation. Geometric match validity at keyframe-pair baselines, gg, is computed at every factor-graph edge, and across a 24-run grid on 8-bit ETH3D it separates the confident collapse from tracking operation with no overlap (Sec. IV-B). A spuriously high match rate is the alarm. It is a property of the system’s state, not of the input: on the same frames stock reads 0.929 and the adapted model 0.371. It does not certify the map that remains, and its healthy level is a property of the camera.

Our contributions are: (1) a mechanism, verified on held-out sequences and by per-gate intervention, for why dense learned SLAM fails silently in low light: the network does not lose confidence in the dark, it manufactures it, and the same number that starves keyframing makes relocalization accept everything; (2) a detector that needs no ground truth and no extra computation, with an operating point and its error rates over 66 labeled runs; (3) a controlled comparison of remedies, retuning, an enhancement front-end, weight adaptation and a training-free dose between stock and adapted weights, in which, at the shipped acceptance radius, only adaptation leaves the degenerate regime, and a partial dose removes its one measured good-light degeneracy while its ATE cost scales with the dose; (4) a scope test on a robot: on a Jetson AGX Orin (memory law, Orin NX ceiling, flat power) and a quadruped’s 8-bit camera over four routes, the mechanism’s signature reproduces on the two darkest routes, the adaptation covers a level stock loses on two of three turn-free routes, and which face of the fault appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding.

title: Toward Open Room-Scale Scanning with Consumer LiDAR via Depth-Inertial Odometry
authors: Minsuk Jang
abstract: Room scanning with consumer LiDAR today depends on ARKit, whose tracking and map update are a black box: an application receives depth and poses but cannot inspect how they were produced, so an error in a scan cannot be traced to its cause. This paper examines whether an open alternative, one whose every stage can be inspected, is feasible on the device. Mobile-LIO is a depth–inertial odometry pipeline that uses the phone’s depth and inertial data and no ARKit poses. On seven ScanNet++ iPhone recordings it completed every scene with 0.2–2.0 m deviation from the ARKit-derived reference, where six open LiDAR–inertial estimators run as configured for dedicated scanners had at least 4.46 m in 41 of 42 runs (two of the six also failed a noise-free adapter check, and Mobile-LIO has a speed cap they lack; the comparison is not controlled and does not rank algorithms). On an iPhone 15 Pro Max, a build with corrected phone code kept up with the sensor in 14 of 15 replay runs of three 7–13 s recordings; the dataset results use the estimator before those corrections. Laser-scanned meshes show how far this is from the closed pipeline. Within 3 m, recorded depth differed from the mesh by a median of 1–5 cm; on three held-out scenes, maps fused with ARKit poses that the dataset scales and aligns to the mesh lay a median 1.8–2.3 cm from it, and Mobile-LIO maps 8–17 cm. Because the pipeline is open, the gap could be examined: in the scene with the largest error, noise-free rendered depth cut the deviation from 1.97 m to 0.04 m, so recorded depth, whose error reached 20–54 cm at 5–7 m, contributed alongside the estimator. Open room-scale scanning on the device is therefore feasible but not yet as accurate as ARKit-pose maps, which themselves indicatively reach only the coarsest USIBD accuracy level (LOA10).
introduction:
Geometric digital twins of buildings lose value unless their geometry is reacquired as the asset changes (Osadcha et al. 2023; Davletshina et al. 2026). Terrestrial laser scanning delivers the accuracy that scan-to-BIM needs, but each update is costly. In one comparison over about 350 m2 of indoor space, a terrestrial scanning and manual modeling workflow took 20 h and a tablet-based workflow 32 min, with larger geometric discrepancies (Ersoz and Bosché 2026). Low-cost, repeatable capture is therefore attractive.

Studies in geomatics, geoscience, and civil engineering have evaluated the output of LiDAR-equipped iPhones and iPads for indoor mapping and building documentation (Teo and Yang 2023; Askar and Sternberg 2023; Abdel-Majeed et al. 2024; Treccani et al. 2024) and for geoscience surveys (Luetzenburg et al. 2021). The pose tracking and map update behind these outputs belong to the proprietary ARKit framework, which exposes depth, confidence, and camera pose but not its internal decisions. When an export shows depth smeared across object edges or a corridor loop that does not close (Jang and Yu 2026), the user cannot trace the error to a stage.

An application-level accuracy number therefore mixes the error of the depth sensor, the error of the estimated pose, and the choices of the fusion software. Open-source LiDAR–inertial odometry (LIO), which estimates the pose of a moving device from range and motion sensors, offers inspectable estimation, yet representative systems are designed for dedicated scanners (Xu et al. 2022; Chen et al. 2023). Smartphone depth is a different observation regime: a 256 ×\times 192 depth image with a three-level confidence map and no per-point timing.

This paper examines whether room-scale scanning is feasible with an open pipeline, meaning one whose every stage is specified and can be inspected, and measures how far such a pipeline is from the closed one by separating those terms. It makes five contributions: (1) a measurement of recorded iPhone depth error against a laser-scanned mesh as a function of range; (2) an error budget on the same recordings, giving the surface error when the same depth is fused with mesh-aligned ARKit poses and with the poses of Mobile-LIO, an inspectable depth–inertial pipeline whose settings are listed in the Appendix, and the deviation of Mobile-LIO from that ARKit-derived reference; (3) a controlled experiment, made possible by the inspectable pipeline, that fixes the estimator and varies only the depth input; (4) a comparison with six open LiDAR–inertial estimators on the same input; and (5) supporting checks: an on-device replay before and after code corrections and qualitative scans exported by the phone application. The results are related to the accuracy levels used to specify building documentation. The scope is single indoor scenes and local estimation without loop closure (the correction of drift when a route returns to a known place); on-device evidence comes from three short recordings of one room replayed on one phone (timing and agreement with ARKit over a few seconds), qualitative scans exported by the phone application, and one corridor compared with a scanner map; it is separate from the held-out evaluation.

title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading
authors: Tianle Zeng,Hanjing Ye,Bingyi Xia,Yuchen Zhou,Zibo Zhang,Yufei Huang,Yonggen Ling,Hong Zhang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Abstract:
Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower.
Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response.
We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation.
To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes.
LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning.
introduction:
Robot leading is an active human–robot navigation task in which a robot guides a designated follower along an intended route to a target destination, with applications in airports, retail spaces, campuses, and other public environments.
During leading, the follower may slow down, stop, fall behind, become temporarily unobservable, or briefly disengage, requiring the robot to adapt without losing the intended route.
The task therefore requires both reliable route execution and responsive human–robot interaction.

Existing robot-leading systems have made substantial progress on both aspects.
Classical methods typically rely on explicit geometric representations, interaction rules, and planning logic [1, 2, 3], while learning-based approaches increasingly learn follower dynamics or guiding behavior from data [4, 5].
More recently, foundation models have introduced richer language grounding and semantic understanding [6, 7, 8], yet follower understanding and physical route execution are still often connected through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces [9].
In contrast, people naturally adjust their pace and local motion to a follower while preserving the intended route.
This motivates a direct embodied learning question: can a robot learn a unified policy that executes a given route while adapting its actions to a designated follower?

A natural intuition is to predict the complete leading trajectory end-to-end from route, visual, and language inputs.
However, we observe that this direct formulation can entangle route execution with follower response: changes in follower behavior that should mainly affect execution may also distort the underlying route geometry.
This motivates a simple structured formulation: preserve the route as a stable execution reference while learning how to adapt its execution to the follower and local scene.
Based on this idea, we introduce LeadVLA, which uses the given route as an explicit Path reference, a learned Pace to regulate progress along it, and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation.

Learning follower-aware route execution at scale also requires suitable training supervision and closed-loop evaluation.
Existing public resources do not yet jointly provide scalable action-level supervision and standardized evaluation tailored to this setting [10, 7, 11].
We therefore develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based infrastructure that composes diverse routes, scenes, follower behaviors, and single- or multi-person configurations into closed-loop robot-leading episodes, together with LeadBench, a standardized closed-loop benchmark.
For this work, we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus with LeadInfra and evaluate on 108 fully held-out LeadBench episodes from disjoint environments, routes, actors, and scene instantiations under the same task definition and interaction contract.

On LeadBench, LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness.
Real-world closed-loop experiments further show transfer to unseen environments without real-world policy fine-tuning.
Our main contributions are:

(1) We formulate robot leading as a follower-aware route-execution problem and introduce LeadVLA, which preserves the route as a stable execution reference while learning follower-aware adaptation.

(2) We develop LeadInfra and LeadBench, providing scalable closed-loop interaction supervision and standardized evaluation for follower-aware robot leading.

(3) We validate the formulation through controlled closed-loop experiments and real-robot deployment, and will release LeadVLA checkpoints, LeadInfra, and LeadBench to support continued research.

title: Value function based Reward shaping for safety in quadrupeds
authors: Janani S K,Manan Tayal,Shishir N.Y Kolathaya
abstract:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has progressed
from simple control tasks to complex real-world challenges with
large state spaces. While RL excels in these tasks, training time
remains a limitation. Reward shaping is a popular solution,
but existing methods often rely on value functions, which face
scalability issues. This paper presents a novel safety-oriented
reward-shaping framework inspired by barrier functions, offering simplicity and ease of implementation across various
environments and tasks. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed reward formulations, we conduct simulation experiments on the Unitree Go1 quadruped robot in Isaacgym. The policy was better than the existing baselines and reduced safety violations from 27%27\% to 0.1%0.1\% without almost any compromise on the performance.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has moved from simple control benchmarks to high-dimensional, real-world problems, and legged locomotion is one of its clearest successes. Policies trained in simulation now let quadrupeds walk, run and climb across varied terrain, including stairs and uneven ground [1]. In these settings the reward function does most of the work. It specifies task objectives such as velocity tracking, and also regularisers such as joint power, action rate and smoothness. The resulting policies are optimised for expected return, but nothing in the reward guarantees that the robot stays within its safe operating limits. On hardware, joint angles that exceed their limits can damage the actuators and the robot.

A common way to enforce such limits is to clip the actions or joint targets. Clipping is simple, but it acts only at the output of the policy and gives the learner no signal about how close it is to the boundary and also it doesn’t guarantee that performance will be maintained. The policy therefore keeps operating at the edge of the safe set, and clipping alone produced safety violations in 27%27\% of our test steps. Safety can instead be built into the reward through reward shaping. Many shaping schemes depend on learned value functions, which are hard to scale to high-dimensional state spaces and make the shaping term difficult to implement and tune.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) offer a principled alternative. A CBF defines a safe set as the superlevel set of a function l⁡(x)l(x) and requires l˙​(x)+κ⁡(l⁡(x))≥0\dot{l}(x)+\kappa(l(x))\geq 0, which makes the set forward invariant. This condition can be turned directly into a reward term. Hand-designed CBFs have two weaknesses. They are reactive, so they only guarantee safety one step ahead and do not account for control-input constraints.Using CBFs in the QP formulation completely overwrites the performance controller and thus there is no guarantee on the performance of the system. They also need the system dynamics, which are rarely available in closed form for legged robots. Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability addresses the first weakness: the safe value function it computes is a valid barrier function that accounts for future behavior under input constraints [2]. However, for solving the HJ equation still system dynamics is needed. Recently, value-guided offline control barrier functions (V-OCBF) [3] learn this kind of safe value function directly from offline transition data {xt,ut,xt+1}\{x_{t},u_{t},x_{t+1}\} and the safe set function l⁡(x)l(x) with no knowledge of the dynamics.

In this paper we bring these ideas together into a safety-oriented reward-shaping framework for quadruped locomotion. We consider box constraints of the form xmin≤x≤xmaxx_{\min}\leq x\leq x_{\max} on the joint angles. We first construct a smooth barrier function for each joint and then learn a V-OCBF safe value function BψjB_{\psi}^{j} for each joint from data collected with random actions. The per-joint values are combined with a softmin, which keeps the result differentiable, and the final barrier Bψ​(s)B_{\psi}(s) is used to shape the reward through

title: RoboThink: Let the Agent Think, Let the Policy Act
authors: Yunbei Zhang,Zijian Jin,Janet Wang,Xingchen Zhao,Zhenyu Zhang,Weirui Ye,Yilun Du

abstract:
Robot policies act in real time but fail without knowing why, whereas a reasoning agent that watches the robot can
often tell what went wrong. Existing systems either hand the agent control, which takes minutes per episode, or let it
send instructions. Yet a policy follows a new instruction only from a fresh start, since a half-finished task leaves
it in states outside its training data. Nor can an instruction fix how the robot moves. If a small drift on its motion commands keeps pulling the hand to the left, feedback such as “push right, slightly” is not a task the policy has learned to follow. We propose RoboThink,
in which the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent’s guidance. An instruction channel tells the
policy what to do. When the user says “the milk, not the butter” after the robot has started, the agent rewrites the instruction and the robot undoes its own motion, with no training. A feedback channel tells it how to move. It is taught
from the agent alone with agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens and counterfactual feedback, and is read only by the
policy’s action module. On LIBERO, RoboThink with Claude Opus 5.5 raises success from 0.09 to 0.87 under an unknown
constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one. It also completes misheard and changed requests in 0.91 to
1.00 of the episodes. GPT-6 Astra, the strongest agent we tested, needs 2.1 min per success and over a million tokens
per episode when acting alone, whereas RoboThink needs 55 s and 8 k tokens. The same recipe works across
policies, for both vision-language-action models and world action models, and across robots, from one arm to two arms
and a mobile manipulator. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with two arms, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 under the
constant drift and from 0.31 to 0.56 under the random one. Finally, the agent is a plug-in. A policy taught by one
agent works with other agents, including open-weight ones, and grows stronger with a stronger agent, without
retraining.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) [4, 18, 3, 30, 28] and
world action models (WAMs) [8, 21, 45, 17, 37, 39]
map camera images and an instruction to chunks of actions in real time. However, outside their training conditions
they fail without knowing why. At deployment, two things can go wrong. The execution can drift away from a correct
plan. Asked to pick up the orange juice, the policy plans the right motion, yet a small unknown drift on every motion
command, which we call a drift, keeps pushing the hand away from the bottle (Fig. 3a). The policy can also
pursue the wrong goal, because the instruction it acts on is not what the user wants. The user’s request may be worded unlike any training instruction, such as “the stove needs to be on now” for “turn on the stove”, and the policy often
misunderstands it. It may be misheard, so that the robot fetches the cream cheese when the user wanted the milk
(Fig. 3b). Or the user may change their mind after the robot has started (“the milk, not the butter”). In
both cases, a reasoning agent that watches the robot, such as a vision-language model (VLM), can detect the failure
and explain its cause [9, 14, 34] (Fig. 1).

How should a robot policy and a reasoning agent work together? Existing systems take one of three routes. The agent
can take over and control the robot through code or tool calls [22, 6, 15]. This can
handle both a wrong execution and a wrong goal, but at a high cost. In our experiments, GPT-6 Astra acting alone needs
2.1 min per success and over a million tokens per episode. On RoboDojo, it spends 8.6 minutes per episode [15]. The agent can instead instruct the
policy [1, 14, 33]. A new instruction fixes a wrong goal, but the
policy can follow it only from familiar states, not from the middle of the wrong task. Given the corrected task after
three chunks, a trained WAM completes it in only 0.07 of the episodes. Moreover, a wrong execution cannot be fixed this way at all, because “push right, slightly” is not a task. Appending such a correction to the prompt of a strong WAM [39] even lowers its success under a random drift from 0.42 to 0.16. Finally, reasoning can be trained into the policy [43, 26], but this locks it into the weights, preventing the policy from correcting a drift it has not seen (Appendix E) or improving with a stronger agent. In short, each route either gives up the policy’s speed or cannot pass the agent’s understanding of what went wrong to the policy.

Our key insight is that the agent and the policy complement each other. The policy knows how to act but cannot see why it fails, whereas the agent sees why but acts too slowly. Existing routes do not play to these strengths. They either make the agent act or the policy reason, or they let the agent speak to the policy in words the policy cannot act on. The difficulty lies in the policy, not the agent. A policy is trained only to follow task instructions. It therefore cannot follow feedback on how to correct its motion, since it has never learned what such feedback means. What is missing is a channel through which the policy learns to understand what the agent tells it. To this end, we propose RoboThink, where the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent’s guidance (Fig. 1). The agent is called only every few chunks, as a bias on the motion commands or the user’s request usually persists from one chunk to the next, and between calls the policy acts in real time on the agent’s latest guidance. This guidance reaches the policy through two channels, one for a wrong goal and one for a wrong execution.

The instruction channel [INST] fixes a wrong goal by telling the policy what to do. The agent knows the user’s request and checks whether the instruction that the policy acts on aligns with it. If the request is worded unclearly, the agent rewrites it as a plain instruction, such as “turn on the stove” for “the stove needs to be on now”. If the request was misheard or changed, the agent writes the correct one, such as “put the milk in the basket” when the robot was told the cream cheese. A corrected instruction alone is not enough once the robot has started on the wrong task, since the policy can follow it only from familiar states. The robot therefore first retraces its own motion back to such a state and then acts on the new instruction, which we call undo before redo. This channel needs no training and works with any policy.

The feedback channel [FB] fixes a wrong execution by telling the policy how to move. It carries the agent’s estimate of the drift, such as “push right, slightly”. Unlike the instruction channel, it must be learned, since the policy has never seen such feedback, and we teach the policy to read it from the agent alone (Fig. 2). With agent-labelled DAgger [31], we run the policy on training tasks under drift. The robot executes the policy’s plan, corrected by the agent for the drift it estimates, and these corrected plans become the training targets, so the true drift is never needed. Learned role tokens keep the feedback separate from the instruction. Counterfactual feedback pairs the same state with different feedback and different corrected plans, so that the policy cannot guess the plan from the state and must learn to read the feedback. Finally, only the policy’s action module reads the feedback, while its world module keeps reading the task alone. The world module imagines how the scene will unfold from the task, and feedback there distorts what it imagines. The action module turns this imagined future into motion, so it is where a correction belongs.

We evaluate RoboThink with two WAMs and a VLA, and with ten proprietary and open-weight agents, in three simulators. On LIBERO [23], we test unknown drifts, reworded, misheard and changed requests, and perturbed scenes [10, 16, 42]. On RoboTwin 2.0 [5], the policy controls two arms in joint space, and on RoboCasa [27], a mobile manipulator works in unseen kitchens. Our contributions are threefold:

RoboThink, a way for a robot policy and a reasoning agent to work together, in which the agent thinks and the policy acts. The agent’s guidance reaches the policy through an instruction channel, which fixes a wrong goal with undo before redo and needs no training, and a feedback channel, which fixes a wrong execution.

A recipe that teaches the feedback channel from the agent alone, and the finding that the feedback must reach the action module, not the world module. The recipe needs neither the true drift nor human labels, works from about a hundred agent-labelled episodes, and carries over to a VLA, a second WAM, two arms and a mobile manipulator.

Evidence across three policies, three simulators and ten agents. On LIBERO, success rises from 0.09 to 0.87 under a constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one, and misheard or changed requests are completed in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 and from 0.31 to 0.56. RoboThink succeeds at least as often as the strongest agent acting alone, in 55 s instead of 2.1 min per success. Its success grows with the accuracy of the agent, so a policy trained once improves as reasoning agents improve.

1. RoboThink, a way for a robot policy and a reasoning agent to work together, in which the agent thinks and the policy acts. The agent’s guidance reaches the policy through an instruction channel, which fixes a wrong goal with undo before redo and needs no training, and a feedback channel, which fixes a wrong execution.

2. A recipe that teaches the feedback channel from the agent alone, and the finding that the feedback must reach the action module, not the world module. The recipe needs neither the true drift nor human labels, works from about a hundred agent-labelled episodes, and carries over to a VLA, a second WAM, two arms and a mobile manipulator.

3. Evidence across three policies, three simulators and ten agents. On LIBERO, success rises from 0.09 to 0.87 under a constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one, and misheard or changed requests are completed in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 and from 0.31 to 0.56. RoboThink succeeds at least as often as the strongest agent acting alone, in 55 s instead of 2.1 min per success. Its success grows with the accuracy of the agent, so a policy trained once improves as reasoning agents improve.

title: Agent on Guard: Self-Improving Runtime Intervention for Robust Robotic Manipulation
authors: Gengming Cui,Mingfei Han,Jiawei Zhang,Mozheng Liao,Yunkai Guo,Minghao Jin,Tingwen Du,Salman Khan,Xiaojun Chang,Zhihui Li
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) learn reusable manipulation skills from large-scale data [17, 34, 48]. Adapting these skills to new task constraints, changing scenes, and execution errors remains challenging [3, 38]. Programming agents interpret goals, compose control programs, and revise them through execution feedback [20, 13, 8], while reliable grasping and fine contact control remain bottlenecks [19, 9]. Physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) retains and revises programs, skills, and decision rules from physical experience [44, 42]. These complementary strengths raise the question of how agent reasoning and program adaptation can extend the policy’s capabilities while preserving its reliable execution.

Existing physical RSI systems remain constrained in when they can revise execution plans and control decisions as physical conditions change. Physical RSI 1.0 [29] selects a skill composition at the start of each episode and keeps it bound throughout execution. EmbodiedEvo [19] and ASPIRE [25] organize observation, execution, and verification into discrete interaction rounds, with decision updates tied to round boundaries. A correction derived from an earlier observation may no longer suit the state in which it takes effect, while a locally successful repair may consume the time needed for subsequent execution. Control allocation must therefore evolve with recovery capabilities, accounting for when a recovery remains feasible and whether it leaves sufficient time for subsequent execution.

We introduce AoG, a self-improving harness that enables a programming agent to monitor and assist a frozen robot policy throughout execution (Fig. 1a). An evolving planner allocates control according to the physical state and the time available for recovery and task completion. Coupled inner RSI loops refine when to intervene, how to recover, and when the policy can resume. The agent learns from what happens after recovery, using complete trajectories to refine both the planner and the inner loops. Recovery capabilities and control allocation thus evolve together: improved recovery changes the planner’s choices, while the resulting execution provides new experience for refining both.
On RoboDojo-Sim [3], AoG achieves a success rate of 50.57% and a task score of 57.26, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline, WorldScape-R2SI [28], by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, respectively. Figure 1c presents the comparison
across five task categories. It also achieves the lowest end-to-end episode latency and online token consumption among the evaluated methods (Fig. 1b), reducing them by 80.4% and 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent [51].
Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce AoG, a physical RSI framework that learns when to intervene, how to recover, and when to return control to a frozen policy under physical time constraints.

We develop a mechanism that jointly evolves control allocation and recovery programs from complete trajectories, learning how the agent can complement a frozen policy and restore conditions for continued task execution.

AoG improves success rate and task score over the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, while reducing end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent.

1. We introduce AoG, a physical RSI framework that learns when to intervene, how to recover, and when to return control to a frozen policy under physical time constraints.

2. We develop a mechanism that jointly evolves control allocation and recovery programs from complete trajectories, learning how the agent can complement a frozen policy and restore conditions for continued task execution.

3. AoG improves success rate and task score over the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, while reducing end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent.

title: Policy-intrinsic Demonstration Curation
authors: Sunjae Jeong,Geunhyeok Yu,Dowoon Lee,Hyoseok Hwang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: (including of references and of appendices), 5 figures, 7 tables
abstract:
Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available.
Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates.
Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations.
Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score.
Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy.
However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time.
We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time.
It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training.
We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors).
It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations.
PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation.
Its selection is also stable across seeds.
introduction:
Robot policies are pretrained on large and diverse collections of demonstrations [25, 12, 30] and then fine-tuned for new target tasks [24, 13, 3, 2].
Fine-tuning requires demonstrations of each target task, which we call target demonstrations.
Each of them is recorded by a human operator who guides the robot, so only a few are available.
Far more demonstrations have already been recorded for other tasks, and adding these candidates to the target demonstrations can fill this gap.
However, Figure 1 shows that adding all of them can even lower the success rate, and so can adding a random subset.
This is because only some candidates are useful for the target tasks, while others are unrelated to them or even conflict with them.
Demonstration curation therefore selects the useful candidates, and its result depends on how their usefulness is measured.

Existing methods measure this usefulness in one of two ways (Figure 2), and the basic approach is to measure it by similarity.
Retrieval-based methods [6, 18, 22] select the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations in the feature space of a separate model.
Their premise is that a candidate that resembles the target demonstrations is also useful for the target tasks.
However, this similarity does not depend on the policy, so a similar candidate receives a high score even when training on it harms the policy.
For example, a candidate from the scene of a target task looks similar even when its action differs from that of the target demonstrations.
Training on such a candidate can move the prediction of the policy away from the target action.
Similarity alone is therefore not enough to determine whether a candidate helps the policy.

Performance-aware methods [16, 5, 34] instead score a candidate by its effect on the policy, that is, by how training on the candidate would change the policy.
They estimate this effect with tools from data attribution [14, 28, 11], which relate the behavior of a trained model to its training data.
This estimate, however, is itself obtained by training.
A policy is typically first trained on the candidates, and a backward pass is then run for every candidate to obtain its gradient.
Curation thus becomes a training run of its own, which takes a long time.
Its selection also changes with the random seed of this run.
In effect, these methods train a policy to determine where training will lead it.

We start from the observation that this need not be determined by training.
On every demonstration, the pretrained policy makes an error that points from its predicted action to the demonstrated action.
To first order, a training step moves the prediction along this error, so the error shows in advance where training will lead the policy.
On the target demonstrations, these errors show what the policy has yet to learn, and we call them the target errors.
The errors on a candidate can therefore be compared with the target errors.
The comparison indicates whether this candidate would move the policy toward what it has yet to learn.
All of these errors are obtained from forward passes, in which the pretrained policy is evaluated but not updated.

This observation leads to a third branch of curation, which we call policy-intrinsic curation because all of its evidence comes from the pretrained policy itself.
A policy-intrinsic method scores a candidate by its effect on the policy, as performance-aware methods do.
Unlike them, it estimates this effect from forward passes of the pretrained policy alone.
It trains no model and computes no gradient, so curation takes little time.
Policy-intrinsic curation thus combines the strengths of both existing branches (Figure 1).

We instantiate this branch with PICKER.
We call a candidate useful for a target demonstration when the policy represents their states similarly and makes errors in the same direction on both.
The first condition matters because training on a candidate changes the prediction mainly in states that the policy represents similarly.
However, it is not obvious that forward passes suffice, because the effect of one demonstration on another is given by their gradient alignment.
This alignment is the inner product of their gradients.
We show that, at the layer that reads the observation, it separates into one term in the observation representations and one in the errors.
PICKER estimates both terms with forward passes and selects the candidates whose errors agree best with the target errors.

Our contributions are as follows:

We propose policy-intrinsic curation, a third branch of demonstration curation that estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy from forward passes alone.

We present PICKER, which derives a forward-only score from gradient alignment and selects the candidates whose errors agree with the target errors.

On three benchmarks, PICKER reaches the success rates of performance-aware curation at the cost of retrieval-based curation. Its selection is stable across seeds.

1. We propose policy-intrinsic curation, a third branch of demonstration curation that estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy from forward passes alone.

2. We present PICKER, which derives a forward-only score from gradient alignment and selects the candidates whose errors agree with the target errors.

3. On three benchmarks, PICKER reaches the success rates of performance-aware curation at the cost of retrieval-based curation. Its selection is stable across seeds.

title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
authors: Zikang Wen,Yuning Zhang,Dong Yuan
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision–language–action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot’s execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv’s WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model’s lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
introduction:
Robotic arms are widely deployed across automotive, electronics, and general manufacturing to perform diverse manipulation tasks (Keshvarparast et al., 2024). A single automotive spot-welding operation can involve 42 robots across 13 workstations (Lopes et al., 2017). Vision–language–action (VLA) models offer a common foundation for manipulation, mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions and supporting adaptation to new robot settings through fine-tuning (Kim et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2025a). A fleet performing different tasks may therefore require multiple fine-tuned variants of a common VLA. As the fleet grows, serving these variants with a dedicated GPU for each robot becomes increasingly costly, motivating centralized inference on a shared GPU server. On a shared server, however, hosting each variant as a separate model instance duplicates backbone weights and splits requests across instances that cannot be batched together (Sheng et al., 2024). Because these variants originate from the same VLA, fine-tuning them with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) resolves both issues. Each variant then becomes a lightweight adapter over one shared frozen backbone, which reduces model-weight memory and allows requests for different policies to be batched together (Hu et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2025b).

A growing body of multi-LoRA serving work provides the machinery for this sharing. S-LoRA and Punica batch requests that target different adapters over a common language-model backbone (Sheng et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024), and dLoRA further improves efficiency through dynamic adapter merging and request placement (Wu et al., 2024). Batching nevertheless trades latency for throughput. Larger batches amortize computation, yet accumulating requests and executing larger batches both lengthen response latency (Crankshaw et al., 2017). For robots, this latency carries a direct physical cost. A robot whose action buffer runs out before new actions arrive must pause, interrupting task progress (Black et al., 2025). Robot serving thus cannot trade latency for throughput freely. The time remaining in each robot’s buffer defines a time budget for serving its next request. This budget differs across robots and shrinks as execution proceeds. Existing multi-LoRA serving systems do not consider such execution-dependent budgets when deciding which requests to batch and when to dispatch them.

Unlike application-defined latency targets in conventional model serving, the time available for robot inference depends on ongoing physical execution and observation timing. With action chunking, each inference produces a sequence of future actions, allowing a robot to observe and request its next chunk before completing the current one while continuing to execute buffered actions (Black et al., 2025). We term the remaining buffered execution time at request generation execution slack. This slack defines the time available for communication, queueing, inference, and result delivery before the robot stalls. Observing earlier leaves more slack for serving, but replanning from an intermediate motion state can disrupt execution and reduce task success (Black et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2026). Observing later reduces the risk of premature replanning but leaves less time for batching. Efficient multi-robot VLA serving therefore requires coordinating two coupled decisions: when each robot observes and how the server batches requests within the resulting execution budgets.

To balance timely robot updates with efficient GPU batching, we propose MotionServe, a multi-LoRA VLA serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with batch formation through execution slack. Its Motion-Guided Pipelined Action Execution (MotionExec) selects observation triggers from predicted motion structure, allowing robots to request new actions while they continue executing buffered actions. Its Slack-Driven Asynchronous Batching (SlackBatch) combines each robot’s remaining slack with estimated outstanding GPU work to decide how long to defer dispatch and which requests to include. Together, these mechanisms enable independent robot updates and cross-policy batching on a shared backbone. With 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU, MotionServe reduces mean stall by 43.4% on X-VLA and 32.6% on OpenVLA-OFT and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points over each model’s lowest-stall baseline. MotionServe also achieves the highest throughput at every fleet size, and backbone sharing reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 91.1–97.6%. Our contributions are:

We propose MotionServe, a framework that brings multi-LoRA serving to multi-robot VLA deployment while exploiting robot execution slack to coordinate observation timing with batch formation. It hosts each robot’s policy as an adapter over one shared VLA backbone and batches action-chunk requests across adapters.

We develop MotionExec, a motion-guided Pipelined action execution mechanism that selects observation triggers from predicted action chunks while overlapping inference with buffered execution.

We develop SlackBatch, a slack-driven scheduler that uses each robot’s execution slack and outstanding GPU work to adapt batch dispatch timing and request selection.

1. We propose MotionServe, a framework that brings multi-LoRA serving to multi-robot VLA deployment while exploiting robot execution slack to coordinate observation timing with batch formation. It hosts each robot’s policy as an adapter over one shared VLA backbone and batches action-chunk requests across adapters.

2. We develop MotionExec, a motion-guided Pipelined action execution mechanism that selects observation triggers from predicted action chunks while overlapping inference with buffered execution.

3. We develop SlackBatch, a slack-driven scheduler that uses each robot’s execution slack and outstanding GPU work to adapt batch dispatch timing and request selection.
