title: PushMimic: Learning Adaptive Humanoid Box Pushing via Dynamic Motion Augmentation and Reference Distillation
authors: Yulun Zhuang,Hanyu Zhang,Jingyu Liu,Yanran Ding
abstract:
Humanoid box pushing is challenging when the physical properties of the task, such as the box mass and the ramp inclination, are unknown before the push begins.
This paper presents PushMimic, a framework that learns adaptive humanoid box pushing from a single level-ground kinematic reference motion.
The learned policy adapts its pushing posture to these properties without observing them.
PushMimic augments the reference motion into a dynamically feasible motion dataset over these properties with sampling-based trajectory optimization, and distills the dataset into one motion tracking policy in one stage of training.
Simulation results over box masses from 55 to 15​kg15~\mathrm{kg} and ramp inclinations up to 15∘15^{\circ} show that PushMimic raises the success rate from 57.8%57.8\% to 88.8%88.8\% compared with a baseline that tracks the original reference motion.
It also reduces the cost of push of the arms by 22%22\%.
Hardware experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid show that the policy adapts its torso pitch during continuous pushing on an inclined treadmill, with box masses up to 19​kg19~\mathrm{kg} and ramp inclinations up to 12.6∘12.6^{\circ}.
PushMimic therefore needs only one reference motion, instead of one for every box mass and ramp inclination.
introduction:
Humanoid robots are increasingly used in repetitive and physically demanding loco-manipulation tasks in manufacturing and logistics, such as sorting parcels and relocating boxes [1, 2, 3], mostly in structured factory settings. However, pushing a large box is still challenging, since the physical properties of the task, such as the box mass, the friction, and the ground inclination, are unknown to the robot before the push begins and vary from one task to another. For example, pushing a box up a ramp requires the robot to lean its torso further forward than on level ground. A human adjusts this posture through the interaction with the box after the push begins. A humanoid robot that keeps the same posture for every task consumes more energy and can fail to deliver the box accurately. Therefore, the humanoid robot should also adapt its posture during the push through the interaction with the box.

Existing solutions for humanoid box pushing are often based on reinforcement learning (RL), either from task rewards [4, 3, 5, 6] or by tracking human reference motions [7, 8, 9, 10, 11] retargeted from motion capture datasets [12, 13, 14].
A task reward alone allows many feasible ways to push a box, such as different gaits and different body parts in contact with the box.
Choosing one of them through reward design is not intuitive and requires much trial and error.
A human reference motion specifies the gait and the contacts together, so tracking it is a practical alternative [15].
However, the available human pushing motions are few and recorded on level ground [14, 1].
Recording one motion for every combination of the physical properties of the task, denoted as task parameters, is impractical.
Therefore, a practical setting is to start from one level-ground pushing motion, denoted as the nominal reference motion, and derive the reference motions for the other task parameters from it.
The problem is then to learn, from the nominal reference motion, one policy that pushes the box over a range of task parameters and adapts its posture without observing them.

Policies trained from task rewards alone can adapt the pushing force to the task.
FALCON [4] applies increasing external forces at the end effectors during training to learn a force-adaptive whole-body controller.
VOFA [3] builds on FALCON and combines the force-adaptive controller with a visual goal policy to push objects of unknown mass and friction.
FACET [6] tracks a virtual impedance reference, and force control policies [16, 17] estimate the external force from the state history without a force sensor.
However, in these methods, the posture comes from the reward rather than from human motion.
The same holds when the pushing behavior comes from a planning cost [18] or when the policy imitates only part of a reference motion [19].
Choosing the pushing posture therefore remains a reward or cost design problem.
Policies that track a human reference motion take the posture from the reference instead.
This approach has enabled humanoids to carry, push, and stack boxes and to interact with other objects [2, 1, 10, 11, 20].
However, the reference motion is recorded under one task parameter.
Other task parameters are usually covered by domain randomization during training, so the policy keeps the recorded posture for all of them.
Therefore, neither family provides a posture that both follows human motion and adapts to the task parameter.

A reference motion for a new task parameter does not have to be recorded, since recent works generate new reference motions from existing ones.
Motion generators sample them from a learned motion distribution [22, 15].
OmniRetarget [20] re-solves the kinematic retargeting of one reference motion for new object and terrain configurations.
AdaMimic [23] edits the keyframes of one reference motion for a new task parameter and leaves the rest to a motion tracking policy.
However, these methods work at the kinematic level, and the dynamics is only considered when the motion tracking policy is trained.
In box pushing, the task parameters change the posture through the contact forces.
For example, a steeper ramp makes the torso lean further forward and moves the feet further back.
Kinematic methods do not model these forces, so they cannot predict how the posture should change with the task parameters.
Therefore, the reference motions for new task parameters should be generated with the dynamics of the robot and the box.

Dynamically feasible retargeting can generate such reference motions.
It optimizes a control sequence that tracks a kinematic reference motion in a physics simulator, so the resulting motion accounts for the contact forces.
SPIDER [24] guides the sampling with virtual contacts, DynaRetarget [21] optimizes the full motion through expanding horizons, and contact-implicit shooting [25] embeds a differentiable simulation in a nonlinear program.
These methods are mostly used to make a reference motion dynamically feasible under the task parameter at which it was recorded.
DynaRetarget has also augmented one reference motion for objects of different masses and shapes.
Therefore, running the same optimization under a new task parameter gives a dynamically feasible motion that stays close to the nominal reference motion.
Such a motion can serve as the reference motion for that task parameter.

Given a reference motion for each task parameter, one policy still has to follow the reference motion of the current task parameter without observing the task parameter.
This can be achieved by decoupling the observation from the reward, so that the reward tracks a reference motion that the policy does not observe.
Similar decoupling is common in motion imitation, where the reward contains more information about the reference than the policy observes [26, 27, 6].
SoftMimic [28] uses this idea to learn compliance.
It generates compliant responses to external forces from one motion clip with an inverse kinematics model, and rewards the policy for matching these responses while the policy observes only the nominal motion.
Since the policy does not observe which response the reward expects, it learns to estimate the force from its state and to produce the matching response.
This decoupling works when the reward scores the correct response to the unobserved quantity, and when this quantity affects the state that the policy observes.
In box pushing, the reference motions generated for each task parameter give the target posture, and the response of the box to the push depends on the task parameter, as the force-adaptive policies show [4, 3, 6, 16, 17].
Therefore, the posture can be adapted to the task parameter without the task parameter as an input.

This paper presents PushMimic, a framework (Fig. 2) that augments the single level-ground nominal reference motion into an augmented motion dataset with one dynamically feasible reference motion for each task parameter (Section II), and distills this dataset into a single motion tracking policy in one stage of training, where the policy observes only the nominal reference motion (Section III).
In simulation on a Unitree G1 over a range of box masses and ramp inclinations, the policy adapts its posture to the box mass and the ramp inclination without observing them.
Compared with a policy that tracks only the nominal reference motion, it succeeds more often as the box gets heavier and the ramp steeper, and lowers the cost of push of the arms.
On the physical G1, the policy pushes a box continuously on an inclined treadmill and leans further forward as weights are added to the box during the push (Fig. 1).

The main contributions of this paper are:

A framework for adaptive humanoid box pushing from a single kinematic reference motion via dynamically feasible reference augmentation and one-stage policy distillation.

Extensive simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 over box masses from 55 to 15​kg15~\mathrm{kg} and ramp inclinations up to 15∘15^{\circ}, in which the proposed method raises the success rate from 57.8%57.8\% to 88.8%88.8\% compared with the vanilla baseline and lowers the cost of push of the arms by 22%22\%.

A sim-to-real transfer of the policy to the physical G1, which adapts its torso pitch during continuous pushing on an inclined treadmill as the box mass grows from 1010 to 19​kg19~\mathrm{kg} and as the ramp inclination rises from 0∘0^{\circ} to 12.6∘12.6^{\circ}.

1. A framework for adaptive humanoid box pushing from a single kinematic reference motion via dynamically feasible reference augmentation and one-stage policy distillation.

2. Extensive simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 over box masses from 55 to 15​kg15~\mathrm{kg} and ramp inclinations up to 15∘15^{\circ}, in which the proposed method raises the success rate from 57.8%57.8\% to 88.8%88.8\% compared with the vanilla baseline and lowers the cost of push of the arms by 22%22\%.

3. A sim-to-real transfer of the policy to the physical G1, which adapts its torso pitch during continuous pushing on an inclined treadmill as the box mass grows from 1010 to 19​kg19~\mathrm{kg} and as the ramp inclination rises from 0∘0^{\circ} to 12.6∘12.6^{\circ}.

title: HERO: Hierarchical Region-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Exploration
authors: Xulin Xiao,Shengyi Liang,Mingjie Zhang,Chengkai Wu,Chen Chen,Zhigang Li,Jinni Zhou,Jun Ma,Boyu Zhou
abstract: Autonomous exploration is widely used to map unknown environments, yet maintaining both path efficiency and low online computation remains difficult as environment scale increases. Hierarchical planners reduce global search through coarse regional representations but often rely on handcrafted local viewpoint-selection rules. Graph-based reinforcement learning can improve local decisions, but its inference cost grows with the exploration graph and global direction is usually represented only implicitly. To address these limitations, we present HERO, a hierarchical framework that assigns distinct responsibilities to global planning and learned local decision-making, enabling each level to focus on the function it is best suited to perform. To reduce the growing inference cost of graph-based policies, HERO restricts learned target selection to reachable candidates within the current region while using region-level planning to provide long-horizon guidance. To avoid informative targets causing excessive deviation from this global direction, the proposed Dual-Branch Graph Policy balances Frontier Utility with guidance toward the next region, improving both local exploration and global progress. Experiments on unseen 2D maps show the lowest overall mean path length and target-decision cost among the evaluated methods. MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites further demonstrate the framework’s applicability with LiDAR-based mapping and chassis dynamics.
introduction:
Autonomous exploration is essential for robots operating in unknown environments, underpinning applications like search-and-rescue and industrial inspection. The fundamental goal is to maximize map coverage while minimizing travel cost. However, achieving efficient exploration in large-scale environments remains a significant challenge. Extensive research therefore continues to investigate how to make effective exploration decisions with low computational overhead.

Despite extensive research, both classical and learning-based exploration methods face fundamental bottlenecks. Classical methods can provide deterministic, long-horizon global path that directs exploration toward complete coverage. However, their handcrafted rules struggle to adapt to diverse, complex environments. Conversely, reinforcement learning (RL) enables environment-adaptive target selection through data-driven training, which is effective within small, bounded regions. Yet as environment scale grows, exploration becomes a long-horizon task: rewards are sparse and delayed, each episode spans hundreds of sequential decisions before coverage completes, and the exploration graph grows continuously with the mapped area, making both training convergence and online inference increasingly costly. Without explicit global direction, RL decisions in unseen environments can drift from the overall coverage objective, accumulating unnecessary detours.

To resolve these complementary limitations, we present HERO, a hierarchical framework that establishes a novel division of labor between structured global planning and learned local decision-making. Our design assigns each layer the role it excels at. At the global level, an explicit region-level coverage plan provides long-horizon global guidance that end-to-end RL struggles to learn. At the local level, an RL policy performs environment-adaptive target selection within a bounded candidate graph, offering the adaptive flexibility that handcrafted rules lack. Restricting the graph locally keeps the policy inference cost bounded as the explored map grows. Meanwhile, the explicit global order relieves the policy from learning the entire exploration sequence, enabling it to focus strictly on balancing local frontier utility against global progress.

Realizing this hierarchy, however, is not straightforward. The first challenge is a gap between the two levels: the global planner specifies which region to visit next, but this region-level intent does not directly translate into actionable local decisions. The local policy must select among individual candidate nodes, yet it lacks explicit knowledge of how each candidate actually connects to the target region. We address this by introducing the Guidance-Distance Feature (GDF), which converts the region-level visitation order into a candidate-level path signal that the policy can utilize directly. The second challenge concerns how these two sources of information should be represented. We observe that local exploration value and global progress exhibit distinct, potentially conflicting objectives; a shared representation risks allowing one to dominate the other, degrading either coverage or path efficiency. This observation motivates our Dual-Branch Graph Policy, which encodes the two signals independently before fusing them, preserving their distinct semantics while enabling the policy to balance information gain against global progress at decision time.

We evaluate HERO in comparative experiments and ablation studies, assessing environment coverage, path efficiency, and online decision-making efficiency. The results show that our method maintains high coverage in largescale unknown environments while reducing unproductive detours and the computational costs. By deriving GDF, which represents global guidance, and combining it with local frontier utility through a Dual-Branch Graph Policy, the framework connects explicit global planning with learned local decision making. It thus offers a new approach to autonomous exploration tasks that require both global task prioritization and flexible local decisions. Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose a hierarchical framework that assigns structured global planning and RL-based exploration policy their complementary roles, providing long-horizon guidance while retaining environment-adaptive flexibility within a bounded decision scope.

We propose a hierarchical framework that assigns structured global planning and RL-based exploration policy their complementary roles, providing long-horizon guidance while retaining environment-adaptive flexibility within a bounded decision scope.

We introduce a Dual-Branch Graph Policy, equipped with GDF as explicit guidance, that learns to balance local frontier information against progress along the global path.

We conduct comprehensive experiments in simulation and the real world to demonstrate the feasibility, stability, and real-time performance of the proposed method.

title: RoboLiveMem: Is Robot Memory Solved When the World Does Not Wait?
authors: Yunbei Zhang,Yuyou Zhang,Janet Wang,Ming Liu,Yijiang Li,Yikai Wang,Weirui Ye,Ding Zhao,Jihun Hamm
abstract:
Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can
remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot
answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so
whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory
tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task
families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled
ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed
strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting
too late.
Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a
remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on
average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude
Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and
models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see
the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the
realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to
memory.
introduction:
A robot that works in a home has to remember what it can no longer see: which of three identical mugs is Grandpa’s,
whether the soup has already been salted, where the keys were put. Memory has therefore become a standard test for
robot policies, and several recent benchmarks measure
it [10, 7, 6, 18, 8]. Agents built
on frontier vision-language models now solve most of these tasks, often as well as people
do [16, 32, 24, 37]. Robot memory, at least for such agents,
looks nearly solved.

All of these benchmarks share one assumption: the simulator stops while the model thinks. A frontier model needs
seconds for each decision. In a paused world nothing changes during that time, so whatever the robot remembers when it
starts to decide is still true when its command runs. A real home does not wait. In Fig. 1, the robot sees
Grandpa’s mug at mark 1 and starts to think. Meanwhile the son, who is setting the table, swaps the two mugs. When the
robot acts, its memory is wrong, even though its own camera recorded the swap while it was thinking. With the simulator
paused, the same episode succeeds.

We call the missing ability live memory: keeping what the robot remembers correct while people or machines
change it during the robot’s own decision. No existing benchmark measures it (Tab. 1). Memory benchmarks
such as RoboMME [10], MIKASA-Robo [7], RMBench [6] and
RoboMemArena [18] hide state from the robot, but the world moves only when the policy acts.
Real-time benchmarks such as Realtime-Bench [27], Gaia2 [12],
Robo-bench [30] and a mode of Embodied First Exam [22] let time run while the model
thinks, but the state that matters is mostly in view when the agent acts, so they test speed rather than memory. When a
model fails in a moving world, there are three possible reasons, and a benchmark has to tell them apart: the model may
be too slow; it may not look at the right moment, since most agents stop watching while they think; or it may lose
track of what changed.

We build RoboLiveMem to measure live memory and to separate these three reasons. It runs every task under two clocks: a
paused clock, as in earlier benchmarks, and a live clock that charges the model’s thinking time to the world. Eight
checkable conditions keep the live version fair (Sec. 3): the change is not announced, the agent does not
trigger it, and real changes are mixed with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy
wins. Most tasks also have a twin in which the change stays in view, which lets us tell forgetting apart from acting
too late. Its 29 task families come in
three tiers (Fig. 2): 16 BEHAVIOR-1K [19] scenes in which people, robots and machines make
the changes, a MuJoCo kitchen, and 5 ManiSkill tasks.

We test 16 models from eight providers on 34,176 episodes (Sec. 5) and find the following.
(1) Paused success does not predict live success. When a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the
8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused but in only 50%
with the world running. Their paused scores are nearly equal and their live scores are not: Opus, perfect when paused,
succeeds in 44%, while Fable 5.1, tied for the lowest paused score, succeeds in 86% (Figs. 1 and 3).
The eight models we run in our own agent also all lose success live. (2) Speed is not the fix. Slower models do no worse,
and each of nine models given only 2 s per decision still falls at least 36 points below its paused success
(Fig. 4). (3) The models see the change. Asked afterwards about the frames they had, they describe it
correctly; they fail because they act on frames taken before the change was over (Fig. 6). Looking again just
before acting recovers most of the realistic gap. (4) What remains is memory. When identical objects are swapped
several times, each of nine models still does at least 12 points worse than when the swaps stay in view, even when it looks
again before acting (Tab. 5).

Contributions.   (1) We define live memory by letting the world run while the model thinks, with eight checkable
conditions for a valid task and a protocol that separates speed, observation and memory. (2) We build RoboLiveMem, to our knowledge the first
robot memory benchmark that runs identical tasks with the world paused and running. (3) We evaluate 16 models and
show that paused benchmarks overstate the memory of frontier agents.

title: Spiking World-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Mingquan Liu,Peng Zhou,Shanming Yao,Shuai Wang,Simo Wu,Malu Zhang
abstract:
World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots.
Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power.
However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background.
We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state.
Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images.
Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan.
On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus.
Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness.
These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence.
Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam
introduction:
World action models (WAMs) [48, 49, 15, 29, 18] let a robot learn in one model how to act and how the world changes in response.
They offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence.
However, most existing WAMs use videos or visual latents as the world state [48, 49, 15, 18].
These models are large and hard to run on robots with limited resources.
To this end, recent work skips future generation at inference [49, 29], which reduces computation.
These models still rely on dense multiply and accumulate operations, and each plan runs the network several times for multistep sampling.
A robot in closed loop control plans again and again, so this cost adds up.
Lowering the energy of each plan is therefore key to deploying WAMs on board.

Neurons in spiking neural networks (SNNs) communicate with discrete spikes and fire only when the membrane potential crosses a threshold.
On neuromorphic hardware, this event-driven computation replaces multiply and accumulate with accumulate, so its energy grows with the number of events [28].
SNNs have recently moved from visual perception [46] to embodied control.
Spiking vision-language-action models (VLAs) [31, 38] and spiking diffusion policies [10, 35] generate actions, and a spiking world model [33] predicts the next state after an action.
However, WAMs are hard to implement directly with SNNs.
Mainstream WAMs are built on large video generation models [48, 49, 15, 18], and there is still no mature way to turn such models into SNNs.
Even if this were done, dense video representations would still spend most events on a background unrelated to the task.
Small jitter in the image would also keep triggering new events.
Running the network several times per plan further cancels the savings from sparsity.
Existing approaches therefore cannot exploit the sparse and event-driven nature of SNNs.
Integer spikes also struggle to keep the millimetre precision of fine manipulation.

In contrast, biological motor control attends to the key positions of a task and represents space relative to the body.
When people manipulate objects, their gaze falls almost only on grasp points and targets [12].
The premotor and posterior parietal cortices represent targets relative to the arm or the hand [7, 3].
Grid cells encode position with periodic firing [8], and cortical neurons can detect spikes that arrive at the same time [16].
This suggests that the world state only needs the key positions of the arm and the task objects.
Once coordinates are written into spikes relative to the body, the positions of hand and object can be compared by spike coincidence.
Following the event-driven principle, only changes pass between consecutive plans.

Based on these ideas, we propose a sparse and event-driven paradigm for spiking WAMs and build SpikingWAM on it.
To our knowledge, SpikingWAM is the first spiking world action model.
A single spiking network trained from scratch learns future skeletons and action chunks together, and it generates only the action chunks at inference (Fig. 2).
First, we propose the Task Skeleton State (TSS), which uses only the keypoints of the arm and the task objects as the world state.
A small spiking perception front end estimates the object keypoints from images.
Next, we propose Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA).
BFSC encodes coordinates relative to the body and GCA compares positions by spike coincidence, so the geometry keeps millimetre precision.
Finally, we propose the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR).
It runs the network once per plan and passes only the changes between consecutive plans.
On LIBERO [21] and LIBERO-Plus [5], SpikingWAM reaches success rates comparable to state-of-the-art (SOTA) artificial neural network (ANN) methods.
On bimanual manipulation in RoboTwin 2.0 [4], it reaches a mean success rate of 80.20% without pretraining on robot data.
On LIBERO, it needs only 1.467 mJ per plan including the perception front end, which is more than an order of magnitude below every compared method (Fig. 1).
On a real robot arm, SpikingWAM completes a pick and place task given by a language instruction, with a success rate comparable to ANN VLAs and only 3.07 mJ per plan.
Our main contributions are as follows.

We design TSS and a small spiking perception front end that estimates its object keypoints from images.
They focus the events and attention of the policy on the parts that matter for the task, which lowers the energy of each plan.

We propose BFSC and GCA to recover the millimetre precision that integer spikes lose.
We propose PSR and an offline check that tells when it applies, so the network runs only once per plan.

We propose a sparse and event-driven paradigm for spiking WAMs and build on it SpikingWAM, the first spiking world action model.
It reaches 98.25%, 88.76% and 80.20% on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0.
On LIBERO-Plus, it exceeds all compared methods.

1. We design TSS and a small spiking perception front end that estimates its object keypoints from images.
They focus the events and attention of the policy on the parts that matter for the task, which lowers the energy of each plan.

2. We propose BFSC and GCA to recover the millimetre precision that integer spikes lose.
We propose PSR and an offline check that tells when it applies, so the network runs only once per plan.

3. We propose a sparse and event-driven paradigm for spiking WAMs and build on it SpikingWAM, the first spiking world action model.
It reaches 98.25%, 88.76% and 80.20% on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0.
On LIBERO-Plus, it exceeds all compared methods.

title: Design of a Compact Cable-driven 4-DoF Salamander Robotic Limb with Large Range of Motion and High Load Capacity
authors: Zhuowen Li,Qiyuan Fu,Auke Ijspeert
abstract:
A compact yet agile and powerful limb is essential for amphibious legged robots that transition between spine-based swimming and leg-based terrestrial walking, as salamanders do. Salamander limbs combine large ranges of motion (ROM), multiple degrees of freedom (DoFs), and high load capacity. These features enable fore–aft swinging and body-weight support during walking, as well as folding alongside the body during swimming. Their proximal kinematics can be represented by three rotational DoFs at the hip and one at the knee. Replicating these capabilities within a compact robotic limb is challenging with direct-drive architectures, because multiple joint-mounted actuators must be sufficiently spaced or placed distally to avoid self-collision, increasing limb size and rotational inertia.
Here we present a cable-driven 4-DoF salamander robotic limb with a spatial cable-routing architecture that relocates actuators proximally while preserving large ROM and load capacity. Transmission-induced coupling is mitigated by mechanically compensating multi-segment cable paths, model-based feedforward decoupling, and output-side joint angle feedback. Compared with a direct-drive limb, the proposed design reduces mass by 20.4%, projected envelope area by 20.5%, and estimated effective yaw-axis inertia by 31.9%. Experiments verify independent, decoupled control over joint-angle ranges of 45∘45^{\circ}, 118∘118^{\circ}, 118∘118^{\circ}, and 135∘135^{\circ} for hip pitch, yaw, roll, and knee flexion/extension, respectively. During lifting tests, the limb supported an equivalent vertical load of at least 5.4 times its own weight. The proposed limb provides a compact, biologically representative platform for future studies of salamander locomotion and neural control.
introduction:
Owing to their foldable limb morphology as well as the flexible spine, salamander robots are promising platforms for combining agile legged locomotion on land with efficient, spine-dominated swimming in fluids [1, 2]. However, whereas salamanders rely on coordinated, complex motions of both the limbs and body for multimodal locomotion [3], most existing salamander robots [4] simplify each limb to only one or two degrees of freedom (DoFs). Although sufficient for basic walking, these reduced limb designs cannot reproduce the full kinematic capacity of salamander limbs, limiting the locomotion capacity of salamander robots in complex environments [2, 4].

To effectively reproduce the versatile multi-modal locomotion of salamanders, salamander-inspired robotic hindlimbs should retain four principal DoFs: three mutually orthogonal rotational degrees of freedom at the hip and one flexion-extension degree of freedom at the knee [3]. The three hip DoFs act together to generate three-dimensional limb retraction and positioning, contributing to propulsion, stride length, and adaptation to uneven terrain, while knee flexion–extension modulates effective limb length and provides foot clearance during swing. Moreover, the three hip joint axes intersect at a single point, providing a closer anatomical abstraction of the salamander hip [5].

Some previous salamander robots [2, 6] incorporated a 3-DoF hip to better approximate salamander limb kinematics. However, the limb design adopted a direct-drive configuration in which each geared servo is mounted directly at its corresponding joint, without an additional external transmission. Although this simplified the mechanical design, the available joint torque was limited by the servo output, while the hip motors had to be spaced sufficiently apart to avoid self-collision, increasing limb rotational inertia and projected area.

These limitations motivate a transmission system that enables actuator relocation toward the trunk while providing the required joint torque. Several transmission mechanisms have been investigated for robotic limbs [7].
Linkages offer stable load transmission [8], but they either require substantial space for link rotation or make it difficult to achieve large ranges of motion without encountering dead points. Gears provide reliable short-distance transmission [9] but add a significant mass when driving all four DoFs. Belt drives [10] transmit torque over longer distances, but their planar routing and limited torque capacity at the required scale conflict with the limb’s design requirements.

In contrast, cable-driven mechanisms offer a powerful yet flexible transmission approach that can transmit large torques over long distances. Researchers have developed high-performance cable-driven robotic arms and dexterous hands[11][12][13], as well as robotic legs with impressive dynamic locomotion capabilities[14].

Despite these advantages, compact multi-DoF cable-driven mechanisms require effective cable pretensioning. Pretensioning mechanisms typically rely on unidirectional transmission to increase cable tension by extending the cable path. Various studies have employed one-way bearings[15], clutches[16], and worm gears[17] for pretensioning. However, these mechanisms require high manufacturing precision that is hard to achieve for customized compact components using 3D printing. Spring-based tensioning methods have also been widely utilized in dexterous hands [13][18], but under high-load conditions, high-stiffness springs may result in bulky components.

Another challenge in using cable-driven mechanisms is to decouple the four non-planar DoFs. Many cable-decoupling methods are designed for planar mechanisms, including rolling contact joints[11, 19, 20], four-bar linkages[21], and movable pulleys [22]. Adapting these mechanisms to the present intersecting-axis hip would require additional routing or decoupling components, increasing the packaging volume. Three-dimensional mechanical decoupling solutions have also been developed [23, 24, 20], but they rely on separate decoupling assemblies that occupy additional volume rather than being integrated into the joint structure. This packaging overhead conflicts with the compact three-axis hip required here.

In this work, we present a compact cable-driven 4-DoF robotic limb that preserves the biological joint configuration through spatial cable routing. To preserve compactness, screw- and ratchet-based [25] pretensioning mechanisms are integrated into load-bearing components. To mitigate transmission errors arising from DoF coupling and long cable paths, we developed mechanically compensating cable routing to suppress variations in total cable length, geometric feedforward decoupling to compensate for differential-length coupling, and output-side feedback to correct residual tracking errors.

Compared with a direct-drive limb, the proposed limb reduces mass by 20.4%, projected envelope area by 20.5%, and estimated effective yaw-axis rotational inertia by 31.9%.
Experiments demonstrate that it preserves a large ROM while suppressing transmission-induced errors and maintaining high load capacity. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating the proposed limb into a robotic platform for future studies of multimodal amphibious locomotion.

title: FlexWAM: Learning Flexible Visual Routing for World Action Models
authors: Mingyu Mei,Haojie Xu,Zibo Dai,Hongjie Fang,Shirun Tang,Zhengrui Lv,Yang Liu,Chen Guang,Xingyue Zhao,Huiliang Shen,Zaixing He
abstract: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view’s contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [6, 5, 22] and World Action Models (WAMs) [53, 55, 24] commonly use multi-camera observations for robotic manipulation. External cameras provide global workspace context, while wrist cameras capture local gripper–object relationships. In Fig. 1(a), the robot arm occludes the placement area in the external view, and the area lies outside the right wrist camera’s field of view. Only the left wrist view reveals the local geometry needed for placement. Several WAMs tile camera images onto a fixed canvas, allocating fewer pixels and visual tokens to wrist views and making these fine details harder to preserve [53, 4, 55, 15, 47, 51].

For video prediction, these models mix tokens from different cameras at every layer. When other views offer little relevant evidence, repeated mixing may interfere with modeling the local structure and motion in the left wrist view. (1)Does predicting each view’s future require cross-view interaction at every layer? For action generation, standard action–video cross-attention assigns weights at the token level, leaving each camera’s contribution implicit as observations and control demands change. (2)How can the action expert integrate complementary information while prioritizing views most relevant to the current action?

Human perception dynamically prioritizes task-relevant sensory cues while integrating complementary evidence across modalities  [39]. At different manipulation stages, people adjust their reliance on sensory cues as control demands change [37, 20]. When plugging in an Ethernet cable, for example, vision guides the approach and initial alignment of the connector. Once the connector touches the port, touch and force provide a more direct cue for detecting misalignment and making fine adjustments [36].

Inspired by this flexibility, we propose FlexWAM to address both questions(Fig. 1(b)) . (1) For video prediction, FlexWAM encodes each view independently and integrates complementary context through cross-view attention at alternating layers, with within-view attention modeling view-specific structure. (2) For action generation, an observation-conditioned router assigns per-view weights, and View-Routed Action Attention uses these weights to combine complementary cues while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action.

When trained end to end with the action prediction loss alone, the action expert can improve by adapting to a nearly fixed mixture of views, leaving the routing weights close to their uniform initialization. To address this limitation, we introduce counterfactual view credit. We estimate each view’s contribution by how much masking that view alone increases the action prediction loss. A larger increase indicates greater view importance. A view critic uses these credits to provide stable supervision for the router, enabling it to learn observation-dependent view weights without predefined task stages or view-importance annotations.

Our contributions are threefold:

We explore an effective multi-view modeling strategy alternating within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and cross-view complementarity.

We introduce flexible view routing to estimate view relative importance and View-Routed Action Attention to flexibly regulate visual attention during action generation.

We propose counterfactual view credit assignment to estimate
each view’s relative contribution to action. A critic network uses these estimates to calibrate the router, mitigating shortcuts from action-loss-only training.

Experiments on five challenging real-world tasks using two robot platforms and two video-generation backbones demonstrate FlexWAM’s effectiveness. With Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [42] and LingBot-Video-Dense (1.3B) [31, 38], FlexWAM achieves mean task success rates of 77.2% and 83.8%, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points, respectively.

1. We explore an effective multi-view modeling strategy alternating within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and cross-view complementarity.

2. We introduce flexible view routing to estimate view relative importance and View-Routed Action Attention to flexibly regulate visual attention during action generation.

3. We propose counterfactual view credit assignment to estimate
each view’s relative contribution to action. A critic network uses these estimates to calibrate the router, mitigating shortcuts from action-loss-only training.

title: One Latent World for Heterogeneous LiDARs: A Scan Pattern Agnostic 4D World Model via Direct Ray Decoding
authors: Minwoo Jung,Dongjae Lee,DongGuw Lee,Yeong Sang Park,Maurice Fallon,Ayoung Kim
abstract:
LiDAR world models generate and predict metric 3D observations in the form of LiDAR scans.
They typically synthesize scans following the scan pattern of their training sensor or render them from an intermediate 3D surface or field.
However, following one scan pattern limits transfer to LiDARs with other patterns, and rendering from intermediate geometry can cause incorrect depths and false returns.
In this paper, we propose a scan pattern agnostic 4D LiDAR world model that decouples the scene from sensor observation, so one spatial latent can be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration.
Our decoder predicts the hit probability and depth of each ray directly from the latent, combining global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth.
Without an intermediate surface or field, it reduces incorrect depths and false returns, and as each ray is decoded independently from one latent, LiDARs that share a ray receive the same return and observe one consistent scene.
Finally, a diffusion transformer generates scenes in this latent and predicts 4D sequences from observed latents warped by the given ego and object motion.
On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, our model generates realistic scenes and reduces the registration error between predicted frames by about 70% relative to the best compared world model.
Its decoder yields 19 to 28% lower depth error than the rendering used by other world models, and generated scans benefit several downstream tasks.
Our code will be open-sourced.
More details are available at https://minwoo0611.github.io/OneLatentWorld.
introduction:
World models learn representations that predict how an environment evolves under actions [2].
In autonomous driving, they simulate scenes and their evolution, allowing scenarios to be revisited without collecting new data [3].
Driving world models have been built on video [4], semantic occupancy [5], and  LiDAR (LiDAR) scans [6, 7, 8, 9].
Among them, LiDAR world models generate metric observations in the scan format that perception and localization modules use.

Since autonomous platforms carry LiDAR with different scan patterns, from rotating to solid-state sensors [1], a LiDAR world model should be able to produce observations for each pattern.
A representative approach to LiDAR scene generation uses range images [10, 11, 12, 13] and produces ranges on the angular raster of the training sensor, as illustrated in Fig. 1a.
However, this ties the representation to that scan pattern and makes non-repetitive scans hard to handle.
Range imaging at variable resolutions [14] relaxes the fixed raster, but its multiscale processing depends on the requested grid. A ray shared by different grids can then have different ranges.

One way to avoid this dependence is to represent the scene in space and render observations along the requested rays, as illustrated in Fig. 1b.
Several world models take this approach and decode a generated latent into meshes, semantic occupancy, or an implicit occupancy field [7, 15, 6, 8].
Rendering supports flexible scan patterns, and learned fields can be fitted to sensor measurements, but each range is still read from the intermediate geometry along the ray.
Spurious or coarsely discretized geometry in front of the visible surface pulls the range toward the sensor, and geometry on a ray without a measured return creates a false return.

These limitations motivate separating scene generation from sensor observation without an intermediate geometry step.
This requires a scene representation independent of the target scan pattern, from which the return and depth of each ray can be predicted directly.
Spatial latents such as  BEV (BEV) and  HCS (HCS) [16, 6, 17] suit this role by placing heterogeneous scans in shared spatial coordinates.
However, for efficient generation, such latents use coarse grids and are often encoded from binary occupancy [16, 8, 17], which discards where points lie within each cell.
Both factors limit the geometric detail needed for accurate depth along each ray.

To tackle these issues, we present a LiDAR world model built on a spatial latent decoupled from scan patterns, outlined in Fig. 1c.
As a shared encoder maps scans of different patterns into this latent, the autoencoder learns from all of them.
To retain detail within each cell, the encoder input also stores the point count and the mean radial offset of the points.
Since only the decoder receives the rays of the target scan pattern, one generated scene can be observed by different LiDAR (Fig. 1d) without regeneration.
Furthermore, unlike rendering, our decoder predicts the hit probability and depth of each ray directly from the latent and learns from labeled hits and misses to reduce false returns.
Finally, a  DiT (DiT) generates scenes in this latent with or without layouts and predicts future scenes from observed latents warped by the given motion (Fig. 1e), so different LiDAR can observe these 4D sequences.
Our contributions are as follows:

Scan pattern agnostic LiDAR world modeling. Our world model separates scene generation and prediction from scan patterns, enabling a single latent scene or sequence to be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration.

Scan pattern agnostic LiDAR world modeling. Our world model separates scene generation and prediction from scan patterns, enabling a single latent scene or sequence to be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration.

Direct latent-to-ray decoding. A depth-guided ray decoder combines global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth to predict ray returns directly, reducing false returns and depth errors without reconstructing an intermediate surface or field.

Temporally consistent scene prediction. The motion-aligned latent conditioning warps the observed latents to the predicted frames under given ego and object motion, which improves temporal consistency.

Generation quality and downstream utility. Experiments on KITTI-360 and nuScenes show strong generation quality, 66–72% lower registration errors between predicted frames than the compared world models, and 19–28% lower depth errors than their rendering. Predicted scans for unseen sensors improve place recognition, moving object segmentation, and object detection.

2. Direct latent-to-ray decoding. A depth-guided ray decoder combines global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth to predict ray returns directly, reducing false returns and depth errors without reconstructing an intermediate surface or field.

3. Temporally consistent scene prediction. The motion-aligned latent conditioning warps the observed latents to the predicted frames under given ego and object motion, which improves temporal consistency.

4. Generation quality and downstream utility. Experiments on KITTI-360 and nuScenes show strong generation quality, 66–72% lower registration errors between predicted frames than the compared world models, and 19–28% lower depth errors than their rendering. Predicted scans for unseen sensors improve place recognition, moving object segmentation, and object detection.

title: TeleMultiStream: An Integrated Robot Teleoperation System with Low-Latency Multi-Stream Video Feedback
authors: Chenchen Lv,Lingchen Hu,Yaosai Zhang,Chunlan Li,Gengkui Wei,Wei Xin,Li Li
abstract: Training embodied-intelligence models requires large-scale, high-quality demonstration data. Robot teleoperation provides an important means of collecting these data. Low-latency teleoperation also helps human operators take control promptly and provide corrective demonstrations in DAgger-based interactive learning. This paper presents TeleMultiStream, a robot teleoperation system that combines multi-stream WebRTC video feedback with UDP pose downlink. The system supports heterogeneous video sources and uses buffer reuse, bounded queues, and native XR rendering to reduce processing and waiting. In wired-LAN ZED Mini tests, TeleMultiStream’s software and high-performance hardware encoding modes achieved dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass latency medians of 60 and 66 ms, respectively. These medians were 26.8% and 19.5% lower than the 82-ms RobotVision-PC reference, respectively. At the lower tested resolutions, the two TeleMultiStream encoding modes provided comparable visual latency. Their respective medians in three-stream Configuration 1 were 72 and 66 ms. In the higher-resolution Configuration 2, high-performance hardware encoding outperformed software encoding in latency and CPU utilization. It reduced mean encoding time from 11.85 to 8.80 ms and the dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass median from 94 to 88 ms. Its CPU utilization was approximately 67%, compared with 265% for software encoding. During three-stream reception with high-performance hardware encoding, the mean corrected one-way UDP latencies at 100 Hz were 1.576 and 1.800 ms in Configurations 1 and 2, respectively. Mean estimated packet loss was 0.0033% in both configurations. These results support responsive teleoperation for robot demonstration collection.
introduction:
Progress in embodied intelligence increasingly depends on robot models trained with large-scale, high-quality interaction data [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Teleoperation supplies human demonstrations, whose usefulness depends on interface design and data quality [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. DAgger training additionally collects expert corrections at states visited by a learned policy [11]. Human-gated variants let operators take over, demonstrate recovery, and return control to the policy [12]. Both data collection and timely intervention require low-latency teleoperation: delayed video obscures the current scene, while delayed commands postpone corrective motion and disturb observation–action alignment [13, 14, 15].

Multiple camera views further complicate this requirement. Stereo head cameras provide workspace context and depth cues, while wrist cameras expose contact and local manipulation [16]. Concurrent streams share host computation, network bandwidth, and headset decoding resources. Maintaining responsive feedback therefore requires reducing processing and waiting throughout the video path [17].

To meet these requirements, this paper presents TeleMultiStream, an integrated low-latency robot teleoperation system. Its Streaming Service sends multiple robot-camera views over WebRTC to a native XR receiver, while a UDP downlink carries operator poses to the robot. The system supports teleoperation across heterogeneous XR headsets and robot platforms, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Fig. 2 presents the system’s video-feedback and pose-downlink data flow.

The main contributions are as follows:

Low-latency multi-stream video feedback. Source adaptation, buffer reuse, bounded queues, and native XR rendering reduce latency. Common-source dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass medians were 60 ms with software encoding and 66 ms with high-performance hardware encoding, versus 82 ms for RobotVision-PC [18].

Real-time video transport and stage-level latency analysis. Per-track scheduling over WebRTC supports timely multi-stream transmission [19, 20]. Pipeline instrumentation quantifies conversion, encoding, queueing, decoding, and rendering delays, enabling detailed analysis of where latency accumulates.

Flexible video sources and encoding backends. Common interfaces combine RealSense, ZED-M, and raw or compressed ROS image inputs, including compatible encoded passthrough. Cross-platform software encoding and platform-specific hardware backends adapt the system to different camera layouts, host resources, and deployment platforms.

The evaluation uses PICO 4 Ultra and PICO Swan headsets. It measures Glass-to-Glass video latency, local processing times, CPU utilization, and the GPU/SoC-rail power change during video transmission. It also assesses corrected one-way pose latency and estimated packet loss during concurrent video reception. By integrating responsive pose delivery with low-latency multi-stream visual feedback, TeleMultiStream provides a reusable foundation for robot demonstration collection and the development of embodied-intelligence applications.

Section II distinguishes the relevant formats, protocols, and reference implementations. Section III describes the video sender and receiver, timing instrumentation, and UDP pose downlink. Section IV reports video comparisons and concurrent pose-downlink measurements. Section V summarizes the system’s capabilities and measured performance.

title: TidyFlow: Geometry-Aware Tabletop Arrangement Generation with Human-Aligned Tidiness Evaluation
authors: Jiahui Qian,Tiandong Wang,Shubao Fan,Chenyu Niu,Erqi Wu
abstract: Generating tidy tabletop arrangements that align with human organizational preferences requires considering both functional relationships among objects and geometric constraints within limited tabletop space. We present TidyFlow, a tabletop arrangement generation framework that integrates conditional Flow Matching with topology-aware geometric refinement. We construct two tabletop arrangement datasets based on functional grouping and geometric constraints, namely General Tabletop Layouts (GTL) and Workstation Tabletop Layouts (WTL), and introduce a six-dimensional tidiness scoring function. Conditional Flow Matching is employed to learn a multimodal distribution of target arrangements conditioned on object attributes and tabletop geometry. To address geometric errors in generated layouts, we construct topology-aware refinement data based on collision and boundary-violation patterns, and employ a pair-aware attention network to iteratively refine object poses. Experiments demonstrate that, after three refinement iterations, TidyFlow improves geometric validity from 23.21% to 88.91% on GTL and from 10.58% to 57.91% on WTL. Furthermore, a human preference study demonstrates a positive correlation between the proposed tidiness scores and human rankings, achieving a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.5543.
introduction:
In robotic manipulation, tabletop target-layout generation
serves as an important intermediate step between scene
perception and robotic-arm planning. Rather than simply moving
objects into available space, tidy arrangements that reflect
human preferences must account for the relative positions,
orientations, and functional relationships of objects, as well
as the use of tabletop space. For example, a keyboard and mouse
typically form a workspace around a monitor, stationery items
are often placed together, and groups serving different
purposes should be maintain appropriate separation. Moreover,
even with the same objects and tabletop conditions, multiple
reasonable arrangements may exist, which are difficult to
represent with a single deterministic pose prediction. Figure 1 illustrates the two
tabletop layout settings considered in this work.

Previous research has explored object arrangement through
functional semantics [20],
layout generation [10],
and geometric constraints [7, 2].
Tidy Up the Table [26] and
Set It Up! [27] use functional relationships
among objects to guide arrangement generation, while
LEGO-Net [22] and
SceneFlow [25] learn spatial relationships
among objects to generate different configurations.
To improve geometric feasibility,
SceneFlow [25] and
STABLE [18] incorporate geometric constraints
and layout refinement. In addition,
SceneScore [9] and
Tidiness Score-Guided MCTS [11]
evaluate arrangement quality using learned arrangement costs
or tidiness scores. However, generating diverse arrangements
does not guarantee that all of them satisfy geometric
constraints, and a collision-free, in-bounds arrangement does
not necessarily match human organizational preferences.

Generating tidy layouts from known object attributes and tabletop geometry presents three challenges. First, Reference Layouts used for training must reflect functional relationships among objects while accounting for object dimensions and tabletop boundary constraints. Second, generated Raw Layouts can exhibit heterogeneous geometric errors, including multiple objects involved in shared collisions, several disconnected collision regions, and simultaneous collisions and boundary violations. Generic geometric correction may reduce individual overlaps without resolving coupled conflicts, or may disturb spatial relationships that were already valid. Refinement must therefore address different error structures while distinguishing objects requiring repair from those whose arrangements should be preserved. Third, even a geometrically valid layout must be assessed for its functional grouping, alignment, and spacing, and the resulting scores must be evaluated for consistency with human tidiness preferences.

To address these challenges, we propose TidyFlow,
a tabletop target-layout generation framework combining
conditional layout generation, geometric refinement,
and tidiness evaluation.
First, we construct geometrically valid reference layouts
with meaningful functional organization through semantic
planning and geometry-constrained search, and train a
conditional Flow Matching model [15]
to learn a distribution over target layouts and generate
multiple candidate configurations.
We then analyze collisions and boundary violations produced
by the generator on the training set and use these error
patterns to construct refinement data with diverse error
structures. Refiner models geometric relationships between objects
to predict local pose adjustments, while safety constraints
prevent the introduction of new collisions and boundary
violations during refinement.
Finally, we select a target layout from geometrically
valid candidates using an interpretable six-dimensional
tidiness score and assess the score’s agreement with
human organizational preferences through subjective evaluations.

On General Tabletop Layouts (GTL) and Workstation Tabletop
Layouts (WTL), geometric refinement increases the
candidate-level Geometric Validity Rate (GVR) from 23.21% to
88.91% and from 10.58% to 57.91%, respectively. To sum up, we contribute:

Two tabletop layout datasets, GTL and WTL,
that incorporate functional organization and
geometric validity across varying scene complexity.

Two tabletop layout datasets, GTL and WTL,
that incorporate functional organization and
geometric validity across varying scene complexity.

A conditional Flow Matching framework for
diverse layout generation, coupled with a
topology-aware Refiner that uses generator-induced
errors, pairwise geometry, and repair-preservation
supervision to reduce violations and unnecessary
pose changes.

A six-dimensional tidiness score for evaluating
functional organization and spatial arrangement,
together with human-rating and preference-ranking
experiments to assess its agreement with human
preferences.

that incorporate functional organization and
geometric validity across varying scene complexity.

2. A conditional Flow Matching framework for
diverse layout generation, coupled with a
topology-aware Refiner that uses generator-induced
errors, pairwise geometry, and repair-preservation
supervision to reduce violations and unnecessary
pose changes.

3. A six-dimensional tidiness score for evaluating
functional organization and spatial arrangement,
together with human-rating and preference-ranking
experiments to assess its agreement with human
preferences.

title: MoMa-NMP: Scene-Scale Neural Motion Planning for Mobile Manipulators
authors: Adam Kan,Jason Jingzhou Liu,Jiahui Yang,Kenneth Shaw,Deepak Pathak
abstract: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. We train MoMa-NMP on these demonstrations through behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation, achieving 87.0% success on our simulation benchmark and 77.5% across 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes. See video results at adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.
introduction:
Robots operating throughout homes, offices, and other complex environments must coordinate mobility and manipulation across entire scenes. They must withdraw an end-effector from confined spaces, navigate around obstacles, coordinate whole-body motion through narrow passages, and reposition to access new workspaces. These capabilities require precise whole-body control, long-horizon planning, and global reasoning under partial observability.

Classical motion planners have long been used during robot deployment to address such problems. However, classical planners generally rely on explicit scene geometry and can become computationally expensive as scene scale, planning horizon, and robot dimensionality increase. Neural motion planners offer an alternative: they can generate actions with low latency, operate directly from partial observations, and replan continuously at runtime as new geometry becomes visible.

Training such neural motion planners, however, requires large datasets that are particularly difficult to generate at room scale. Demonstrations must capture long, nonlinear whole-body motions around multiple obstacles while remaining collision-free and suitable for imitation. Classical motion planners can provide this supervision, but generating high-quality trajectories reliably and at sufficient throughput becomes increasingly difficult as scene scale and geometric constraints grow.

To address this challenge, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a parallelizable demonstration-generation pipeline for room-scale mobile manipulation. DemoSmith first procedurally constructs multi-workspace environments with dense obstacles and constrained start and goal regions. It must then generate learning-ready whole-body trajectories through these environments. However, cuRobo [1], a state-of-the-art GPU-accelerated motion-generation framework, often struggles to discover the long, nonlinear base trajectories required to maneuver around obstacles in complex scenes.

Our key insight is to relax cuRobo’s collision margin and velocity limits to improve global path discovery, allowing it to identify the high-level whole-body route between start and goal configurations. However, these relaxed constraints can produce trajectories that pass too close to obstacles and contain unrealistic base velocities. We therefore use Geometric Fabrics [2], a reactive motion generator with access to ground-truth obstacle geometry, to generate high-clearance action targets along the cuRobo route for imitation learning.

Finally, we use these demonstrations to train a closed-loop neural policy, MoMa-NMP. We first use behavior cloning to train a policy from demonstrations generated by MoMa-DemoSmith. However, over long, scene-spanning trajectories, small prediction errors can compound and drive the policy into collisions. During on-policy fine-tuning, we use Geometric Fabrics to correct action chunks predicted by a frozen BC policy. Through on-policy student-teacher distillation, these corrected actions supervise a student policy that operates on partially observable scenes in deployment.

To our knowledge, MoMa-NMP is the first general-purpose neural motion planner to demonstrate closed-loop whole-body planning for a mobile manipulator in unseen cluttered real-world scenes. The policy learns to execute globally constrained motions—coordinating base and arm around multiple obstacles and into narrow or initially occluded workspaces—using only partial onboard observations, without a precomputed global route or task-specific training. Across 80 trials spanning 20 tasks and 10 unseen scenes, MoMa-NMP achieves 77.5% success.

title: SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
authors: Jiarui Guo,Jinkai Zhang,Yuanhong Yu,Yongchen Zai,Futang Zhu,Ruizhen Hu,Sida Peng,Xiaowei Zhou
abstract:
This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals.
Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image–text records.
However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image–text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes.
To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent.
The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes.
This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations.
For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map.
Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals.
Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency.
Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system’s applicability.
introduction:
Reliable navigation requires understanding current observations and remembering the environment beyond the robot’s immediate view.
For instance, within a single search, a robot should distinguish explored from unexplored areas to avoid redundant exploration [4].
Across successive goals or repeated visits, it should reuse past experience to reach remembered destinations efficiently [3].
Together, these settings require persistent spatial memory that is both easy for an agent to query and geometrically grounded for navigation.

Existing approaches to spatial memory broadly fall into two categories: graph-based representations and recallable image–text records.
Graph-based spatial memories provide explicit structure but can be costly for an agent to process.
Scene graphs organize objects and rooms as nodes connected by relational edges [27], while observation-based topological memories retain visual features from past observations [13, 7].
As exploration adds nodes and relations, exposing the full accumulated representation can increase context and reasoning costs, motivating selective memory access [7].
The challenge is to expose useful spatial knowledge without overwhelming the agent with scene detail.

Recallable image–text records provide access to past visual observations and textual summary  [14, 15].
Although these systems retain spatial evidence, retrieving an image or textual record does not by itself specify a traversable route to a distant destination.
The remaining challenge is therefore to couple compact semantic recall with a geometric representation that can provide executable navigation route.

We introduce SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system with structured spatial memory that the agent selectively constructs and uses.
Our key insight is to use a geometric map as the spatial backbone while letting the agent decide where to retain useful memories.
During navigation, a real-time two-dimensional simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) system  [10] builds an occupancy map partitioned into areas.
The agent adaptively creates memory nodes at selected map locations, grounding retained scene information in a shared spatial reference.
This design simplifies memory access and management, while grounding memory nodes in the map enables efficient navigation to known areas.

This structured spatial memory supports both exploration and navigation to remembered locations.
During initial exploration, the occupancy map distinguishes explored from unexplored areas, guiding the agent toward unvisited regions.
To reach an unvisited area or revisit a remembered location, the agent selects the corresponding destination on the map. A map-based geometric tool then plans and executes the route, avoiding the need for the agent to infer step-by-step semantic instructions.

When reusing memory across navigation sessions, the robot must first determine its location within the stored map.
Our agent-guided relocalization combines agent reasoning with geometric relocalization to estimate this location using limited geometric observations from the current session.
Once relocalized, the system reuses stored memory nodes and map geometry to navigate to subsequent goals.

Experiments evaluate SuperNav-1.5 on single-object, multi-object, demand-driven, and multi-session navigation.
On HM3D-OVON [29] val-unseen, our method achieves an 80.00% success rate at the 1 m evaluation threshold, outperforming the reported baselines.
On Habitat-GS [24] multi-object tasks, it improves success weighted by path length (SPL) from SuperNav’s 0.1388 to 0.2494.
In second-session navigation from a different spawn position, memory reuse raises SPL from 0.4364 to 0.5022 compared with the no-memory setting.
These results support the value of geometry-grounded memory for long-horizon navigation and multi-session reuse.

Our contributions are threefold:

A structured spatial memory with agent-selected nodes grounded in a persistent two-dimensional occupancy map, linking scene recall to navigable locations.

An agent-guided relocalization method that locates the robot in a stored map using limited geometric observations from the current session.

A unified agentic navigation system integrating map-guided exploration, geometric navigation, and relocalization for long-horizon navigation and multi-session memory reuse.

1. A structured spatial memory with agent-selected nodes grounded in a persistent two-dimensional occupancy map, linking scene recall to navigable locations.

2. An agent-guided relocalization method that locates the robot in a stored map using limited geometric observations from the current session.

3. A unified agentic navigation system integrating map-guided exploration, geometric navigation, and relocalization for long-horizon navigation and multi-session memory reuse.

title: UnderGrasp: Envelopment-Oriented Grasp Refinement for an Underactuated Gripper
authors: Zhiwen Song,Ruidi Liu,Guanglu Jia,Zuowei Chen,Hao Wen,Qing Shi
abstract:
Underactuated grippers can form enveloping grasps through passive compliance,
while the terminal pose and single width predicted by generic grasp generators
do not fully capture the approach–closure process. Conventional collision
filtering also struggles to distinguish harmful interference from acceptable
contact.
We present UnderGrasp, a post-hoc grasp refinement and evaluation framework
for an underactuated gripper that reuses grasp candidates and quality priors
from a frozen generator.
The model jointly encodes the target, local
environment, support surface, and approach-path geometry to propose diverse
combinations of insertion depth, pre-grasp width, and target closing width
for each candidate. These actions are ranked by combining separately
predicted envelopment and interaction quality with upstream priors,
balancing grasp feasibility, envelopment, and scene disturbance rather
than rejecting all environmental contact. The back end is trained solely
on configuration and interaction labels generated by gripper-specific
simulations, without real-robot grasp labels. Real-robot experiments with an
underactuated gripper show that UnderGrasp improves the overall success rate (SR)
and the envelopment rate among successful grasps (ER) from 0.55/0.12 to
0.82/0.55 with AnyGrasp, and from
0.42/0.08 to 0.65/0.36 with GraspNet. In contrast, increasing the fixed
insertion depth to 40 mm improves ER to 0.35 but reduces SR to 0.52,
supporting the value of adaptive refinement. For trials involving target
or environmental contact during approach, the conditional success rates increase from 0.36
to 0.89 and from 0.25 to 0.86, respectively, demonstrating more reliable
execution under contact.
