introduction:
Stable and robust grasping of unknown objects in unstructured environments is
a key capability for general-purpose robotic manipulation [1, 2].
Underactuated grippers combine multi-link fingers with a single actuator
and passive compliance, allowing them to conform to object geometry
and achieve both parallel and enveloping grasps [3, 4].
Enveloping grasps provide stronger geometric constraints and
greater robustness to perception errors, execution deviations,
and external disturbances [5],
as shown in Fig. 1(a).
Realizing these benefits requires grasp poses, contact geometry, and closing actions
that exploit the gripper’s mechanical characteristics [6, 7].
Large-scale grasp datasets and 3D deep networks have enabled 7-DoF
grasp generators, such as AnyGrasp and GraspNet [8, 9], to efficiently generate and rank
candidates from RGB observations or point clouds while generalizing to unseen
objects and cluttered scenes. These methods are typically designed for
rigid parallel-jaw grippers and represent each grasp using a terminal end-effector
pose and a single gripper width, while the gripper’s closing action must still
be specified by the downstream execution policy.

Furthermore, existing methods often approximate grippers as combinations of simple
geometric primitives for collision checking, limiting their ability to accurately
represent the spatial occupancy of real multi-link grippers and its evolution during motion [9, 10].
Beyond this geometric limitation, collision-avoidance strategies for rigid parallel-jaw grippers
typically regard environmental contact as undesirable interference [11, 12]. For underactuated grippers,
however, some contact is not necessarily detrimental, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b).
Appropriate early contact with the environment or the target object may induce only minor disturbance
while guiding the fingers toward a more favorable enveloping configuration,
potentially improving subsequent grasp stability [13, 14]. Such contacts should therefore be evaluated
by balancing the resulting gains in grasp quality against the associated disturbance costs.
Accordingly, post-processing of grasp candidates would benefit from considering not only
the gripper’s actual geometry but also the effects of contact on both grasp execution and
the surrounding environment, thereby determining whether a contact is beneficial or acceptable.

To address these challenges, we propose
a post-hoc grasp refinement and evaluation framework
for an underactuated gripper (UnderGrasp), which reuses grasp candidates and their quality scores from
a frozen grasp generator.
It jointly encodes the target, local environment, support surface, and candidate-specific
approach-path point clouds to predict
an insertion depth offset along the approach axis, a pre-grasp width offset, and
a target closing width offset,
yielding a refined stage-wise action from a generic grasp candidate. Ranking combines upstream grasp quality with predicted envelopment
and interaction quality, balancing grasp feasibility, envelopment, and environmental
contact costs and benefits. Trained solely on gripper-specific simulations,
the network uses geometry-focused supervision from enveloping configurations,
target capture, and scene changes to reduce reliance on precise physical parameter
identification. Real-robot experiments demonstrate transfer without real-world grasp labels.

The primary contributions are as follows:

We introduce UnderGrasp, a post-hoc framework that reuses candidates and quality priors
from a frozen grasp generator.
It refines the generic grasp candidate into a stage-wise action,
adapting execution to target geometry and surrounding spatial constraints.

We propose a refinement-evaluation architecture.
The refinement module generates local variants of each input grasp candidate,
while the evaluation module predicts physical quantities used to
evaluate their envelopment and interaction qualities. These results,
together with the upstream grasp score, are used to rank the refined candidates
based on grasp feasibility, envelopment quality, and the costs
and benefits of environmental contact.

Real-robot experiments demonstrate that, with the back end trained solely
in simulation and without real-robot grasp labels, the proposed method
achieves effective enveloping grasps on diverse objects not used in back-end training while
better balancing grasp robustness and environmental interaction,
thereby reducing harmful interference.

1. We introduce UnderGrasp, a post-hoc framework that reuses candidates and quality priors
from a frozen grasp generator.
It refines the generic grasp candidate into a stage-wise action,
adapting execution to target geometry and surrounding spatial constraints.

2. We propose a refinement-evaluation architecture.
The refinement module generates local variants of each input grasp candidate,
while the evaluation module predicts physical quantities used to
evaluate their envelopment and interaction qualities. These results,
together with the upstream grasp score, are used to rank the refined candidates
based on grasp feasibility, envelopment quality, and the costs
and benefits of environmental contact.

3. Real-robot experiments demonstrate that, with the back end trained solely
in simulation and without real-robot grasp labels, the proposed method
achieves effective enveloping grasps on diverse objects not used in back-end training while
better balancing grasp robustness and environmental interaction,
thereby reducing harmful interference.

title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
authors: Yue Huang,Tianshan Zhang,Zeyu Zhang,Jayeon Kang,Akide Liu,Sungjoon Choi,Dacheng Tao,Hao Tang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Code:this https URL. Website:this https URL
abstract:
Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root–body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text–motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138×\times while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts.
Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

introduction:
Generating long-horizon motion from changing instructions is a central problem in interactive animation and humanoid robotics.
A useful generator must interpret an action description, accommodate spatial constraints, and continue from the motion already produced.
These requirements extend beyond synthesizing an isolated clip: a user may change direction during walking, request an upper-body action, or specify a future target while the current motion is still being executed.
The resulting references must be available quickly enough for interactive use and remain compatible with a downstream tracking system.
Unlike offline text-to-motion synthesis, the future instruction sequence need not be known when generation begins.
An interactive generator must therefore preserve useful context while incorporating newly arriving commands, rather than simply replaying a completed trajectory.

Diffusion models produce diverse text-conditioned human motion [1, 2, 3].
Recent methods extend this formulation through temporal composition, autoregressive prediction, and direct spatial conditioning [4, 5, 6, 7].
Temporal composition allows multiple descriptions to define a longer sequence, while causal latent models and hierarchical motion tokens support incremental synthesis [8, 9].
Spatially constrained methods further specify where selected joints or the character should move [10, 11, 12, 7].
In particular, generating one window at a time provides a practical interface for online instructions.
However, two difficulties remain closely connected.
A bounded attention cache discards older motion features, whereas an unbounded cache increases storage and computation as the sequence grows.
Moreover, repeated denoising of short windows can incur substantial execution overhead even when each individual model evaluation is small.
An interactive system therefore requires both a suitable representation of motion history and an efficient implementation of its repeated updates.
These requirements concern different aspects of the problem: reducing the number of sampling steps does not extend the history available to the model, and a compact historical state alone does not eliminate denoising overhead.

State-space models provide an alternative to storing every historical token by summarizing a sequence in a recurrent state [13, 14].
Their use in motion generation has shown the value of efficient temporal modeling [15, 16].
Recent studies also combine Mamba with autoregressive diffusion or use recurrent temporal representations for sustained and interactive motion [17, 18, 19].
Nevertheless, a compressed recurrent state and an attention cache expose history differently: the former carries evolving context, while the latter permits direct retrieval of explicit features.
Simply placing both branches in a network does not make the recurrent history directly accessible to attention.
This distinction motivates a learned interface between accumulated recurrent motion state and attention-accessible content, rather than relying on either mechanism alone.
Diffusion introduces an additional requirement: successive noisy candidates describe alternatives for the same output window, not successive moments of the accepted motion stream.
Persisting those intermediate candidates would mix sampling iterations with physical time.
We therefore treat the boundary between prediction and history commitment as part of the model’s streaming formulation.

We propose Motion Mamba 2.0, an autoregressive diffusion model for long-horizon, real-time controllable G1 motion.
The model follows a root–body decomposition [7]: explicit root predictions determine local trajectory features for body generation.
Within both denoisers, local attention is combined with a resumable Mamba branch.
Our persistent content memory (PCM) learns to map compressed Mamba state summaries, successive state changes, and text-conditioned features into dynamically updated slots accessible to local attention.
The slots complement recent motion features in the bounded cache and aim to support terminal spatial constraint satisfaction and command-conditioned generation over extended rollouts; they are not designed to reproduce arbitrary early instructions verbatim.
Recurrent states, cached features, and slots are committed only after a clean motion window is accepted; intermediate denoising candidates read the same immutable history snapshot.
The fixed-size recurrent state, cache, and PCM slots bound stored context without guaranteeing retention of every detail from arbitrarily distant motion.
The accepted-history separation also guides efficient inference.
Read-only denoising avoids materializing unused state proposals, selective fusion reduces intermediate memory traffic, and CUDA Graphs reduce repeated host dispatch [20, 21].
These changes preserve root-to-body ordering and the canonical clean-history update.
Our objective is to accelerate the same sampling computation, complementing methods that obtain faster generation through compact representations or altered sampling procedures [3, 22, 23].
We measure their contributions separately, since the effect of local fusion differs from that of graph replay.
The complete scheme generates a 52-frame window in 276.14 ms at the median on an RTX 4090; this steady-state generation time is distinct from the delay between a user command and its visible execution.

We evaluate the method on three G1 motion benchmarks under a matched 100,000-update training budget (App. C).
We first examine short- and long-horizon generation on retargeted HiPHI [24], followed by short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed [25] and retargeted HumanML3D [26]; BONES Seed retains its officially provided G1 trajectories.
The results demonstrate accurate control over extended rollouts together with strong short-horizon performance, while architectural ablations examine the contributions of recurrent state and history-dependent content memory.
Finally, we conduct real-world evaluation on a physical Unitree G1,
which demonstrates sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We propose Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based autoregressive diffusion model with persistent content memory, connecting accepted recurrent history to local attention for long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation.

We develop and evaluate state-preserving inference optimizations for this architecture, combining execution-flow simplification, fusion kernel, and CUDA Graph replay. On an RTX 4090, the complete optimization achieves a 6.138×6.138\times median paired speedup.

We evaluate the proposed framework on a physical Unitree G1 through multi-stage text-guided action composition and interactive keyboard/mouse control, demonstrating continuous motion execution under changing instructions and spatial commands. The system achieves 94% full-task success across 100 trials without observed falls.

A preliminary version of this work appeared in our ECCV 2024 conference paper, Motion Mamba [15]. The present manuscript substantially extends the
conference version in both methodology and experimental evaluation in the following six aspects.
(1) We reformulate the original text-conditioned latent diffusion framework into an autoregressive root–body diffusion architecture for long-horizon humanoid motion generation. Instead of synthesizing
a motion sequence as a single clip, the new framework generates successive 52-frame windows while accommodating changing text instructions and time-indexed spatial constraints.
(2) We redesign the temporal modeling architecture beyond the original Hierarchical Temporal Mamba (HTM) and Bidirectional Spatial Mamba (BSM) blocks. The new denoisers integrate resumable Mamba-3 recurrence with local attention and persistent content memory (PCM). PCM converts accepted recurrent-state summaries and their changes into gated content slots, providing attention-accessible representations of compressed motion history alongside the sliding cache.
(3) We introduce an accepted-only history update mechanism for autoregressive diffusion. Intermediate noisy predictions read an immutable historical snapshot, whereas the attention cache, recurrent states, and PCM slots are updated together only after a clean motion window is accepted. This separates diffusion sampling iterations from the temporal evolution of generated motion.
(4) We develop a hardware-aware inference pipeline that combines execution-flow simplification, custom fused kernel and CUDA Graph replay across three guidance branches.
(5) We extend the evaluation from the original
HumanML3D and KIT-ML text-to-motion benchmarks
to a unified G1 motion setting involving retargeted HiPHI, BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D. The new protocol evaluates spatial controllability, instruction matching, motion quality, and inference efficiency over autoregressive rollouts of up to 39.52 s.
(6) We further extend our evaluation to physics-based simulation and real-world deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid, assessing multi-stage text-guided actions alongside interactive spatial control via keyboard
and mouse.

1. We propose Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based autoregressive diffusion model with persistent content memory, connecting accepted recurrent history to local attention for long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation.

2. We develop and evaluate state-preserving inference optimizations for this architecture, combining execution-flow simplification, fusion kernel, and CUDA Graph replay. On an RTX 4090, the complete optimization achieves a 6.138×6.138\times median paired speedup.

3. We evaluate the proposed framework on a physical Unitree G1 through multi-stage text-guided action composition and interactive keyboard/mouse control, demonstrating continuous motion execution under changing instructions and spatial commands. The system achieves 94% full-task success across 100 trials without observed falls.

title: ProMix: Efficient Data Mixture Optimization for Robotic Imitation via Proxy-Reference DRO
authors: Qie Sima,Wei Xue,Yike Guo
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. We further provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model’s role in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy, low-quality domains (−3.8%-3.8\% average and −14.3%-14.3\% worst-domain success rate), and that entropy regularization is needed to prevent weight collapse. Evaluated on 9500 real-world episodes from the Open-X Embodiment dataset, ProMix improves the average success rate over uniform mixing from 68.4% to 76.2%, matching Re-Mix within evaluation noise while reducing mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours—versus 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B for full-scale searches—with a +17.1%+17.1\% absolute gain on the worst-case domain.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are rapidly transforming the robotics landscape, enabling agents to execute complex, open-world tasks from natural language instructions. The impressive generalization capabilities of these foundation models, such as RT-1 [1], are a direct result of pre-training on massive, diverse multimodal datasets. Recently, the field has gravitated toward “general-purpose physical intelligence” with the emergence of the π\pi model family [2, 3], which achieves state-of-the-art control through sophisticated data curation and distillation. Beyond proprietary efforts, open datasets such as Open-X [4] and DROID [5] and open models such as OpenVLA [6] and GR00T N1 [7] have made large-scale pre-training broadly accessible. However, a critical bottleneck is shifting from architecture to data: effectively blending heterogeneous data collected from disparate robots, platforms, and tasks. Naively pooling these domains causes performance saturation, and the curation recipes used by industrial labs are neither public nor reproducible.

Recent research has started to bridge LLM data optimization and robotics. DoReMi [8] showed that in LLM pre-training, domain weights can be learned cheaply by a small proxy model trained against a frozen reference model, so that the expensive weight search never touches the final large model. Re-Mix [9] ported this distributionally robust optimization (DRO) objective to large-scale imitation learning and demonstrated substantial gains over uniform and hand-tuned mixtures on Open-X Embodiment. However, Re-Mix’s instantiation retains a prohibitive cost structure: both the reference model and the robust proxy are trained on the full corpus at (near-)final policy scale, so the weight search roughly doubles the training budget before the final policy is even trained—a limitation the authors themselves highlight. Moreover, two questions that determine whether such methods are practical at the scale of modern VLA training remain unquantified. First, is the reference model actually load-bearing in robotics, where continuous action spaces and heteroscedastic demonstration noise dominate the loss? Without it, a standalone proxy may become overly pessimistic, disproportionately assigning weights to inherently chaotic or noisy trajectories rather than to domains with the most headroom for cross-domain generalization. Second, do weights learned at a small proxy scale transfer to the large backbones where the savings matter most? This transfer is asserted in prior work but has not been systematically measured for robotic policies.

This paper introduces ProMix, a framework that makes proxy-reference data mixture optimization practical for robotic imitation learning. ProMix learns mixture weights with a 15M-parameter proxy guided by a frozen, standardly-trained reference model, at a cost of 11 GPU-hours that is fixed regardless of the final backbone—under matched accounting, a full-scale search in our reimplementation of Re-Mix costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at the 7B scale—and transfers the learned weights, without re-tuning, to 50M and 7B VLA backbones. Beyond efficiency, we use ProMix as an experimental probe of the proxy-reference design itself: we provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled ablation of the reference model in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy domains (−3.8%-3.8\% average and −14.3%-14.3\% worst-domain success rate), and that an entropy regularizer on the weight simplex is essential to prevent weight collapse. This offers a practical path for researchers to achieve competitive performance without industrial-scale computing clusters, aligning with the industry trend toward compact yet capable models like π0.5\pi_{0.5} [3].

Our key contributions are as follows:

We present ProMix, a compute-efficient proxy-reference framework for data mixture optimization in robotic imitation learning, which reduces mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours—versus 16 GPU-hours at 50M and 192 GPU-hours at 7B (17×17\times) for full-scale searches—by performing the entire search with a 15M proxy rather than full-scale policies.

We provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model in robotic DRO, demonstrating that the excess-loss objective is essential for mitigating over-pessimism on noisy, heterogeneous robotic data, and we identify entropy regularization as the stabilizer that prevents weight collapse.

We quantify cross-scale transferability on the Open-X Embodiment dataset: weights learned by the 15M proxy consistently improve 50M and 7B VLA models, lifting the average success rate from 68.4% to 76.2% and the worst-domain rate from 51.4% to 68.5%.

title: Arcadian: Open-Source Humanoid Ecosystem for Accessible and Customizable Research and Education
authors: Zelin Shen,Gabriel Ramos Salinas,Qiyu Zhang,Yue Qin,Chen Qian,Yanran Ding
abstract:
Reproducing and modifying a meter-scale humanoid remains challenging for research and teaching groups with limited fabrication resources and engineering support.
This paper presents Arcadian, an open-source humanoid ecosystem that offers accessible and customizable humanoid hardware and software with community support.
Arcadian aims to strike a balance among cost-effectiveness, structural durability, and full customizability, lowering the barrier to entry for research and education.
Specifically, this meter-scale humanoid adopts metal-embedded 3D printing to achieve a high strength-to-cost ratio, eliminating the need for computer numerical control (CNC) machining while retaining design flexibility.
Extensive simulation and hardware tests validate the design: a reinforcement-learning (RL) locomotion policy trained in simulation transfers to the hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) teleoperation interface drives both arms for simple manipulation tasks.
The robot is around one meter tall and costs approximately $6,800 to build.
All computer-aided design (CAD) models, the bill of materials, assembly documentation, and training and deployment code are publicly released, distributed through Tnkr.ai and MakerWorld and supported by a Discord server and a project forum through which community feedback informs design updates.
The ecosystem resources are available at 
https://anonymous-humanoid.gitbook.io/docs.
introduction:
The rise of Artificial Intelligence combined with the maturity of actuators has sparked unprecedented interest in humanoid research. Commercial platforms have become affordable for a well-funded research lab, exemplified by the Unitree G1 humanoid, democratizing research in locomotion, whole-body skill learning and teleoperation [1, 2], to name a few. Although the Unitree G1 is relatively affordable, import restrictions can limit the options available to U.S. labs, and domestic alternatives can be expensive. Even when labs can obtain a platform, proprietary hardware designs can restrict hardware modifications, and secondary development is often limited to the manufacturer’s application programming interface (API). Furthermore, the tightly integrated hardware is often treated as a black box, whose actuator, transmission, and electronics are inaccessible for modification, making research on humanoid hardware difficult.
Some manufacturers market their humanoids as open platforms that researchers can modify. K-Scale Labs, for example, publishes the mechanical and electrical designs for K-Bot along with its control software [3].

Research labs have also developed their own humanoid platforms to adapt the hardware to specific research needs. Examples include the MIT Humanoid [4], Berkeley Humanoid [5], and HECTOR [6]. These platforms have supported research on dynamic locomotion and loco-manipulation. The academic publications documented the overall system architectures and key design decisions, allowing researchers from other labs to examine how the platforms are constructed and potentially reproduce the results. However, reproducing a complete robot requires detailed build documentation and a team with experience in fabrication, electronics integration, and control.

Fully open-source humanoid platforms such as ToddlerBot [8] and Berkeley Humanoid Lite [9] released hardware designs, software, and detailed construction documentation. Both projects made print-ready designs available on MakerWorld and set up Discord servers. ToddlerBot also provided an interactive assembly guide on Tnkr.ai. Builders can fabricate replacement parts for both platforms on desktop printers.
Their compact size makes these robots easier to handle in the lab, but it can limit their ability to reach tools on a workbench designed for human operators.

Building a larger robot for these tasks also places greater loads on its leg structures. The open-source ARTEMIS [10] and Duke Humanoid [11] platforms address these demands with structural components produced by CNC machining, which provide greater structural strength and load capacity. Nevertheless, CNC machining is not always available in a laboratory or classroom, and outsourcing these components adds to the build cost and iteration time. Labs building meter-scale humanoids need an accessible, low-cost way to make load-bearing parts.

This paper presents Arcadian, a low-cost, reproducible, open-source humanoid with an ecosystem to support its wide adoption, as shown in Fig. 1. The robot is 1.111.11 m high and can be built with a budget of around $6,800. To achieve structural strength and durability while maintaining reproducibility and low cost, we adopt a composite material framework. Specifically, waterjet-cut metal is placed along the load-bearing paths, and the remaining custom structural components are produced using desktop 3D printers and can be reprinted for replacement.
The design requires no custom printed circuit boards (PCBs), custom actuators, or CNC-machined components. Beyond the waterjet-cut and 3D-printed parts, all components are commercially available.
Table I compares Arcadian with representative academic humanoids in physical specifications, fabrication requirements, open-source resources, and community support.
Arcadian’s CAD, bill of materials, detailed reproduction documentation, training code, and deployment code are all released as open source.
We distribute them through Tnkr.ai and MakerWorld and provide a Discord server and a project forum, aiming to close the loop between developers and users: replication issues and quick fixes reported by users flow back into the design, so that the platform continues to improve after publication.

title: How Should a Home Robot Update Its Memories When Human Routines Change?
authors: Oliver Wang,Mani Srivastava
comment: Non-archival version presented at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Continually Self-Improving Robots and the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Robot Memory. Code:this https URL
abstract: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot’s memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot’s own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule’s gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.
introduction:
Robots deployed in homes must keep learning about the specific home they work in. A robot that helps with chores should know where objects are, and where objects are depends on the people who live there and on what those people are doing. If someone gets sick and stays home for a week, maybe their laptop that was usually stored in a backpack now tends to be open all day on their bedroom desk. When they recover, the laptop goes back to the backpack. A robot’s memory has to do three things at once. It must adapt during the sick period, recognize when to switch back to the healthy routine, and remember the sick-week experience (so that the next time this person is sick the robot already knows where to look).

One approach is to give the robot a language model that maintains written summaries of the home, revising them each night from what the robot saw and reading them each day when deciding where to search [1, 2, 3, 4]. A language model could notice that several objects moved for one shared reason, or recognize a situation it has seen before. However, Zhang et al. [5] show that when a language model repeatedly rewrites its own memory, the memory accumulates errors, and that simply keeping the raw episodes is competitive with every summarization method they test. Their worlds never change. Robot memory benchmarks test recall within one episode or as unrelated sessions accumulate [6, 7, 8], and scene memories keep a map current as objects move [9, 10, 11]. None of these test whether a memory written over weeks keeps what one routine taught it for the day that routine returns.

We test this in simulated households where one resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. The robot answers object-location questions by observing up to three rooms, learns only from what it sees, and is never told that anyone is sick. We compare a simple rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. Two conclusions come out of this. First, what helped the robot search was keeping its past sightings available. The summaries carried less than the sighting history, and a model that read the history did no better for also writing summaries. Second, the summaries adapted to the illness but did not retain it: they recorded where objects went and never that anyone was sick. When the illness returned, the methods that kept the history did better, mostly by reusing stored sightings. We argue that written robot memories should also be evaluated on what they keep for a routine that returns.

title: Superellipse Function: A Powerful Geometric Tool for the Design and Deformation Modeling of Tendon-Driven Continuum Manipulators With Flexural Patterns Experiencing Tension Loss
authors: Yang Liu,Farshid Alambeigi
abstract:
In this article, we feature the Superellipse function
as a geometric and versatile tool
for effective design and modeling of flexural patterns (FPs) in tendon-driven continuum manipulators (TD-CMs) with discontinuous cross-section geometries. We also propose a unique complementary mathematical framework and solution algorithm for modeling the effects of distributed and concentrated friction forces– caused by partially-constrained tendons– on tension loss and deformation behavior of a TD-CM designed using a Superellipse function.
Particularly, by employing this geometric function, we establish four intuitive functional mappings relating the manipulator’s geometric parameters, kinematics, and deformation behavior.
Thanks to the features of these intuitive mappings and Superellipse function, we then introduce the concepts of design space and design curve to facilitate intuitive design of a TD-CM with a generic FP geometry experiencing tendon tension loss.
To thoroughly evaluate the performance of this novel framework and its aforementioned features, we performed various simulation and experimental studies on TD-CMs designed and fabricated based on a Superellipse function. Results were then analyzed and compared using different error metrics.
introduction:
Tendon-Driven Continuum Manipulators (TD-CMs) are designed to imitate the flexibility and dexterity of natural biological systems [1]. These robots are often made of a flexible backbone actuated by tendons that extend along the structure’s length, allowing for controlling the shape, stiffness, and deformation of the robot [2]. As opposed to the conventional robots, TD-CMs lack rigid links and recognizable rotational joints, resulting in infinite degrees of freedom (DoF) and the ability to bend continuously through elastic deformation along their body [2] (see Fig. 1). These unique characteristics allow TD-CMs to offer several benefits over rigid-body robots, such as inherent compliance, light weight, small form-factor, excellent accessibility, dexterity, and safe interaction with the environment [2]. Such features make them a great candidate for various medical procedures in which a TD-CM can safely navigate through tight spaces for diagnosis or treatment purposes [3]. Examples include different minimally invasive surgeries in orthopedics [4], single-incision laparoscopic procedures [5], and eye surgeries [6].

The steerability, flexibility, and bending behavior of TD-CMs directly depend on their material constitution (e.g., Nitinol [7] or silicon [8]) and geometrical structure (e.g., their shape [1], and continuous [9] or discontinuous [10] geometry), and number of segments (e.g. [11]).
Using these parameters, various types of TD-CMs have been introduced by researchers. Nevertheless, design and development of this type of manipulators typically suffer from various challenges that need to be addressed [1].
First, a review of the literature shows that design of TD-CMs with discontinuous geometry (i.e., including notch or flexure patterns (FPs) along the body of robot) is often presumed (e.g., [12]) or selected based on finite element analysis (FEA) (e.g., [13], [14]) and not a generic analytical modeling framework to thoroughly study the effect of these patterns on the deformation behavior of the manipulator.
For example, in [15], [16], and [17], authors have pre-selected a rectangular FP for their TD-CM whereas in [12] and [10], a circular pattern has been used and presumed without optimally designing this pattern by performing an analytical design procedure. It is worth highlighting that although FEA has been suggested as a tool for the design and deformation modeling of soft robots (e.g., [13, 14, 17, 18]), performing reliable and valid FEA of a TD-CM with discontinuous geometry is often time-consuming and very challenging, especially when considering large deformation for these robots and interactions between tendons and the robot body causing hysteresis and tension loss due to friction [19, 20, 21].
Therefore, there is a crucial need for a more comprehensive and generic mathematical framework that can readily enable design of a wide range of TD-CMs with distinct flexural patterns and analyzing their effects on the deformation behavior of TD-CMs.

Aside from the effect of FPs on the deformation behavior of TD-CMs,
this important design parameter also directly affects the tension loss and hysteresis of these robots. As shown in [3, 22, 23, 20, 24, 21], the deformation behavior and tension-loss of TD-CMs are inter-related and need to be simultaneously considered during the design and modeling of such manipulators.
Nevertheless, to simplify this complex and nonlinear problem, most of the existing literature neglect to consider the concurrent effect of robot geometry and loss of tendons’ tensions because of friction on robot deformation behavior. Examples include but not limited to the studies using piecewise constant-curvature (e.g., [25], [26]) and variable-curvature methods (e.g., [8], [27]) solely focusing on modeling deformation behavior of TD-CM in an ideal friction-less situation. Although there exist studies that have considered the effects of friction in modeling deformation behavior of TD-CMs and tendon-sheath systems, they typically rely on simplifying assumptions or models such as models using lumped parameters [28], pre-defined or known tendon configurations (e.g., tendon wrap angle [29] and tendon curvature distribution [30]), or experimentally-tuned parameters that are not generic and can be applied on particular types of TD-CMs and experimental conditions [31].

To partially address the above-mentioned limitations, in [23], [32], [20] and [24], we proposed analytical modelling frameworks that fully describe the unknown correlation between internal forces and deformation behaviors of TD-CMs with continuous geometries without relying on a priori known information or experimentally-tuned parameters. However, similar to the most friction-less and friction-based models in the literature (e.g., [1]), our model did not account for the effect of discontinuous cross-section geometries or FPs on TD-CM design and deformation behavior. Particularly, the proposed models, cannot completely describe the effect of distributed and concentrated point friction forces caused by partially-constrained tendons inside the tendon channels of TD-CMs.

To address the aforementioned limitations, and as our main contributions, in this work,
(1) we propose a unique mathematical framework that
features the superellipse functions [33] (see Fig. 1) as a geometric and versatile tool for effective design and modeling of a generic FP (e.g., triangular, rectangular, or circular) in TD-CMs with discontinuous cross-section geometries;
(2) We also propose a unique complementary mathematical framework and solution algorithm for modeling the effects of distributed and concentrated friction forces– caused by partially-constrained tendons– on tension loss and deformation behavior of a TD-CM designed and modeled by a superellipse function.
Particularly, by employing this geometric function, we establish four intuitive functional mappings relating the manipulator’s geometric parameters, kinematics, and deformation behavior enabling efficient design and optimization of TD-CMs with complex FP geometries;
(3) Thanks to the features of these intuitive mappings and superellipse function, we also introduce the concepts of design space and design curve to intuitively design a generic TD-CM with FPs experiencing tension loss; and
(4) To thoroughly evaluate the performance of this novel framework and its aforementioned features,
we performed various simulation and experimental studies on TD-CMs designed based on a superellipse function. Results were then analyzed and compared using different error metrics.

title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
authors: Zifan Zeng,Qunli Zhang,Peng Wang,Shiming Liu,Feng Liu,Zheng Hu
comment: Manuscript submitted to IEEE OJ-ITS and is currently under review
abstract:
Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a
signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may
change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack
onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model’s samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the
attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the
same specification decides acceptance.
On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the
specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per
scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the
public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner’s failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label
requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.
introduction:
Motion planners of automated vehicles have to be tested in safety-critical
interactions, and learned planners need such interactions in their training data. An example is a
vehicle that cuts in at a short gap in front of the vehicle under test, the ego vehicle. Such interactions
are rare in recorded driving data, and scenarios that contain them therefore have to be
generated [1].
At the trajectory level, a scenario is the motion of all agents on a map. The content of a scenario is
specified and checked at this level, and the levels below take it as input. Traffic layouts and agent
trajectories condition the generation of driving video and sensor
data [2, 3], and end-to-end driving policies are tested in closed
loop on scenarios defined at this level [4].
Trajectory diffusion models trained on recorded data generate realistic multi-agent
behavior [5, 6, 7], and guiding their sampling
with differentiable objectives makes them controllable [5, 8, 9].
In both uses, the generated trajectory of the ego vehicle has a role of its own. In testing, it shows
that the attack can be avoided, so that a failure of the planner under test is meaningful. In
training, it is the label that the planner imitates.

A generator of such scenarios is useful at scale if it has three capabilities. It has to generalize, that is, cover the scenario types that matter, such as the pre-crash types of the National Highway
Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) [10], at a low cost for each new type. Its
scenarios have to be valid: the attack takes place as specified, and the ego vehicle has a legitimate
response once the attack is observable. Finally, it has to be efficient and yield many valid scenarios per compute hour and per recorded input, since processing a recorded input
further, for example by sensor-level reconstruction, is expensive. This paper addresses scenarios at
the trajectory level. It does not address sensor simulation or the training of the generative model.

A recent survey of foundation models for scenario generation [11]
lists problems that limit these capabilities. Gradient-guided diffusion models require carefully tuned
objective weights, and adapting them to new constraints is costly. The objectives are hand-written
terms [5] or loss code, weights included, that a large language model (LLM) writes from a description [12, 13]. Either way, each new scenario type needs its own terms.
Since the objective is separate from the check that later decides validity, a sample can minimize the
objective and still fail the check, and no output carries a mark of validity. The survey also lists the
computational cost of generation among the open problems. Formal specifications are the established way
to state the content of a test scenario, and scenarios are synthesized from
them [14, 15]. Signal temporal logic (STL) offers
both a guidance objective, through its quantitative semantics, and a
monitor [5, 16].

A further problem concerns validity (Fig. 1). Guided diffusion models that generate
all agents, the ego vehicle included, optimize the terms of the attacker and of the ego vehicle in one
objective [5, 12]. This objective does not represent the roles of the scenario. A
safety term of the ego vehicle then sends its gradient to the attacker as well and moves it back, which
cancels the attack. The attack is defined with respect to the ego vehicle that has not yet
reacted, but it is optimized against the ego vehicle that is responding. As a result, the attacker chases the response, and a cut-in can become a collision with the unreacted ego vehicle. Generators that run the ego vehicle as an
external planner in closed loop [8, 9, 13] avoid these
interactions, but they produce no trajectory of the ego vehicle that could serve as a reference or a
label. Optimizing the attack first and a response afterwards has been used to find failures of a given
planner and their solutions [17, 18]. In guided generation, which terms may
move which agent and in which order have so far been designed for a given pair of roles or scenario
type [19, 20].

In each of these problems, the objective does not represent which agent attacks, which agent responds,
and from which time on it may respond. We therefore state each
scenario as a role-typed, causal STL specification (Fig. 2). Every clause names the
agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the clauses of the ego vehicle may read the attacker
only from the attack onset on. An LLM drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker
returns errors for repair. From the checked specification, a compiler derives how it is solved: each
clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted seed of the ego vehicle and
fixed before the response is solved, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. The
solver edits a seed scene (a diffusion sample or a planner’s trajectory).

The contributions of this paper are the following.

We introduce a role-typed, causal fragment of signal temporal logic for adversarial scenarios, in
which every clause has an owner role and a causal type and clauses compose without weights.
Specifications are drafted by an LLM from a description and accepted by a type system that enforces
ownership and causality and drives a repair loop. A new scenario type needs a description and no new
weights. The rule that binds the attacker and the judge of the type remain fixed per type.

We derive a role-structured solve from the specification: the ownership of every clause, the order
of the roles, which solves the attack against the unreacted ego vehicle before the response, the attack
onset that releases the response, and the monitor as the acceptance gate. The response can then neither
cancel the attack nor draw it toward itself, and the monitor marks which outputs satisfy the specification.

We make the compiled specification efficient to solve at scale. The compiled objective is one tensor
program per specification, so the seeds of many windows are solved in one batch on an accelerator; a pre-check
skips seeds that cannot satisfy the specification, the monitor ends accepted roles early, and each distinct
accepted seed is a further scenario from the same input. Under a fixed budget this yields about nine times as many
solved windows per hour as one window at a time, and more valid scenarios per recorded input.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work.
Section III formalizes the scenario and the generation problem, and
Section IV presents the method. Section V reports the experiments,
Section VI discusses limitations, and Section VII concludes the
paper.

title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
authors: Wenjie Lin,Jin Wei-Kocsis
abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control have enabled teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. To address this challenge, we propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our world model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. These results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
introduction:
Physics-based human-object interaction (HOI) requires coordinating body motion, contact, and object dynamics [28, 15, 8, 29]. In cooperative transport, the shared object further couples the humanoids’ movements: each agent must respond to both the load and its teammates. Recent approaches have enabled such coordination across different objects and team sizes [5, 14, 11, 3]. However, constrained environments require the team to adapt both its route and its configuration around the object [16, 19, 1]. Narrow passages may require humanoids to reposition, while blocking walls demand coordinated detours. These decisions must account for the entire team. For example, a collision-free path for the object may still cause a humanoid to collide with obstacles. We therefore study whether pretrained cooperative transport skills can meet these demands through shared temporary waypoints, avoiding repeated policy retraining for new layouts and team sizes. The central challenge is to predict how each waypoint affects the coupled team and object.

Hierarchical skill reuse [25, 21, 17, 22, 13, 18]
and predictive planning with world models [6, 7, 33]
provide a basis for this adaptation.
However, adapting cooperative transport to constrained environments remains challenging, as alternative waypoint commands can affect not only object motion but also the collective behavior of the humanoid team. Effective guidance must therefore consider object progress alongside team-level obstacle contacts and failure risks. To address this challenge, we introduce CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built on a relational world model, CarlWM. CarlWM represents humanoids, the carried object, and obstacles as interacting entities and learns from counterfactual simulator rollouts to imagine how alternative waypoint commands affect the coupled team and object. Counterfactual anchoring expresses command effects relative to unchanged guidance. CarlHOI then selects shared waypoints using predicted progress, failure and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, while the frozen transport policy coordinates individual movements.

Our contributions are threefold:

Counterfactual predictive guidance for cooperative transport.
We propose CarlHOI and its relational world model, CarlWM, to predict and compare collective responses to alternative shared waypoints. Counterfactual anchoring, branched-rollout supervision, and long-horizon value estimation enable adaptive guidance of frozen transport policies.

A benchmark for constrained multi-humanoid transport.
We introduce narrow-passage, wall-detour, and multi-obstacle tasks that require coordinated transport under environmental constraints, with matched initial states and a common arrival criterion for systematic evaluation.

Zero-shot generalization to unseen teams, objects, and controllers.
Trained with four humanoids, one object, and one controller, CarlWM transfers without retraining to teams of 2-10, unseen objects, controllers, and obstacle configurations, improving transport success over evaluated baselines.

1. Counterfactual predictive guidance for cooperative transport.
We propose CarlHOI and its relational world model, CarlWM, to predict and compare collective responses to alternative shared waypoints. Counterfactual anchoring, branched-rollout supervision, and long-horizon value estimation enable adaptive guidance of frozen transport policies.

2. A benchmark for constrained multi-humanoid transport.
We introduce narrow-passage, wall-detour, and multi-obstacle tasks that require coordinated transport under environmental constraints, with matched initial states and a common arrival criterion for systematic evaluation.

3. Zero-shot generalization to unseen teams, objects, and controllers.
Trained with four humanoids, one object, and one controller, CarlWM transfers without retraining to teams of 2-10, unseen objects, controllers, and obstacle configurations, improving transport success over evaluated baselines.

title: SparQ4D: Learning to Act through Sparse 4D Queries
authors: Siyuan Xie,Jinxi Xiao,Ran Ji,Yikai Liu,Mingxi Li,Xuebing Li,Ye Shi,Yuxiang Gao,Jiayuan Gu
abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces SparQ4D, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, SparQ4D achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to 5×5\times faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
introduction:
Successful manipulation is inherently spatiotemporal: it depends on knowing where things are and how they will move. To hang a mug, a robot must grasp it, align its handle with a rack, and relate wrist and external camera views as it moves. Action demonstrations supervise the desired behavior but leave these relationships implicit. Efficiently teaching a policy this spatiotemporal structure is thus a central question.

One approach to supervising spatiotemporal understanding is through future prediction. World action models (WAMs) jointly model future visual observations and robot actions [26], while X-WAM [11] extends this paradigm to multi-view RGB-D prediction. Reconstructing the full future supervises scene dynamics richly, but requires dense prediction over many visual tokens, substantially increasing training cost. Fast-WAM [27] removes future generation at inference yet retains strong performance, suggesting that much of the benefit comes from the training signal itself.
Another line injects geometric knowledge into vision-language-action models (VLAs) through pretrained 3D representations: R3DP [30] incorporates foundation-model features via a fast-slow perception system, and Spatial Forcing [14] aligns VLA representations with 3D teacher features during training. Although effective, these methods likewise rely on dense, per-token supervision. This leads to our central question: can sparse, explicit supervision teach a robot policy both geometry and motion at substantially lower training cost, without additional inference overhead or sacrificing expressivity?

We introduce SparQ4D, a lightweight framework that injects holistic 4D understanding into robot policies through unified sparse supervision (Fig. ). Inspired by D4RT [29], our key idea is to formulate diverse spatiotemporal tasks as a single query: where is a selected point at a specified time, in a specified view or coordinate frame? Given a query specifying the point, time, and reference frame, a lightweight decoder predicts its location. By varying these attributes, the same decoder provides supervision for depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations. We attach this decoder to intermediate VLA representations and jointly optimize auxiliary predictions with action learning, encouraging the policy to encode rich geometric and temporal structure. Crucially, this unified formulation eliminates the need for dense reconstruction. During training, we sample only a small budget of queries across points, times, and views, directly controlling auxiliary decoding cost while retaining diverse spatiotemporal supervision. At inference, the decoder is simply removed, leaving the original policy architecture and computation unchanged. Thus, SparQ4D decouples rich training-time supervision from inference-time complexity.

Across simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, SparQ4D achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance with both π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5}, reducing failures by up to 60%. These gains span RoboTwin 2.0 [6], LIBERO-Plus [9], and five real-world tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our unified supervision. Beyond performance, SparQ4D requires up to 5×5\times fewer training GPU-hours than WAM-based approaches, while introducing no additional inference overhead. Finally, probing analyses reveal recoverable 4D structure, suggesting that the policy itself internalizes this structure rather than relying on the auxiliary decoder.
Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce SparQ4D, a lightweight yet expressive framework that injects holistic 4D understanding into robot policies through a unified query-based supervision interface.

We enable efficient training through a small, controllable budget of sparse 4D queries, reducing auxiliary supervision cost without sacrificing expressivity or inference speed.

We demonstrate improved manipulation performance across multiple backbones, simulation environments and the real world. We also systematically examine supervision content, density, placement and internal representation through controlled ablations.

1. We introduce SparQ4D, a lightweight yet expressive framework that injects holistic 4D understanding into robot policies through a unified query-based supervision interface.

2. We enable efficient training through a small, controllable budget of sparse 4D queries, reducing auxiliary supervision cost without sacrificing expressivity or inference speed.

3. We demonstrate improved manipulation performance across multiple backbones, simulation environments and the real world. We also systematically examine supervision content, density, placement and internal representation through controlled ablations.

title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
authors: Siyeon Kim,Mohanraj Devendran Shanthi,Joseph C. Liechty,Tucker Hermans
comment: Under review. Project page:this https URL. The second and third authors contributed equally
abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.
introduction:
Learned manipulation models must generalize beyond their training data, yet contact-rich skills make this difficult: small changes in contact conditions, object geometry, or inertial properties can produce qualitatively different outcomes such as sliding, toppling, or rotating. Real-world deployment further introduces perception errors, motion execution errors [1], and sim-to-real mismatch [2, 3, 4], especially when models operate across objects from partial perceptual inputs such as images or point clouds. These factors do not merely broaden predictions around a single mean; they induce distinct, physically plausible outcome modes under nearly identical states and actions. We therefore argue for skill-effect models (SEMs) that explicitly represent multimodal robot action effects.

Robots with reliable action-outcome uncertainty estimates can act more safely [5] and efficiently [6]. For example, a planner that anticipates multiple possible effects can avoid pushes likely to topple a crate rather than slide it, preventing unsafe states and costly recovery actions. While probabilistic safety filters can mitigate some planning failures [5, 6], their effectiveness depends on the fidelity and structure of the underlying action-effect model. More generally, robots that reason about and visualize alternative futures can solicit human intervention under high uncertainty [7, 8, 9] or communicate uncertainty to nearby humans, improving trust and transparency [9, 10, 11].

Stochastic dynamics models have a long history in robot manipulation, including Gaussian process regression [12], Gaussian mixture models of state-space dynamics [13], and neural network ensembles [14]. Because these methods model low-level transitions or represent uncertainty indirectly, they do not directly support reasoning about mode probabilities or visualizing alternative outcomes. SEMs [15] instead abstract away low-level dynamics by predicting the outcomes of temporally extended skills, and prior work shows that explicitly modeling skill-effect uncertainty with mixture density networks (MDNs) [16] can improve planning under uncertainty [17]. The MDN-based SEM in [17], however, assumes known object identities and trains separate models per object.

In this paper, we propose learning multimodal, probabilistic SEMs directly from partial point clouds. We train three representative classes of multimodal architectures: explicit mixture densities, state tokenization, and flow matching. We study their tradeoffs for predicting and reasoning about skill outcomes under uncertainty; see Figure  and Table I.
In summary, we make the following contributions:

Object-generalizable multimodal skill-effect models — We learn probabilistic skill effects from partial point clouds across seen and unseen objects, without object-specific models;

Comparison of multimodal representations — We compare mixture densities, state tokenization, and flow matching against deterministic and Gaussian baselines on push, pick, and place; and

Benefits of multimodality for prediction and planning — We show that the multimodal heads predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and single Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill in simulation, and on a real robot the probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often. Flow matching is the most accurate of these heads and the MDN the fastest to plan with.

title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
authors: Jiyong Kwon,Yikun Bai,Amirhossein Mollaali,Guang Lin
abstract:
Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π0,π0.5\pi_{0},\pi_{0.5} generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions:
(1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete cc-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularization.
(2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera images, language instructions, and proprioceptive states to robot actions, which allows a single policy to perform diverse manipulation tasks from natural-language commands. Flow-based VLAs such as π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [5, 21] build an action expert on a pretrained vision-language model and generate continuous action chunks by flow matching [27, 31], which supports high-frequency and dexterous control. These models are trained by pretraining on large demonstration datasets followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the target task. SFT requires costly expert trajectories, its performance is bounded by the quality of these demonstrations, and the resulting policy tends to overfit to them. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a post-training stage that improves the policy through interaction with the environment, which allows it to exceed the demonstrations and to generalize better to new conditions.

Online RL has recently achieved strong results in generative modeling. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [46] estimates advantages from a group of samples without a value network and has improved the reasoning ability of large language models [19]. Flow-GRPO [29] brings GRPO to flow-matching models by converting the deterministic sampler into a stochastic differential equation, which gives a tractable likelihood for each denoising step, and it improves text-to-image generation in compositional accuracy and text rendering. πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} [9] extends this approach to flow-based VLAs with learned or converted noise injection, and it raises the success rates of few-shot SFT policies to the level of policies trained on full demonstration datasets. These methods update the policy through clipped likelihood ratios or a Kullback–Leibler (KL) penalty, which can be viewed as a KL proximal step whose continuous-time limit is the Fisher–Rao gradient flow. In this geometry, the update reweights the sampled actions according to their advantages and keeps their positions fixed.

Optimal transport (OT) provides a complementary geometry, in which an update moves samples. The Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto (JKO) scheme [22] discretizes a Wasserstein gradient flow as a sequence of proximal steps under the Wasserstein distance, and it has been used to train generative models, including input-convex neural networks for large-scale gradient flows [37, 16] and normalizing flows trained block by block [54]. Wasserstein gradient flows have also been applied to RL: policy optimization can be interpreted as a Wasserstein gradient flow over policies [59, 61], and Wasserstein Policy Optimization [40] projects this flow onto the policy parameters, using the action gradient of a learned action-value function, and SWFP [48] implements each JKO step of a flow policy against a learned soft Q-function. These methods require a learned critic, whereas a GRPO group provides only scalar rewards at the sampled actions. For robot control, the Wasserstein geometry is natural, since distances between action chunks measure differences in physical motion. In this paper, we augment the clipped likelihood-ratio update of Flow-GRPO with a Wasserstein proximal step and propose JKO-GRPO, a new RL method for flow-based VLA policies.

Our contributions are as follows.

At each state, we treat the group of actions sampled by the old policy as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a JKO step of the advantage. Restricted to the group, this step has a closed-form solution given by a discrete cc-transform: each sampled action moves to the sampled action with the highest advantage net of the transport cost. We soften this discrete update and fit the deterministic flow sampler to the resulting targets by regression through the shared noise, which requires no policy density, and combine this loss with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective, so that the update both reweights and moves the sampled actions.

We show that, at the old parameters, the negative gradient of our transport loss is proportional to a masked empirical pathwise update whose action-space direction is constructed from the group without a critic.

We extend JKO-GRPO to the πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} setting through random-time branching, which restores the simulator state at selected decision times along each trajectory and applies the update at multiple action chunks. Experiments yield favorable results on ManiSkill, LIBERO, and MetaWorld, with improved success on all 13 unseen ManiSkill scenes.
