title: TASC: Time-to-Collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd Attention for Non-Holonomic Service Robots
authors: Mohammadhossein Malmir,Mohammadali Rahmati,Mohammad Reza Kolani,Alois Knoll
comment: . Accepted for publication at the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII)
abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.
introduction:
Service robots are moving out of structured industrial cells and into airports, hospitals, shopping centers, and offices. There, a robot shares the floor with people who neither coordinate with it nor stand still, and navigation becomes a prerequisite for deployment: the robot must reach its goal safely and predictably, without making the people around it uncomfortable.

Classical planners handle this setting poorly because they treat people as moving obstacles, not as agents who react to the robot. In dense crowds, the result is unnecessary detours or a complete stop, known as the freezing robot problem [2]. Deep reinforcement learning instead learns interaction behavior directly, without a map [3], and recent architectures encode the relations between agents with graph networks and attention [4, 5, 6].

Two practical gaps separate this line of work from a deployable platform. First, the attention- and graph-based policies of the standard crowd benchmark [4, 5] are trained for a holonomic disk, whereas a service robot usually has a differential-drive base. Second, the methods that model a unicycle either select from a discrete action set [7, 6], which produces a jerky velocity profile, or output continuous commands [8, 9] but do not select among pedestrians. Non-holonomic kinematics, continuous commands, and hardware deployment each exist in prior work, but not together with selective attention (Section II-D). This paper addresses that combination as a system-integration problem rather than as an isolated algorithm. The target platform is MiPA (My Intelligent Personal Assistant), a commercial differential-drive service robot from NEURA Robotics [10]. We refer to the integrated system as TASC (Time-to-collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd attention).

Our contributions are of three types:

Adapted method. We adapt the dual-selection attention module (DSAM) [6], designed for discrete-action value-based learning, to proximal policy optimization (PPO) [11] for continuous non-holonomic velocity control, and pair it with a closing-speed time-to-collision (TTC) feature that enters both the observation and the reward.

Adapted method. We adapt the dual-selection attention module (DSAM) [6], designed for discrete-action value-based learning, to proximal policy optimization (PPO) [11] for continuous non-holonomic velocity control, and pair it with a closing-speed time-to-collision (TTC) feature that enters both the observation and the reward.

System integration. We implement the complete pipeline from training to hardware: a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab [12] with 10,000 GPU-parallel environments, social force model (SFM) [13] pedestrians with stochastic stopping, crowd-size randomization, and a ROS 2 package that runs the policy on the physical robot in under 10 ms per inference.

Empirical characterization. We report the resulting behavior together with its main weakness: in 30,000 evaluation episodes, the policy times out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density, but its pedestrian collision rate grows from 4.5% to 17.4% as the crowd grows from five to ten pedestrians. We quantify this trade-off between liveness (continued progress) and safety and test the TTC feature in a retrained ablation.

title: Dr. Grasp-RL: Diverse and Robust Dexterous Grasping via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Kunqi Xu,Xiaokang Sun,Xueyan Zou
abstract:
Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with
PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and
robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.
introduction:
What is the essence of human’s ability to manipulate objects? How can we make robots exhibit human-level intelligence in their object manipulation performance? This remains an unsolved and even poorly understood problem [1, 17]. Humans can grasp the same object in many different ways, adapting their wrist pose and finger configuration to the current situation [7]. This flexibility suggests a desirable capability for robotic grasping: a single policy should support multiple effective grasping modes and select suitable actions from the current hand–object state. Diversity and feedback are complementary [18, 4]. Alternative grasping modes provide options when an approach is unfavorable, while closed-loop control allows the robot to adjust its actions and retry after failed contact [15]. The challenge is to learn a policy that retains this repertoire while realizing its behaviors through continuous physical interaction.

A useful perspective on this challenge comes from the distinction
between evaluating candidate solutions and generating them [8, 2].
Generative modeling offers an expressive means of representing
multiple plausible solutions, as illustrated by advances in image
and video generation [12, 13].
In dexterous grasping, grasp-synthesis approaches have similarly explored
large-scale grasp data and diverse grasp-pose distributions.
However, a grasp proposal alone does not specify how to reach, maintain, or recover it through physical interaction.
Conversely, some policy-learning approaches integrate grasping more
directly with feedback close-loop control, either through reinforcement
learning or subsequent policy distillation.
Yet optimizing task success does not necessarily encourage a
policy to preserve multiple successful grasping modes:
learning can concentrate on a narrow repertoire of effective
behaviors [6, 11].
Despite progress along both directions, jointly learning diverse
grasping strategies and reliable close-loop execution remains
a central challenge.

We revisit this challenge from a value-function perspective.
Rather than explicitly generating a target grasp pose, we seek to
learn a state-value landscape—a
scalar field over grasping states—with two key properties:
multiple high-value peaks and dense, informative guidance.
Each peak should correspond to a distinct effective grasp
configuration, allowing the landscape to represent multiple
valid ways of grasping the same object.
Far from the object, the value should generally increase as the
hand approaches a feasible grasp from different directions;
near contact, it should distinguish effective wrist poses and
finger configurations according to the object’s geometry.
Importantly, this guidance should extend beyond successful
grasp configurations to the intermediate states encountered
during approach, contact, and recovery.
Intuitively, a controller could then select actions that produce
the greatest expected increase in value under the robot’s
dynamics, repeatedly updating its decisions from the current
state.
Multiple peaks would preserve alternative grasping strategies,
while dense value guidance would support closed-loop execution
and adaptation after failures or disturbances.

This intuition naturally motivates an actor–critic approach [16]:
the critic learns to evaluate states associated with different
grasping modes, while the actor learns feedback actions that
lead toward high-return outcomes.
We therefore introduce Dr. Grasp-RL, which uses PPO [26] with simple
multilayer perceptron (MLP) networks to learn diverse, closed-loop
dexterous grasping.
Through a time-reversed training curriculum and diverse,
instructive reset states, we progressively extend learning from
states near successful grasps to earlier and more challenging
stages of the interaction.
We just use a simple reward proportional to object lift height.
Our experiments demonstrate diverse grasping behaviors, robust
closed-loop execution, and strong generalization across object
geometries. Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Dr. Grasp-RL, a framework for learning a
diverse repertoire of dexterous grasping behaviors within a
single closed-loop policy using MLP-based PPO.

We develop a time-reversed curriculum coupled with
diverse, curriculum-aligned reset states to facilitate
learning across multiple grasping modes with a simple
lift-height reward, without requiring an explicit
grasp-pose generator at execution time.

We evaluate the learned policy on more than 20,000
unseen objects after training on no more than 420 objects,
and analyze its grasp diversity, closed-loop recovery
behaviors, and generalization.

1. We introduce Dr. Grasp-RL, a framework for learning a
diverse repertoire of dexterous grasping behaviors within a
single closed-loop policy using MLP-based PPO.

2. We develop a time-reversed curriculum coupled with
diverse, curriculum-aligned reset states to facilitate
learning across multiple grasping modes with a simple
lift-height reward, without requiring an explicit
grasp-pose generator at execution time.

3. We evaluate the learned policy on more than 20,000
unseen objects after training on no more than 420 objects,
and analyze its grasp diversity, closed-loop recovery
behaviors, and generalization.

title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding
authors: Taekyung Kim,Ege Yuceel,Steven Hong,Georgios Fainekos,Dimitra Panagou,Bardh Hoxha
abstract:
Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.

introduction:
Planning from images requires more than predicting what a robot
will see next. A candidate maneuver must avoid obstacles, remain
within the workspace, and, for articulated vehicles, avoid jackknifing.
These requirements concern physical motion and geometry, not
similarity to a goal image. Optimization-based planning can enforce
explicitly modeled constraints, but errors in perception and scene
reconstruction can make their evaluation
unreliable [1].

World Models (WMs) learn predictive representations from
observation-action trajectories, enabling image-based control through
imagined rollouts [2, 3, 4].
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict representations
rather than reconstructing pixels [5].
LeWorldModel (Le-WM), for example, learns action-conditioned latent
dynamics through next-embedding prediction and
regularization [6, 7],
then plans toward encoded visual goals. Such representations support
predictive control but need not expose the task-space quantities
on which physical constraints are defined.

A downstream probe can predict safety values from latent rollouts,
but its outputs reflect errors in both the predicted latent trajectory
and the learned safety mapping. Near a
constraint boundary, an optimistic prediction can make an unsafe
maneuver appear acceptable. Thus, a favorable predicted safety
value alone does not establish physical constraint satisfaction.
Recent work has begun to address this gap. Kim et al.
calibrate a learned binary failure predictor for model-predictive
shielding [8]; SLS2 calibrates latent-dynamics and
constraint-prediction errors and propagates uncertainty sets through
robust model predictive control (MPC) [9]; and
concurrent work by Zhong et al. calibrates learned risk and
progress predictions before applying a separate deterministic
safety shield [10].

We propose JEPA-Shield with a guiding principle:
predict in latent space, evaluate constraints in physical
space, and account for prediction error before accepting an action trajectory.
A motion predictor converts the latent rollouts of a frozen JEPA
world model into multi-horizon relative trajectories, while a spatial
decoder estimates current unsafe geometry from encoder features.
Split conformal prediction calibrates the end-to-end motion error
to construct tubes for robust constraint evaluation.
A backup-based shield integrates these checks into diffusion-inspired
sampling-based MPC, retaining nominal prefixes only when their
backup-completed trajectories satisfy the robust constraints.
Under the stated initial-backup, exchangeability, and
conservative constraint-evaluation assumptions, the method provides

title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation
authors: Haoxiang Zhan,Haoqin Hong,Congcong Zhu,Jingrun Chen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks.
However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially.
In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution.
Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens.
We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time.
Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration.
Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.
introduction:
Everyday tasks often require intervening while physical conditions still permit success, whether bonding a handle before glue dries, stopping heating before milk overflows, or catching a falling cup before impact. Recent vision-language model (VLM) agents have expanded the capabilities available for robotic manipulation by combining general-purpose models with perception tools and executable programs [27, 24]. As these agents achieve leading scores on a public manipulation benchmark [2], evaluating their capabilities in time-sensitive everyday tasks becomes increasingly important. Such evaluation must determine whether agents complete the required intervention in time to achieve the task goal.

Recent benchmarks evaluate dynamic manipulation with ongoing environmental evolution and explicit inference delays [16, 3, 19]. Industrial manipulation evaluations also incorporate finite execution windows into task specifications [28]. Understanding timely intervention further requires relating an agent’s complete decision and execution sequence to the interval in which intervention can succeed. Task scores and individual decision times alone do not explain how agents use this interval.

For this analysis, we use action windows: process-dependent intervals during which the required intervention can achieve the task goal (Fig. ). Timely intervention requires recognizing window onset and completing the required operations before closure. Window duration provides the corresponding time budget for model inference, tool computation, and physical execution. Even when each decision takes less time than the window duration, successive decisions and movements can exhaust this budget.

We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark comprising 18 tasks across self-triggered, cued, and sudden-onset windows (Fig. 2). The tasks span rigid-body interactions, liquid transfer, inflation, and surface-state changes in photorealistic environments built with our scene generation pipeline. The evaluation protocol accounts for computation and physical execution on a shared simulation clock, with measured-time and controlled-delay conditions that preserve the same physical execution rules. We evaluate VLM agents across decision costs normalized by window duration and use execution traces to examine how their decisions and movements consume the available time.

Our contributions are:

An action-window task suite covering diverse physical processes with explicit window boundaries and task-specific success conditions.

A computation-aware evaluation protocol that measures decision costs relative to available intervention time while preserving physical execution rules.

A behavioral analysis of timely intervention linking decision and motion sequences to window use and task outcomes.

1. An action-window task suite covering diverse physical processes with explicit window boundaries and task-specific success conditions.

2. A computation-aware evaluation protocol that measures decision costs relative to available intervention time while preserving physical execution rules.

3. A behavioral analysis of timely intervention linking decision and motion sequences to window use and task outcomes.

title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
authors: Thanish Bolla
comment: . Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop "Do Robots Need World Models?". OpenReview:this https URL
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of π0.5\pi_{0.5} on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps π0.5\pi_{0.5} on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy’s data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551–0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator’s state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18  mm removes 70 % of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56  mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies now complete most tasks in standard manipulation benchmarks, but often unsafely. On LIBERO-10, π0.5\pi_{0.5} succeeds in 88.0 % of our episodes, yet only 70.5 % are free of violations such as pushing a non-target object, excessive contact force or tilting a carried object (Table 1). Because the policies are stochastic, a simple remedy at test time is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that is predicted to be safe. This requires a world model. The question is what kind of model, and how accurate it must be.

Two families of approaches could make this prediction. Implicit approaches learn a critic or value function that scores candidates directly [1, 2, 3]. Explicit approaches predict the future and evaluate it, as in latent safety filters [4, 5], Cosmos Policy [6] and learned predictive models combined with a geometric shield [7]. Both are usually judged in closed loop or by how well they separate safe from unsafe states pooled over a dataset. RoboMonkey’s offline comparisons at one state use the demonstrated action, not safety, as the reference [2]. A safety filter needs something narrower: at a single state, it must tell which of the policy’s own candidates is safe.

We study this question with the most accurate world model available, the simulator itself. A lookahead safety filter rolls the policy’s candidates forward from an exact copy of the simulator state and executes the one with the fewest predicted violations. For these candidates and this rule, no model can predict better, although another rule might be safer. Against it we place learned critics, dynamics and video models, and state estimators, and degrade the simulator’s state by known amounts.

With the exact model, the filter raises safety in all 8 policy–benchmark pairs (11.5 to 25.7 points on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus), for π0.5\pi_{0.5} largely via fallbacks. The learned critics we train detect dangerous states no better than a critic that never sees the candidate, and within a state they rank candidates near chance, as do the explicit models we test. Selection degrades with state error long before detection, and real estimators lose more than their median error predicts. Our answer to the workshop’s question: such a filter needs a world model that ranks actions at one state, and among the models and data we tested only the exact simulator does. Its state must also be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, where the median error says little. The test is therefore within-state ranking rather than pooled AUROC, and simulator labels make it cheap.

title: Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning
authors: Jiarui Li,Runyu Zhang,Gioele Zardini
abstract:
Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds.
Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed.
We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots.
TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice.
A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance.
For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it.
With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost.
They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.
introduction:
Large teams of robots that share a workspace are central to applications ranging from automated warehouse fulfillment [1, 2] and autonomous intersection management [3] to coordinated quadrotor swarms [4, 5], with commercial facilities deploying hundreds of robots in a single shared workspace [1].
In these settings, each robot must navigate from its start position to its goal without colliding with static obstacles or other robots.
Physical execution further requires that the motions obey the robot dynamics and actuation limits, which defines the Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning Problem (KMAMPP).
A solution assigns one time-parametrized trajectory to each robot.
The trajectories must be conflict-free, so that robot bodies remain disjoint from obstacles and one another at every instant, and dynamically feasible, so that the robot dynamics and actuation limits are satisfied [6].

In practice, the planning runtime governs both the fleet size that can be deployed and how quickly the fleet responds to change.
First, in offline planning, i.e., before execution begins, the computational burden grows with the number of robots, so the available planning time caps the fleet size that can be coordinated.
Second, a sufficiently fast planner can update the trajectories while the robots keep moving (Fig. 1), provided that each update returns within the lead time before it is executed.
Such real-time planning [7, 8] tightens the time budget further as the fleet grows.
Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners remain several orders of magnitude slower than such time budgets for large fleets.
Joint methods explore the combined state space of the fleet through sampling [9, 10] or optimize continuous trajectories under pairwise collision constraints [11].
Both couple inter-robot coordination with dynamics-constrained motion synthesis, so the state dimension and the number of collision constraints grow with every robot, which restricts these planners to relatively small teams [12].

By contrast, solvers for the related problem of MAPF scale to thousands of agents.
Standard MAPF coordinates point agents on a graph through synchronized moves and waits, avoiding simultaneous vertex occupancy and opposing edge traversals [13].
Within this abstraction, PIBT constructs joint moves through priority inheritance and backtracking [14], and LaCAM embeds this efficient successor generation in a complete configuration search that has solved instances with thousands of agents in tens of seconds [15, 16].

Its solutions, however, are discrete schedules that abstract away robot-body geometry and dynamics, and not the continuous, dynamically feasible trajectories required by the KMAMPP.
Several planners build on MAPF to solve the KMAMPP and differ in where they enforce dynamic feasibility.
One class incorporates the dynamics during the search: db-CBS and db-LaCAM [17, 12] run MAPF search over kinodynamic motion primitives, while K-CBS [18] coordinates single-robot kinodynamic planners within Conflict-Based Search (CBS).
Searching over higher-dimensional kinodynamic states and primitives is expensive, however, which limits scalability to tens of robots [12].
A second class enforces the dynamics after the discrete search through continuous postprocessing.
MAPF/C+POST [4] constructs a discrete schedule and then solves constrained trajectory optimization problems within safe corridors, and Park et al. [19] additionally guarantee that these problems are feasible, reporting an average planning time of 6.4 s for 64 robots.
Because postprocessing can reduce obstacle clearance and inter-robot separation, these pipelines must enforce continuous-time collision constraints during trajectory optimization, which takes several minutes for hundreds of robots [4].
In both classes, executable motion thus requires additional computation, either to generate and evaluate kinodynamic motions during the search or to solve trajectory optimization problems after it.
As the fleet grows, this computation limits how much of the speed and scalability of MAPF carries over to kinodynamic planning, particularly within the tighter time budgets of real-time planning.

We resolve this bottleneck by accounting for the robot dynamics before the discrete search.
Specifically, we analytically bound the clearance lost when a discrete plan is reconstructed into continuous trajectories under the prescribed speed and acceleration caps, and we reserve the corresponding margin in the discrete search.
A closed-form reconstruction, applied independently to each robot, then converts any valid discrete plan into smooth, dynamically feasible trajectories that are provably conflict-free in continuous time.
This approach needs neither kinodynamic search nor trajectory optimization.
The discrete search still ranges over synchronized moves and waits only, so the speed of MAPF solvers carries over, and any discrete solver that returns valid plans becomes a certified kinodynamic planner.

This paper presents Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that certifies dynamic feasibility and continuous-time collision avoidance through discrete coordination, together with two fast planners built on it.
TAKT brings kinodynamic multi-agent motion planning to real-time speeds for fleets of hundreds of robots and scales to more than a thousand robots, more than an order of magnitude beyond the largest fleets solved by existing baselines.
We model the robots as equal-radius closed balls in 2D and 3D with double-integrator dynamics and common speed and acceleration caps.
Our contributions are threefold.

First, we formulate TAKT as a pipeline of three stages, namely Discretization, Discrete Coordination, and Continuous Reconstruction (Section IV).
Discretization embeds a lattice in the workspace, reserves a certified clearance radius around each robot, and reduces the KMAMPP to a discrete search problem (Problem IV.1).
Discrete Coordination solves this problem with synchronized moves and waits, and Continuous Reconstruction filters the motion of each robot into a smooth trajectory.
We prove that every valid discrete plan reconstructs into conflict-free trajectories that satisfy the speed and acceleration caps, independently of the discrete solver (Theorem VII.1).
We also derive sufficient clearance conditions under which a discrete plan exists, both at a fixed lattice resolution and under lattice refinement (Theorems VII.2, VII.2 and VII.3).

Second, we introduce a diamond formulation of the discrete problem and two planners that solve it.
On a fine lattice, a robot spans many vertices, and a Euclidean separation rule can prevent it from yielding sideways in the same tick in which another robot advances.
The diamond formulation restores this one-tick sideways yielding, and we derive a sharp condition on the diamond size that guarantees the Euclidean separation required by reconstruction (Section V).
We then adapt PIBT and LaCAM to this formulation through backtracking over simultaneous blockers, priority reshuffling in stationary groups, Euclidean candidate ordering, and memory-efficient goal-distance queries, which yields TAKT-PIBT and TAKT-LaCAM (Section VI).
With 50 robots, TAKT-LaCAM is 2,200 to 2,600 times faster than MAPF/C+POST [4] in four 2D halls and 105 to 415 times faster on three 3D maps, with comparable or lower makespan and cost (Section IX-B).
Both planners compute trajectories for about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D and in tens of seconds in 3D (Section IX-C), and ablation studies isolate the effect of each design element (Section IX-D).
In physics simulation, fleets of up to 1,082 differential-drive robots and 1,010 quadrotors track the planned trajectories without collisions (Section IX-E).

Third, we develop two paradigms for real-time replanning under online changes to goals and to the environment (Section VIII).
Whole-fleet replanning computes a complete new plan and, in our experiments, returns within 500 ms for up to 763 robots in an empty hall and 335 quadrotors around a central pillar.
Incremental replanning extends the plan with TAKT-PIBT by one configuration per tick, faster than the robots execute it, for up to 1,018 robots and 671 quadrotors on the same maps (Section IX-F).

Organization: Section II reviews related work, and Section III states the problem.
Section IV presents the TAKT framework, Section V the diamond formulation, and Section VI the two planners.
Section VII establishes the guarantees, Section VIII presents real-time planning, Section IX reports the experiments, and Section X concludes the paper.

title: Feedback Completion Certificates for Repeated Dwell Tasks with Time Windows
authors: Jiaxun Sun,Yuqi Yang,Senlan Yao,Hengyu Xue,Hongming Fu,Zhimu Zhou
comment: including appendices with full proofs and experimental details
abstract:
An inspection robot may owe several measurements at the same station, each
with a different window in which a dwell can begin. We ask what a feedback
controller must retain about earlier visits to guarantee all remaining
deadlines under bounded disturbances. For a common spatial predicate and
dwell length, removing redundant windows orders the remaining obligations
by both endpoints. On every history without an expired obligation, the
served windows form a suffix. One boundary and one capped run length
therefore preserve the future satisfaction of the original task. On a
verified library of branching motion primitives we use this state to
recover a feedback policy. For one task type a scalar threshold per run
length suffices, with work linear in the number of listed branches per
time layer for fixed dwell. Multiple types require a joint recursion.
On a quadrotor inspection library the threshold sweep reduced the cost
of constructing a reusable full-domain policy, while a sparse Boolean
baseline answered a single initial query faster. In a two-station MuJoCo patrol, three task-aware filters all met every
window in twelve paired runs each. Of eight initially certified runs, the
completion filter retained the certificate in all eight, compared with
three for safety-only filtering.
introduction:
An inspection robot checks two stations several times during a shift.
The first reading at one station might be allowed in a narrow start window
and the next reading in a wider one. A reading takes several consecutive
samples. When the robot leaves a station to do other work, its position and
the clock do not tell the controller which visits it still owes. Even a
flag recording that the station has been visited loses the distinction
between an early and a late reading. The controller needs enough of the
executed history to decide whether it can still meet each deadline after
the next disturbance.
Figure 5(a) shows what that distinction costs:
at the same state and clock, returning from A or from B leaves disjoint
sets of certified actions. Figure 2 shows how a
short-horizon controller can certify a return that lies beyond its plan.

We study finite lists of such obligations known before execution. A
measurement may count for every window containing its start. This convention
fits an inspection record that can satisfy overlapping requirements, or a
single request whose actual service window is one of several candidates.
It also gives the usual constant-clock-offset interpretation when the
candidate windows are equal-width translations. Separate work orders that
each consume a measurement require a different assignment rule.

Our first result describes exactly what to remember. Removing a window that
contains another preserves the task. Among the retained windows the served
ones are consecutive in endpoint order on every history that can still meet
its deadlines. A boundary index and the current dwell length therefore
determine the response to every continuation. Second, we use this order to
solve a feedback game on verified motion primitives. With one task type the
winning boundary for each run length satisfies a scalar backward recursion.
Several types share the same physical game but may compete for the next
action and require a joint state. Third, we compare executable policies on
identical queries and test the role of memory and branching in closed-loop
robot simulation. We report the cost of constructing a certificate alongside
the cost of querying it.

title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
authors: Kevin Qiu,Zhao Yang,Marek Cygan
comment: NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. . Code and run records:this https URL
abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot’s torso falls below a height threshold. We train PPO controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body’s starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and SAC. Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol’s best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: reset-dependence.github.io.
introduction:
Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. Co-design methods search over bodies, and recent studies also vary the task, but each commits to a single recipe for training the controllers that score the bodies (Gupta et al., 2021b; Lu et al., 2025; Ai et al., 2025). Such training and evaluation protocols are known to shape the learned controller (Henderson et al., 2018; Pardo et al., 2018; Machado et al., 2018). We ask whether they also change which body appears optimal.

We study one part of the protocol, the reset rule. During training, an episode ends when the robot’s torso falls below a height threshold, and the robot starts again from its initial pose. Real robots often cannot rely on cheap fall resets (Sharma et al., 2022; Eysenbach et al., 2018), so a body selected under reset-rich training may be optimized for resets that are unavailable at deployment.

We test this on 100 bodies from the UNIMAL design space, evolved by Deep Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (DERL) (Gupta et al., 2021b) in three families: on flat ground (Floor), on variable terrain (VT), and for pushing a box across variable terrain (MVT). Here every controller is trained from scratch on the same task, walking forward on flat ground. We compare three training protocols that set the reset threshold to a fraction τ\tau of the body’s starting torso height: Standard (τ=0.20\tau{=}0.20), Strict (τ=0.50\tau{=}0.50), and Reset-free (τ=0\tau{=}0), which never resets after a fall. Each protocol is run with three seeds, and every other episode setting is specified identically. We change the rule only during training and score every controller with the same evaluator. Our contributions are:

The reset rule is part of the benchmark specification. Changing the reset rule during training reorders the bodies. After Strict and Reset-free training, the rankings of all 100100 bodies correlate at Spearman ρ=0.21\rho=0.21, against about 0.890.89 if seed noise were the only difference, and the reordering persists when runs are scored without a cutoff. As a control, retraining 60 bodies with a threshold below the torso’s resting height leaves their Reset-free ranking almost unchanged. A morphology ranking is therefore underspecified without the reset rule that produced it.

After Strict and Reset-free training, the rankings of all 100100 bodies correlate at Spearman ρ=0.21\rho=0.21, against about 0.890.89 if seed noise were the only difference, and the reordering persists when runs are scored without a cutoff. As a control, retraining 60 bodies with a threshold below the torso’s resting height leaves their Reset-free ranking almost unchanged. A morphology ranking is therefore underspecified without the reset rule that produced it.

Reset dependence is embodied. How much a body loses without fall resets differs across evolutionary families. Under proximal policy optimization (PPO), Floor bodies lose 45%45\% of their per-step reward under Reset-free training relative to Standard training, but VT bodies lose only 16%16\%. The difference holds in permutation tests over bodies and when runs are scored without a cutoff, and on 24 bodies, Floor bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC; Table 1, Figure 3, Sections 4.5 and 4.6).

Selecting for robustness costs little reward. In sample, bodies chosen by their worst per-step reward across the three protocols keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol’s own best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds (Section 4.3, Table 3). Section 5 turns this into a short audit for benchmark authors that also checks whether the reset rule acts on every body.

Every controller is trained from scratch, so the family difference does not come from controllers inherited from evolution. One explanation is what the bodies were selected for. Floor bodies were evolved for speed on predictable surfaces, so once a fall no longer ends the episode, they must act from states that were rare during their evolution. VT bodies were evolved on rough terrain that exposes them to such states. Our experiments are consistent with this account. The audit applies to any co-design benchmark that scores bodies under a reset rule. We release the code, the records of all 900 runs, and a script that recomputes 2,401 values from the released records on a CPU (Section 5).

title: A ROS2 based Human-In-The-Loop Framework for UAV Search and Rescue Operations
authors: Anubhav Pandey,Harshit Nagpal,Aditya Agarwal,Tejasvi Alladi,Fei Richard Yu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Submitted to and under review in "International Journal of Intelligent Systems" of Wiley
abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates this migration to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations, a critical factor for UAVs that enables situational awareness during SAR operations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework further demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We further implement the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation and evaluate them on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation provides a structured pathway for SAR-UAV platforms transitioning from ROS1, ensuring seamless integration of human intent. This work bridges critical gaps in human-robot collaboration, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning, thus advancing mission-critical ROS2 deployments in SAR operations.
introduction:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become a game changer in search-and-rescue (SAR) operations [1]. Their ability to quickly provide aerial surveillance in disaster zones, collapsed buildings, and remote terrain is unparalleled. However, while autonomous UAVs perform exceptionally well in controlled environments, their reliance on pre-programmed flight paths and sensor-based navigation can limit their flexibility in dynamic SAR scenarios [2]. In these real-world situations, conditions are constantly changing – shifting debris, victims may be hidden from view, and new obstacles can appear without warning. This is where human judgement becomes more valuable than rigid, pre-programmed algorithms. For example, a firefighter controlling a UAV inside a smoke-filled building may need to override the system quickly, but traditional joystick interfaces can struggle to provide the precision required in high-stress moments.

HITL systems aim to combine human expertise with machine autonomy, but current solutions often come with challenges such as high latency and operator overload [3]. As user interaction plays a critical role in operational efficiency, voice commands, while intuitive, tend to be unreliable in noisy environments, and touchscreen interfaces pull the operator’s attention away from more critical responsibilities at the worst possible moment. Gesture-based control offers a promising alternative, allowing human operators to interact with UAVs through simple, natural hand gestures—such as halt or move left—which require minimal training [4]. This provides a more seamless, intuitive connection between the operator and the UAV, enabling faster, more effective responses when it matters most.

Robot Operating System (ROS) [5] is an open-source framework for building robotics applications more efficiently. It is a middleware, a set of tools, libraries, and conventions that simplify communication between hardware and software components in a robot or a drone. In ROS, topics act as communication channels for nodes, allowing the broadcast of information that multiple other nodes can receive. A node is an executable that communicates with other nodes via ROS by publishing or subscribing to topics. ROS has two versions: ROS1 and ROS2 [6]. While ROS1 laid the foundation for robotic communication with its publisher-subscriber model, its real-time performance, security, and scalability limitations make it less ideal for mission-critical SAR operations. Referring to Fig. 1, ROS2, however, addresses these challenges head-on with several important features [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12] :

Secure, Priority-Based Communication: By integrating the Data Distribution Service (DDS), ROS2 ensures secure, low-latency transmission of gesture commands.

Secure, Priority-Based Communication: By integrating the Data Distribution Service (DDS), ROS2 ensures secure, low-latency transmission of gesture commands.

Deterministic Execution: With thread-safe executors and lock-free memory management and real-time optimisations, ROS2 ensures high reliability, especially in real-time tasks like obstacle avoidance and path planning, even in complex and dynamic environments.

High-Fidelity Simulation Support: ROS2’s integration with Gazebo allows for thorough testing in simulated SAR environments, ensuring optimal UAV performance before deployment.

Improved Build System and Scalability: Introduced a more modern and flexible build system and tooling ecosystem, such as “ament” and “colcon”.

Modular Architecture: The flexible middleware and language-agnostic communication in ROS2 make it an ideal framework for seamlessly integrating components, such as a YOLOv11-based gesture recognition module (in Python).

Cross-Platform and Embedded Support: The supported platforms for ROS2 are Ubuntu, Debian, Windows, Mac OS, etc. Also, Micro-ROS extends ROS2 to microcontrollers, enabling lightweight embedded applications.

These advancements make ROS2 the ideal framework [14, 15] for developing next-generation HITL systems for SAR UAVs, where real-time responsiveness and security are critical.

This paper introduces a ROS2-based framework using Gazebo simulator, PX4 Autopilot and YOLOv11 algorithm that integrates gesture-driven control for SAR UAVs. The following are the main contributions of this paper:

ROS2 Migration Support: We propose a modular, hardware-agnostic algorithmic framework to simplify the transition from ROS1 to ROS2 for SAR-UAV developers. The framework outlines the integration of gesture recognition nodes, PX4-compatible flight control, providing a clear conceptual basis for implementation and field deployment.

ROS2 Migration Support: We propose a modular, hardware-agnostic algorithmic framework to simplify the transition from ROS1 to ROS2 for SAR-UAV developers. The framework outlines the integration of gesture recognition nodes, PX4-compatible flight control, providing a clear conceptual basis for implementation and field deployment.

Unified Vision-Based Gesture Pipeline for UAV Control: We design a unified pipeline that combines RGB and depth data to estimate human pose, calculate distance, and classify pointing gestures using YOLOv11, enabling intuitive HITL UAV guidance in complex SAR missions.

Robustness in Cluttered and Degraded Environments: We deploy a YOLOv11 model on RGB and depth data to detect directional gestures, which enhances recognition accuracy in cluttered environments. Furthermore, we quantify the framework’s resilience in degraded visual conditions, demonstrating a 46.7% average improvement in detection confidence under fog compared to RGB-only baselines, ensuring operational viability where conventional vision fails.

Mission Efficiency Validation: Through Gazebo simulations with PX4 autopilot, we demonstrate that the framework’s direct gesture-to-command mapping minimises computational overhead, which is critical for time-sensitive SAR operations.

Extended Evaluation on Datasets: We implement the modified YOLOv11 (YOLOv11-ℒt​o​t​a​l\mathcal{L}_{total}) and the depth-weighted pose estimation, and test them together with Algorithm 1 on a fixed simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in two fog models (Section 7). As the framework is modular, its perception model, gesture rules and UAV commands can be exchanged for other UAV tasks and evaluated on other datasets in the same way.
